News.title: What we know about Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's legal action against police
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has begun legal proceedings against Thames Valley Police over the lawfulness of the search warrants that led to his arrest in February.

The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after information emerged regarding his dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging search warrants used to access the former Prince's residences' at Sandringham and the Royal Lodge in Windsor, as first reported by the Telegraph.

The BBC's Noor Nanji has what we know so far.

Read more here.

News.title: Twelve arrests after protest over migrant boat arrival
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested for offences including assaulting a police officer after a protest over migrant arrivals in a south coast town.

The Home Office said 149 migrants had been picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport.

Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during the stand-off at a marina in the Hampshire town, involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators on Sunday.

Eleven men and one woman were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order. All remain in custody.

The migrants were taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent.

It is the second known landing of large numbers of migrants this far west along the south coast in recent years.

A police cordon was in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful.

Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".

News.title: BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news
News.content:
Rachel Jupp has been appointed the new director of BBC News, nearly a year after the previous CEO resigned.

Deborah Turness announced last November that she would step down from the role following the fallout over how Panorama edited a speech by President Trump.

Jupp is a former deputy editor of BBC Two's Newsnight and has also served as Panorama's editor, but left several years before the controversial Trump episode aired.

In a statement, Jupp said she was "honoured to be asked to lead BBC News", while the corporation's director-general Matt Brittin described her as "an outstanding editorial leader".

The appointment comes as the BBC continues to make sweeping cuts to its news division. Around 550 job closures have been announced so far, with more expected to follow.

The BBC as a whole will cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

In a statement, Brittin said Jupp was "widely regarded for her news judgement, fairness and high standards".

"She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News," he added.

News.title: Pickford 'almost caused crash' with careless driving
News.content:
England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford nearly caused a crash with two other cars during a bout of careless driving in his Â£200,000 Lamborghini supercar, a court has heard.

The 32-year-old was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to slam on the brakes, and then speeding off into the distance.

The incident happened in the Cheshire town of Knutsford on 14 April, sparking a criminal prosecution for driving without due care or attention.

Pickford, who has 336 appearances for Everton and 92 England caps, has pleaded guilty to the charge and will next appear at Chester Magistrates' Court on 7 December.

According to court documents, PC Cecil Ricardo, from Cheshire Police, said he had just left the station when he saw Pickford's blue Lamborghini Urus complete with personalised number plates.

"I was stationary on Bexton Road, Knutsford, waiting for traffic signals to turn green," he wrote.

"I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street.

"It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision.

"The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford."

News.title: Man detained for stabbing dog walker to death
News.content:
Safi, who appeared for his sentencing hearing on a video link from the high-security Broadmoor hospital, was born in the Kapisa province of northern Afghanistan.

He was smuggled in to the UK on the back of a lorry in November 2020 and lied about his age - saying he was 17 instead of 22 - to stand a better chance of asylum.

He worked as an Uber driver, studied for a mechanics qualification at Uxbridge College and had no convictions since entering the country.

He had sought help from doctors for his deteriorating mental health prior to the stabbings, which began at his home in Midhurst Gardens.

The court was told that in the three days before the stabbings, Safi had attended an appointment at his GP, had a mental health assessment at Hillingdon Hospital and had sought help at Hayes police station.

After the stabbings, doctors concluded Safi was suffering from psychotic depression which had led to the violent offences.

Dr Elliott Carthy, who assessed Safi at Broadmoor, said he had "paranoid and persecutory beliefs", and voices in his head contributed to his actions that day.

He said a hospital order with restrictions was the best way to protect the public "going forward now and in anticipation of his release into the community".

He said Safi was likely to spend at least five years at Broadmoor before being considered for transfer to a medium security facility where he would stay for several more years, and if he is released into the community he would be under strict conditions and subject to lifelong monitoring.

Safi admitted manslaughter by diminished responsibility, was found guilty by a jury of attempting to murder Farrukh and pleaded guilty to causing actual bodily harm against the teenage boy as well as possession of the knife.

Prosecutors dropped a charge of murder after the guilty plea to manslaughter was entered, and after receiving expert reports on Safi's mental health.

The judge told the court she would have sentenced Safi to life in prison with a minimum term of eight years if he had not been mentally unwell.

News.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution, which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

News.title: Failed asylum seeker jailed for life over knife attack attempt at Israeli embassy in London
News.content:
A failed asylum seeker who tried to break into the Israeli embassy in London to carry out a knife attack has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 20 years.

Abdullah Albadri was carrying two knives when police officers caught him as he tried to climb over a fence into the Kensington embassy on 28 April 2025.

The 34-year-old from Kuwait had arrived in the UK on a small boat 16 days earlier, having first entered country illegally four years earlier.

He was previously found guilty by majority verdict after a trial at the Old Bailey of preparation of terrorist acts and possession of two bladed articles.

The court heard how he was motivated to plot the attack by the death of Palestinians in Gaza and planned the attack after sleeping rough in the capital.

Albadri first travelled to the UK on a small boat in August 2021 and applied for asylum but returned to France before a decision was made.

He crossed the Channel again in April 2025 and was housed in a hotel in Basingstoke for three days, before being told he was not eligible for accommodation due to his outstanding asylum application.

On the day of the attempted attack, he walked to the west London embassy from north London wearing a red and white traditional Arabic scarf wrapped around his head and sunglasses.

The embassy is located on a street which is home to several large diplomatic buildings and has a round-the-clock police presence.

At around 18:00, he saluted in the direction of two nearby diplomatic protection officers before trying to scale a security fence.

The armed officers dragged him down from the railings and detained him.

News.title: Ex-Manchester leader defends deals with Man City owners
News.content:
The former leader of Manchester City Council has defended the council's relationship with the owners of Manchester City amid questions over land deals.

Sir Richard Leese, who was head of the council for 25 years until 2021 and is also honorary president of the club, said a decade-old deal with Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was "good for the city".

The partnership between the authority and the company owned by Sheik Mansour bin zayed Al Nahyan has come under renewed scrutiny since City was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations with "sham" commercial contracts.

The club has denied any wrongdoing is appealing against the charges.

The council entered into a partnership with ADUG in 2014 when they formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.

It planned to invest more than Â£1bn over the next decade and develop thousands of homes in the Ancoats and New Islington areas, on the edge of the city centre close to the club's Etihad stadium.

But in 2022, a report by the University of Sheffield, called Manchester Offshored, raised questions about the wider public value of the schemes, and a lack of transparency around their finances.

It highlighted the absence of any affordable housing in the projects, and that the joint venture companies were ultimately owned by ADUG through firms registered offshore.

News.title: Andrew takes legal action over search warrants before his arrest
News.content:
"As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further," a spokesperson for the force that carried out the arrest said.

Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.

A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon to begin considering this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The judge will initially hear a request by the police to keep some documents private.

The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor had been arrested - and the legal challenge is against the chief constable of Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court.

"Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.

Vamos said such disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search.

"The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.

It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.

For several days after the arrest, police were seen searching Mountbatten-Windsor's property at Marsh Farm in Sandringham and at his former home, Royal Lodge, on the Windsor estate.

The arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.

They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.

Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said those links had been severed.

After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation.

The launch of this legal action against the police over the search warrants is the first public pushback from the former prince, who has lost his home, titles and public status, with charities and businesses distancing themselves from him.

Thames Valley Police says its investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is continuing.

In a previous update it said the force had been "working with the United States Department of Justice to get further information that may be related to this investigation".

Detectives also highlighted that allegations of sexual misconduct could be considered as part of this inquiry into potential misconduct in public office.

Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing in his associations with Epstein.

News.title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk
News.content:
The UK's biggest broadband provider, BT, has agreed to buy rival operator TalkTalk to save the company from collapse.

The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal.

BT boss Alison Kirkby said it provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers. The administrator, Alvarez & Marsal, said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff based in Salford, Greater Manchester.

However, Virgin Media called it a "stitch-up" which allows BT to "tighten its grip" over the market. The government has given itself the power to have the final say on the deal, citing its importance to vital public services.

TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK.

BT's Kirkby told the BBC's Today programme: "Two and a half million customers, including vulnerable households, and key emergency services might have lost their services if Talk Talk had failed, which it was on track to do.

"So BT stepped in as we were the only viable option to take the business forward."

Ernest Doku from comparison website Uswitch said the deal means "nothing changes today".

"Your broadband and landline carry on as normal, and there is nothing you need to do right now," he added.

However, he said that BT should explain "quickly and plainly what this means for contracts, prices and service in the future, so nobody is left guessing".

The regulator, Ofcom, says broadband customers should have the right to leave a contract without an exit fee, external if a new owner puts the price up beyond what was in the contract.

TalkTalk began as a challenger to BT in the broadband market. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange, but was taken over by private equity in 2021.

Since then, the firm has built up debt while losing customers, leaving it unable to pay some of those it owes money to.

Despite this, TalkTalk remained the fourth biggest broadband provider in the UK, with 6.6% of customers, during the March to June period of this year, according to figures from analytic firm Opensignal.

BT has 32.5% of customers, Sky 19.9%, and Virgin Media 19.1%.

Rivals who were beaten to the deal by BT have said it will be bad for consumers.

Tom O'Hagan, a former TalkTalk executive who was leading a takeover bid for the firm, told the BBC he was worried about "reduced choice and potentially an increase in price for consumers and for businesses" because of the BT deal.

He added that he was particularly concerned about competition in the wholesale market, where TalkTalk's subsidiary PXC was BT's main rival.

Virgin Media, which has also reportedly tried to buy TalkTalk in the past, said the BT takeover has "all the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest".

It added that the purchase means BT can "roll its tanks over competition and further tighten its grip on the market. The logic simply doesn't add up."

News.title: Mother killed by falling bricks, court told
News.content:
A mother on the school run sustained fatal injuries when a large pile of bricks fell on her head as she walked past a building site in east London, a court has heard.

Michaela Boor, 29, was on Burdett Road in Bow on the morning of 27 March 2018 when the accident happened. She suffered a fractured skull and died two days later.

Higgins Homes is on trial at the Old Bailey charged with corporate manslaughter and a health and safety offence.

Four construction workers contracted by Higgins Homes - Thomas Anstis, Stephen Coulson, Dawood Maan and Alexander McInnes - are accused of the same offences. Both the company and the four men deny the charges.

Opening the case on Monday, prosecutor Alexandra Healy KC said Boor had been walking towards some shops with a friend, Chelsea Mustafa, when the bricks fell from a crane.

News.title: Shadow chancellor to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
News.content:
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.

Griffith and his colleagues will also use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion, and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency.

Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.

Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".

Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Griffith said infrastructure development was key to his plan, throwing his support behind the expansion of Heathrow airport.

"Someone, sooner or later, has to get serious about getting this country growing again," he said.

"It's a national embarrassment that we can't get that third runway built - we've said we will get full square behind that and the government should do that right now.

"Whether it's reservoirs or reactors we need a system of getting infrastructure in this country that really works."

Pressed on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing, he said: "We are going to keep it."

In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others".

Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable.

Griffith will accuse Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn."

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.

This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard.

The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to Â£50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.

A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

Prospect general secretary Mike Clancy, whose union represents members in Natural England and the Environment Agency, said: "Conservative budget cuts have left these regulators struggling to perform their vital functions with 'lack of resources' the most common reason for planning delays.

"The solution is to restore their funding to adequate levels, not scrap vital safeguards."

News.title: Two men die in Channel crossing attempt off northern France
News.content:
Two men have died after trying to cross the English Channel off the coast of Berck in northern France.

According to local media, police saw migrants leaving the beach on a boat at about 22:00 local time on Sunday, and when rescuers arrived, they were bailing water out of the overloaded vessel with their shoes.

"When we arrived, there were at least 80 people on board and a terrible smell of gasoline,"Jean-Marc Lamblin, director of the French national sea rescue service (SNSM) told La Voix du Nord newspaper.

Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns that were caused by the mixture of gasoline in the seawater. Their condition has been described as not life-threatening.

Lamblin told the newspaper that there were so many people on the boat, including children, that about 20 people were left stranded in the water because they could not get on board.

He explained that when SNSM arrived, the two men, aged in their 30s and 40s, were in cardiac arrest.

The men and injured women were brought back to shore where firefighters and paramedics helped them, but the men died at about midnight.

Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation to determine the circumstances of their death.

The two women were from Somalia and aged 20 and 26, La Voix du Nord reported, adding that they are now recovering in Rang-du-Fliers hospital.

News.title: Town's 215-year-old chapel goes to auction for £1
News.content:
A 19th Century revivalist chapel is going to auction with a guide price of just a Â£1.

The Grade II listed Ebenezer Chapel once held up to 900 worshippers but the building, with its long curved pews and high arched windows, was last used in 2009 and is now overgrown and derelict.

Paul Fosh Auctions said the "substantial detached property" in Aberdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had partial renovation work done but its planning permission for conversion to five flats had now lapsed.

"This large former chapel which also has a domestic-sized single garage is in the sought-after location of Trecynon," said auctioneer Sean Roper.

News.title: Death of girl, 11, 'unexplained' after body found in park
News.content:
An 11-year-old's death is being treated as unexplained by police who say they are investigating after her body was found in a Worcestershire park.

The girl was reported missing at about 23:20 BST on Sunday and she was later found in the park near the cricket ground in Elmley Castle, near Evesham, detectives said.

Inquiries were ongoing into the circumstances surrounding her death, a West Mercia Police spokesperson said.

Nearby residents were told by the force that there would be an increased police presence in the area as they investigate.

The girl's family were being supported by specially trained officers, said the force.

Her death was "deeply upsetting" for the community, said Ch Insp Daniel Pilkington.

"We are carrying out inquiries to fully understand the circumstances and provide her family with the answers they deserve," he added.

The small village, about four miles from Pershore, has a population of about 500, according to the parish council.

The castle it is named after, dating back to the 11th Century, is on the side of nearby Bredon Hill.

News.title: Priest pleads guilty to 109 sex offences
News.content:
In a statement on Monday, Bishop Router said his thoughts were "first and foremost" with those affected by the case, "particularly the children who have suffered harm and those who continue to live with the consequences of abuse and exploitation".

The bishop said he would "move immediately to seek the most serious penalty available under church law" - Gallagher's dismissal from the priesthood.

"I can confirm that I am petitioning the Holy See to submit the case directly to the Holy Father with a recommendation that Father Edward Gallagher be immediately dismissed from the clerical state," he said.

The bishop said the Catholic Church could not "undo the harm that has been caused" but had "a responsibility to respond truthfully, justly and decisively".

He said the Diocese of Derry had cooperated fully with the PSNI and all relevant statutory authorities throughout their investigations in the Gallagher case - and would "continue to do so".

News.title: Kim Kardashian reveals number of nannies she has for her and Kanye West’s four kids
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Kardashian-West kids are outnumbered by their nannies.

Kim Kardashian shares her four children — North, 13, Saint, 10, Chicago, eight, and Psalm, seven — with her ex-husband Kanye West.

In a new interview, the reality star told The Sunday Times Style magazine she has five nannies who work on rotation to help look after her children.

The billionaire Skims founder explained that although one nanny is always on duty, Kardashian is the one who drops her kids off and picks them up from school each day — and that they all have dinner together every night.

“I think I am an intermediate-strict parent,” Kardashian, 45, told the magazine. “I’m extremely patient and loving. I still have a kid sleep in my bed when they want. I read books with the kids every night.”

open image in gallery Kim Kardashian said she always has dinner with her four children ( Reuters )

The reality TV star said that she takes it upon herself to discuss wealth and privilege with her children.

“It’s something I talk to my kids about constantly, about hard work, never taking things for granted, always having gratitude,” she said. “I lead by example. I’m really open with them about my work, all of the hard work that I put into my law studies, and they’re proud. I think that you can have a big life and still have that spirit in you. But it is more challenging.”

Kardashian spoke briefly in the interview about how she co-parents with 49-year-old West, to whom she was married from 2014 to 2022, when it comes to North’s solo music career.

“That is something that her dad and I have better communication about,” Kardashian said. “We make sure we’re aligned and that she’s in projects that we both approve.”

open image in gallery Kardashian said she communicates well with Kanye West about North West’s music career ( Getty )

open image in gallery Kim Kardashian and Kanye West were married from 2014 to 2022 ( AFP/Getty )

Kardashian and West have had a publicly turbulent co-parenting relationship since the businesswoman filed for divorce in 2021.

In October 2025, Kardashian said during her interview on Call Her Daddy that sharing custody with the famous rapper has been “a lot of work.”

“It’s not easy, but I raise the kids full time,” she said on the podcast. “They live with me. I welcome a great, healthy relationship with my kids and their dad. He knows that. I push for it all the time. But I also protect them when it's time for that... it’s a lot of work.”

She added: “The one thing that gets me is that there’s this narrative that I keep the kids...away from him. I never once [have] done that.”

News.title: Daniil Medvedev disqualified against Novak Djokovic after controversial fan incident
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Daniil Medvedev has been defaulted from his China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic after hitting a fan in the crowd with the ball.

The Russian player was down 7-5, 5-3 with Djokovic serving for the match at 15-15, when world No 5 Medvedev failed to reach a Djokovic winner.

The ball then rebounded off the backboard and Medvedev hit the ball into the face of a fan sitting in the front row, who clutched his eye in pain and was taken away from the court.

Chair umpire Mohammed Lahyani, after discussion with an ATP official, then defaulted 30-year-old Medvedev, in scenes not dissimilar to Novak Djokovic’s disqualification from the 2020 US Open – when the Serb hit a line umpire with the ball.

"It's a bit of a shock to be honest, I hope that person is not badly injured," 24-time major winner Djokovic said.

"I also feel sorry for Daniil. I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match. I am sure that Daniil did not want to do this intentionally."

It is not Medvedev’s first disciplinary mishap in recent times. Last year, he was fined £31,500 after a meltdown at the US Open when a photographer walked onto the court, while in April 2026 he was fined for unsportsmanlike conduct after smashing his racket in a 6-0, 6-0 defeat to Matteo Berrettini in Monte-Carlo.

Yet this default handed Djokovic a place in the final in Bejing, where he will face Australian No 1 Alex de Minaur on Tuesday.

open image in gallery Daniil Medvedev after being disqualified from his semi-final with Novak Djokovic ( AP )

In the women’s draw, Sonay Kartal’s WTA Tour comeback at the China Open has ended after she lost in straight sets to Alina Charaeva in the third round.

The Masters event represented Kartal’s first WTA tournament since March after a six-month absence with a stress fracture in the back.

Kartal, who made the fourth round of Wimbledon last year, showed good form in China to beat Andrea Lazaro Garcia and Wang Xinyu, but exited in the last 32 following a 6-4, 6-1 loss to Charaeva, who stunned world number one Elena Rybakina in round two.

British No 5 Kartal played her part in a competitive 91-minute battle on Moon Court and broke Charaeva in the first set, but struggled on her own serve to lose the opener.

Further opportunities were presented in the second and yet with Kartal unable to convert any of her five break points, Charaeva cruised into the fourth round.

Elsewhere, Carlos Alcaraz earlier rallied from a set down to get the better of Jaume Munar and reach a second consecutive Japan Open final.

open image in gallery Carlos Alcaraz has reached a second consecutive Japan Open final ( Reuters )

Defending champion Alcaraz was only on court for 83 minutes of Sunday’s quarter-final after Denis Shapovalov retired, but compatriot Munar pushed the world number three all the way a day later.

Munar won four games in a row to claim the first set against the top seed in Tokyo, but Alcaraz regrouped after an exchange of breaks at the start of the second and outlasted his opponent to clinch a 5-7, 6-3, 6-1 victory.

Alcaraz will face Jiri Lehecka, a 6-4, 6-2 winner over eighth seed Valentin Vacherot.

Additional reporting from PA

News.title: My top tips for shopping the Amazon Prime Day sale
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Amazon’s biggest sale event over the year, Prime Big Deal Days, is back for October bringing two days of member-exclusive deals across top brands including Apple, Dyson, Ninja, Samsung and more.

I’ve been covering Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day deals for eight years, so I’ve picked up a few useful tips and tricks for getting the most out of the sales. I’m an expert at spotting the real savings among the flood of offers on Amazon, and I’ll also flag when a deal isn’t quite as good as it looks or you can get a better saving elsewhere.

To help you get the best deals during this year’s event, I’ve pulled together my top tips for shopping the Prime Big Deal Days sale. Before you check out, take a moment to make sure you’re really getting the best value for money. From spotting inflated discounts to checking a product’s price history, keep scrolling for my advice on how to navigate Amazon’s October Prime Day sale.

1. See if you can get an Amazon Prime free trial

The first thing to remember is that you need to be a Prime member to access the discounts on Prime Day. But the sale isn’t the only benefit; the membership also includes benefits like free next-day delivery and, on eligible orders, even same-day delivery at no extra cost.

Amazon Prime costs £8.99 per month or £95 per year. If you’re not already a Prime member, you might be eligible for a free 30-day trial of Prime. It’s only available to Amazon customers who have never been a Prime member before or haven’t been a Prime member in the past 12 months. You may also be offered a half price membership for three months, bringing the price down to £4.49 a month.

If you’re between the ages of 18 and 22, you can get a six-month free trial, as well as half-price memberships, meaning you’ll pay just £4.49 instead of £8.99 per month.

2. Make a wishlist

It’s easy to get swept up in the excitement of Amazon Prime Day and end up adding things to your basket that you don’t actually need. A discount only really counts as a saving if it’s on something you were planning to buy anyway.

I recommend making a wishlist of the things you’ve been eyeing up this year, as well as Christmas gifts for loved ones. For example, I’ve had my eye on the Oura ring, plus I’m on the lookout for a new coffee machine. If I see significant price drops on these items, I’ll add them to my basket.

3. Compare the price of the product against other retailers

Amazon can sometimes be a little sneaky when it comes to adjusting the RRP of its products. It reportedly changes prices on its website up to 2.5 million times a day, so it’s not always clear whether the “original” price reflects what the manufacturer actually charges. I’d recommend doing a quick Google search to compare prices across other retailers before you buy.

For example, if I’m looking for a new iPad, and it’s currently on sale at Amazon, I’ll check Apple’s website for the original price, just so I know whether the apparent discount is legit. If it is, I’ll head to other retailers, such as Argos, John Lewis, Currys and AO.com, to make sure the iPad isn’t the same price (or cheaper) there. If it is, I might consider shopping at the other retailer if it offers better perks, such as a longer warranty or a better trade-in deal.

4. Be wary of electric toothbrush deals

Amazon is notorious for playing with the RRP of leading electric toothbrushes during sales periods. The retailer sometimes raises the RRP of an item to an exorbitant price, and then discounts it by upwards of half price, so it looks like a much better deal than it actually is.

For example, a £50 electric toothbrush might be given a new RRP of £100 in the run-up to the sale. During the sale, Amazon will then “discount” it to the original £50 price. If you’re coming to the deal that day, it looks like a huge 50 per cent discount, but you’re really paying the retail price.

Some of the more expensive brushes bounce up and down in price, spending two weeks at full price, then two weeks at half price – rinse and repeat. Again, check other retailers for the actual price of the electric toothbrush and make a call. You’ll still find good savings on Oral-B and others, they just won’t be as big as Amazon might have you think.

5. Use Amazon price history tools

It’s sometimes difficult to know if a deal is exclusive to the sale. That TV or laptop you’ve been considering could have been discounted to that sale price weeks before Amazon Prime Day even started. A deal that looks great today could have been even better a few months ago, and the new sale price could even be higher than the old retail price.

To find out if a discount is actually exclusive to Prime Day, use Amazon price history tools such as Camelcamelcamel, which records price changes at Amazon. These tools give you historical data on a product’s lowest, highest and average prices, giving you an idea of whether it’s a deal you should pick up now or leave until it goes down even further.

6. Watch out for no-name brands

There’s a host of no-name brands on Amazon that churn out poorly made products, including laptops, just to exploit the Prime Day sale. These products usually have steep discounts but are not worth your hard-earned money.

It’s easy to be caught out by this because of how difficult it can be to decode the technical jargon of a laptop. We will only bring you deals on laptops that we’ve tested or that hail from well-respected brands. This applies to every product category on Amazon, but particularly so for laptops.

7. Check out our Amazon Prime Day live blog

As well as curating guides to the standout offers, we’ll also be running a rolling live blog of the best Prime Day deals until the same ends. The live blog is run by a team of deals experts, who will be busy rifling through thousands of discounts to bring you the offers worth caring about.

You’ll also find more shopping tips on the live blog and even more coverage across our entire directory of Amazon Prime Day shopping guides, so stay tuned.

Follow live: Best Amazon Prime Day deals

News.title: Voices: I’m a death row lawyer – the botched execution of Christa Pike has done us a favour
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Every now and then, America’s 27 “executing states” do everyone a favour by illustrating why their practice is both barbaric and utterly pointless.

It might be the state of Georgia, putting the profoundly intellectually disabled Jerome Bowden to death (he did not eat all his final meal, saying he would save the dessert for later). It might be the state of Texas, killing Leonel Herrera, after the Supreme Court told us that merely being innocent would not be a reason to spare him. You have the constitutional right, apparently, to a “fair trial”, but not one that reaches the correct result.

The state of Tennessee followed the pattern, delegitimising capital punishment while trying to execute Christa Pike as midnight loomed on Wednesday.

The run-up was relatively typical, at least since the conservative Supreme Court majority decided to speed the process up. Some of my American colleagues struggled mightily and got a stay from the Sixth Circuit two hours before the execution was to begin. That is traumatic, but not abnormal: as a lawyer working on death penalty cases, I once got a stay 58 seconds before the allotted time.

In Christa’s case, the state attorney general appealed, and the Supreme Court predictably voted 6-to-3 to sanction the death penalty, over a despairing dissent by the three liberals.

I have been there, and it leaves one with great empathy for all those involved. I kept tabs on what was happening to Christa until the Supreme Court ruled, but stopped when it all seemed inevitable.

Christa Pike survived her execution attempt (Tennessee Department of Correction) ( Tennessee Department of Correction )

The odds were good that there would be some type of botch, as the executing states are just not very good at killing people. Most of our clients have bad veins, often from when they self-medicated the pain of their childhood abuse away with drugs. Christa was known to have veins that were naturally narrow, and her lawyers had warned everyone that the rather amateur executioners would struggle to insert an IV properly. (Medical professionals are barred by their Hippocratic oath from taking part.)

Equally, Tennessee uses shoddy drugs. This dates back to when pharmaceutical giant Hospira decided to no longer sell certain drugs, because what they had patented as life-saving medicine was being used to kill people, which was very bad PR for a profit of about 90 cents a vial. The executing states have struggled to find their materiel ever since.

Some years back, Tennessee bought a batch of drugs from a one-man enterprise in west London. So the pentobarbital used on Christa ran the risk of being defective, even if they could get it into her veins.

And so it proved. She was in great pain as the needles were apparently badly set and the drug was not readily absorbed, swelling and burning her arm. By the second dose, she was asleep, but still breathing.

However, this is really a story of absurdity. We now wait to hear whether she will pull through, or is she so brain damaged that she no longer understands where she is and why. The most obvious irony is that the prison rushed Christa to the hospital to try to preserve her life, so they can try again to execute her.

Another incongruity arises from Christa’s age. The US Supreme Court has ruled that it would be “cruel and unusual” to execute someone under 18. While the media made out that the murder of Colleen Slemmer was a satanic ritual, it was Christa’s 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who carved a pentagram on the poor victim’s chest. Because Christa was 10 months past her 18th birthday, that qualified her to die.

There is also the issue of whether Christa was the victim of several capital crimes, as well as an author of one. The Supreme Court has ruled that for anyone who did not actually commit murder to face execution would be a disproportionate punishment.

In 2024, the state of Tennessee decided to challenge the Court by making child sexual abuse a death penalty offence. Aged three, Christa was sexually molested over and over; aged 11, it happened some more; this led her, aged 12, to attempt suicide; and, aged 17, she was raped. So according to the Tennessean authorities, Christa has been the victim of multiple offences, most that would now be capital. All of this was reported to the authorities at the time, yet nothing was done.

I must admit that, after 42 years doing death cases, I find the arguments made in favour of the death penalty unwise on every level. Colleen’s family were promised that, after 32 years of appeals, an execution will make her feel better. But it is never truly a catharsis: the victim’s relatives emerge from witnessing the execution with the same trauma or more, and their loved one still dead. Imagine how Colleen’s mother feels after this week’s farce?

I have myself come out of the death chamber six times, always around midnight, and looked up at the stars. I ask myself a simple question, as I did when, in 1987, the BBC was filming its Fourteen Days in May documentary: did systematically gassing Edward Johnson with Zyklon B really make the world a better, safer and more civilised place? I suspect most people are asking the same thing about Christa’s torment.

Clive Stafford Smith is a human rights lawyer and founder of the Justice League

News.title: Emilia Fox explains ‘decision to not talk about’ cousin Laurence Fox publicly
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Emilia Fox has explained why she’s decided not to talk publicly about her controversial cousin Laurence Fox, who has swapped acting for right-wing politics in recent years.

Having followed their famous parents into the entertainment industry, Emilia and Laurence are both part of a younger generation of famous Foxes, which also includes the former’s brother, House of the Dragon star Freddie Fox, and the latter’s sister, Submarine actor Lydia Fox.

And while the family is still best-known for its acting prowess, Reclaim Party founder Laurence has hit headlines for his politics and social media presence in recent years, posing in blackface and sharing an image of a swastika, as well as multiple court cases.

In March last year, he was charged with a sexual offence after allegedly sharing an intimate picture of a TV star without her consent. He has pleaded not guilty.

When asked about Laurence in a new interview with The Telegraph, Emilia replied: “I understand why there is an interest in knowing about Laurence. But I’ve made a decision to not talk about Laurence in interviews, because of what I’ve said in the past.”

open image in gallery Emilia Fox ( PA Archive )

In 2021 – a year after her brother Freddie was reportedly spat at in the street over their cousin’s views – Emilia told The Times: “We’ve had very different life experiences and Laurence’s political life is nothing to do with my relationship with him. We’ve had some amazing times together and we’ve been very mutually supportive of our personal lives.”

Asked if she was worried about him, the Silent Witness actor replied: “Why should I be worried? What are the things you are worried about?”

Freddie, meanwhile, has been direct in his criticism of Laurence. “I fundamentally and completely oppose Laurence’s political views and the way he chooses to express them,” he told The Independent in 2023. “His views both shock and appall me. And that’s all I’ve got to say about it. It’s not something I relish talking about.”

open image in gallery Laurence Fox ( AFP/Getty )

Laurence’s last acting project was a 2022 film distributed by far-right website Breitbart, in which he played Joe Biden’s son, Hunter.

Prior to his pivot to politics, Laurence was best known for playing Detective Sergeant James Hathaway in the ITV drama Lewis. His credits also include Gosford Park, Victoria and Elizabeth: The Golden Age.

Laurence began becoming increasingly involved in political commentary in early 2020 and launched his Reclaim Party later that year, before unsuccessfully standing for London mayor in 2021.

Earlier this year, he stood against Nigel Farage in the Clacton by-election and, having received less than 500 votes, lost his £500 deposit.

News.title: Army secretary who quit Pentagon after clashes with Hegseth breaks silence
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll has given his first interview since resigning from the Pentagon in September after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Driscoll is just one of a series of high profile departures since Hegseth took over, with the secretary carrying out a purge so substantial it reportedly even raised President Donald Trump’s concerns.

Speaking to Rolling Stone, Driscoll acknowledged the pair had disagreements on a number of issues, without going into specifics.

“Once he makes a decision, there’s nothing I can do about it. I don’t have to like it,” he said of Hegseth. “But I think it’s unfair to describe our relationship so flatly – that every interaction was bad, or that we disagreed on everything.

“If you polled us, we probably agreed on more than 50 percent of things. What’s been reported is all the things we disagree on.

“I’ll never talk about our private conversations but we were both very passionate about our positions, and I would advocate as strongly as I possibly could – knowing I’m talking to my boss, and the final decision-maker.”

open image in gallery Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll has given his first interview since leaving the Pentagon, saying of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decision-making: ‘I don’t have to like it’ ( Getty )

Driscoll said his role had been “to advocate as hard as I could for leaders who I thought were good.”

An Iraq War veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance – whom he befriended while they were contemporaries at Yale Law School – Driscoll is characterized in the piece as a keen modernizer of the U.S. military, interested in innovation and ensuring the Armed Forces had the equipment necessary to meet the challenges of a 21st century battlefield.

While Hegseth was also interested in making changes to the operation of the military, reports suggest he has been concerned about instilling a “warfighter” mentality in the troops and focussing on appearance.

Driscoll, the youngest person ever to hold his position after sailing through his confirmation hearing in the Senate in February 2025, recounts how he approached Hegseth early on with what he considered a “gift” – his close friendship with Vance – which he believed would help the Pentagon get what it needed from the White House.

open image in gallery Hegseth has been characterized as preoccupied with priotizing culture wars over technological innovation ( Getty )

But, the magazine reported: “Hegseth blew up at him… telling Driscoll that he needed to go through his office before reaching out to the White House, creating a tension between the two men.”

The friction worsened as Hegseth dismissed more and more top generals and admirals, culminating in the removal of Gen. Randy George and then Gen. Christopher Donahue, two men with whom Driscoll had found common cause in pursuing his modernizing agenda.

Driscoll reached the end of his tether in late August and informed President Donald Trump of his intention to resign, reportedly telling the commander-in-chief that he was leaving because Hegseth had fired everyone working towards the goal he held dear.

open image in gallery Driscoll reportedly informed President Donald Trump of his resignation at a meeting in the Oval Office, at which he complained that Hegseth had fired everyone working towards his modernization initiative ( Getty )

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, responded to The Independent’s inquiry about Driscoll’s comments by calling Rolling Stone “a fake news rag regurgitating months-old false narratives in an attempt to stay relevant to their ever-dwindling audience” and alleging that its interview “is riddled with made-up claims regarding Secretary Hegseth’s historic achievements and transformative leadership.”

“Since Day One, Secretary Hegseth has focused on modernization across every branch of our Armed Forces and has moved with urgency to deliver on President Trump’s vision of Peace Through Strength,” Parnell said.

“From slashing bureaucracy, to untying the hands of our warfighters, to re-energizing our defense industrial base, Secretary Hegseth has been a generational Secretary for the Pentagon. With President Trump and Secretary Hegseth at the helm, our military will remain the greatest fighting force on the planet.”

Driscoll was praised by White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly when he left his post as “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more.”

"The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

News.title: Taskmaster set for first-ever UK live show after selling out US debut in 13 minutes
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Taskmaster is heading out on stage, with its first-ever UK live show confirmed for Manchester.

Greg Davies, the show's host, and his assistant Alex Horne will perform at the AO Arena on 26 May next year. A second date follows at The Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles on 22 June.

The production, titled Taskmaster Live On Stage, will feature special guests as contestants. The remaining contestant places will be up for grabs from the audience.

Davies said: “I am thrilled that my tiny assistant and I are to bring Taskmaster to such illustrious venues. Whilst on one hand it feels daunting, on the other it feels like destiny.

“Rest assured my judgements will remain even-handed, and every effort will be made for everyone to have a good time, except Alex.”

Taskmaster will be heading to the AO Arena in Manchester ( Channel 4 )

Show creator Horne added: “This is one of the maddest moments of my life. For me the Hollywood Bowl means Monty Python and the Manchester Arena means Oasis.

“Now it’s our turn?! Luckily I’m with my biggest friend Greg, so I’m going to be so brave.”

The live format has already been tested in America, where Taskmaster Live On Stage debuted earlier this year. Tickets for that run sold out in 13 minutes.

Davies and Horne were joined there by comedians John Oliver, Seth Meyers, Lisa Gilrow and Jason Manztoukas as special guest contestants.

Tickets for the new dates will be released for pre-sale exclusively on the Taskmaster mailing list on October 14. General sale follows on October 16.

The TV series, which premiered in 2015, sees a panel of five celebrities take part in various challenges, with points awarded by the taskmaster. The 22nd series began airing in September 2026.

Taskmaster Live On Stage will arrive at the AO Arena on May 26, with the Los Angeles show following at The Hollywood Bowl on June 22.

Davies and Horne will front both performances, with special guests and audience members making up the contestant line-up.

Pre-sale tickets open on October 14 via the Taskmaster mailing list, ahead of general sale on October 16.

The Manchester date will be the show's first-ever UK live performance.

News.title: Laid-off Ohio union workers turn on Trump days after rally as economic pain shapes election battle
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Drinking tea out of beer mugs alongside his colleagues, Kyle Bos reflected on the ways his life is changing.

Bos is a father of two, with a third daughter expected in January. At his local grocery store, five items now cost as much as an entire cart once did. On Wednesday, Bos and nearly 1,400 other people were laid off from their jobs at what had been the Navistar truck factory in southwestern Ohio.

The layoffs, occurring just three days before President Donald Trump’s rally on Saturday at a nearby high school, were large enough to basically erase an entire year of job growth in the greater Dayton, Ohio, area. And they are one reason why Bos, 30, plans to spend the final weeks before the November election canvassing votes for Democrats.

Asked how many times he had voted for Trump, Bos held up three tattooed fingers. But he said he is done with the president.

"Something has to change politically in this country," said Bos, a member of the United Auto Workers who identifies as a centrist. "Seems like it just kept getting worse and worse and worse."

This year’s election is a test for the working-class coalition that lifted Trump into the White House and gave majorities to Republicans in the House and Senate.

The outcome will be decided in places like Dayton, which once sprouted factories because it led America in patents per capita. The Wright brothers’ airplane, the cash register, the stepladder and the electric car starter were all invented in this city of 137,000.

Trump's blunt talk and status as a celebrity businessman initially helped him around Dayton, where voters felt traditional politics had failed them. Republicans secured wins across the broader metro area, but this year the party is vulnerable among voters disgruntled about inflation, the Iran war, and a president who seems unsympathetic to their daily struggles.

An Ohio race could help determine control of the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is attempting to harness that disenchantment as he seeks a comeback two years after losing his seat.

Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of living, with just 17% approving of his handling of the issue.

open image in gallery Drinking tea out of beer mugs alongside his colleagues, Kyle Bos reflected on the ways his life is changing ( AP (AP photo /Carolyn Kaster) )

Trump did not discuss grocery prices, gas prices, or factory layoffs during his Saturday night rally in Vandalia, part of what he says will be a 32-day marathon of events aimed at convincing the public that the economy is performing better than they think.

"The fake news media, they refuse to talk about our record-setting numbers. So tonight, if you don’t mind, I’m going to do it myself," he told the rally.

Trump has largely sneered at concerns about affordability, but he is promising to give people $5,000 checks if Republicans win the House and Senate next month — something Bos said he found offensive.

"It feels like a bribe, a slap in the face, and, like, that we’re all ignorant," Bos said.

The Dayton area has shed roughly half of its 90,000 manufacturing jobs since 1990, according to federal figures, after the North American Free Trade Agreement shifted many jobs to Mexico where auto components could be produced more cheaply. That trend accelerated after China joined the World Trade Organization.

As steady paychecks vanished, drug addiction and crime increased across the area. Conditions reached a low point following the 2008 financial crisis, prompting Phil Plummer — who was then Montgomery County Sheriff — to enter political life.

"My jail was 40% drug addicts, 50% mental health patients, 10% criminals," said Plummer, who has been a Republican state representative since 2019. "We got it upside down — that’s what drove me to the state house."

Plummer, the Montgomery County Republican chairman, is now on the ballot for the Ohio state Senate and stressed that Trump remains the force keeping the GOP's coalition of corporate interests and working-class families together.

In recent years, the local economy showed signs of improvement as Wright-Patterson Air Force Base expanded, now directly employing 38,000 people. The facility's innovations have drawn new aerospace companies to the region, including Joby Aviation, Sierra Nevada Corporation, and Electra.

Trump pointed to an $850 million investment by aircraft manufacturer Electra — alongside a new project in Ohio from Stellantis and a Friday announcement from Bayer regarding a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical plant near Columbus — as evidence his policies were creating jobs.

Dayton rebounded because Republicans and Democrats alike recognized the value coming out of Wright-Patterson over the past two decades, according to Jeff Hoagland, CEO of the Dayton Development Coalition.

"In economic development, it takes time, and you have got to give it a little bit of time to bake, and then once it does, then you’re going to have something special," Hoagland said.

Downtown Dayton has added residential lofts, while the historic Dayton Arcade complex, featuring its glass dome and mosaic-tiled floors, has been renovated into shops, an art gallery, and eateries.

On Monday, the gallery echoed with the sound of an acoustic guitar and flute during a fundraiser for Rose Lounsbury, a former schoolteacher making her second run as a Democrat for state representative.

Guests expressed optimism that Democrats could pick up a U.S. Senate seat, a governorship, and enough seats in the Ohio House of Representatives to end a Republican supermajority.

"There is a gap between what people want and what they feel is available," Lounsbury said. "People don’t want to live a life of subsistence. They want to live the middle-class dream and they feel it’s not available like it once was."

Lounsbury’s Republican opponent, State Rep. Andrea White, spent time in the state capital of Columbus over the past week helping lead an effort to pass a temporary suspension of the state gas tax of 38.5 cents per gallon to provide relief at the pump.

White argued that the Republican-led state government has cushioned the impact of inflation by flattening state income tax rates and checking property tax increases.

"The concept is, put it back in the hands of the people who pay the taxes — so they have more of their own money," White said.

The White House said Trump's tax cuts and trade agreements have assisted Ohio. However, experiences at the former Navistar facility demonstrate that policies intended to support the working class fell short.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump dances during a campaign rally in Vandalia, Ohio ( AFP/Getty )

His broad tariffs failed to drive demand, and the plant's former owner, International Motors, chose to offload the facility. Meanwhile, Trump's primary legislative achievement — the One Big Beautiful Bill — added little to take-home pay, even as it temporarily eliminated taxes on tips and overtime.

"We weren’t getting a lot of overtime because of the economy," said Marianne Donnelly, who drove a forklift at the factory. "There just wasn’t any to be had, very little to be had."

At the same time, household costs have continued to climb. Donnelly buys marked-down beef, pork, and chicken to store in her freezer, and she canceled her subscriptions to The Columbus Dispatch and The Washington Post, along with several streaming platforms.

Laid-off workers like Donnelly expect to be rehired within six to 12 months by Roshel, a Canadian producer of armored vehicles acquiring the plant. Roshel stated it is "working with everyone involved not only to protect the current workforce, but to more than double it over the coming years through a phased process."

On the Monday prior to the layoffs, Morgan Hughes and JoJo Burkhard were canvassing neighborhoods in Kettering, a Dayton suburb named after the inventor of the electric car starter. They were working to persuade union members and retirees to vote for Democrats.

The Navistar job had enabled Hughes, 35, to buy a home at age 21 and work beside her father.

When her working hours were reduced, Hughes drove for DoorDash and earned a real estate license. On her wrist is a tattoo of a cross and the words "Be Still And Know," referencing Psalm 46:10, which speaks to how faith in God helps overcome fear.

Hughes noted that union members and retirees simply want to be heard after feeling neglected by politicians. Burkhard said inflation and economic stress have made it easier to convert swing voters.

"It isn’t a hard pitch at all," she said. "And even if they don’t want to stay Democratic long-term, they’ll at least give the candidates a chance this election, which could be a turning point for us."

After spending the morning speaking with voters, the pair stopped at a Chinese restaurant for potstickers as the weight of the week set in.

Burkhard opened a fortune cookie and tears welled in her eyes. The layoffs meant no income for her, her boyfriend, and her mother — making the message inside feel almost prophetic. She said she needed the hope it offered.

Her fortune read, "You’ll find your inner strength to overcome challenges."

News.title: This is when to upgrade your tech (and when not to bother)
News.content:
The tech giants’ attempts to persuade people to upgrade to new gadgets every two years are proving less and less effective. According to YouGov polling, Brits are increasingly deciding to stick with the devices they have for longer, and it isn’t altogether surprising.

As well as the inherent wastefulness of the bi-annual upgrade cycle, year-on-year improvements are less dramatic than they used to be, and tech prices are sky-rocketing thanks to the growing needs of AI data centres.

Inevitably, however, there will come a time when you need to bite the bullet and buy a new model. These are the questions to ask yourself to decide whether that should be today, or whether you can kick the can a little further down the road.

How’s the performance?

A good place to start is to evaluate how your device functions day-to-day versus the day you bought it. Tech inevitably slows down over time, but the drop isn’t equal among devices: a five-year-old flagship smartphone may still outperform a budget model from last year.

If it’s still running smoothly enough, and isn’t broken in an unfixable way, then it probably pays to wait until it no longer passes this test. The longer you wait, the more appealing the upgrade choices will be.

The exception to this is if you’re bumping up against storage problems. If there’s no way to add more, and cloud storage isn’t cutting it, then you may need to upgrade early.

Are you missing key features?

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

News.title: Brilliant Hamilton storms to podium despite another Ferrari blunder
News.content:
One of the big talking points heading into the weekend has been the cooling vests drivers wear under their overalls (as opposed to the jacket-like ones they wear when they’re out of their cars). Russell told us in our Brits media session on Thursday that Mercedes had decided to forego the vests here, since the technology was not yet refined. The system works by pumping a coolant through thin tubes stitched into the vest.

Drivers have complained that the connecting valve to the pump, which was originally placed on the side of the vest, proved uncomfortable when combined with the high G-forces experienced in an F1 car. On some vests the connector has been moved to find a more comfortable position, but the thick material and tubing have also proved cumbersome under the driver’s fireproof overalls. There are also concerns over the reliability of some systems and the possibility that a failure will mean the vest will have the opposite effect and work as a heat insulator.preferring to spend that money instead on car upgrades. The money to develop the vests comes out of the budget cap.

But Russell added that the FIA should make the tech mandatory and develop it themselves, describing this race as like being in a “sauna”.The Briton’s comments prompted a sarcastic response from Verstappen - who doesn’t wear the vests either, out of choice - who said Russell “shouldn’t make a fuss”.

“I don’t need it,” Verstappen said. “Maybe I suffer a bit less from the heat.. I find a Finnish sauna at 85 degrees a lot hotter... You shouldn’t make a fuss. Yes, it is hot, but that’s part of it. You have to train for that.”

The Dutchman added: “When I was 18, I had a bit more trouble with these conditions. But after that, I started training more in the heat, such as in the sauna and a steam room, so that I can handle the sweating better and the fact that your head gets very hot. Maybe I should take him (Russell) to the sauna a few times.”

These two have history, of course. They’ve sniped at each other for years. In 2024, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, it reached a peak when Verstappen described Russell as being “two-faced” and said he had lost all respect for him. Russell responded by saying Verstappen was “a bully”. Earlier this year, the Mercedes driver said Verstappen could always retire from the sport and drive sports cars if he didn’t like the regs.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

News.title: Sublime England thrash Croatia in best performance for a decade
News.content:
We came out of the World Cup wondering if Tuchel really had an idea of how he can get England over the line. After last Saturday’s defeat by world and European champions Spain, followed by Tuesday’s win over the Czech Republic we still did not know.

But here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their new head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

News.title: Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying
News.content:
The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”
