News.title: Bath complete revenge mission on Exeter despite imperious Feyi-Waboso
News.content:
Bath held off a furious comeback from Exeter, led by the irrepressible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to avenge their Gallagher Prem semi-final defeat here in June.

It felt as if lightning might strike Bath twice. Once again Exeter overturned a 26-10 half-time deficit, to manufacture a second-half lead thanks to a pair of blistering finishes by Feyi-Waboso. Four months ago, Bath failed to take a drop goal in the closing stages, but this time with the reassuring presence of Finn Russell at fly-half, they kept their cool.

The Scotland playmaker twice sent penalties deep into the Exeter 22 from where Stephen Varney conceded a yellow card and penalty try before Bath replacement Ted Hill powered through a thicket of Exeter tacklers.

“Finn is one of the best 10s in the world and I thought he had a very good game,” Johann van Graan, the Bath head of rugby, said. “His decision making is above most players in the world and I thought that came through tonight.”

Despite the appearance of yet another high-scoring shoot-out, both teams defended with real bite, although Bath struggled to lay a finger on Feyi-Waboso who ended up in a scrap with a fan in the stands here when he was a spectator in May. He exacted a measure of revenge beating eight defenders and carried for 132 metres.

“Manny still needs game time,” Rob Baxter, the Exeter director of rugby, said. “When he’s on the ball, you see something incredible, but it is his ability to get on the ball again. He is just getting his game minutes and match fitness up.”

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

However, the youngster was shown a straight red card in the 73rd minute of England’s 2-1 victory over the US last Friday.

The injury is yet another blow to Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, who has already lost a host of players during the extended three-week international break.

MARK Chapman has been spotted for the first time since The Sun revealed he was dating his Match of the Day co-host Kelly Cates.

Chappers, 52, was spotted keeping it casual in a hoodie and jeans while picking up some ready meals and a coffee in Cheshire.



He was seen balancing a stack of M&S ready meals, including ravioli and spaghetti carbonara, in one hand while looking at his phone.

The BBC star split from ex-partner Clere Collier in April after a three-year relationship with the Dubai-based estate agent.



Insiders told The Sun the 43-year-old then confronted Mark with suspicions about him and Kelly, 51.

But while admitting his relationship with Kelly – who hosts the BBC1 sports show with him – Mark maintained he had been faithful.

A source said: “Mark admitted the relationship but insisted there was no overlap between the two women and that he hadn’t cheated on her.”

Mark, one of the BBC’s highest paid broadcasters on £335,000 to £340,000 a year, was seen house-hunting with Clere last year.



The mum-of-two regularly travelled from Dubai to see Mark and their relationship had been “going strong” before their sudden split.

An associate of the former couple said: “Mark split with Clere out of the blue, without much explanation.

“They had been making plans for the future and their relationship had been going strong.

“They stayed in touch after the split, but Clere soon realised that Mark and Kelly were close and she accused Mark of dating Kelly.

Sports.title: Man City set for ‘a reception like you’ve never seen’ with Liverpool trip first after Premier League guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY’S shell-shocked players will need some answers as they drift back to the Etihad this week.

But what they really do NOT need is a trip to a “brutal” Anfield looming large on Sunday.



Many of Enzo Maresca’s squad are newcomers and will not have experienced this high-octane fixture too often.

No doubt Phil Foden — among the non-international players who will clock back on first — will be able to fill them in.



City and Liverpool was called the “biggest rivalry” in English football history by former Red Jamie Carragher in 2022.

The two camps have gone head to head for over a decade and came to blows once — when Raheem Sterling and Joe Gomez had a bust-up in the England canteen.

That was seven years ago as an argument on the pitch at Anfield 24 hours earlier spilled over into the Three Lions camp.

Sterling, a former Liverpool player whose transfer to City in 2015 was acrimonious, admitted his “emotions got the better of him” as he was dropped from the squad for the Euro 2020 qualifier.

Emotions have been running high on both sides since they first battled it out for the title in the spring of 2014.

And the events of the last ten days will only have intensified the bad feeling ahead of Sunday’s clash in front of the Kop.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Gary Neville – no stranger to the power of Anfield during his playing days – says this time it is going to be on another level.

He said: “If they want an understanding of how angry the game is, Anfield will tell them.

“It will be brutal — a reception like you’ve never seen.”

A lot of calls for City to be relegated and stripped of titles have come from the red half of Merseyside — and no wonder.

Liverpool finished runners-up to them three times in the Premier League over the last decade and also lost a League Cup final to Manuel Pellegrini’s side in 2016.



If it was not for City, there would be several more honours on the board at Anfield.

So tensions will be running high when City make the short journey along the M62 — and there will be no sympathy from the stands.

They really are heading right into the eye of the storm. Talks have already taken place about security around the stadium.

Merseyside Police and Liverpool’s security companies will already have an idea what to expect. Not long ago, it was Liverpool’s clashes with Manchester United that were the biggest draw on these shores.

And who can forget the infamous tunnel rows between the Red Devils and Arsene Wenger’s Arsenal back in the Noughties.



But as Carragher said, there is certainly a case for this game topping both — although history may see it differently unless the lawyers can clear the name of the shamed Etihad giants.

Tension has been simmering both on the pitch and in the boardroom ever since that nail-biting title scrap in 2014.

It emerged around that time that Liverpool had paid £1million into the City coffers amid suspicions the scouting database at the Etihad had been hacked.



Later, City’s bus was targeted as it left Anfield after the Reds had appeared to strike a major blow in the title race between the pair.

The visitors did not complain as it occurred on a day when the 25th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster had been marked.

However the amount of praise Liverpool got for finishing second that season clearly rankled in the blue half of Manchester.

It was when the City team bus came under attack again four years later as it edged towards the stadium for a Champions League quarter-final that things started to ramp up.

Significant damage was done to the vehicle — and it was deemed unfit to take Pep Guardiola and his players back after the match.



However nobody was ever arrested by Merseyside police – while Uefa issued a measly £17,500 fine, much to the dismay of the visitors.

Vincent Kompany, City’s skipper that night, later said: “The moment that happened things changed between City and Liverpool.

“The rivalry increased and they became our No 1 team to beat. The mood among City fans towards these games against Liverpool had changed.”



In the years that followed, the clashes between Guardiola’s side and Jurgen Klopp’s Reds became unmissable.

In 2022, Pep was pelted by coins from the stands as he argued with officials over a disallowed goal – while Liverpool condemned “vile chants” from the away end.

There were allegations that some City coaches had been spat on by supporters seated near the dugout in previous years.

Privately, the club were also unhappy about Klopp’s pre-match comments about their spending and how they had “no ceiling”.

All the while, Guardiola’s all–conquering team could not win in front of fans at Anfield — although they did manage it once when the Kop was empty during Covid.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

They finally laid that hoodoo to rest with a dramatic late win earlier this year. But Sunday will be an enormous test of character for Maresca and his new-look squad.

Everyone at City will have to brace themselves.

OFFICE romances may look a little different in sport – but they certainly do happen.

Swap out the work canteen and a sweaty tube journey together for pre-match pasta meals and luxury drives to the training ground or studio in swanky expensive motors.



SunSport revealed Match of the Day hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates are dating.

The pair of presenters share the anchoring duties for the BBC’s Premier League highlights show alongside Gabby Logan.



But Chapman and Cates – who both also work for Sky Sports and even featured on Celebrity Gogglebox together – started going out after he ended a three-year relationship with Dubai-based estate agent Clere Collier in April.

The broadcasting romantics, though, are not the first colleagues in the world of sport to get together…



BETH MEAD & VIVIANNE MIEDEMA

One of the most high-profile recent examples has been Beth Mead and Vivianne Miedema.

Both players joined Arsenal in 2017 but it was not until 2022 that they started going out.



Miedema moved to Manchester City in 2024 – and Mead followed her this year – while they have also faced each other on the international stage.

LAURA & JASON KENNY

Jason and Laura Kenny are Britain’s ultimate sporting power couple.

CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

As team-mates for Team GB across four Olympics, they boast a staggering 15 cycling medals including 12 golds between them.



Jason holds the overall Team GB record while Laura is Britain’s most decorated female Olympian.

The velodrome speed stars married in September 2016, weeks after their Rio exploits, and now have three children together.

ROGER & MIRKA FEDERER

From British cycling royalty to the Swiss king of tennis. Roger Federer racked up 20 Grand Slam titles and is one of the greatest players to ever grace a court.

But as Federer quickly pointed out when he was inducted into the Hall of Fame, he has his long-term partner Mirka to thank.



The pair were both part of Switzerland’s Olympic tennis team at Sydney 2000 and they practised together before Mirka retired with injuries and dedicated herself to supporting her man become one the best ever.

They tied the knot in 2009 and, incredibly, had identical twin girls followed by identical twin boys.

DOUGLAS LUIZ & ALISHA LEHMANN

It was fun while it lasted but sadly Douglas Luiz and Alisha Lehmann proved not all office romances quite work out.

The footballers met when they were both at Aston Villa in 2021 and were in a relationship for four years.



That included a rarely-seen double-transfer to Juventus in 2024.

However, after a year in Italy, they split up – with Luiz going public with Duda Gaspar, Edu’s daughter, while Lehmann is now with former Love Islander Montel McKenzie.

CHARLOTTE JACKSON & CHRIS COLEMAN

Charlotte Jackson made her name as a presenter on Sky Sports – and it was there that her and Chris Coleman’s relationship blossomed.



Ex-Wales defender Coleman regularly visited the studios as a guest pundit and that is said to be how things started.

Now married, they have a son and a daughter and have kept largely out of the football limelight with Coleman managing in China, Greece, Cyprus and Belgium since his last job in England with Sunderland in 2018.

Instead, she has launched an acting career, starring in various productions including Secrets on Prime Video.



SUSIE & TOTO WOLFF

F1’s ultimate power couple is Susie and Toto Wolff.

Susie was an accomplished motorsport driver, featuring for Mercedez-Benz in DTM where she connected with Toto, a former driver who was then co-owner of HWA AG.

They were then at Williams F1 team together, Susie as a development driver and Toto a shareholder.



He proposed on a boat in Venice and they married in 2011, now with three kids together.

Susie remains in F1 as the F1 Academy managing director while her husband has been Mercedes’ team principal since 2013.

KARREN BRADY & PAUL PESCHISOLIDO

Karren Brady became managing director of Birmingham City aged just 23 following David Sullivan’s takeover back in 1993.

Two years later, she married Canadian international Paul Peschisolido, who was in the Blues’ first team for two seasons.

RECOMMENDED STORIES



She even sold him to Stoke in 1994, the year before they wed, before he returned briefly to St Mary’s in 1996, the year Brady gave birth to their first child, daughter Sophia – son Paolo followed.

The couple have properties in the West Midlands and Canada but are based in Knightsbridge.

Sports.title: How Jude Bellingham compares to England’s best players at 23 as he stakes claim to be Three Lions GOAT
Sports.content:
Next

PAUL GASCOIGNE has long been revered as the Geordie genius that put the weight of a country on his shoulders and nearly led them to glory.

He’s England‘s biggest what-if, in many ways. But the first five or so years of his career showed him to be one of the greatest talents England ever produced.



While we can romanticise about the playmaker’s fearless dribbling and his iconic tears in Italy, Jude Bellingham has completely changed the bar for what a young England star is.

It’s hard to believe he isn’t 24 until next June, but he has already played in four major tournaments which included two finals for England and a third-place finish.



The Real Madrid superstar has been within touching distance of becoming the Three Lions greatest ever already if those fine margins had fallen England’s way.

Many believe he already is. Gary Lineker, an England legend himself, believes he’s at least the best midfielder the country has seen.



Lineker said: “Where does he stand in all-time midfielders for England? Because I put him top, and we were only talking about perhaps this century.

“So I think he’s got the power and the pace and the ability of Gerrard. I think he’s almost got the passing ability of Scholes, but not quite, and he’s definitely got the finishing and the arrival in the box of Frank Lampard.

“So he’s close on all three of the primary strengths of all three players. He might be slightly behind on each one, but overall, as a package, he’s got all three.”

Roy Keane doesn’t just think he will be England’s best – he thinks Bellingham has the potential to be one of the greatest players of all-time, period.

So how does Jude stack up against the legendary Three Lions that have donned the shirt since Gazza arrived on the scene 38 years ago?

Jude Bellingham

The Birmingham export – who has his number 22 shirt retired by the club – has 59 England caps and 14 goals and he’s not 24 for another eight months.

Eight of Jude’s England goals have come across three major tournaments, and he’s actually played in four after coming off the bench at Euro 2020.

He was an unused sub in the Euro 2020 final loss, started in the quarter-final loss to France in 2022 World Cup as well as the Euro final loss to Spain in 2024 before securing third at the World Cup this summer.

He won the DFB-Pokal with Dortmund before moving to Real Madrid and has won five more honours including LaLiga and a Champions League where he scored in the final.



Paul Gascoigne

Gazza had won the FA Cup with Spurs (with THAT famous knee injury) and he had 20 caps before turning 24, making his debut in 1988.

He led England to the semi-finals of Italia 90 with nothing short of a mercurial display, truly dragging the country to the business end of the tournament. His tears after picking up a yellow card in the semi-final to rule him out of the final is the stuff of legends.

Sadly, he was injured for Euro 1992 with the aforementioned knee injury and England were awful without him, failing to win a single game.



Steven Gerrard

The Liverpool legend had 24 caps and had won five trophies – with the Uefa Cup and FA Cup the pick of the bunch – by the time he turned 24.

The all-action midfielder was 20 when he took part in England’s Euro 2000 disaster and he was ruled out of the World Cup two years later through injury.

Paul Scholes

Whilst Scholes has one of the most ridiculous CVs the Premier League has ever seen, he didn’t burst onto the scene early like Bellingham or Gazza.

He had two Premier League titles and an FA Cup by 23, which is not to be scoffed at by any means.

Scholes had 14 caps and went to the 1998 World Cup as a 23 year old, starting every game and scoring in the opener against Tunisia.



Frank Lampard

Harry Redknapp‘s prediction that Frank Lampard would reach the top was proven right and then some in the end, but it took a while.

He had just seven caps before his 24th birthday. He had only won the Intertoto Cup at that point and did not go to a major tournament before he turned 24.

His first 15-goal season for Chelsea came in 2003-04 when he was 25.



Michael Owen

Owen had 53 of his 89 England caps before he turned 24 and he had 25 goals – not enough respect gets put on his name.

Like Gerrard, he won six major honours but also won the Ballon d’Or in 2001 aged 22.

He was literally crowned the best player in the world; he’s only the fourth Englishman to ever win it and he’s the most-recent one right now (prayers for Harry Kane on October 26).

He burst onto the scene as one of the world’s brightest talents at the 1998 World Cup scoring that iconic goal vs Argentina, but was sent packing in the second round.



Euro 2000 was horrendous with a group stage exit before a quarter-final loss at the 2002 World Cup to eventual winners Brazil – though he did score.

Harry Kane

Kane was a little bit of a slow starter in the pro ranks, enduring four loan spells before Tottenham gave him a real chance.

He had 18 international caps before 24 and he already had 12 England goals. We should have known then he’d become the country’s all-time goalscorer.

Obviously, no major honours at club level at that point and Kane was a part of the England squad that was embarrassingly knocked out by Iceland at Euro 2016 just before he turned 24.



David Beckham

Then Manchester United darling, Beckham had 22 caps before 24 and went on to skipper England when he was 25.

Becks had six major honours with three Premier Leagues, two FA Cups and the Champions League as the Red Devils dominated the turn of the millennium.

Becks was 23 when he got sent off against Argentina at the 1998 World Cup in the second round.



Wayne Rooney

Rooney exploded onto the scene at 16 with Everton and made his England debut against Australia at just 17.

Thought of as the biggest talent the country had seen since Gascoigne, it wasn’t long before Man Utd splashed £30m on the teenager.

He had seven major honours by 24, including three Premier Leagues, the Champions League, the Club World Cup and two League Cups – he was yet to win the FA Cup at that point.

Rooney had a massive 56 caps before turning 24 with 25 goals, just like Owen.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He got to two quarter-final appearances with England before 24, including lighting up Euro 2004 where England might have done better had he not been struck down by injury.



Now that’s a what-if.

Sports.title: Medvedev defaulted for hitting spectator with ball as Djokovic makes Beijing final
Sports.content:
Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting a spectator with a ball as Novak Djokovic took his impeccable record at the China Open to 33-0 and moved one win away from a first title of 2026.

Medvedev accidentally struck the fan while trailing 7-5 5-3 and three points from defeat in Monday's punishing semi-final in Beijing, during which Djokovic saved 16 of the 18 break points he faced.

Medvedev, who will now lose all points and prize money earned from the event, hit the ball into the stands after it deflected off a wall, with the spectator subsequently helped out of the arena.

Tournament organisers said he had been taken to hospital.

Djokovic, 39, won the China Open six times in seven years between 2009 and 2015 but had not returned prior to this campaign.

Image: Djokovic's record at the China Open is a flawless 33-0

The Serb, who secured a come-from-behind quarter-final victory over world No 2 Alexander Zverev on Sunday, will meet Alex De Minaur in Tuesday's final as he looks to clinch a 102nd career title and first since the Hellenic Championship little under a year ago.

Speaking on court afterwards, Djokovic, defaulted at the 2020 US Open for hitting a line judge with a ball, said: "It is a bit of a shock, to be honest. I am sorry for the person.

"I didn't see what happened. I hope the person is not badly injured. I feel sorry for Daniil as I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match. I'm sure he didn't want to do this intentionally."

Djokovic: Always a battle against Medvedev

Djokovic reached the Australian Open final in January, losing to Carlos Alcaraz in four sets, but has struggled for fitness and form since and dropped out of the world's top 10, although this run in Beijing has returned him to that elite level.

The 24-time Grand Slam champion, who has played just eight tournaments this year, recently revealed an ongoing medical condition that has led to fatigue and vomiting on court, with the issue exacerbated in hot and humid conditions.

Image: Djokovic is targeting a seventh title in Beijing

Djokovic was made to work by Medvedev in a marathon match that lasted just shy of two and a half hours, recovering from a break down to claim the opening set.

He then broke Medvedev twice in the second set and was serving for victory prior to the premature finish.

Djokovic added: "It was a gruelling battle that I definitely didn't want to take to a third set. It was looking like that.

"It is always a big battle with Daniil, so hard to play him when he is feeling the ball in slower conditions with his big serve.

"I always believe in myself and felt I played really well in training bit obviously it is different in an official match.

"My draw wasn't favourable, very tough matches from the beginning, but it makes the run the final sweeter. Something about Beijing keeps me going."

De Minaur was leading Hubert Hurkacz 6-4 3-2 in the first semi-final when his opponent pulled out through injury.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sonay Kartal's run in Beijing was ended by Elena Rybakina's conqueror Alina Charaeva in the third round

In the women's event, Britain's Sonay Kartal saw her WTA Tour comeback end in the third round with a 6-4 6-1 loss to Alina Charaeva - the player who dumped out world No 1 Elena Rybakina.

The Beijing event was Kartal's first WTA tournament since March after a stress fracture of the back and she picked up wins over Andrea Lazaro Garcia and Wang Xinyu before falling to Charaeva.

Iga Swiatek, reached the fourth round after rallying from a set and 5-2 down to beat Donna Vekic 4-7 6-7 (7-0) 6-2.

Alcaraz wins - despite losing 16 points in a row

Over at the Japan Open, defending champion Alcaraz fought from a set down to beat fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5-7 6-3 6-1 and make his first final since April's Monte-Carlo Masters.

World No 3 Alcaraz led 5-3 in the first set against his compatriot but then lost 16 points in a row to ship it before the players traded breaks at the start of the second set.

The seven-time major champion eventually took control to secure a meeting with Jiri Leheckat in Tokyo on Tuesday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from Carlos Alcaraz's semi-final clash against Juame Munar at the Japan Open

Alcaraz said: "I don't know what happened in the first set. It seems that I'm struggling in every first set, but I've come back every time and I'm really happy about it."

Alcaraz's season has been disrupted by a wrist injury that caused him to miss his French Open defence as well as Wimbledon.

He returned for the final Grand Slam of the year, the US Open in New York, where he reached the quarter-finals before losing in five sets to home player Ben Shelton.

If Alcaraz takes the title in Japan for the second straight year - he beat Taylor Fritz in the 2025 final - it will be his third of the campaign, after the Australian Open and Qatar Open, and 27th of his career.

Sports.title: Macklin: Does Whittaker have the toughness to win a world title?
Sports.content:
Ben Whittaker's recent scare against Conor Wallace has raised questions about whether he has the attributes needed to win a world title, says Sky Sports expert Matthew Macklin.

After controlling the fight from the start, Whittaker was troubled by a left hand from Wallace in the 10th round and then looked ragged in the 12th as he repeatedly slipped to the canvas before clinging on to claim a points win on Saturday in Birmingham.

Whittaker's victory lined up a shot at the IBF light-heavyweight belt which is held by unified champion Dmitry Bivol, but Macklin believes the Olympic silver medallist is not yet ready to challenge the Russian.

Macklin told Sky Sports: "Ben has been on a run of pretty spectacular performances, hasn't he? That said, if we're honest about the calibre of opposition, we know it's pretty low for him and where he is aiming towards being.

"All of a sudden, they stepped it up again with Conor Wallace. He boxed really well for most of the fight, but nonetheless, at the end of the fight, he struggled.

Image: Ben Whittaker fought through some adversity late on to beat Conor Wallace on Saturday

"He got caught and then struggled to shake off the effects of that shot. He recovered momentarily, but not properly. He got his head together a little bit, but was still hurt because you could see he didn't really regain control of the fight.

"I think he needs more than one [fight before Bivol], probably a few.

"While Conor Wallace is a nice boxer, you wouldn't put him in the category of your Bivols and your Callum Smiths.

"Look at the fight between Callum Smith and Joshua Buatsi, and what those two went through in that fight, and then you see how Whittaker unravelled on Saturday night, there's no way you'd say he beats those two guys.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player You won't see a better round of boxing! Watch the phenomenal sixth between Joshua Buatsi and Callum Smith which had both fighters in big trouble.

"He has the skill, the sleekness, the speed and the savvy to mix it with those guys, but has he got the toughness, the chin, the stamina, the power, the hardness to mix it with those guys over 12 hard rounds? He hasn't shown that so far.

"That's not to say that Ben isn't tough or hard. But we can only judge him on what we've seen, and we've seen him unravel a couple of times.

"In the first Liam Cameron fight, he was unravelling and then obviously they both fell out the ring. Fair play to him, in the rematch, he came out and looked brilliant, but against Conor Wallace, he was boxing well, controlling it, but then gets nailed a couple of times and, all of a sudden, he starts to unravel.

"Fair play again, he got through it. But against a Bivol or a Callum Smith, or a Buatsi or William Hutchinson, would he have got through it against those guys? Probably not.

Image: Is Ben Whittaker ready to fight IBF light-heavyweight title holder Dmitry Bivol?

"I think [his trainer] Andy Lee has done a great job with him, but I also think that there's only so much you can do in the gym. You've still got to get the experience on the night, under the lights, in a real fight against real high calibre opposition.

"What's happened with Ben in his career, is he hasn't fought enough high level opposition. If you look at who he has boxed, outside of Cameron and Conor Wallace, he's boxed absolutely nobody.

"For someone who was a top-class amateur, to be a professional as long as he has and to have fought the level of opposition he has, he's missed years of learning - and that could be a problem at the top level.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Ben Whittaker's US fighting debut against Richard Rivera earlier this year. Courtesy of DAZN.

"It's great getting the highlight-reel knockouts - it's great for your ego, for the perception of you and from a promotional point of view, to create the star quality and the hype. That's important when you're trying to build a star, but you also need to build the fighter.

"You can't just build a star without building a fighter, because at some point he's going to be in a battle against another real fighter, who is of a high level, who wants it as much as he does, and can take a shot and give a shot.

"If you're not getting seasoned, if you're not putting the stuff that you're learning in the gym into practice, on the night and when you need it, it won't be there because you haven't developed it.

"By the way, I like him a lot and I want him to do well, but he hasn't been managed well in his career in terms of the opponents he's fought. He needs some proper fights."

Sports.title: Slegers can no longer hide behind 'fine margins' in defence of Arsenal
Sports.content:
Sky Sports columnist Laura Hunter analyses the big talking points from the second round of Women's Super League matches, bringing you closer to the key stories at the heart of the women's game.

Slegers 'fine margins' defence failing to stand up

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Manchester City against Arsenal in the Women's Super League

Renee Slegers has had to put a brave face on things over the past couple of weeks. Arsenal are winless in each of their last four league outings, their worst start to a campaign since 2014. To judge their alarming league position paints a bleaker picture still.

There are not many defensible aspects of such underperformance, despite Slegers' consistent claim that her side are falling foul of fine margins. That argument becomes less and less credible the longer such a stagnant run continues.

Perhaps it even lost its legitimacy completely when Slegers admitted after defeat to Man City that the club will use the upcoming international break to stage a comprehensive review of "not only what we see on matchday, but everything in the background". She added: "We have to turn over every stone."

Small margins do not tend to require such investigation. To suggest Arsenal have been hard done by up until now surely misses the point. Tweaks are not enough to arrest such a talented team from its current malaise. If they were, plenty of stones could be saved from the scour that Slegers has promised over these next two weeks.

In reality, Arsenal appear to be suffering a crisis of confidence, a self-doubt that is particularly noticeable in the pressure moments of big games. It's a multi-pronged problem with tough consequences.

Lisa Baum offered exhibit A within three minutes of kick-off at the Etihad on Sunday, escaping the advances of Niamh Charles, as she did many times throughout the game, only to snatch at a near-post effort instead of squaring the ball to Alessia Russo for a tap-in.

In isolation, that poor decision is easy to write off. Baum is new to the league; a young, dynamic winger with a hunger to impress. Having created the chance, she had every right to take the shot on herself. But choosing the low-probability option seems to be a trend that is harming Arsenal in the final third.

It happened again when Georgia Stanway played a superb raking pass out to Emily Fox on the right and she tried to beat Ayaka Yamashita from an impossible angle. Had she delayed by a fraction of a second, Russo was making a clever run on the blindside of Jade Rose and would have been free at the back post.

Stanway's off-target strike from 30 yards shortly after bore all the same hallmarks, and so a problem becomes a pattern, and that cycle of uncertainty is ruining Arsenal's chances of winning games.

Simply, Arsenal have lost any semblance of nuance. The numbers back that up. Their xG differential is the worst in the division, their conversion rate just as damning. Shots are being snatched at as desperation sets in, doubt stalking the patterns of play by which Arsenal are so known.

This was not a defeat by margins. Man City have killers in their ranks. Arsenal do not. The current conditioning of each side, broken down, is actually quite stark. Nothing about the way City operate under Andree Jeglertz is inhibited. They play with a full range of motion and balanced flow through the thirds when they progress the ball. Each phase has purpose.

Jeglertz lept to the aid of Slegers after the game, calling Arsenal a "great football team" but also made a point to praise his own side's "very fluent" attacking play, adding "we score in different ways".

The creative paralysis Arsenal are suffering does not allow for that, scoring twice because of faults attributed to City's defending. Albeit Russo did offer a timely reminder of her finishing quality in the second half. Her first goal of the domestic campaign is perhaps something to build on; she is one of many with form issues greater than any off-day can accept responsibility for.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alessia Russo's brilliant strike put Arsenal back in front against Manchester City during their Women's Super League clash

Slegers and her coaching staff have serious work to do; by far the toughest examination of her Arsenal tenure so far lies in the next block of fixtures. The north London derby is later this month.

The Dutchwoman has cultivated a discernibly strong bond with her squad and, importantly, retains the backing of the club despite being unable to deliver consistency of results in this moment. Arsenal's stance is not expected to change over the course of this international window.

The time for a reality check is now, though. No more talk of fine margins. Arsenal need big impact from this break and a more intentional way of accepting responsibility for what has already gone wrong in order to find their way back.

The gap to leaders Man City is anything but small or fine. It's a whopping 10 points.

Sports.title: Man City's rivals do not expect them to be in Premier League next season
Sports.content:
Sympathy is in short supply at other clubs after an independent commission laid bare the scale of Manchester City's rule breaking across nine seasons in a devastating decision published last week.

As City's legal team prepare for their appeal and sanctions hearing after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's rules, their rivals in England and across Europe believe "the punishment should fit the crime".

With the looming prospect of City taking their bid to clear their name all the way to the High Court, rival clubs are becomingly increasingly concerned about the damage that is being done to the image and integrity of the Premier League, the cost of the dispute and what they see as City's failure to take any responsibility or accountability for their actions.

City are adamant they have done nothing wrong, insisting they are innocent and that a "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists" to support their position as they lodged their appeal.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol breaks down how long it may take for a final judgement to be reached following Man City's appeal after being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules

But even a cursory reading of the decision which was published by the independent disciplinary commission puts into sharp focus the scale of the task facing City's lawyers when an appeal hearing takes place before Christmas.

The commission's finding are about as serious as it gets when it comes to financial rule-breaking and the fact that it was carried out over nine seasons and distorted the competition means City's rivals are not expecting Enzo Maresca's team to be playing in the Premier League next season.

Many believe that a points deduction is not a sufficient punishment if it would lead to City spending just one season outside the top flight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville gives his thoughts on a potential punishment for Manchester City after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission. City deny all charges

It is only natural for clubs to think of their own self-interest and City's relegation would mean one fewer club going down this season as well as removing one of the favourites from the title race and opening up another European place. Self-interest is not the over-riding consideration though.

The consensus appears to be that rules have to be respected by all clubs, no matter their size or status - and it would not be sufficient to hand City a punishment that would last only one season for rules which were broken across multiple seasons.

City's rival Premier League clubs will not be involved in the sanction hearing, which could be take place while the appeal process runs its course.

The same three-person panel which heard the evidence at the 42-day hearing in 2024 and delivered its core decision last Tuesday will decide on sanctions after the Premier League, as the prosecutors, put forward their recommendation and City's lawyers argue their case.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol answers your questions after Manchester City launched an appeal after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission

It will be down to the Premier League board to decide what recommended sanction their lawyers should present to the panel.

In 2023, the Premier League argued that Everton deserved a 12-point deduction for one breach of the Profitability and Sustainability Rules.

Everton, who were in a desperate financial position at the time, eventually ended up with a six-point deduction after they appealed the original 10-point sanction.

With both sides allowed to appeal the sanctions, and City appealing the judgment, Premier League clubs are prepared for this marathon dispute to keep on running until at least next year.

Clubs have been trying to draw a line under the legal disputes which have become a feature of the English game as they try to move towards what some executives call "the NFL model" where the league speaks with one voice.

That will not happen until the final chapter of the 115 charges case is finally written.

Sports.title: Moore inducted into Hall of Fame
Sports.content:
Ryan Moore paid tribute to the "brilliant people" who have helped build his magnificent career in the saddle after it was announced he has been inducted into the British Racing Hall of Fame.

The three-time champion jockey, who has ridden an astonishing 230 Group/Grade One winners during a highly decorated career, will be honoured in an official ceremony at Ascot on Qatar Racing British Champions Day on October 17.

The Aga Khan's ill-fated Shergar will be inducted on the same day.

Moore was keen to namecheck those who have helped him build from his initial rides as a jump jockey for his father Gary to globetrotting international superstar.

"I'm honoured to be inducted into the British Racing Hall of Fame. I've been fortunate to work with some brilliant people throughout my career," he said.

"My family's support was so important when I was starting out, and Richard Hannon showed lots of faith in me in the early days as well. I'm also particularly grateful to Sir Michael Stoute and Aidan O'Brien for the opportunities they've given me over the years.

"It means a lot to be recognised alongside them and others who have achieved so much in the sport."

Moore becomes the 14th person inducted into the Hall of Fame following Lester Piggott, Vincent O'Brien, Pat Eddery, Queen Elizabeth II, Frankie Dettori, Willie Carson, Sir Henry Cecil, Sir Michael Stoute, Prince Khalid Abdullah, Steve Cauthen, Aidan O'Brien, Jack Berry and Major Dick Hern.

Shergar, who won the 1981 Epsom Derby by a record-breaking 10 lengths and followed up in the Irish Derby and the King George VI And Queen Elizabeth Stakes at Ascot, is remembered as much for a sad end after being kidnapped in February 1983.

The middle-distance star, who was never seen again, becomes the 14th horse to be inducted after Frankel, Brigadier Gerard, Nijinsky, Mill Reef, Dayjur, Dancing Brave, Galileo, Sea The Stars, Stradivarius, Pebbles, Dubai Millennium, Goldikova and Enable.

Sophie Able, co-chair of the Hall of Fame panel, said: "It was the unanimous decision of the panel that Shergar and Ryan Moore are both truly deserving inductees to the British Racing Hall of Fame.

"Shergar remains one of the most celebrated and iconic horses in British racing history, while Ryan's outstanding career and achievements in the saddle have established him as one of the great jockeys of his generation."

Sports.title: England to play white-ball warm-up in Australia after pre-Ashes criticism
Sports.content:
England will play a Western Australia XI in a 50-over warm-up game at the WACA ahead of their ODI series against Australia in November - having been criticised for not facing any local opposition prior to their Ashes humbling last winter.

England's sole Test match warm-up before being thrashed 4-1 was an intra-squad fixture held at club ground Lilac Hill, which in no way replicated the bouncy conditions they ultimately came up against in the series opener in Perth, a contest they lost inside two days.

White-ball coach Brendon McCullum, who was in charge of the Test side during the Ashes thrashing, had said last month that he was hoping to arrange some warm-up games this time around and his team will now take on the Western Australia XI on November 7.

The first one-day international against Australia on November 13 is also in Perth, at Optus Stadium, followed by matches in Adelaide on November 15 and Hobart on November 18.

McCullum's side will then meet their hosts in five T20 internationals, across Melbourne, Carrara, Brisbane, Sydney and Canberra.

Image: Joe Root is a key member of England's ODI side

England are yet to name their squads for the tour but hope Jacob Bethell will be fit to return having missed the back end of the home summer following a knee injury and subsequent surgery.

Before that assignment, they will play an ODI tri-series in Pakistan, also featuring Sri Lanka, from October 20.

'Crane a better leg-spinner than Ahmed'

Glamorgan leg-spinner Mason Crane has been called up, in place of the dropped Rehan Ahmed, and is eyeing a first international appearance since the 2017-18 Ashes.

Crane recorded bowling figures of 1-193 from 48 overs on a trying red-ball debut in Sydney back then but has enjoyed a fine season domestically in 2026, playing all 14 County Championship games and backing up his 34 wickets with two hundreds.

The former Hampshire bowler also claimed 15 Vitality Blast wickets.

Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, former England captain Michael Atherton said: "Crane's call-up is a great story.

Image: Mason Crane could play for England for the first time since 2018 after being named in the squad for the ODI tri-series in Pakistan

"He had a hellish introduction to Test cricket but I thought he showed a lot of character in that game and didn't bowl as badly as his figures suggested.

"He has reaped the benefit of both a bit of experience - he is 29 now and been around the block - and being at a county where he is getting plenty of game time.

"His batting has come on as well which is not going to harm his chances at all.

Image: Rehan Ahmed played two ODIs in the recent series win over Sri Lanka, recording figures of 1-46 from seven overs in Durham and 2-48 from eight at Headingley

"I am happy England have moved on from Ahmed from a spin-bowling side as I feel there are better leg-spinners than him.

"To my mind, Ahmed is principally a batter first who bowls leg-spin whereas I see Crane the other way.

"There is time for Ahmed to come back but England have to work out how they see his role and he does, too.

"Crane is definitely a better leg-spinner than him for me and England may be looking at him for the rest of the winter [with a Test series in Bangladesh in February]."

Sports.title: Humphries ready to win another World title - and wants Littler in the final
Sports.content:
Luke Humphries says his World Grand Prix triumph has left him feeling ready to win a second World Championship - and hopes to face Luke Littler in the final.

Humphries landed a first major title since the 2025 Premier League as he recovered from 3-0 down to beat Gerwyn Price 6-4 in the final of the double-start event, sealing victory with an 11-darter having broken his opponents in 10 to clinch the ninth set.

'Cool Hand' defeated Littler to win the 2024 World Championship and last year's Premier League but has lost his last four major finals against 'The Nuke', including at the 2025 World Grand Prx.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Wayne Mardle looks at how Humphries' win sets him up for the rest of the year

Humphries, who played four days in a row in Leicester last week, says winning in set-play has given him confidence ahead of the similar format at Alexandra Palace from December 11, live on Sky Sports.

The world No 2 told Sky Sports: "Four days on the trot is hard but I have done it so many times before. I know in the Worlds you have three gruelling days - quarters, semis, final.

"Now I have got that major tournament, it is going to put me in a good frame of mind that I can go on and win the World Championship again.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries' 105 checkout to deny Price a 4-0 lead in the final proved crucial in Leicester

"My goal now is to make the World final and play [Littler] in it again and let's see what can happen. The real fans of darts know I am still here and capable of winning stuff.

"I have come so close to beating Luke in some majors in the last six to eight months and I think he enjoys the battle as well.

"He deserves credit for what he has done in the sport. He is one of my closest friends on tour. I know a lot of people don't like that but I do because he is such a great kid.

"He is amazing for the sport and the hate he gets is unjust."

'If I am in this game for another 15, 20 years, how much more can I win?

Humphries now has nine PDC major trophies, placing him outright fifth on the all-time list, behind only Phil Taylor, Michael van Gerwen, reigning world champion Littler and James Wade.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Humphries claimed the ninth set against Price with a 10-dart break of throw

"Nine major titles and two World Cups is insane and it's been done in such a short space of time as well - three years to the day," said Humphries, whose maiden major came at the 2023 World Grand Prix when he also beat Price in the final.

"If I am in this game for another 15, 20 years, how much more can I win?

"It's not just one player winning everything. There are so many opportunities now, so many major tournaments. This is great for my confidence and hopefully I can pick up another big one this year.

"I am here and I'm still going to win some stuff. Those last four legs [against Price], I don't think anyone would have stopped me. I felt so focused, so determined.

"After three or four months of not playing your best, people discredit you and think, 'he is finished, he won't win anything' but I always seem to bounce back and pop up with a major tournament or final."

Image: Humphries joked that 'Harry Potter did well' after winning the World Grand Prix

Humphries sported a scab on his head during the World Grand Prix, which he attributed to an allergic reaction to make-up applied during filming for TV show bullseye.

The 31-year-old joked 'Harry Potter did well, didn't he?!' when speaking on stage after beating Price and later added to Sky Sports: "It has been a big story of the week.

"I think I am alright but maybe it got infected or something so I will get that sorted."

What's next?

The European Tour season continues with the Swiss Darts Trophy (October 9-11) and the Dutch Darts Championship (October 16-18) before the European Championship takes place in Dortmund, Germany from October 22-25.

Sky Sports remains the home of darts with the Grand Slam of Darts (November 14-22) and World Darts Championship (December 10-January 3) both live. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

Sports.title: Why Verstappen's 'special' Malaysia win was so significant
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says his victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was a “really special and emotional moment” after Red Bull claimed their first win of 2026.

Verstappen was at his imperious best as he mastered the mixed conditions and Safety Car restarts to beat championship leader Kimi Antonelli and maintain his streak of winning at least one race every season since joining Red Bull in 2016.

Only two months ago, Verstappen's future was in the spotlight but he signed a new Red Bull contract during the summer break to stay with the team until at least the end of 2030, and Malaysia highlighted why the Dutchman had so much faith in the Milton Keynes squad.

How have Red Bull suddenly turned things around?

Having come within two points of becoming a five-time world champion last year, it became clear Verstappen would be unable to challenge for the title this season for the first time since 2020.

Red Bull, in collaboration with Ford, built their own power unit but it was actually the chassis which was a major weak point at the start of the season. In fact, the Red Bull-Ford engine was deemed to be the benchmark on the grid by the FIA after the first ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) review.

Verstappen has the ability to drive and get the most out of any racing car but even he struggled to have confidence in the unpredictable handling of the RB22 as he claimed just one podium in the opening seven races.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Relive Max Verstappen's troublesome first half of the 2026 season where he suffered several issues

Red Bull brought a major upgrade package to June's Austrian Grand Prix which got rid of the car's excess weight and changed the aerodynamics.

It had an immediate effect as Verstappen finished less than two seconds behind race-winner George Russell on his way to second, was on course for third a week later at Silverstone until his rear wing failed, and took two more podiums before the summer break in Belgium and Hungary.

A rare mistake at his home race in Zandvoort saw Verstappen crash out on the opening lap but he was back on the podium in Monza and Madrid.

Red Bull brought more upgrades to Baku where Verstappen finished just two tenths behind Russell in Azerbaijan in F1's closest finish since 2002.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Azerbaijan GP saw a dramatic ending as Valtteri Bottas crashed on the final lap as George Russell just beat Max Verstappen to victory by one tenth of a second

Outside of his crashes at the British and Dutch Grands Prix, Verstappen has been on the podium in the other seven races since the Austria upgrades. In some ways, his dominant weekend in Malaysia should not be a surprise because Red Bull have been on an upward trajectory.

"We had a very complicated and tough start to the year with all sorts of problems and just not being competitive enough," said Verstappen.

"But throughout the year, the team has been working very hard to understand our issues and bring good performance upgrades to the car and make it more driveable. Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and Sunday, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form, so it's amazing.

"Very enjoyable to win here and also have our first victory for our own engine. It's an incredible project with a lot of partners and a lot of people that are dedicated to be where we are now, so a fantastic feeling."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player SkyPad analysis of Max Verstappen's first pole position in 2026

A new Red Bull era

Much credit must go to former team principal Christian Horner for the success of Red Bull-Ford powertrains, the venture he set up that has delivered far above expectations during its first campaign as an engine manufacturer.

However, Red Bull was somewhat in turmoil during Horner's final years at the team due to a power struggle following the death of co-founder Dietrich Mateschitz in 2022.

Several key members left the team including legendary F1 designer Adrian Newey, chief engineering officer Rob Marshall, sporting director Jonathan Wheatley, advisor Helmut Marko - and eventually Horner himself.

With it came question marks about Verstappen's own future at the team in 2024 and 2025, particularly when his father Jos Verstappen fell out with Horner.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Christian Horner says he's looking at doing the right thing if he were to make a return for Formula 1 when he was in the Silverstone paddock in July

Laurent Mekies replaced Horner as team principal in July 2025 and the Verstappen camp appears to have a far more harmonious relationship with the Frenchman, with Max especially appreciating Mekies' engineering background.

Twelve months ago, Red Bull suddenly found plenty of performance that saw Verstappen claim eight consecutive podiums, including four wins, to unexpectedly push Lando Norris close to the title.

How much of that was down to Mekies is hard to judge, given how quickly that step was made, but the development this year can certainly be put down to his leadership.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen go wheel to wheel on the restart, before Verstappen slips through to take the lead in Malaysia

Mekies said following Verstappen's win on Sunday: "The credit goes to all the people involved who have been working incredibly hard on this project over the past five years. Everyone in Milton Keynes and at the track deserves this moment and should celebrate it as an important step towards many more victories in the future.

"This result confirms the progress we have been making in recent months. We were already close several times, and today we converted that pace. The team has been working tirelessly to improve our package, and weekends like this are the reward for that effort."

Verstappen's new contract justified?

It's far too early to say Verstappen has definitely made the right decision by committing his future to Red Bull, and this can only be truly answered in 2027.

However, it has become clear the combination of Mekies as team principal, trust in technical director Pierre Wache and chief performance engineer Ben Waterhouse - both of whom have been with Red Bull for over a decade - are key parts of the puzzle to effectively rebuild a new Red Bull era around Verstappen.

"Everyone is contributing a lot and always trying to find performance, upgrades and push the team forward," Verstappen told Sky Sports F1.

"In Baku we were quick in the corners but not on the straights compared to Mercedes. In Malaysia, we were decent in the corners and quick on the straights.

"Sometimes we just need to understand the whole package - why we are quick, why we were not so quick and take it step by step."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Max Verstappen win the Bahrain GP in Malaysia!

Red Bull have a history of developing their cars strongly and appear to be exhibiting that once more this season, so there's no reason to think Verstappen won't add to his 72 career wins during the seven remaining rounds.

Malaysia was just another reminder that the Red Bull-Verstappen combination is still an almighty force that was never likely to sleep for long, and may now be wide awake once more.
