Sports.title: Bournemouth unhappy over Scott injury but Tuchel says England took ‘zero risk’
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel insisted England took zero risk with Alex Scott after the midfielder’s withdrawal with a thigh injury left Bournemouth unhappy over his treatment.

Scott excelled during the 7-0 win over Croatia in the Nations League on Saturday but will play no further part in this international break and could be out for two months after exacerbating a muscle issue during his full debut for the national team.

The frustration for Bournemouth is that the 23-year-old played through the pain after feeling discomfort before facing Croatia. Scott, who was in line to start again when England host Czechia in their fourth and final game of this camp on Tuesday, made way for James Garner after 70 minutes in Rijeka and underwent tests on the problem on Sunday.

Bournemouth, who are also without the French forward Eli Junior Kroupi, face being without one of their most important players as they enter a busy part of the season. They are looking for their first win in the Premier League and are in the Europa League. But Tuchel is adamant that England, who have also lost the Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa to a quad injury, followed the proper medical procedure with Scott.

“With Alex, it’s a strange one,” the head coach said. “I’m very sad about it. He trained in full before Croatia, did extra work after the training sessions. We knew he was in treatment but there were only green lights from him and the medics.

“When we were aware there was slight discomfort during the match and asked if he wanted to come off he said no. After the match, he said he could have played 90 minutes and didn’t feel an injury. Even before the scan he didn’t feel injured so it’s a strange one. There was zero risk taken from our side. On a human level, I feel bad that he has not the next cap tomorrow.”

Asked if he had a clear conscience, Tuchel said: “Yeah, 100%. I would not have taken any risk.”

Scott’s determination to represent his country was underlined by his decision to stay with the squad after the recent death of his grandfather. The former Bristol City midfielder, who remains a key target for Chelsea, made his debut when he came on during last week’s win over Czechia in Prague. He earned a starting place against Croatia and reprised his excellent partnership with Elliot Anderson from last year’s Under-21 European Championship.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel praised Harry Kane, who is poised to win a record-equalling 125th England cap on Tuesday. Photograph: John Walton/PA

Scott is unlikely to be unavailable when England face Croatia and Spain in their final two games in Nations League Group A3 next month. It is a headache for Tuchel after Scott emerged as competition for Declan Rice during the past fortnight. However the German maintained that England had not let Bournemouth down.

“The medical and physical department is in constant contact,” he said. “We are sharing information and this is a totally open process. We are not on the phone to clubs asking for advice because then it would be an empty camp.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel has questioned Fifa’s decision to extend this international window, saying the format is testing from a physical perspective because of the amount of travel and training time after the 48-team World Cup. England last week lost the Manchester City left-back Nico O’Reilly, whose place has been taken by Rico Lewis.

Rice and Kobbie Mainoo withdrew at the start of this camp, leaving Tuchel with Anderson, Garner and Myles Lewis-Skelly as his midfield options against Czechia. England are second in their group, well placed to make March’s two-leg quarter-finals. A major talking point against Czechia will be Harry Kane equalling Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England men’s appearances.

“I’m not sure I have any more words,” Tuchel said of the England captain. “He’s on the shortlist for the Ballon d’Or. We’ve spoken so often about him and I try to find new words which then make no sense.

“Everything he does, he does it on the highest level. Since he took this major role for Bayern Munich, he found a new level. It’s the highest level, on and off the pitch.”

Trevoh Chalobah is likely to replace Konsa. Tuchel has not decided how heavily to rotate. He said that Trent Alexander-Arnold had a chance to replace Jarell Quansah at right-back.

Sports.title: Czechia’s Santi Denia: ‘Anthony Gordon? What a player! He’s at the same level as Lamine Yamal’
Sports.content:
At the end of a 2-0 defeat by England in Prague, the Czechia coach turned left, walked along the touchline, shook Thomas Tuchel’s hand and said something he thinks he had never said at full-time: “See you soon.” To which Tuchel said back: “See you soon.” Seven days later, via Oviedo and Rijeka respectively, they meet again, at Wembley. “Four matches in 11 days, no time to train, for anything; I haven’t heard a single national coach say they like the new setup,” Santi Denia says, but it’s not all bad and there’s a big smile too.

This is the start of a new life, yet familiar faces await, warmth in every word. Very familiar faces. If Czechia’s opponents in this Nations League could not have been much worse, they could not have been much better either. In Oviedo, Denia’s team played his country, his players; in London, for the second time in a week, they play the nation he knows better than any other, more footballers he has seen grown up. Hello, again.

The opportunity to become Czechia’s coach came during a conversation with an old friend, at the World Cup where Denia watched Spain beat Argentina, the culmination of a long journey shared. Of Spain’s 26 champions in New Jersey, 23 had played under him during his 15 years at the federation, coaching the under-15s, 17s, 19s, 21s and 23s and working across the academy structure: those were his kids lifting the cup, stories to tell about when Rodri was tiny and Lamine Yamal tinier. Along the way, if there were kids whose path he kept crossing, they were England’s.

And so, as Czechia’s manager chats between matches – England, Spain, England again – and phone calls, mobile buzzing on the table, there is affection and admiration. Optimism, too. There’s a fondness for Phil Foden going back a decade – “differential”, Denia calls him – and a defence of the Football Association and this England generation. “You’re this close to winning a World Cup,” he says, signalling the tiniest of gaps between thumb and forefinger.

A European champion and Olympic gold medal-winning coach who helped restructure Spain’s academy system, Denia can see it coming. It was England his under-17s beat to win the European Championship on penalties in 2017, before England took revenge in that year’s World Cup final; and England who defeated Spain in the European under-21 final in 2023, Curtis Jones scoring the winner and James Trafford saving a penalty. It was also England against whom he coached his last Spain game in 2025 and it is, he says, fitting to encounter England, twice, in his first games with Czechia.

“When you work for Spain, it’s normal to cross paths with England,” he says. “There have been many finals, many moments. I see St George’s Park with Luis de la Fuente. I see England in Huelva. They came to see us work; we went to Bisham Abbey to see them. I arrived at the Spanish federation in 2010 and the English FA is one that has grown the most. You win an under-17 euros, an under-17 World Cup in India, an under-21 Euros because you have believed in investing in youth, supported their development. You provide them with opportunities and experiences that end up playing out at senior level. The FA saw that. You depend on clubs, the talent pool, but infrastructure and player development is the basis of everything.”

Among those Denia met often is Anthony Gordon. What does he make of Gordon’s comments suggesting that England should not try to replicate Spain? “Gordon? What a player!” Denia replies.“What a footballer, my God. He’s at the same level as … I don’t know, I was going to say Lamine. Young, daring, one-on-one, speed. And what great work English football has done bringing through players like him. Look, every country has its essence, you have to respect that, embrace it. You also can’t change overnight; success isn’t immediate, it’s a process. You will make mistakes but you have to be clear where you’re going. In 15 years with the inferiores, we developed, evolved, adapted. See what other federations do. That’s not copying, it’s learning.

View image in fullscreen Santi Denia admires English football and knows the ability his team will face. Photograph: Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty Images

“England are very, very good; they’re no distance from a World Cup final. None. I defend the English FA a lot. England are among the two or three best in the world, always there. The FA saw, invested, and I would encourage them to keep doing so: in young players, in St George’s Park, in forming coaches. That’s the key. In 2006, Spain had as many trophies as Czechia.”

And now they are double world champions. “There’s something beyond football,” Denia says. “A player said once: ‘You’re not a coach, you’re a teacher.’ Especially with the inferiories. You want to win, sure, but you have to teach. There’s a psychological, paternal element. Every kid, and they are kids, has an emotional development. You know their personal problems, help them mature. There have been times when Luis or I have left players out for the good of the group: ‘He’s some player but he’ll create problems.’ No player wins alone. One: Messi. No one else.

“When they win you feel so proud. I sat with David Gordo [Spain’s under-21 coach] at the World Cup final. We hugged each other, didn’t say anything, but shared a look that said: ‘We did our part.’ We’re not responsible but we contributed our little grain of sand. In 15 years, almost all of them have been through our hands.” Only David Raya, Víctor Muñoz and Aymeric Laporte had not been, and Denia competed against Laporte.

Now he competes against them. “And I want to beat them,” he laughs. “I’ll call Luis, say: ‘That’s enough now’. Luis has the best players but you have to manage them and he’s a maestro, the best in the world without doubt.”

It wasn’t enough; in Oviedo on Saturday Czechia became the latest victims as Spain won 3-1. The fondness though is not diminished, the pride in seeing his players lift the World Cup.

Seeing Ferran Torres score Spain’s World Cup final winner felt familiar to Denia. “When Ferran scores in the final you get a deja vu. He scored in the final of the under-19s Euros, won the under-17s Euros, and that’s taken to the seniors. You’ve got Lamine and [Pau] Cubarsí who came to an under-15s tournament in Sweden. I’ve worked with some players, eh: Isco was incredible. Thiago [Alcântara]. [Sergio] Canales. But that was the first time I saw spectators with their heads in their hands going: ‘Oh! What is this?!’ José Lana was coach. I asked him: ‘Where did you get these guys from?!’ I was the lucky one. I had the under-19s and took Lamine up. He was 14, a record. ‘That one’s for me!’”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Fortnightly Sign up to The Hotspot A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sure, but as under-19 or under-21 coach, the best get taken off you too. “Delighted!” Denia says. “When a player reaches the seniors it’s your proudest moment. I used to joke with Luis: ‘You haven’t got the guts to take my players.’ He would reply: ‘Don’t tempt me; I’ll take all of them.’ There’s no fear, none. Don’t look at the date of birth. If they’re ready, they’re ready. We know them but you need the clubs. You encourage them to put players in young, but who plays Cubarsí and Lamine at 16!”

The phone goes, Denia has a look – a Czech number – then returns to Spain and their captain. “I can’t be objective about Rodri,” he says. “I first saw him at Atlético with José María Amorrortu, the academy head. Watching an infantil [under-14] session from a balcony above the pitch, there’s this little lad who is amazing. Josema [Amorrortu] says: ‘That’s Rodri.’ I say: ‘He’s a second ahead of everyone but he’s tiny.’ He says: ‘Yeah, but look …’ Rodri’s parents are in the stands and they were so tall. ‘He’ll grow! I think we can wait for him!’ I remember his under-17 debut in Sweden. I said: ‘Don’t go to war: they’ll win. You’re the smart kid, you think faster: that’s how you win.’ His spurt came later, at Villarreal. Talk to him and you’re talking to a coach, a grandad. He’ll give you advice.”

View image in fullscreen Santi Denia on the touchline during the Nations League match between Czechia and Croatia. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

If Rodri raising the World Cup was the culmination of the work Denia and his federation colleagues had done, the end of one journey in the US, another began there too. The Czechia coach Miroslav Koubek had resigned and Denia was watching a game with Radek Bejbl, the former Czech Republic international with whom he played at Atlético. “Radek says: ‘I know Pavel Nedved [Czechia’s general manager]. Send me a résumé, what you did with Spain.’ The federation president, David Trunda, was in New York too. We met there and again in Prague, with Nedved. We talked about how we would build. And I’m delighted.” Bejbl is now on Denia’s staff.

Denia leans forward. “Czechia is incredible. Prague is … wow,” he says. All the way through the conversation, the occasional English word or concept has slipped in; now, that makes more sense. “We talk to them in English,” Denia says. “Pablo Amo, my assistant, speaks great English. Radek translates some things. The occasional Spanish swearword slips out. If you have three or four key words [in Czech] and speak some English, it’s OK: football is a universal language. Getting to the World Cup was an achievement; now we want to develop, grow, open a pathway. We know the football we want and the players have identified with the style.

“There’s a structure to build. Departments which all work together, clear roles. Medical, media, marketing, travel. If the federation wants us to, we can advise and work on the inferiores, maybe bring ideas from Spain. But we’ve just arrived and haven’t had time yet. The first thing, the thing you have to do best, is choose the right players. Scout, watch games, define the profile we want, select the players that fit. Then you have a few days to shape it. Time is always limited; with this format it’s even harder. We lost to Croatia but competed. England too. We and the federation have no doubts about the pathway. David and Pavel trust in us. We have to be faithful to the essence of Czechia and leave our mark too. The immediate objective set is qualification for the Euros.”

England again. “Sign me up!” Denia says, glancing at the phone buzzing, time to go. “A Euros in England. I know the stadiums and training grounds, remember visiting [Aitor] Karanka at Middlesbrough. The hard part was driving; the other part, the football, I love. I’d be delighted to play there again. And imagine another final with England! I’m dreaming here, aiming high, but why not?”

Sports.title: WSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal and Putellas and Diani shine
Sports.content:
1 Fans stay connected to Slegers

Travelling Arsenal fans showed no animosity towards the head coach, Renée Slegers, despite their side’s run of one win in six games in all competitions and slipping 10 points behind Manchester City. Slegers walked over to applaud the 2,000 away fans after the 4-2 defeat at Etihad Stadium, on Sunday and they applauded her back. Slegers said: “I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and appreciate them coming to Manchester. And also to show them that I feel – not sorry for them because I’m a big part of it and things are within my control – but they’re coming here and they’re not getting the rewards, just like the team. I wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding.” Tom Garry

View image in fullscreen Lauren Hemp celebrates scoring Manchester City’s third goal. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

2 Forward-thinking Walsh lifts Chelsea

Chelsea’s midfield came to the fore again in their 3-0 win over West Ham. Keira Walsh was the heartbeat of the team, collecting her third straight player of the match award with the 29-year-old enjoying a more attacking role this season. With the introduction of Lexi Potter at half-time, Walsh was able to push forward fruitfully again. She scored her second WSL goal of 2026-27 – the same as she managed last season – and took more shots (five) and completed more dribbles (three) than anyone else. “It helps us a lot in terms of creating opportunities,” said her coach, Sonia Bompastor. “We know how good she is at the edge of the box … It’s good to have a player who is confident and brings us the solution to scoring goals.” Sophie Downey

3 Lionesses flex their muscles

London City showed their Champions League qualification credentials with a 6-1 rout of Tottenham to move above them into third. They were at their fluid and clinical best against a team many believe will rival them as challengers to the traditional top three, with 47.6% of shots on target compared with Tottenham’s 11%. Superstar signings Alexia Putellas and Kadidiatou Diani both scored twice, but most impressive was the muscle the squad showed. They looked more robust and hungrier than Tottenham, their physical presence combined with an aggressive press making the home team look pedestrian and lightweight despite an unbeaten start to the season. With lots of summer changes it can take time for players to gel and that physical presence can make a difference when things aren’t clicking. When things are clicking, though, it appears anything is possible. Suzanne Wrack

4 Pointless Charlton neglect basics

The Charlton manager, Karen Hills, did not mince her words after her side conceded five despite taking the lead at Brighton. “It’s unacceptable if we can’t deal with one v ones,” she said. “The game is about one v one duels, about tackling, doing the basics and doing them really well. Unfortunately, we didn’t do that today. We found ourselves on the end of the scoreline which isn’t very flattering for us. We need to be more accountable for some individual stuff, but at the same time I take full responsibility because that’s my team out there.” The international break comes at a critical time for the team, who are yet to pick up a point. Even with some time to work on their unacceptable handling of the basics, it is hard to where Charlton’s first point is coming from. SW

5 Liverpool unsuccessfully copy United

Gareth Taylor admitted surprise at Manchester United’s directness after his Liverpool team succumbed to a 1-0 defeat at Leigh Sports Village. Possession was split almost evenly, with 51% for Liverpool, and the hosts created more goalmouth opportunities, but could not convert them. Taylor told the BBC: “We ended up becoming what they are, very direct. We have got to be braver – and do what we do.” TG

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Julia Zigiotti Olme of Manchester United (left) celebrates after her goal settled the match against Liverpool. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

6 Familiar problems for Sørensen at Villa

Brian Sørensen’s first WSL game as Aston Villa’s interim manager ended in a 1-1 draw with Crystal Palace. The Dane took over on Tuesday after Natalia Arroyo’s dismissal, with Villa having won two points from their opening four league matches. Villa took the lead through Noelle Maritz in the 55th minute, but Abbie Larkin’s equaliser 19 minutes later ensured Villa remain without a league win. Villa were fortunate not to concede again as Palace’s confidence grew and created several chances late on, and the draw leaves them 12th. Villa and Sørensen have work to do, whether his appointment remains temporary or becomes permanent. Réshma Rao

7 Mace ends Everton’s goal wait

It was quite a feat for Everton to be in the top five without registering anything other than an own goal and their luck continues. They finally scored goals of their own in a 2-1 victory against Birmingham. It was all thanks to Ruby Mace, who scored them both. Her most recent WSL goal came playing for the visitors in 2021. The first was a stunning left-foot strike into the far corner; the second a deflected shot from the edge of the area. “I’m really happy. I have [been working on my shooting], putting in the extra work, and luckily today I managed to score,” she said. Renuka Odedra

Sports.title: Celtic celebrate heated win over Rangers in final of revived Tennent’s Sixes
Sports.content:
The intensity of the football rivalry in Glasgow was evident on Sunday night as Celtic turned the tables on Rangers to win the Tennent’s Sixes. Celtic beat their rivals 5-4 in the final at Braehead Arena after being on the end of a 7-1 defeat by Rangers in the group stage on Saturday.

The tournament was for retired players from all 12 Premiership teams as the SPFL revived a tournament that took place between first teams from 1984 to 1993. But the reactions were similar to any major trophy final.

Celtic’s Charlie Mulgrew admitted he got carried away in his celebrations after he ignored handshake attempts from the Rangers captain, Andy Halliday, in order to salute the crowd, and exchanged words with the Rangers manager, Barry Ferguson.

There was a heated post-match analysis in the Rangers dressing room. In a video leaked on social media, Kirk Broadfoot appears to be heavily criticising the goalkeeper Lee Robinson.

Mulgrew had calmed only slightly when he spoke to Premier Sports. “A lot of adrenaline was flowing, a few nasty tackles,” the 40-year-old said. “I mean, I know it was the Tennent’s Sixes, but you get caught up in the moment.

“You don’t like to get beat from Rangers, our closest rivals, 7-1, so that hurt. We had a few beers, a wee chat, a wee night out, so we managed to turn it around. We got a few things ironed out, although I was a wee bit rough in the morning.

“It feels like I’ve won an actual, real cup. It’s mental. I got a bit carried away at the end there but it builds up. There was a lot of emotion in that. Sometimes that’s what happens, it spills over.

“Football’s like that. I got nutmegged a couple of times by [Martyn] Waghorn, and exchanged words with him, then that was me, I was just fired up and fired into a few tackles. In the end, because we had that spirit, we won.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Celtic’s manager, Tom Boyd, said he was “pretty angry” with his players on Saturday night and that it “feels like winning the league”.

His assistant, Simon Donnelly, admitted they were all “embarrassed” by Saturday’s heavy defeat and told Celtic Player after the final: “It’s against Rangers, so it’s as if it’s a Scottish Cup final there. That’s the feeling. You could play Rangers at tiddlywinks and you’d still want to win.”

Sports.title: Hallgrímsson calls on Uefa to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after bad-tempered draw
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he said “has been tough on us all”. Ireland were pegged back to a draw in another tetchy encounter on Sunday, played without fans at TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia.

Hallgrímsson did not want to comment on a half-time confrontation, after which a member of his backroom staff alleged he was spat at by an Israeli player. The Icelandic manager said that was better left to a disciplinary committee.

“We need now some time to reflect and go forward,” he said. “It’s also the best time to find your enemies when you’re lying on the ground and people are kicking you. It’s easy to see who was trying to kick you.”

Asked on RTÉ whether the two sides should be playing in the future, he said: “No, they shouldn’t. That’s not ours to decide, that’s Uefa. I wouldn’t want or wish any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks. Uefa needs to step in and do something.”

On Monday, a spokesperson for the Israel FA denied anyone had spat “towards the coach”, understood to be the fitness coach Damian Doyle. They added that “our dream is still to play against [Ireland] in Dublin at Euro 2028”.

Troy Parrott’s first-half ­penalty was cancelled out after the break in the Group B3 game. Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his past seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two ­minutes after the restart.

Ireland players again wore black armbands and bowed their heads ­during the Israel national anthem. The Israel players wore black armbands in memory of the people killed in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.

The Ireland goalkeeper, Caoimhín Kelleher, stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea – who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child – and he pointedly avoided shaking hands with Peretz, the Israel captain, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants.

That was a repeat of O’Shea’s actions before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary last week, when he declined to shake Manor Solomon’s hand. Ireland went on to win that game 3-0 through three first-half goals.

Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday’s match. The Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for being sent off after his goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria last month.

Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Ireland substitutes after starting against Austria on Thursday.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen The Ireland goalkeeper, Caoimhín Kelleher, avoids shaking hands with the Israel captain, Dor Peretz, before the game. Photograph: Andrej Čukić/EPA

Ireland had started to find some fluidity when Dunne won a penalty. The Israel goalkeeper, Assaf Tzur, scrambled to smother the ball and Jimmy Dunne was brought down under the challenge, with the spot-kick confirmed after a lengthy video assistant referee check.

Peretz levelled the scoring two minutes after the restart. An Oscar Gloukh effort took a favourable deflection off Liam Scales and into the path of the acting captain, who gave ­Kelleher no chance with a low finish.

The game was supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland moved the game to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June after widespread calls for a boycott in protest against Israel’s actions in Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present. It followed the FAI’s own motion in November calling on Uefa to ban Israel from club and international competitions.

The difficult atmosphere between the sides spilled over as the sides entered the tunnel at half-time. Officials broke up a second altercation in added time and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

Sports.title: Let’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the target | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Move fast and fix things. It has been a fine week so far for Thomas Tuchel as he attempts the cyclical task of soldering together not just an England team, but a way of looking like one, all the while being battered by the to-and-fro conflicting winds of England managerdom.

There is nothing new here. This is a job that involves not just picking the right players and making high-stakes calculations over your second-half substitutions, but carrying out these basic duties while wrestling with aggrieved members of the Thuggee cult on a collapsing rope bridge outside the Temple of Doom, and simultaneously having your heart ripped out.

No other nation makes quite the same twin-track demands. Manage the games. Yeah, do that obviously. But also tell us who we are and how we should play. This is why the job will always take its pound of mince meat, why these people end up drained and hollowed out, an empty tracksuit resigning in the Wembley toilets, Roy Hodgson in Nice looking like a desiccated vampire, saying “I don’t know why I’m here”.

It is also why it was heartening in Rijeka to see Tuchel gripped with the familiar energies, still whirling about on the touchline in penitent black shoes and black trousers, looking as ever like a famine-ridden earl out taking the hounds for a walk, while simultaneously cracking the Enigma code in his hunting shed.

It feels absurd to say that Tuchel is now safe in the job, if only because the idea he wouldn’t be is so hysterical. Tuchel was never realistically in any trouble. But such is the nature of a role where you’re only ever a few rapid-fire defeats away from the incredible twin feat of a greatest-ever overseas World Cup and a near-instant heaving from the job.

We should of course keep a sense of scale over a couple of Nations League wins against underpowered opponents. The 7-0 steamrollering of Croatia was always a strange affair. From the moment the doors opened the whole occasion felt like a youth club association sports day, where everyone gets a medal at the end and the teachers do a disco dance routine.

It was an atmosphere that seemed to communicate itself to the Croatia players even as they were warming up in a notably fun and jokey way, cheered by shrill groups of junior ultras, and blasted by the Croatian version of We Didn’t Start the Fire through the ear-shredding speaker system.

Croatia played from the first minute like a team recovering from a dose of herbal sleeping tablets. Luka Modric’s every touch was met with the kind of noise more usually associated with an appearance by a Korean boyband at an Apple Store launch event, but one of the great players of the age was simply run over by England’s youthful and hungry midfield.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham was superb in the win over Croatia, as he was during the World Cup. Photograph: Igor Soban/Pixsell/MB Media/Getty Images

These are also the teams you play, however. Croatia were decent enough at the World Cup. Mainly, though this came at an absolutely vital moment in the age of Tuchelism. The next 20 months are basically it, the engine room, the space where Tuchel gets to decide how good his team can be, leading in to a tournament England will never have a better chance of winning.

The only questions that really matter right now are: is there vision of a team and a way to play? And do we have forward progress? The answers to both of which are yes.

England were good in an interesting way in Croatia. We’re used to England teams that seem powerful but also flawed. In Rijeka they looked like a World Cup semi-finalist that has used that experience to improve, strong in every area, physically, technically and in its basic balance.

At times in the current era England have brought to mind the Gareth Southgate team of 2019 into 2020, when some key new players entered a blooming environment, and suddenly they were blowing away mid-range opponents. The Covid break would complicate that arc. An unprovable counter-factual: nudge those first Southgate Euros forward a year and England might have had the momentum to overpower Italy in the final.

There are two aspects to Tuchel’s England this time around. First, the reckoning up with the mistakes of the recent past. Why, oh why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, maybe for the same reason Palmer’s not here now. Well, why of why, then, didn’t he take Phil Foden? This has also answered itself. The same goes for not selecting the back-up striker who is now, it turns out, playing in Saudi Arabia. It is entirely legitimate to still disagree with all these things. But it feels clearer that there was logic and reasoning here.

The past can re-litigate itself. The second key element is the sense of progress. This was always likely to be the case. It takes time to get to know your players. Tuchel had never been to an international tournament before. He was never the knockout specialist some seemed to assume. Just take a look at his record. He’s a process guy. And we are now right in the middle of that process.

View image in fullscreen Lewis Hall has enjoyed a fine international break and looks to be first choice for England at left-back. Photograph: Darko Bandić/AP

So what has changed? Most obviously making Jude Bellingham the hub of this team is an excellent idea, and not just because of his astonishing talent. Rallying around Bellingham is Tuchel’s version of Southgate’s inflatable unicorns, the talk about Spitfires, the away-days with the SAS crawling through an assault course made entirely from Cheddar cheese and Eccles cakes.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How do you make players want to play for England? Here’s a short cut. Give them aura, brand power, magnetism. Put the big guy right at the centre. Everyone’s turning up if Jude is loving it, and you have a chance for two weeks to exist in his forcefield.

Then there’s the way England have played. There is always talk about “a Premier League style”, which has never been a single thing. But these players are definitely best suited to high-intensity, hard-running, duel-winning football. This wasn’t only there in successfully outmuscling an ageing Mateo Kovacic, who even in his pomp had the air of a frail Victorian child masquerading as an elite modern midfielder, shorts hiked up, skinny legs gamely covering the turf.

England also played like this for half an hour against the world champions, and narrowly lost a game where they went 1-0 down after a minute and missed a late penalty. This felt like an evolved version of the “packet-ball” intensity that blew Croatia away at the World Cup for 20 minutes then could never quite click into gear again. The next Euros are in England. Cancel the heatwave, and they can play like this for longer.

Then there is the issue of balance. Lewis Hall: yes, a proper left-back with a left foot. Jarell Quansah makes lots of sense now, offering something of the Kyle Walker-style recovery athleticism. Alex Scott looked really good in Rijeka, a genuinely smart, head-up, surging midfield presence.

Tuchel is right. He can’t roll into a tournament with two first-choice midfielders. Scott offered something different in the exact area England lose these high-stakes, high-intensity games. He even knows who his back-up centre-forward is now, and it is of course Jude. Ask any question right now. The answer is likely to be the same.

Here is another unprovable counter-factual. England would have beaten that Argentina team in Atlanta with this team in Rijeka. This should not be a source of why-oh-why frustration. It’s forward momentum, learning new patterns, adding new tricks. Stick Bellingham up front in the second half, pack Scott into a three-man midfield, and they’ve got a far better chance of seeing that game out.

The process is also far from done. England need competition on the right wing. Bukayo Saka is an excellent footballer. But he’s not a weapon other teams will fear. Add an England-issue Michael Olise, for example, and this team looks entirely different in its threat levels. Max Dowman is still just a very nice idea at this point. But there’s time. And he doesn’t need to be perfect.

Finally, and back to the key figure in this cycle, there is the total weaponising of Bellingham, whose role in the team is now beautifully clarified. Station him in forward areas and he will still press and harry and add a defensive function. But turning, running, breaking in transitions, making risky creative passes, he is just a supreme footballer. Not to mention a one-man mission statement of the way this team wants to play.

Tournaments aren’t won with a 7-0 win on the Adriatic coast in front of 6,000 over-caffeinated schoolchildren. But there is progress here. And that time will pass in a wink.

Sports.title: How former Premier League goalkeeper David Stockdale rescued and revamped FC Farsley
Sports.content:
They held a sweepstake in the FC Farsley office. How many fans would come for the first men’s game at their Throstle Nest ground in more than two years? David Stockdale, the owner and first-team manager, was cautious, predicting 140. After all, the old club, Farsley Celtic, played in Buxton for much of the 2024-25 season and missed the 2025-26 campaign after going into liquidation.

When 480 came through the gates to watch the all-new FC Farsley play Collegians FC in a Yorkshire Amateur League contest, Stockdale realised the scale of his achievement in getting the club back on their feet. There remains an enormous amount of work still to do – and Stockdale was operating a digger before this interview – but it was the first step of a fresh journey for the Leeds-based club.

The former Premier League goalkeeper, once of Birmingham, Brighton and Fulham among a host of other clubs, is aware his situation is abnormal. He never expected to be running a club when he took on the job of Farsley Celtic manager 19 months ago. By that stage, the club, playing in the National League North, owed about £750,000 in debts and was on the verge of being wound up.

“When I came in to help, I had no idea what had gone on,” Stockdale says. “I told them: ‘You’d better start telling me everything.’ They owed a lot of people money. This place was derelict.

“I don’t know how the club finished that [2024-25] season. Players were not getting paid. I helped out as manager because I live in the area. But it was in a sad, sorry state. It was about managing people and getting through the season. You might get £5,000 per game, but we were playing in Buxton – that was a deal made by the last owner. A lot of money was going out.”

By the summer of 2025, Stockdale was putting in his own money in an effort to save the club. Farsley Celtic were relegated from the sixth tier initially to the ninth tier, then the 11th, before withdrawing from competition in June. Six months later Stockdale was forced into liquidating the club and established FC Farsley.

View image in fullscreen A view of one of the Farsley ticket gates before the club’s renovation. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

Stockdale says: “The bank was going to repossess it, so I had a chat with the bank, stakeholders and my financial guy to see if it was possible … and my wife was last on that list! It was a very worrying time for those three or four months, and it was ironic that we bought it on Mad Friday [the last before Christmas Eve], which I think sums it up. We’ve gone from really bad, to bad stress, to stress, to now having good stress where things are turning.”

The manager and his family have become fully immersed in the club, not just on the football side but in helping a local sports facility rediscover a place at the heart of its community. The club has a sports hall – which previously could not run because electricity bills went unpaid for months – and clubs have returned to play badminton, netball and five-a-side football. There is a cafe – from Ikea – and soft play, bought and fitted by Stockdale. His wife, Katie, is running the cafe, his daughters Molly and Daisy help out with activities for children and his son Billy is the kit man. Stockdale’s father, also David, a painter and decorator, has been involved in the refit.

“It’s been absolutely relentless,” says the club’s manager, who is also a qualified electrician. “People laugh, but I’ve always grown up being shown how to do things, DIY, helping yourself before people help you. If people see you do the work they’re more willing to help you. But secretly I love it. I’ve been on a digger, on a dumper. We’ve got to keep going.”

The next goal is the biggest: spending £1.5m on a state-of-the-art artificial pitch. It is hard to envisage looking at the main pitch, overgrown and in disrepair, having been neglected since April 2024 – the new team play on an adjacent grass pitch – but Stockdale knows it would be transformative.

“I want this to be a premium sports facility,” he says. “We’ve put in cricket nets in the sports hall, we want a new floor, we want to host netball and badminton finals. If we’ve got a 3G pitch on the main pitch and a good grass pitch, plus junior pitches, a kitchen, a beer garden – it’s hopefully everything you would want.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I’m not stupid, I know what football costs. That’s why it’s two different entities here, the sports facility and the football side of things. I want to be the place where clubs who are playing Leeds United can come and practise – somewhere people can come to, somewhere people can be proud of. Historically, it’s never had the best facilities and it is run down; not much money has been spent on the place in the last seven years.”

View image in fullscreen The club was liquidated under David Stockdale, who then set about rebuilding it. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

The Stockdale family have the backing of their close friend Adebayo Akinfenwa, who played with Stockdale at Wycombe and has joined as a shareholder. Stockdale jokes that Akinfenwa is their “hype man” and says: “It’s not like he’s thought: ‘This is a great investment or a business move.’ It’s more a friendship thing. It was years in the making and it’s very organic.”

Stockdale hopes to engage more local fans and sponsors and cannot rest on his laurels, even after a successful relaunch. One look around the place tells him that. So it’s back on the digger when this interview concludes.

“It’s great when you sit back and have a pint of Guinness at the end of a game now and be like: ‘Yeah this is great, it’s going forward,’” he says. “But I’ve got this five- and 10-year vision in my head, and I’m only 10 months in. It might not get fulfilled, but this is my area, west Leeds – I grew up down the road. I won’t let this go.”

Sports.title: England star Jordan Pickford set to face court following 50mph Lamborghini chase after 'almost causing car pile-up'
Sports.content:
England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford faces a court appearance after being chased by police for exceeding the speed limit by 20mph earlier this year.

Pickford, 32, is believed to have hit the 50mph mark in a 30mph zone in his £165,000 Lamborghini Urus when driving in in Knutsford, Cheshire.

The incident took place five days before April's Merseyside derby, in which Pickford's Everton lost 2-1 to bitter rivals Liverpool.

On April 14, PC Cecil Ricardo was leaving Knutsford station when he noticed Pickford's car exceeding the speed limit, forcing two fellow road users to slam on their brakes, and then speeding away.

The officer then flicked on his blue lights and pursued Pickford, before eventually managing to pull over the footballer and his blue Lamborghini, which can hit 62mph in just 3.5seconds.

Under the Single Justice Procedure, Cheshire Police charged Pickford on September 23 and the Everton and Three Lions shot-stopper has since entered a guilty plea, and requested to attend court in an effort to avoid a ban.

Jordan Pickford has entered a guilty plea for exceeding the speed limit by roughly 20mph back in April

Pickford is believed to have hit the 50mph mark in a 30mph zone in his £165,000 Lamborghini Urus

In a witness statement provided by PC Ricardo, he said: 'I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street. It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision.

'The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford. I activated my emergency equipment, lights and sirens and attempted to catch up with the vehicle.

'At one point on Toft Road my vehicle’s speedometer indicated I was travelling at 50mph and the Lamborghini was still pulling away. The speed limit on that stretch of Toft Road is 30mph.'

Pickford is said to have not initially responded to the blue lights, but after a brief pursuit did pull over.

'I approached the driver’s side and the driver identified himself as Jordan Pickford,' PC Ricardo added. 'I cautioned Pickford, pointed out the offence of driving without due care and attention and issued a traffic offence report. He made no reply.'

Pickford requested a court hearing and in a brief submission wrote that he would like 'to put forward my mitigation'.

The incident occured five days before Everton's 2-1 derby defeat to Liverpool back in April

Careless driving could lead to a potential ban but if the offence does not meet that threshold then Pickford could possibly receive three to nine penalty points. A court date at Warrington magistrates’ is yet to be confirmed.

Pickford is currently on international duty with England, with the Three Lions facing the Czech Republic in their final Nations League fixture of the current break on Tuesday evening.

The Everton keeper, who lives near Knutsford with his wife Megan and their three young children, started in goal in the Three Lions' 7-0 win over Croatia on Saturday and has earned 91 caps for his country.

Sports.title: Tennis bad boy Daniil Medvedev is THROWN OUT of the China Open after hitting a fan in the face with a rogue shot - putting Novak Djokovic into the final
Sports.content:
Daniil Medvedev was dramatically disqualified from the China Open after hitting a fan with a rogue shot.

Medvedev, who has a reputation as a combustible character, inexplicably hammered a ball into the stands in frustration after losing a point against Novak Djokovic.

The ball hit a spectator in Beijing, with the affected fan seen holding their left eye before they were escorted away for medical treatment.

One of the fan's counterparts appeared to remonstrate with Medvedev, who was spoken to by both the umpire, Mohamed Lahyani and an ATP official.

As a result of his misdemeanour, Medvedev was defaulted - the tennis term for an immediate disqualification of a player from a match or tournament due to a serious rule violation or misconduct - with Djokovic progressing from the semi-final clash.

Medvedev didn't contest the decision and walked sheepishly off court after shaking hands with his opponent.

Not the ending we expected 😮 @DjokerNole advances to the Beijing final after Medvedev is defaulted whilst down 5-7 3-5#ChinaOpen pic.twitter.com/Pae5eNrJ6W — Tennis TV (@TennisTV) October 5, 2026

Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from the China Open after hitting a fan with a rogue shot

The Russian had been been up against it given he was down 5-7, 3-5 in the match at the time - with the score in the decisive game 15-15 - yet it still proved to be a remarkable ending to the encounter.

And, speaking after the match, the Serbian expressed his surprise at what had gone on and offered his support to Medvedev.

'Well, at this moment, I am a little bit shocked to be honest with the turn of events,' he said. 'I feel sorry for Daniil. Also for the person, who I hope is not injured.

'I didn’t see what happened to be honest. I turned around. Look, I was disqualified from the US Open for something similar six years ago. So I know the feeling. It’s horrible.

'I am sure that Daniil (didn’t mean it). It happened by accident. Sorry for the crowd. For the match to end like this, I was only three points from winning.

'It was an incredible level, probably the most physical level I have experienced at this tournament.

'You know, you had to work for your points. I gave it my all. I knew it would be a big challenge.'

Medvedev has a reputation of causing chaos on court, with the Russian famously having a meltdown at the US Open in 2025 when a photographer walked on court.

That is one of several memorable tantrums, while he has been known to frequently argue with umpires, crowds and smash racquets during matches.

Following his antics in Beijing, Medvedev will lose the points and prize money he had earned during his run to the semi-finals, with Djokovic set to take on Alex de Minaur in Tuesday's final.

MORE TO FOLLOW

Sports.title: Former Miss Germany, 33, set to move into professional boxing... four years after being crowned the nation's most beautiful woman
Sports.content:
Former Miss Germany, 33, set to move into professional boxing... four years after being crowned the nation's most beautiful woman

A former winner of Miss Germany has announced a surprise career switch - and will swap the catwalk for the boxing ring at the age of 33.

Tatjana Genrich was voted Germany's most beautiful woman in 2022 and has now announced she will make her professional boxing debut next month in Magdeburg, rekindling her childhood love of the sport.

Genrich was the Saxony-Anhalt state champion in the flyweight division for amateur boxers between 2007 and 2009. And she recently opened up on why she originally went into the sport, saying: 'At school I was often bullied and I wanted to find a way to defend myself. That's how it all started.'

This then led to her attending a sports school in Halle, Germany where she was picked up by boxing promoter Ulf Steinforth. Years later he reconnected with the model after her fame and stature had grown and suggested the former amateur champion try her hand in the professional ranks.

When asked about their talks, Genrich said: 'Since I sponsor the ring girls at his boxing events, he approached me one day and asked if I wouldn't like to get back in the ring. I finally agreed and am now about to make my professional debut.'

Only four years ago she was Miss Germany... now Tatjana Genrich has her sights set on a career in boxing

The supermodel turned boxer still posts regularly to her 44,500 Instagram followers and owns her own modelling agency

Genrich will be hoping to her journey will inspire a new generation of young women into different sports

View this post on Instagram

Promoter SES Boxing are backing Genrich to become the country's next big superstar, saying: 'Tatjana can follow in Regina Halmich's footsteps. She has all the necessary qualities, an incredible presence, and is extremely ambitious.'

Halmich won 54 of her 56 fights during a storied career between 1994 and 2017 which saw her become one of the most successful female boxers of all time, and also modelled for German magazines.

To prepare for her first fight fight on November 14, Genrich - who also runs her own modelling agency with 80 models under contract - has begun a rigorous training routine that sees her spending five full days a week in the gym.

In her corner she will have coach Dirk Dzemski, who guided Robert Stieglitz to world champion status in the 2010s.

Genrich also detailed another motivation to succeed in her new career, saying:' I want to be a role model for young women and show them that you can be successful in both your career and sports.

'I train in areas like posture, running and choreography. This prepares me for competitions as well as events like fashion shows.'

Sports.title: Match of the Day! Hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates 'are dating' after his ex confronted him over suspicions
Sports.content:
Match of the Day! Hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates 'are dating' after his ex confronted him over suspicions

Match Of The Day presenters Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates are said to be dating - amid accusations from his ex that he started the new relationship while they were still together.

Chapman, 52, reportedly split suddenly from Clere Collier, a mother-of-two and estate agent who lives in Dubai, in April after three years together. He insists there was no overlap between the relationships and that he had remained faithful.

A source said: 'Mark split with Clere out of the blue, without much explanation.

'They had been making plans for the future and their relationship had been going strong.

'They stayed in touch after the split, but Clere soon realised that Mark and Kelly were close and she accused Mark of dating Kelly.

Match Of The Day presenters Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates on Celebrity Gogglebox

The duo became the main presenters of Match Of The Day last season alongside Gabby Logan

'Mark admitted the relationship, but insisted there was no overlap between the two women and that he hadn’t cheated on her.'

The source told The Sun: 'He told her that he had been a single man when he started spending time with Kelly. Of course, it left a bad taste in Clere’s mouth and she didn’t believe him.'

Chapman and Cates, 51, became the main co-presenters for Match Of The Day alongside Gabby Logan last season after Gary Lineker left.

While their shifts presenting the show do not overlap, Chapman and Cates did appear on Celebrity Gogglebox on the same sofa together in July.

Chapman, a highly respected broadcaster paid between £335,000 and £340,000 a year by the BBC, was already heavily involved with the show as Match Of The Day 2 presenter before his promotion.

He was married to his wife Sara for 19 years until she died aged 44 in 2020 after a battle with cancer. They had three children.

Chapman was accused by ex-girlfriend Clere Collier of dating Cates while they were together

The Greater Manchester-born TV star is believed to have started dating Collier in 2023, with her making regular trips to the United Kingdom from the United Arab Emirates.

Meanwhile, Cates is the daughter of Scotland and Liverpool legend Kenny Dalglish.

She was previously married to TV producer husband Tom Cates, with whom she has two children, but they split in 2021.

Sports.title: Antonio Conte reveals desire for next job to be with a fallen giant that has 'lost sight of its history... and make it shine again' - having previously been linked with Man United job
Sports.content:
Antonio Conte has revealed his desire to resurrect a falling giant in his next managerial role. Legendary Italian coach Conte, 57, is out of work after leaving Napoli at the end of last season following a two-year stint where he won Serie A and the Italian Super Cup. And Conte, who previously coached Chelsea and Tottenham in the Premier League, discussed his potential next move in an interview with The Athletic. The 57-year-old has been linked with the managerial role at Manchester United in the past. Conte said: 'If you go to a club where the history speaks for itself - a history made up of trophies, league titles and victories - you can only honour that history in one way: by having the ambition to bring that club back, if it isn't there today, to fight for those goals. 'I know full well that only one team can win every year, but I must carry in my heart, and instil in the hearts of the fans, my players and my directors, that spark, that hope that makes you say, "f***, we can win". You only make history by winning. Antonio Conte has dropped a hint that he would like to manage Manchester United in the future 'There are many clubs that have somewhat lost sight of their history. I'd like to go to one of these clubs to dust off that history and make it shine once more. 'Clubs where there's pressure, where, ultimately, you know full well that you're not going there just to take part, but to compete.' United continue to endure a tough period, with the club having not won the Premier League title since Sir Alex Ferguson's last season in 2012-13. In the subsequent 13 years, United's only trophies have been the FA Cup twice (in 2016 and 2024), the EFL Cup (in 2017 and 2023) and the Europa League (in 2017), and they have rarely threatened to challenge for the biggest titles. Although Conte didn't specifically mention United, his criteria of a supposed fallen giant was interpreted as referencing a select group of clubs across Europe, including the Red Devils. Another may be Juventus, who Conte previously managed from 2011 to 2014, along with AC Milan. During the interview, Conte also suggested he would be open to another experience in England despite his Tottenham tenure ending in chaotic fashion in March 2023. Speaking more widely about English football he added: 'In England today they’re using bazookas, while everywhere else they’re still using a pistol. 'But we also need to be careful about how the money is spent. That’s why we were talking earlier about making the right assessments, about having a vision, because you may well have the money, but you have to spend it wisely.' Michael Carrick is United's current manager, but they have endured a tough start to the season Conte's comments come with Michael Carrick facing scrutiny after United's poor start to the season. The Red Devils have just five points from their first five matches and have failed to build on the momentum generated during the second half of last season when Carrick led them to third place. Adding to that scrutiny, Conte – who has tended to join clubs in the summer throughout his career – suggested he would consider taking a job in the middle of the season 'if it's worth it'.

Sports.title: The tell-tale signs Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates were growing closer as more than Match of the Day co-hosts, leaving his ex furious at suspicions of an 'overlap'
Sports.content:
The tell-tale signs Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates were growing closer as more than Match of the Day co-hosts, leaving his ex furious at suspicions of an 'overlap'

Perhaps it should have come as little surprise that Match of the Day hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates are now an item.

Eagle-eyed viewers will have seen them featuring in episodes of Channel 4 show Celebrity Gogglebox recently and the pair appear to have got closer between the broadcasts – literally.

In the first, aired in June 2025, the pair were sat apart on the sofa with Chapman having his arms folded and Cates had her hands tightly clasped.

A year later, from episodes in June and July 2026, footage shows them sat closer together and appearing much more relaxed.

And on a clip previewing one episode in June, posted on Gogglebox's Instagram account, Cates brushes crumbs off Chapman's shirt, and he flirtily replies: 'It's because some of the television's been so funny you've spat the crisps all over me!'

Chapman's ex-girlfriend Clere Collier has accused him of starting the relationship with Cates while they were still together - which he denies. They are said to have split in April, before the 2026 round of Gogglebox filming.

Chapman and Cates appeared on Celebrity Gogglebox back in June 2025

... and the chemistry is clear in an episode from July 2026 a year on

View this post on Instagram

News of the relationship between 52-year-old Chapman and Cates, 51, emerged at the weekend, just over a year after they began their roles as co-hosts of Match of the Day alongside Gabby Logan.

And the development appears to have been well-received among many football fans, with X user Joni Cluer posting: 'I hope this is true, always thought there was a connection between them.'

Fellow X user Peter Crowther said: 'I predicted that after seeing them on Gogglebox! The chemistry was there. Good luck to them.'

The pair also enjoyed a day out at an event at which they met the cast of The Traitors, with The Sports Agents, the twice-weekly podcast hosted by Chapman and Logan, posting a picture of the pair with series 4 winner Stephen Libby.

Chapman told Logan on the podcast: 'I do think that, in the cold light of day the following morning, I may have had too much to drink.

'There was a long conversation with Stephen, Kelly and myself about whether one of his jumpsuits would work for me to do the FA Cup final!'

Chapman added that he had effectively acted as Cates' personal assistant for the day as he asked various cast members for photos with her, adding: 'We had such a fun time.'

Chapman recently split with estate agent Clere, who accused him of an overlap in the relationship with Cates while they were together, an allegation he denies.

On salaries of £335,000-£340,000 and £215,000-£220,000 per year respectively, Chapman and Cates are two of the BBC's highest-paid employees.

Chapman was previously married to wife Sara for 19 years until she died in 2020 after a battle with cancer. They had three kids together and lived in Hale in Greater Manchester.

Reacting to the news Chapman and Cates had been dating, talkSPORT Breakfast co-host Gabby Agbonlahor said: 'How fantastic. Great news for a Monday morning. It's set everyone listening off to a great week.'

His co-host Ally McCoist added: 'We're all delighted and we're all thrilled. We wish them all the best. Two great people.'

News of Cates' relationship with Chapman is in stark contrast to her comments on Gabby Logan's The Mid Point podcast in March 2021 when she spoke about the struggles of dating and her own insecurities.

'I don't have a picture in my head of why a middle-aged, slightly overweight mother of two could possibly be attractive,' she said.

'I can't get my head round that. It's not that I'm putting myself down and it's not a lack of confidence or a low self-esteem. It's just I don't know what that would look like.

'The thought of going on a date, spending an evening with someone and at the end of it thinking, "Well, I don't really like you", I would be so resentful of them taking up my time.

'Obviously it's vice versa, too, but I'm not really bothered about it from their perspective.'

High-flying Clere Collier accused Chapman of an overlap in the two relationships

Cates spoke about the struggles of dating and her own insecurities on a podcast

Cates candidly added: 'Bearing in mind I don’t get to see the people I do like quite often, but I do know unless I want to spend the rest of my life alone… and I’ve got no real thoughts about long term relationships or anything like that.

'Imagine sitting there and halfway through you think, "God this guy’s an idiot." You’ve just wasted a babysitter.'

The news comes as BBC Sport faces mutiny over their latest restructuring.

Strike action is now said to be 'inevitable' amid the latest redundancy plans, with staff left furious at a view that while dozens of rank and file jobs will go, well-remunerated senior leadership appears to be 'untouched'.

Daily Mail Sport revealed that a series of job cuts were to be announced ahead of a 'savings' call with all staff.

On the summit, workers were told that 41 roles would be culled, with five new posts created as director of sport Alex Kay-Jelski continues to ring the changes with a series of controversial moves some believe are aimed at chasing clicks, rather than serving all of the licence-paying audience.

'Everyone is furious,' explained one insider. 'The TV sports news department in particular will be decimated. And yet those at the top, unsurprisingly, are untouched. The feeling is that strike action is inevitable.'

Daily Mail Sport understands that while nobody in a senior leadership role is at risk, it would be wrong to suggest that management itself is not impacted and that the highest percentage of the 41 job losses comes from management level.

Sports.title: Bournemouth frustrated as Alex Scott withdraws from England squad with injury after playing through pain against Croatia - as it's revealed star's grandfather died while he was in camp
Sports.content:
Bournemouth frustrated as Alex Scott withdraws from England squad with injury after playing through pain against Croatia - as it's revealed star's grandfather died while he was in camp

Alex Scott is withdrawing from the England squad due to an quad injury aggravated against Croatia - leaving Bournemouth frustrated they could now lose a star player for up to two months.

The 23-year-old Bournemouth midfielder made his first start for the Three Lions on Saturday night, having made his debut off the bench against Czechia days before.

There are now fears that the Guernsey-born star could be sidelined for a couple of months, a blow for the Cherries who remain winless and 17th in the Premier League. Daily Mail Sport understands the club are frustrated at the development.

Scott played on during the international break in honour of his grandfather, who died days before his debut.

He impressed for England, playing 70 minutes against Croatia, and Thomas Tuchel described him as playing at the 'highest level' - but he was said to be playing through pain from a pre-existing issue in order to represent his country.

And on Monday, ahead of the Wembley clash with Czech Republic, Tuchelsuggested that England did not take a risk playing him. ‘With Alex, it’s a strange one,' Tuchel said. ‘I’m very sad about it. Alex trained, both training sessions before the match full against Croatia. He did extra work after the training sessions.

'We knew he was in treatment but there were only green lights from himself, from the medics. When we were aware that there was a slight discomfort through the match, we asked him if he wants to come off. He said, “No”.

'After the match, he said, “Yeah, OK, it was the right thing to do, but I could have played 90 minutes, I don’t feel an injury”. Even the day after, here before we did the scan, he felt he was not injured.

'It’s a strange one because it does not match the objectivity of the scan and the prediction of the time that he is obviously going to miss. It doesn’t match his feelings, and doesn’t match at all the process into the match and during the match.’

Alex Scott is withdrawing from the England international squad due to a quad injury

Thomas Tuchel described Scott as 'the complete package' and at the 'highest level'

It was a surprise when Scott received his first call-up last November - he didn't play in that stint - but there is a growing view that he can have a big future with England.

He soldiered through this international break to honour his grandfather, who he described as one of his 'biggest fans'.

'I will always remember this place now. England debut - it's what dreams are made of,' Scott told BBC Radio 5 Live.

'Something that when I was younger, even 15 or 16, wasn't a reality at all so I've worked really hard and it's a proud moment for me and my family as well.

'My partner, she's been there with me for a good six years so she's seen everything, my parents are massive for me, my brother growing up [we were] playing football non stop, and my grandad passed away last week.

'For him, obviously it was a special thing and it's a shame that he didn't see it but he would have been looking down and proud of it. It was tough last week, I found out on camp just before the Spain game, he was the proudest man, he came to all my matches whenever he could and he was my biggest fan.'

His withdrawal follows that of Nico O'Reilly, with the full-back returning to Manchester City after picking up a knock.

Scott will return to Bournemouth for medical tests instead of potentially playing the Czechs again at Wembley on Tuesday.

Scott is a key player for Bournemouth, who only sit 17th in the Premier League

It robs him of his latest audition against Chelsea, where Bournemouth travel on Saturday.

Xabi Alonso's club are interested in Scott. Chelsea bid for him at least once in the summer, though sources have claimed the Blues submitted three offers, up to £68million.

Scott’s current contract with Bournemouth runs until 2028 and he has so far resisted signing a new deal despite the efforts of those inside the Vitality Stadium.

Daily Mail Sport reported last week how Bournemouth sources have told those interested that they will only entertain negotiations for England’s newest international after they have established themselves in the Premier League once again this season.

They are also not interested in selling this January.

Bournemouth are currently 17th after five games, working under a new head coach in Marco Rose, and juggling Europe for the first time. While winless in the Premier League this term, they won 2-1 away at Real Sociedad in the Europa League, and beat Championship side Lincoln 4-0 in the Carabao Cup.

As well as Chelsea, multiple other clubs enquired about Scott in the summer. That included Arsenal, Liverpool, Manchester United and Manchester City, whose current crisis could deter transfer targets from joining, depending on what happens next in their case.

If Bournemouth stand firm on not selling this January, Chelsea may be forced to look at bringing in an alternative midfielder, such as Monaco's Lamine Camara.

His absence is a blow for Bournemnouth, who are also missing striker Eli Junior Kroupi.

Sports.title: Willian reveals Mikel Arteta's 'broken promises' made him want to quit Arsenal just THREE months after joining - and claims Gunners boss lacked 'human' side of management
Sports.content:
Former Arsenal star Willian has opened up on his nightmare spell at the Emirates and revealed why he left the club after just one season. The Brazilian attacker, now 38, joined the Gunners in August 2020 having shone at Chelsea over the previous seven years in what was a statement signing for Mikel Arteta's side. However, just a year later, Willian departed by mutual consent after struggling badly to replicate the form he had shown at Stamford Bridge. The 38-year-old scored once in 37 appearances. And Willian, who had previously described his Arsenal stint as 'the worst time that he had lived as a professional', provided further context of what happened on The Obi One Podcast with his former Chelsea team-mate John Obi Mikel. Reflecting that 'I know it was a big mistake,' he explained how Chelsea would only offer him a two-year extension to his deal, while Arsenal were prepared to give him a three-year contract. 'I met them couple of times,' he said. 'I met Arteta, I met everyone there. And they said "we want you to be the main guy". Willian has opened up on his nightmare one-year spell with Arsenal after leaving Chelsea Willian's arrival at the Emirates was viewed as a statement signing for Mikel Arteta's side 'Arteta said to me: "We're going to play like this and I want you to be the main guy, I will build the team around you, I want to give you the key to the club". 'When I heard that, obviously I love Chelsea but I was in the last year of my contract, I was 32, and I was thinking three more years in London, stay with my family in London, they love London. And then I decided. 'To be honest I should have stayed but at that moment I was thinking maybe the best solution is to go there, and I signed for three years there but it was not good.' Willian went on to reveal how things didn't materialise as he had expected or been promised and said that by November he informed his agent that he wanted to leave the club. 'I got frustrated,' he added. 'I am not saying it is their fault, but when you heard a lot of things and then you join the club, things that are not the same as what they told me, I got frustrated straight away. 'Three months later I said to my agent I want to leave, and that I made a big mistake leaving Chelsea.' When questioned on what promises were broken, Willian responded: 'It was more due to what I heard. I got frustrated from that because when I was there I saw some situations that I said to myself, it's not going to change. 'But it didn't work and because of that I couldn't play well or perform because I wasn't happy. When you are not happy you cannot perform. Money cannot buy happiness. It was the best contract of my life there, but I wasn't happy.' Following a disappointing personal and collective campaign that saw Arsenal finish eighth, Willian told the club he wanted to depart, and he moved to his boyhood side Corinthians. Willian revealed things were hugely different from his successful period playing at Chelsea Willian's stint at the Emirates did come at a time when Arsenal were worlds away from their current status as Premier League champions, yet the Brazilian was still critical of what he witnessed after joining. 'The mentality was totally different to Chelsea,' he added. 'You cannot compare. That's why I got frustrated also because the mentality was not the same in the club. 'When I left Chelsea they were fighting for titles every season, but Arsenal were in the middle of the situation where people were leaving, people were coming, and it was a difficult situation. But straight away I saw the mentality was different.' The Brazilian highlighted how he felt standards weren't the same in north London, pointing to the fact 'nobody was pushing' younger players, something he found 'very difficult'. Despite his subsequent success, Willian also shared an interesting appraisal of Arteta's management after explaining their relationship was 'not good'. He explained: 'I have nothing against him. He's a great coach inside the pitch, his ideas are great but he missed little bits on how to manage the team. 'The human part, he was missing it. It's important, but inside the pitch he is good. I always joke they sold me a dream and it wasn't a good dream.'

Sports.title: Football fanatic who'd been to every single AFC Wimbledon match for 37 years dies suddenly
Sports.content:
Football fanatic who'd been to every single AFC Wimbledon match for 37 years dies suddenly

Michael Taliadoros, the AFC Wimbledon superfan who had watched every single one of his team's matches since 1989, died last night in news that has rocked the League One club

View 3 Images Michael Taliadoros died on Sunday, the club confirmed (Image: Supplied)

Tributes have been paid to a legendary football fan who had just watched his team play in 2,000 consecutive matches.

‌



‌



Much-loved Michael Taliadoros died last night, leaving supporters and staff of his club AFC Wimbledon devastated. He had watched every single game the Dons had played for 37 years, with not even a global pandemic or his club being uprooted to Milton Keynes holding him back.

‌



Incredibly, Michael, known as MikeyT at Plough Lane, famously could not only remember the score from every game he has ever been to, but when the date the match took place as well. The League One Dons announced his death this afternoon as messages flood in after the loss of their matchday commentator.

‌



Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

View 3 Images Colleague Rob Cornell says he doesn't know if he will ever get used to his friend not being there (Image: Supplied)

Andy Burnham's hope to scrap drinking ban could throw lower league football clubs a survival lifeline READ MORE :

He put his encyclopaedic knowledge of the game to good use when he became a matchday commentator, and said he counted his blessings with his role, allowing him behind-closed-doors during Covid - and the chance to keep his incredible run going.

‌



In total, Mikey watched 2,010 Wimbledon consecutive first-team matches - a run that spanned almost four decades.

"The memories he has given and shared with us will last for many years to come, and we will never forget the dedication he gave to his roles as commentator and stadium announcer," the club said in a statement. "We send our deepest condolences to Mikey’s family and friends at this difficult time.

"Rest in peace Mikey, a Wimbledon legend in every sense."

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The terrace legend sat down with the Mirror at the start of the new season, telling us that he never planned to stop. The voice of the Dons had just celebrated his 56th birthday. His commentary from the club's late win over bitter rivals Milton Keynes went worldwide back in 2024.

He told the Mirror in August: “The run started away to Charlton on May 6 1989, and and the last match I missed was Man U a few days earlier.

‌



"That was the last Wimbledon game I wasn’t at. I had only just started work, and I hadn’t had my first pay packet. I’d just left college but as soon as I'd been paid for the first time, there was no stopping me!

“The next season was our centenary year, so that summer a few of us said we’re going to try and do every game and it snowballed from there really. I did all 47 that year, including the Zenith Data Systems Cup away at Ipswich on a Thursday night just before Christmas!

View 3 Images The League One club are in mourning (Image: Joe Toth/Shutterstock)

Article continues below

“The season after, my friend who had suggested going to every game got a better job so couldn’t carry on, I maintained a more humble existence employment-wise so I just carried on.

"I make sure I am at every first tea, competitive league and domestic cup game. The friendly games don't count, as sometimes they split the squad and play twice in one day."

Heartbreakingly, he added: “I just never want to stop. If I keep eating spinach and keep drinking cans of Lidl’s Red Bull equivalent, then who knows when the run will end. Myself and Rob [Cornell, co-commentator] will be like Statler and Waldorf from the Muppet Show into our 90s!”

Sports.title: England benefiting from Premier League transfer exodus says Trevoh Chalobah
Sports.content:
England benefiting from Premier League transfer exodus says Trevoh Chalobah

Thomas Tuchel's current England squad is packed full of players like Trevoh Chalobah, who decided to leave behind the Premier League to play in Spain, Germany and Italy

View 2 Images Trevoh Chalobah left Chelsea for Como in the summer (Image: John Walton/Getty Images)

Trevoh Chalobah says England’s foreign legion are bringing more experience to Thomas Tuchel’s squad.

‌



‌



Chalobah moved to Como in the summer and part of the former Chelsea defender’s decision was to take himself out of his comfort zone to further his England career. John Stones and Djed Spence also moved to Inter Milan in the summer while Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham are established as superstars at Bayern Munich and Real Madrid.

‌



Bayer Leverkusen defender Jarell Quansah and Barcelona winger Anthony Gordon also made moves abroad and are key members of Tuchel’s England set-up.

‌



Chalobah, 27, who moved from Chelsea to Como for £30million, said: “It's been amazing so far. It's different, obviously playing abroad before in my own spells in France, it's obviously feels a bit similar in terms of the culture, the language.
