Goodnight.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua reveals that Tyson Fury's estranged uncle has joined his camp ahead of £150m mega-fight as Gypsy King claims: 'I've not spoken to him for years'
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua reveals that Tyson Fury's estranged uncle has joined his camp ahead of £150m mega-fight as Gypsy King claims: 'I've not spoken to him for years'

Anthony Joshua made the startling revelation that he has joined forces with Tyson Fury's uncle, Peter, ahead of their eagerly-anticipated super-fight in Cardiff in December.

Never has the calling of a sporting press conference agitated as much, if not more, attention than the event itself.

Without putting Fury and Joshua into the same room in London on Wednesday evening there would have been no chance of them sharing a ring in Cardiff two months from now.

Never has a promo prompted so many startling revelations, either. We might never have known that Fury’s estranged uncle is advising AJ on how to prevent Tyson beating him. Traveller families are usually bonded by such fierce loyalties that we can only wonder about the tensions around the camp fire.

‘Not to worry,’ said the Gypsy King about the defection. ‘I haven’t spoken to him for years.’

Nor might we have learned that Joshua took a mind-blowing pay cut in order to haul the Battle of Britain back home from the clutches of New York.

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Tyson Fury’s ticket-selling appearances

How much of a purse deduction? ‘Twelve figures’ declared his promoter Eddie Hearn. That’s £10million at least.

AJ shrugged and cited another fringe benefit picked up during the maelstrom of doubt as to whether this fight between a pair of British world heavyweight champions would ever take place. He also added Fury’s former trainer Ben Davison to his team.

Joshua said: ‘Ben’s pinpointing details which will make the difference on the night.’

Fury replied: ‘Ben can’t put muscles on that suspect chin.’

He could not resist reminding everyone that Davison has just returned from Las Vegas where he presided over Conor Benn’s two-round devastation by America’s great Latin hope, Ryan Garcia.

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Fury’s ticket-selling appearances.

Instead he advertised ‘probably the greatest fight boxing’s ever seen if you factor in the commercial aspect'.

Which includes the US$150million split equally between the two of them as they put an end to 12 years of public waiting for this fight.

Joshua said: ‘Both of us want to do British boxing proud.’

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles with Fury inviting Joshua to ‘a pint of Guinness as soon as the fight over, win lose or draw'.

Well, they are ten weeks away from them putting on their fight faces.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White

It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: For Scottish boxing, the cupboard is bare. All that remains are memories of better times
Sports.content:
Given the endless nonsense that continues to surround the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight, it’s no surprise that it has dominated all the recent headlines in boxing.

Will they? Won’t they? Does anyone even really care any more? Is it happening in the UK? America? Saudi Arabia? Maybe on the moon? For a gazillion dollars?

It felt like a degree of certainty had been reached last week with the announcement that the fight will go ahead at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in December.

That was until Dana White, the UFC supremo and one of the fight’s chief promoters, said only a few days ago that he ‘doesn’t know’ if it will go ahead.

Perhaps we will get a clearer picture tomorrow afternoon, with Fury and Joshua set to face-off at a media conference in London.

Either way, this tiresome circus act involving two fighters long past their prime continues to be pretty much the only thing anyone is speaking about in boxing right now.

Josh Taylor is dominated by Jack Catterall in Leeds as his ring supremacy is left in ruins

Nathaniel Collins had been Scotland's biggest hope until he suffered two successive defeats

Taylor's rise to the top of the fight game was an incredible achievement that will long be lauded

It perhaps escaped your attention, then, that Scotland’s Nathaniel Collins was back in the ring last weekend. Quite an important fight it was, too.

Taking on European featherweight champion Liam Davies in Birmingham, this was supposed to be Collins’ comeback fight after he lost to Spain’s Cristobal Llorente in Glasgow in April in their world title eliminator.

It did not go well. Collins was floored in the first round and never really recovered, before his trainer put a stop to it all and said enough was enough at the end of the seventh round.

There was a sadness to it all. Not only that Collins had suffered a second successive defeat, but also in terms of the wider implications for himself and for Scottish boxing as a whole.

The defeat to Llorente at The Hydro had been the first loss of Collins’ career. It had been a tough night, albeit not disastrous. There was a chance to bounce back and come again.

But, in terms of challenging at world level, he now looks further away than ever. The same would surely apply to Scottish boxing as a whole after this latest blow.

Not so long ago, Scottish boxing felt like it had a pulse. Josh Taylor climbed the mountain and was, in his pomp, one of the best pound-for-pound fighters on the planet.

The Tartan Tornado put together one of the greatest runs by any British fighter in history to become our first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era. Achieving that in just 18 fights was truly phenomenal.

When Taylor’s career then fizzled out due to a combination of burn-out, inactivity and promotional mismanagement, it had been hoped that Collins would be the next cab off the rank.

The late Ken Buchanan won multiple titles at lightweight and fought between 1965 and 1982

The Nightmare, as he’s known, was supposed to be the fighter who kept the lights on and continued to fly the flag in the post-Taylor era.

That’s not to say he was ever going to be quite as good as Taylor. That always looked unrealistic. But there was genuine hope that Collins could at least be a contender for a world title.

The brutal yet stylish manner in which he dismantled fellow Scot Lee McGregor at The Hydro in May 2025 gave the look of a fighter with all the credentials to go on and box at world level.

But the defeat to Davies in Birmingham last weekend has surely ended that conversation. In the post-Taylor era, the cupboard is depressingly bare for Scottish boxing. Completely and utterly empty.

No one is selling out arenas in Scotland. No one is forcing their way on to Sky Sports and the likes. No one is even close to holding box-office appeal or appearing on pay-per-views.

The amateur and club scene are still doing their bit. The numbers are OK, even if a lot of people use boxing clubs as fitness classes these days rather than having any desire to actually enter a ring.

But when you speak to people involved with boxing clubs across Scotland, the majority of them all share a similar concern.

Plainly, that we have no one even remotely close to following in Taylor’s footsteps and fighting at the top level of the sport. The outlook is bleak.

Listen, Scotland is a relatively small country. We do not have an endless pool of talent. Boxing is not a mainstream sport like football or rugby.

The two successive defeats for Collins have signaled a barren period for Scottish boxing

Kids learn to play football in various different ways; at school, at coaching sessions, or with a club. Maybe even down the local park or on the streets in some very rare and old-fashioned instances.

Rugby is a non-negotiable for those in private education. Even golf now has far more reach and appeal with the younger generation than boxing.

With the awareness around long-term brain damage now greater than ever, you can hardly blame any parent if they aren’t overly enthused by the idea of their kids being involved in a sport where they get punched in the head.

When a generational talent like Taylor comes along and then leaves, the gap is enormous. There is no conveyor belt of world-class operators waiting in the wings.

Sadly, it also now appears that Scotland can’t even offer up any fighters in the bracket just below world level either.

Collins has already come through a serious health scare – a life-threatening twisted bowel caused by infant scar tissue – that put much more than just his boxing career at risk. He has shown heart. No one questions that. He gave it a good go.

But his latest defeat is emblematic of the wider malaise that continues to be so prevalent across Scottish boxing as a whole.

There have been lean times in the past. After Ken Buchanan and Jim Watt, there were quiet periods. After Scott Harrison’s turbulent reign at featherweight the scene thinned out again until Ricky Burns and then Taylor arrived.

Cycles exist. The problem now is that the cycle feels stuck in the downward phase with no obvious sign of it moving back up again.

Where is the next boxing superstar in Scotland? It is beginning to feel like the sport is dying a death. That is the uncomfortable truth.

When Collins fought Llorente at The Hydro in April, it wasn’t even close to being a sell-out. The whole top tier of the arena was closed. Make of that what you will.

And that was a world title eliminator involving the guy who was supposed to be our next big hope. Taylor himself has acknowledged the lack of young fighters breaking through.

The Tornado’s retirement left a void. Collins’ latest defeat has made it wider and deeper. The Hydro still stands ready for big nights, but it’s hard to see a major promoter going back there any time soon.

The Scottish public still loves a fighter who will dig in and go to war. But the fighters of genuine world-class pedigree are simply not here at present.

These are the lean years. The barren stretch. And that should worry anyone who cares about the sport north of the border.

The cupboard is bare. The stars have gone. Until someone steps forward and proves otherwise, Scottish boxing is living on memories of Taylor and on nostalgia about some of the other great names of the past.

Sports.title: The dire consequence of Russell's Bahrain GP in Malaysia retirement
Sports.content:
George Russell’s retirement from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia will have huge consequences on the rest of his 2026 Formula 1 campaign - especially in regards to ADUO.

The Mercedes driver was running third under the safety car with five laps remaining at Sepang on Sunday, until he pulled over at the Turn 1 entry with a power unit failure.

Minds immediately went to what impact it would have on the title race, as second for team-mate Kimi Antonelli stretched his championship lead to 84 points with seven rounds left.

But Mercedes is also now having to reassess its plan of when to give Russell a new engine, considering it will incur a grid penalty as he’s already used the allotted four in a season.

“He came on the radio behind the safety car and said PU's starting to sound funny,” said Mercedes’ deputy team principal Bradley Lord.

“We saw sensors then misbehaving and it was clear we had to pull the car over and we'd had a failure of some sort.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

“Still need to understand what it means for his pool because he's not rich in low mileage power units either. So that may mean we need to alter what had been our previous plan.”

The plan was for Russell’s next power unit to be the updated version under the Additional Development and Upgrades Opportunities system, which grants Mercedes one token.

It’s believed that the 28-year-old was set to take his penalty in Austin, but Sepang means he might need to do it beforehand - Singapore this weekend - and consequently miss out on the upgrade.

When asked if that’s the case, Lord confirmed: “Potentially so, yeah. That's what we need to understand. But yes, there may be a double whammy effect there, which for him after such a gut-wrenching blow today... it was devastating to see him have to pull off as he did.

"Yeah, there may be a sort of double whammy effect there that is just a really unfortunate consequence of that issue.”

Sepang continued what’s been a series of bad luck for the pre-season title favourite, who retired from the lead in Montreal with a power unit failure, as well as other misfortunes in 2026.

Bradley Lord, Mercedes Deputy Team Principal Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

But there’s also been issues on Antonelli’s side, such as his power unit failure late on at Barcelona, so unreliability is the one concern amid an otherwise dominant year for Mercedes.

“I’m so massively annoyed, I’m not in a happy place,” team boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports after the Malaysian race.

“First of all, we didn't have the speed that we were hoping to have before the weekend, so there's a lot of homework to be done in order to recover, which I'm sure we will.

“Then the race literally went, if you consider the fight with Lewis [Hamilton] behind, went against us.

“We had such an advantage, one VSC, two safety cars, you couldn't be more unlucky. And to make things worse, PU failure with a few laps to go to the end with George, which is terrible for his championship and not good at all for our constructor points.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

“So, as much as I love to be here when I look at the pure races, one of my worst experiences, to be honest.”

Mercedes is still on course for its first constructors’ title since 2021 as it leads second-placed Ferrari by 151 points, a gap that stood at 160 heading into Malaysia.

“This overarching topic, the DNFs, that could cost us dearly also for the remaining seven races,” added Wolff. “A championship is quickly turned around against you or for you if you have a DNF, and that's why that can't continue.”

Sports.title: Honda HRC to get new boss with Watanabe set to retire
Sports.content:
Koji Watanabe, the long-time boss of Honda's racing activities under HRC, will retire on 1 January 2027, with Keiichi Yasuda appointed as his successor.

A long-time Honda employee after first joining the Japanese marque in 1987, Watanabe became the head of Honda's racing division in 2022. In that time Watanabe oversaw the company's merger of its four-wheel and two-wheel divisions as well as its U-turn on the decision to leave F1, returning as a works partner of Aston Martin for the 2026 regulations.

But Honda has now announced Watanabe will retire on 1 January, with Keiichi Yasuda his successor as HRC CEO. Yasuda is the current Executive Vice President and Representative Director, and was previously head of HR at Honda's racing division.

"This executive change is part of a planned periodic personnel rotation designed to strengthen the management structure in response to global transformation and to accelerate business expansion for the next generation," Honda stated.

"It is my honour serving as a president of HRC with the wonderful colleagues,” Watanabe said.

“In 2022, I assumed the post of President of the new HRC, unifying both motorcycle and automobile motorsport activities. Since then, we decided on our return to F1, expanded our global motorsport structure by reorganising HPD in the U.S. into HRC US and establishing HRC UK, and worked on building HRC's global brand.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"For the remaining three months of my presidency, I will continue to do my utmost, aiming for victory until the very end."

Speaking on his new role, Yasuda said: "I consider it my mission to firmly inherit the solid foundation built by Watanabe.

"Evolve it further, unite everyone's vector toward the single goal of winning in races, and make HRC even stronger.

"Leveraging my management experience as president of overseas local entities and my background in HR, I will focus on investing in people and strengthening our organisation toward victory."

Sports.title: How FIA software bug caused chaos in Bahrain GP in Malaysia – and the emergency fix that saved the race
Sports.content:
The start of the first wet-weather race of the 2026 Formula 1 season descended into chaos. Leader Max Verstappen was the first to suffer from a lack of power while driving slowly during the formation laps behind the safety car, after which Lewis Hamilton came to a standstill and several other cars followed.

Race control was forced to stop the formation lap with a red flag, after which there was a 40-minute delay before fans actually got to see some F1 action.

Read Also: Formula 1 FIA explains software glitch that caused Bahrain GP in Malaysia race delay

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis confirmed to media including Autosport that a bug in the software supplied by the FIA and developed together with the teams over the course of multiple years was responsible for the chaos.

“We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked because there's been very little wet running this year. There was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in,” Tombazis said during an impromptu media session post-race.

“Basically, on the formation lap, some cars went very slowly and almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars and some cars almost stopped completely. That bug prevented then the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again.”

This is closely related to the reduction in electrical power to 250kW in wet conditions.

Although the software required for this was tested by several teams, including Red Bull and Racing Bulls, it was not tested in the conditions behind the safety car – and therefore not at these extremely low speeds.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing, Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

At the Sepang International Circuit, those low speeds were reached in certain minisectors, with all the consequences that followed.

“It was mainly in some sectors where the full power was reduced. I don't know exactly what speed that was, but some cars reaching this very low speed somehow entered into a loop, which meant they couldn't re-accelerate and then it looked as if they came to a stop.”

In practice, this left drivers feeling as though the throttle pedal was no longer responding, something Oliver Bearman told the media with some surprise.

“I've never seen or felt anything like that. I was shocked that… I didn't even know that the FIA could control our throttle pedal. That was quite scary, actually,” the Haas driver said.

“My throttle pedal just stopped working. It was like it was not connected and the engine was just idling. It was so weird, I mean, shocking.”

One of the questions is why the internal combustion engine was also affected, when that should not be the case at extremely low speeds. The FIA does not yet have a formal answer to that question, but the initial suggestion is that the bug caused all throttle input to go towards recharging the MGU-K, which explains why drivers felt there was no response from the throttle pedal at all.

At first glance, it appeared as though the Mercedes-powered cars were less affected by the issue than other manufacturers, but Tombazis explained that there is no technical reason for that. It was simply related to the speeds reached in certain minisectors.

Nikolas Tombazis, FIA Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

“Not all cars reached the same low speeds on the formation lap. There was a bit of a concertina effect. I think Max slowed down quite a lot, being at the front, and then some cars braked harder as they were surprised and so on. That caused some cars to experience the problem and some others to not experience it.”

How the FIA provided F1 teams with an emergency fix

The FIA then had to react quickly to get the race near Kuala Lumpur under way after all, as Tombazis explained when asked by Autosport.

“Fortunately, our guys understood the issue very, very quickly. I think the update was done very competently. It was obviously a rush job. The priority was to get running as quickly as possible again, so I think the reaction time was quite fast,” he said.

“It wasn't a perfect job and, clearly, we didn't test the updates, but I think it was the way to handle such a case.”

In practice, the update meant that the FIA lifted the energy limit constraint – the restrictions associated with the 250kW limit – for the minisectors in which the low speeds had triggered the bug. Logically, this is not a watertight solution going forward, but it was an emergency measure to ensure the race could go ahead.

“In some of the sectors, some of these reductions of power were overridden,” Tombazis confirmed. “Clearly, we didn't have five days to do the updates. We only had a few minutes, but fortunately, I think we managed to do it without compromising any safety, any racing or fairness.”

How could this happen in the first place?

After the FIA update, all the teams still had to install the modified software, which explains the delay before the restart. The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was saved as a result, but that still does not explain how the FIA could have missed this issue throughout all its preparations and why it only surfaced in round 16 of the championship.

“The software was tested. It just wasn't tested in those specific conditions,” Tombazis replied. “What caught us out was the fact that cars went in that very, very low speed, which was not normally contemplated.”

FIA Safety Car Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

During the tyre tests in which the software was tested, the extremely low speeds were understandably not reached. Nevertheless, there is a crucial counterargument to that: in the rain, the likelihood of a safety car – and therefore low speeds – is very high. Should the FIA not have anticipated that, and was that the governing body’s biggest mistake?

Asked that question by Autosport, Tombazis responded: “Well, any bug is a product of a mistake. I don't know of any software that doesn't have bugs and updates. Your computer probably gets updated every three days and those are all bugs.

“Of course, anticipating these things is what one hopes to do, but sometimes some very combination of events isn't properly anticipated and causes the problem. I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.”

Although the cause of this problem is now known and a temporary fix has been introduced, the FIA still has many questions to answer internally – also to ensure that it does not happen again.

“We would all like it to be simpler, but the fact is when you have as much electrical energy, it does make it more complicated. I think you appreciate that the race has now finished about one hour ago and we haven't done a full debrief of the situation to see how we can avoid such an issue.

“Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards where we identify criticalities. Obviously, that was a major criticality and we need to make sure we avoid it.

“But can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no. But we will do our best to avoid it, of course.”

Sports.title: The slick tyre gamble that hurt McLaren and Ferrari's chances in Bahrain GP in Malaysia
Sports.content:
When the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia eventually got going after an hour and 33 minutes of delays, it became apparent that the intermediate was the tyre to be on among the opening laps - even if the Sepang circuit had looked like it was drying out.

At the front of the field, Ferrari and McLaren chose to go all-in on the dry tyres for the restart; Ferrari opted for the soft compound, while McLaren went for the mediums. When the race got underway behind the safety car, both teams were left to rue their choices as the circuit was still too slippery.

McLaren bailed on the plan early, stopping before the standing start to ensure Oscar Piastri could get a set of intermediates back onto the car, but Lando Norris and the Ferraris stuck with their choices. Charles Leclerc duly fed into the pitlane at the end of the lap, as the slick-tyre runners were swamped and then left behind by those who'd stuck with the intermediate for the start.

Lewis Hamilton and Norris surmised that, since they'd made their beds, they'd lie in them. Hamilton was asked if he wanted to stop again, but the seven-time champion reasoned that Ferrari might as well stick with the gamble given that the team was well behind - and pitting would only cost more time.

By the end of the eighth lap, the slick times were now equal with the intermediate runners; Valtteri Bottas' subsequent off then presented the inter-shod drivers with the chance to switch to slicks.

Speaking about the decision, Norris stated that the idea of starting on the slick was "quite convincing" and that he was unsure of the performance of the inter; on his recon lap to the grid, the Briton reported that the green-walled tyre was already feeling the pain on Sepang's rough surface.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

"It felt maybe a little bit of a risk, because a slick on a wet track is always a bit of a risk," Norris said. "There was enough people on it that it was quite convincing at the time that it was possibly going to be the right decision.

"The laps to the grid on the inter when it was a similar kind of condition, they had so much grip and my Inter was completely shredded after one lap.

"I was convinced a slick tyre would work, but I think it was just the fact I've never really been on the inter before. Things just felt a lot better than they should have done in a way.

"If we would have had a read on an inter from a previous weekend, maybe I would have been able to understand it more. But that convinced us and it clearly convinced a lot of people.

"Oscar probably made the right decision in boxing and we got it wrong today, that's all."

Leclerc theorised that the roughness of the tarmac made it more difficult to read the track surface, as water pooled up in the gaps - and the drop in temperature that accompanied the rain ensured that the circuit took much longer to dry out than expected. Given the length of the downpour, any residual circuit temperature was swiftly extinguished.

Even though the Monegasque switched tyres, the time loss involved in pitting after the start kept him behind Hamilton, who ran longer on his set of soft tyres and quickly began to make up positions.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

Hamilton joked that he wasn't going to "go to the casino with the guys" after the team's gambles didn't pay off, although praised his team's strategy in keeping him out on the road. The Briton was ultimately less enamoured with the medium after making a stop on lap 31, but the late-race VSC (later a full safety car) presented a chance to return to the soft - which he put to use with a pass on Isack Hadjar for third.

"As we pulled out [of the pits], all the spray came out the back of Max’s car and I was like, 'okay, I’m done. My race is really in trouble,'" Hamilton recounted.

"We just had to stick with it. As everyone’s overtaken me, they [the engineers] were like, 'we stop.' I know we’ve already made another 26 seconds. What’s the difference from that with one minute 40 or whatever I was down? So I was just, 'Let’s just wait it out for the track to dry.'

"And once it did, it felt good that I was catching people. The car felt great then after that. Really good pitstops from my guys in the garage and then good strategy. But for us to get back to the podium, I never thought that that was going to be the case. Of course, I’m really, really grateful that we managed to get back here.

"We’ll definitely have an open dialogue, and I’m really so proud of my team. The mechanics every weekend, just the work they’re putting in, the engineers that accompany here every weekend, the catering, everyone really, really comes and gives it their best.

"Their heart’s all in the right spot. We’ve definitely got areas that we need to improve and we know that, and we’re not in any denial of that. So I think we’ll have a constructive chat, we’ll regroup, we’ll take the positives from this weekend, which the car was really good, and we’ll come back next week fighting."

Sports.title: FIA explains software glitch that caused Bahrain GP in Malaysia race delay
Sports.content:
The FIA has given insight into why Formula 1 cars experienced technical issues ahead of Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The start of the Sepang race was delayed by 40 minutes due to a downpour; then a chaotic formation lap saw the likes front-row starters Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton suffer from a glitch which rendered throttle input ineffective, with numerous cars coming to a standstill. The red flag was waved.

The situation was branded “unacceptable” by Sergio Perez, who likened it to ‘being in a rental kart and running out of time’; Lando Norris described it “just horrible” and evidence that “we shouldn't have any of that stuff, the electronic side”, given this was linked to Formula 1’s new machinery, which features 47% electrical power.

FIA single-seater Nikolas Tombazis has now explained that, given F1 had never had competitive running in actual wet conditions this season, it was caught out by the power unit’s reaction to cars driving extremely slowly at that time. A software update therefore had to be carried out, hence a 53-minute delay to get the race restarted.

“We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked, because there's been very little wet running this year, and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in,” Tombazis said.

Nikolas Tombazis, FIA Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

“Basically, the formation lap, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. And that bug prevented the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again. I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.”

Tombazis praised the FIA’s reaction when it came to fixing the issue as swiftly as possible.

“Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars,” he added.

“So all of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting [for] a race and for everybody else, which is understandable, and we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem.”

Not everyone was so upset about some cars running into trouble, with eighth-placed Fernando Alonso joking at the end of an unusually good day for Aston Martin-Honda: “I had 50% DNFs this year, they never stopped the race for us.”

Sports.title: Russell: “You’ve got to laugh” at bad luck as F1 title drifts away
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver George Russell labelled his misfortune as laughable following Formula 1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, where a power unit failure cost him a podium finish late on.

Russell was a lowly seventh on the grid at Sepang, but the correct choice of intermediate tyres on a damp track and a lightning getaway saw him surge to second into Turn 1, behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Russell was however passed by Max Verstappen as early as lap six, but the first safety car period gave him a chance to sweep past Antonelli around the outside of Turn 5 at the restart as the race leader dropped down to third – though the Italian youngster found a way back into second place just eight laps later.

Further drama did not disrupt the status quo in the top three, but a late safety car meant Russell had a chance to challenge his rivals for victory. However, the chance never came as a power unit failure took him out of the race before the final restart.

“You've almost got to laugh,” Russell told Sky Sports F1 after his third retirement this season – his second purely technical DNF. “It's beyond disappointment. It's just, so many times this season it's happened.

“Of course, it's a real shame, but… Just keep on fighting. Just keep on trying to go.

“The podium, of course, looked very certain. Solid race, not amazing race, but solid race.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Not the first time, so I'm pretty used to this feeling and these questions, let's say.”

As he said, Russell will “keep on fighting”, but is equally aware of his deficit to championship rival Antonelli reaching an unprecedented 84 points.

The Briton steered clear of any sensational comments – he won’t say the title is out of reach – but his assessment is bleak nonetheless.

“I don't need to say I think it's gone or whatever,” he added. “But, of course, it’s exceptionally unlikely, and that's just the reality.

“I knew if I wanted to come back I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I've had luck not on my side. So, you know, a three-point loss today being behind Kimi turned into an 18-point loss. Of course, if the issue was on the other side, it would have been an 18-point gain.

“So, yeah, it's a real shame. It's a real shame, but that's just how it is.”

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said the Bahrain GP in Malaysia had been one of his “worst experiences” personally, as Red Bull claimed its first victory of the year over the Silver Arrows and Russell suffered that setback.

“I'm so massively annoyed,” Wolff told Sky. “I'm not in a happy place.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“We didn't have the speed that we were hoping to have before the weekend, so there's a lot of homework to be done in order to recover, which I'm sure we will. Then the race literally went, if you consider the fight with Lewis [Hamilton] behind, went against us. We had such an advantage, one VSC, two safety cars. I mean, you couldn't be more unlucky. And to make things worse, PU failure with a few laps to go to the end with George, which is terrible for his championship and not good at all for our constructor points.”

After praising Antonelli for ‘doing the job’, the Austrian added: “It's just this overarching topic, the DNFs, that could cost us dearly also for the remaining seven races. A championship is quickly turned around against you or for you if you have a DNF, and that's why that can't continue.”

Perhaps Wolff was overdramatic there. At Sepang, Mercedes was outscored by Ferrari for just the first time since the summer break, and the Scuderia still is 151 points in arrears in the constructors’ championship. Meanwhile, Hamilton’s deficit to Antonelli in the drivers’ standings is up to 106 points.

Asked how to pull the team together after such a result, Wolff replied: “I think we have a good action plan. James [Allison, technical director] is really fully on top of it with his leadership team.

“That lifts my mood because I know we have such a tremendous group of people. In the same way as we have with HPP, they're going to sort it out. But that gives me real relief for the moment to know they are the best and they are going to find a solution. And I think we will come back strong.”

Sports.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen wins chaotic race from Antonelli as Russell retires late on
Sports.content:
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen won a disorderly Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, clinching his first victory of the season, as George Russell’s title hopes dwindled further with a late retirement.

After the race was delayed by an hour and a half due to dysfunctional software on a wet track, Verstappen outduelled both Mercedes to triumph as Russell was struck by a technical issue.

After a 40-minute delay due to a downpour, the formation lap began, with Isack Hadjar having a trip through the gravel as the whole field warmed up intermediate tyres. Several cars, including front-row starters Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, suffered software glitches that rendered throttle input ineffective. The red flag was waved, which delayed the race by a further 53 minutes.

When race finally got under way, only nine cars opted for intermediate tyres, including Verstappen, Kimi Antonelli, Russell and Hadjar. Others like Hamilton, Charles Leclerc, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri went for slicks, like Pierre Gasly, who spun out behind the safety car on lap one and dropped to 13th.

A standing start took place at the end of lap two, as Piastri, Gabriel Bortoleto, Lance Stroll, Nico Hulkenberg made late pitstops to switch from slicks to intermediates.

The Silver Arrows of Antonelli and Russell surged to the front of the pack easily at lights out, despite polesitter Verstappen having the same intermediates; the four-time world champion only narrowly held off Liam Lawson for third, with the Racing Bulls man enjoying a blistering getaway too.

Meanwhile, the Ferraris dropped down the order, along with Norris. Having clipped Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi, Leclerc pitted at the end of that lap and moved to intermediates, while team-mate Hamilton and his compatriot lost further dozens of seconds trying to make their gamble work – along with the Alpines, Oliver Bearman, Fernando Alonso and Valtteri Bottas.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Verstappen passed Russell for second place in Turn 4 on lap six, with the top three drivers within three seconds while fourth-placed Lawson was 10 seconds down; he was overtaken by Hadjar at the last corner on that same lap.

Verstappen caught Antonelli and started putting pressure on the race leader on lap eight; Antonelli went wide at the last corner but retained the lead.

Bottas-induced safety car levels the field

Bottas lost control in Turn 13 on lap nine and ended up benched in the gravel, causing a safety car period that was perfect timing for the inter-shod runners to switch to slicks, as the latter had become the quicker tyre compound, while allowing those who gambled on slicks to cut their losses.

Antonelli led from Verstappen, Russell, Hadjar, Lawson, Ocon, Lindblad, Sainz, Bortoleto and Piastri, with a variety of slick tyre compounds out on track – most interestingly the Mercedes drivers on mediums and the Red Bulls on softs – while Hamilton, Norris and Leclerc were down in 15th to 17th, with the Ferraris on softs and Norris on hards.

A ruthless Verstappen went around the outside of Antonelli at the restart in Turn 1, while Russell swept past in Turn 5, with the championship leader dropping to third in a few seconds. Meanwhile, Bortoleto and Sainz collided, with the Williams collapsing to 18th and the Audi driver handed a 10-second penalty.

As Verstappen pulled away from the Silver Arrows by over three seconds, Antonelli was getting impatient behind his team-mate, but team orders were not on the cards, so the Italian youngster found a way past in Turn 4 on lap 21. Further down the field, Hamilton was overtaking his opponents one after another, climbing to fifth by lap 22, while Leclerc broke into the top 10 on the following tour.

Antonelli went wide at the last corner and hit the pit entry bollard on lap 24, losing another two seconds to Verstappen, with the gap up to 7.5 seconds. He was now just one second ahead of Russell, but both gaps subsequently increased.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

The wave of second pitstops began on lap 29 for frontrunners, including Russell on lap 32, moving to softs – too early to his taste. Antonelli logically followed on the next tour to avoid being undercut, and so did Verstappen, now comfortably leading by 11 seconds.

Verstappen (briefly) cedes lead under VSC, Russell retires

As Hadjar found himself under pressure from Hamilton, the virtual safety car neutralised the race, with Alex Albon stopped due to a technical failure. Verstappen opted for a ‘cheap’ pitstop but ceded the lead to Antonelli; both Ferraris also changed tyres.

Mercedes eventually opted to pit both cars on the following tour, along with most frontrunners, until the VSC turned into a full safety car – which swayed the remaining ones.

Ahead of the final laps in green-flag conditions, Verstappen led Antonelli, Russell, Hadjar, Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Lawson and Alonso, who fought his way into the top 10.

But before racing even got back under way, Russell stopped trackside with a technical issue and retired, while Norris was surprised by cars slowing down ahead and had a trip through the gravel and fell to 11th.

There were just four laps remaining when the safety car returned to the pitlane, and Verstappen mastered the restart; he never was at threat from Antonelli and triumphed. Hamilton found a way past Hadjar in Turn 1 on lap 53, clinching his first podium finish since Silverstone. The Frenchman also dropped behind the sister Ferrari of Leclerc.

Piastri finished sixth ahead of Lawson, while a combative Alonso held off Norris for eighth. Lindblad scored the last available point in 10th, underlining another strong day for Racing Bulls relative to the rival Alpine squad.

Having held sixth place early on, Esteban Ocon collapsed to 15th under the chequered flag, behind team-mate Bearman.

Sports.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia descends into chaos as car trouble prompts red flag
Sports.content:
The Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia has been red-flagged after several cars suffered power unit gremlins during a wet set of formation laps.

After a heavy tropical thunderstorm, the action at Malaysian Sepang was set to get underway with a number of laps behind the safety car followed by a standing start.

But ahead of F1's first-ever wet event under the 2026 regulations, a number of cars suffered power unit gremlins in the rain, suspected to be software related.

Initially, polesitter Max Verstappen reported a lack of acceleration from his Red Bull before the Dutchman got going again. Soon after, second-placed Lewis Hamilton reported a similar issue on his Ferrari, with the Briton crawling around the first formation lap as the rest of the field passed him. One lap later, Hamilton too managed to get going again.

More cars, including Racing Bulls man Liam Lawson, Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto and Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas, also appeared to struggle with similar problems, with race control suspending the start procedure and throwing a red flag.

With the grid mixed up as cars streamed into pitlane, race control will revert to the original grid positions when the running is resumed.

Race control eventually announced a start time of 16:33 local time, amounting to what would be a 50-minute delay.

Eventually race control abandoned the attempt to start the race and summoned the field back into the pits so the FIA could issue a software update. The process took the best part of an hour.

The problem was widespread throughout the field and affected drivers in different ways. Here’s how several of them experienced the fault.

Verstappen’s car almost came to a stop at the front of the field. However a switch change on his steering wheel solved the problem for him.

The car accelerates away Lambiase Looks like maybe Lewis has a similar problem to you. He’s still struggling between turn 11 and turn 12.

Lando Norris’s car also lost power around the same time as Verstappen, which led to some confusion between him and race engineer Will Joseph. However the problem cleared up quickly for Norris.

Joseph Lando can we have strat 14, strat 14. Norris Happening? I’ve got no power at all. Joseph Verstappen has an issue, he can’t accelerate. Norris But we all do. Sports.title: Fan’s video shows moment software glitch slowed F1 cars to a crawl on formation lap | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s 2026 engine regulations faced fresh criticism yesterday following the farcical start to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The race, which had already been delayed by rain, was postponed by almost an hour more after a software problem struck cars during the formation lap.

Pole-winner Max Verstappen and several drivers behind him slowed to a crawl as their power units would not allow them to accelerate. The cause was a software parameter set by the FIA, which required the governing body to apply new settings to the cars.

Verstappen said he had as much power as he did when the drivers raced in Lego cars in a promotional event.

“It was like the Lego race,” he said. “Same speed. It was insane, it’s the Lego power.

“At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn’t understand what was going on. Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still.

“That’s not what you want, right, for the sport.”

The FIA said the cars’ loss of power was due to “an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration.”

Sports.title: Mercedes ‘don’t know if upgrade made us faster or slower’ – Antonelli | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The long-awaited upgrade package Mercedes introduced last weekend may have made them less competitive, Andrea Kimi Antonelli has admitted.

Antonelli led the opening stages of yesterday’s race ahead of team mate George Russell . However both were overtaken by Max Verstappen , who went on to win the race.

Mercedes originally planned to introduce their new parts for the W17 at this weekend’s race in Singapore. They brought the upgrade forward after Formula 1 added last weekend’s round in Malaysia to replace the cancelled event in Bahrain.

However the unusually abrasive track surface at the Sepang International Circuit complicated the team’s efforts to understand the performance of its upgraded car. Antonelli qualified half a second slower than Verstappen.

He said the performance of the upgrade is “the question we need to answer because we don’t really know if it made us go faster or worse.”

However he pointed out the team has been less competitive at tracks which share some traits with Sepang. “It’s fair to say that this season, whenever we went on really old Tarmac, we’ve struggled. For example, in Zandvoort, McLaren was much quicker than us, especially on the older Tarmac.

“So I think maybe it’s just a fact that the Tarmac is very old and that for the tyres it’s very, very hard, and maybe we just struggle on this kind of Tarmac.

“But, of course, the track and the Tarmac made our life difficult in understanding whether it made us improve or not.”

The championship leader expects the team will have some answers before this weekend’s race. “I’m sure the team – they have a lot of data, especially after this weekend – and I’m sure for Singapore we will come with a much, much better view on the package and hopefully we can extract the full potential out of it.”

Sports.title: Hamilton suspects he could have fought for win had he not started on slicks | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton believes he could have fought for victory at Sepang had he started on the right tyres.

The Ferrari driver qualified on the front row of the grid alongside Max Verstappen

“We were having a good weekend,” he said. “The car felt great in qualifying. It felt amazing to get to second.

“Me and my engineers were here ’til 11:30 last night just going over everything and I really, really felt today was the opportunity to have at least a good battle with Max.”

The original start was delayed due to rain. A further delay followed after a software problem caused several drivers, including Hamilton and Verstappen, to slow to a crawl during the formation lap.

“My power didn’t come back and I had to stop on-track and restart the car and then we all ended up in the pit lane,” said Hamilton. “Thankfully, we all got back to our positions.”

By the time race control were ready to start the race, the track had dried considerably, though it was still damp. Hamilton and his team chose to start the race on slick tyres.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“There was such a long wait and we were debating what tyre to go on to. And I said, ‘look, there was a lot of spray on the laps to the grid.’

“I went into the pit lane, I looked at the ground, I was like, ‘It’s still wet.’ I went to the pit wall and I was like, ‘It’s still wet.’ And they’re like, ‘Yeah, but because it’s been so long, it’s definitely going to dry up real quick and maybe we’re already in the crossover.’

“So, anyway, as a team we ended up taking that soft and when we were at the end of the pit lane and these two took off their blankets and they were on inters [I knew] we were in trouble.”

The track took a long time to dry and those who opted for intermediates gained a significant advantage at the start. Hamilton urged the team not to bring him into the pits for another change.

“As everyone had overtaken me, they’re like, ‘we stop.’ [But] I know we’ve already [lost] another 26 seconds, what’s the difference from that with one minute 40 or whatever I was down? So I [said] ‘let’s just wait it out for the track to dry.’ And once it did, it felt good that I was catching people.”

Hamilton began to make progress on his softs once the Safety Car came out and he was back within range of other cars.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The car felt great then after that. Really good pit stops from my guys in the garage and then good strategy.

“For us to get back to the podium, I never thought that that was going to be the case. But, of course, I’m really, really grateful that we managed to get back here.”

He said he will have an “open dialogue” with the team about the decision to start the race on slicks.

“We’ve definitely got areas that we need to improve and we know that, and we’re not in any denial of that.

“So I think we’ll have a constructive chat, we’ll regroup, we’ll take the positives from this weekend, which was the car was really good, and we’ll come back next week fighting. I thought today, as I said, was a chance for us potentially to try and fight Max for the win, but maybe we can do that next week.”

Sports.title: Formula 1 must learn lessons from formation lap shambles at Sepang – Hamilton | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were unimpressed with the delay to the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The pair urged Formula 1 to learn lessons from the software problem which struck both their cars during the original formation lap. Both drivers and several of their rivals slowed to a crawl, leading F1 to abandon the attempt to start the race.

“It was insane,” said Verstappen. “At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn’t understand what was going on.

“Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw [Hamilton] crawling.”

“That’s not what you want, right, for the sport,” he added.

Hamilton’s Ferrari came to a complete stop. “I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it,” he said. “I’ve never done that before.”

“I hope there is a lesson learned,” he added.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Race control summoned the field into the pits and distributed revised software parameters to all the teams in order to address the problem. The problem added almost an hour to the original delay, caused by rain.

“They had to update the software and then you have to load it into the car,” said Hamilton. “I guess some had some faster laptops than others.”

The FIA confirmed it “removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release” to address the problem.

“It was just like driving at 35 kilometres, going uphill, actually losing speed,” Verstappen explained. “I don’t know exactly, because when you go too low in speed and too low RPM, for whatever reason, then it just bogs down, and normally it takes one or two seconds and it comes back.

“That’s basically also what I had in the start. But somehow that didn’t trigger in the first software round, and then in the second software round it was a bit better, luckily.”

Sports.title: FIA blames “unprecedented” circumstances for car stoppages on formation lap | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA says an unexpected combination of factors caused the car stoppages which delayed the start of today’s race.

Multiple drivers encountered technical problems during the original attempt to start the race which followed the delay due to rain. Max Verstappen , Lewis Hamilton and others suffered a serious loss of power, causing their cars to slow and delay the rest of the pack.

Race control eventually abandoned the attempt to start the race and summoned the field back into the pits. The race finally started some 50 minutes later after software changes were applied to the cars.

The FIA confirmed the problem originated with its systems and said it would look into it.

“On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars,” it said in a statement.

“As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race.

“This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.”

However Fernando Alonso claimed several drivers “stopped on the formation lap” and should not have been allowed to restart. “It’s the first time I see it,” he said. “I had half of the races this year with DNF and we never stopped the race. I hope they can do it next time we stop.”
