World.title: Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz?
World.content:
Crude exports bypassing Hormuz surged in September, yet oil prices remain high. Could a secret fee be the reason?

Share Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz? on social media

Middle East oil exports have climbed back above levels seen before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, despite Tehran’s attempts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and attack vessels.

Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September, reaching between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day (bpd), according to provisional data from maritime tracking firm Kpler. Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd.

This surge in oil exports from the region has so far largely been attributed to US ships shepherding tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with increasing ship-to-ship transfers that reduce the risks of being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones. Meanwhile, the fact that oil prices have remained high has been explained by analysts as the result of still-elevated insurance rates — driven by fears of Iranian attacks — and a market factoring in the possibility of a return to a hot war.

But a senior Kpler analyst last week offered a different explanation for the rise in oil exports at high prices. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo.

Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

Does this explanation hold up, and what does it mean for the war and oil prices?

What did the Kpler analyst say?

Michelle Brohard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, recently said some countries could be paying Iran for passage through the Strait of Hormuz.



“I suspect there is a toll that’s being paid, which is giving these ships safe passage,” she said in an interview last week with energy analyst Rory Johnston.

“I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added.

“So you’re starting to see like what I would call like a race to get out as much as possible, as quickly as possible before the war restarts.”

The claim has not been independently verified, and Brohard presented it as speculation rather than a finding backed by evidence.

But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait.

The Trump administration, during the course of the war, has repeatedly said Iran will not be permitted to charge a toll under any potential agreement with Washington.

Closure of the strait has caused global fuel costs to soar and has tested agricultural sectors across the world.

What does traffic in the Hormuz look like?

Oil is increasingly getting out of the Middle East, marine trackers report.

In the last week of September, the seven-day average climbed above the roughly 18 million bpd recorded before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February – the first time since the conflict started.

Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September.

The pattern of increasing oil exports has continued into October. Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company on Saturday announced that it had transported two million barrels of crude on a very ‌large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general said was the company’s first such operation in decades.

According to Kpler, “40 percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore”, with much of it flowing through Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pipelines.

The export figures also include supplies moved through the Red Sea, which has become an increasingly important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Moreover, the Kpler figures exclude any vessels that may have crossed the key transit route with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.

Iran, however, disputes suggestions that it has lost control of the waterway.



Senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi said on Sunday only three to four million bpd were travelling along a US-supervised route and described that amount as “negligible” compared with pre-war traffic.

Before the war erupted seven months ago, the strait routinely saw about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships.

Where are oil prices right now?

Oil prices have eased marginally as exports from the Middle East recover. Last week, the Group of Seven countries also announced a decision to release 100 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves.

But crude prices remain significantly higher than pre-war levels. Brent crude was trading at about $101.59 a barrel on Monday, down 0.71 percent, while US West Texas Intermediate fell 1.2 percent to about $90.05.

“Despite exports from the region resurging, much will depend, longer-term, on the security of energy supplies,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, noting that the “situation is still tense”.

“The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with the attack on another tanker on Sunday keeping worries bubbling about the potential for further disruption to supplies, particularly if shipping companies become increasingly reluctant to risk sending vessels through the crucial chokepoint.”

On Monday, an oil tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was instructed by the IRGC to turn back or risk being targeted, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) group that monitors shipping traffic.

Does the Kpler analyst’s claim hold weight?

Academic Abdul Khalique says while Kpler analyst Brohard’s speculation that a transit-fee arrangement has been put in place may be “plausible”, it is best described as an “informal security mechanism rather than a formal maritime levy”.

“No public proof confirms a systematic, state-run Iranian toll system,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.

He said the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) safeguards transit passage through international straits, “rendering formal tolls legally dubious”.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that Brohard’s suspected scenario was “in part” possible.

“Everything appears to be happening under the radar in the Middle East, from the US convoying ships to Iran quietly charging tolls,” he told Al Jazeera.

In September, the US government also imposed sanctions on a digital assets firm, BitBank, that it said had been used by Iran’s Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority — a body set up by the country’s government to collect fees for allowing the safe transit of vessels through the strait — to transfer money to Tehran.

However, Beauchamp said the biggest challenge for oil exports was now what he called the “problem of shipping”.

“The shuttle system in the Gulf is doing wonders in getting oil out, but it requires plenty of ships, and that has pushed freight rates higher while also reducing supply beyond the region itself,” he added.



According to Beauchamp, Asian buyers are having to find crude from further away too, “lengthening transit times”.

“Previously a supply story, this is now one about the underlying mechanics of shipping. While less exciting, it is arguably much more important and trickier to solve,” he said.

“Ships don’t get built overnight.”

World.title: Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism?
World.content:
Israel condemns the move as the party’s vote causes an uproar, including among party members.

Share Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism? on social media

The United Kingdom’s Green Party has voted to define Zionism as a form of racism, drawing condemnation from the Israeli government.

In a binding vote held at the party’s conference over the weekend, members voted to usher in the new definition as well as a series of other strongly pro-Palestine policies.

However, just as the resolution has drawn international criticism, it has also proved internally controversial with four of the party’s five members in parliament opposing it.

Israel on Monday banned party leader Zack Polanski from the country just a day before the politician faces a by-election as he runs in the London constituency that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer represented.

Zionism emerged as a political ideology in the late 19th century. It called for the creation of a Jewish homeland at a time of rising anti-Semitism and persecution of Jews in Europe. Theodore Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist considered the father of political Zionism, originally proposed an independent and colonial Jewish state in either Palestine or Argentina.

Here’s what we know about what the Greens have said:

What is the resolution?

The Greens endorsed the motion to equate Zionism with racism by a vote of 1,022 to 813.

In addition, the party restated its “commitment to Palestinian liberation” and called for the “establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”.



The party also recommitted to its support of Palestinians’ right of return as well as to the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement against Israel.

“The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians,” a Green Party statement said.

A significant number of party members, including four of its five MPs, were against parts of the resolution, exposing divisions within the party.

Codeputy leader Rachel Millward said in a post on X that while the party is committed to “stop the genocide”, the term Zionism means “different things to different people, … so I personally do not think the policy helps us do the work we all want to”.

Meanwhile, Polanski, who is Jewish and was away campaigning during the vote, told journalists afterwards that if Zionism equates to the displacement of Palestinians, “that is clearly racist.”

Polanski said he, however, did not support the reference to a single Palestinian state and external entities should not decide what a future state would look like.

How has Israel responded?

Israel has accused the party of legitimising “terrorism”, and senior officials equated it to anti-Semitism.

“The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on social media.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would “deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the party was “racist”.

The Green Party has rejected equating criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism and reiterated its stance against “any form of discrimination or harassment”.

“We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people,” Polanski and other senior party members said in a statement on Sunday.

Has Zionism been equated to racism before?

Yes. In 1975, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution that “determines that Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”.

The vote was sponsored by the Soviet bloc and the Arab League. It passed after 72 countries, largely from the Middle East and Africa, voted for it. Israel and 34 other countries – chiefly from the West – were against it. Thirty-two other countries abstained.

Just a year before, at the 1974 General Assembly, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat had given his “olive branch” speech at the General Assembly.



About the same time, African countries opposing the apartheid regime in South Africa, which was increasingly allying with Israel, had resolved separately that the Israeli government was “racist” and both had an “imperialist origin.”

Also, in 1975, at the first international women’s conference, held in Mexico City, attendees decided there would be no international peace outside the “elimination of foreign occupation, Zionism, apartheid” and all other forms of “racial discrimination”.

However, the General Assembly vote proved controversial. Chaim Herzog, then-Israeli ambassador to the UN and later president, told the assembly in a speech that it was “based on hatred, falsehood and arrogance” and proceeded to rip up copies of the resolution in front of the audience.

The US too accused the UN of making “anti-Semitism international law”.

In December 1991, the US, under President George HW Bush, stepped up a campaign to revoke the resolution with Bush declaring at the UN that equating Zionism with racism “is to reject Israel itself” and to “challenge its right to exist”.

Israel also insisted it would not participate in the Madrid Peace Process to continue negotiations between Israel and Palestinian leaders if the resolution was not cancelled.

After much pressure from the US, an overwhelming majority of countries voted for its revocation – 111 to 25, including European and African countries.

Who else equates Zionism with racism?

Jewish Voice for Peace, the American anti-Zionist and pro-Palestinian advocacy group, has also named Zionism as a movement that creates a “racist hierarchy with European Jews at the top”.

In a February statement, the group reiterated its stance against what it called the “colonial ideology” of Zionism’s founders.

Similarly, in the United Kingdom, an employment tribunal in 2024 backed anti-Zionist activist and professor David Miller, who was earlier sacked from his post at the University of Bristol in 2021 for his views that the movement was “inherently racist”.

World.title: Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us
World.content:
Analysts say Flavio Bolsonaro is projected to win a run-off vote on October 25 and become Brazil’s next president.

Share Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us on social media

Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has exceeded expectations in the first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio ‌Lula da Silva, triggering a run-off later this month.

“Brazil wants change, and I am very happy with the results,” Bolsonaro told reporters in Brasilia on Sunday as he saluted “the end of the era of [Lula’s] Workers’ Party”.

The 45-year-old ⁠son of right-wing former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, now faces an October 25 showdown with the 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.

‌In the run-up to Sunday’s first-round vote, a series of polls showed a close race between Lula and Bolsonaro, with the incumbent president poised to win by about 3 percentage points against his right-wing challenger.

In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections, Bolsonaro beat Lula with 47 percent of the vote, while Lula got 45.1 percent.

Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro.

Why is Bolsonaro favoured to win Brazil’s election?

Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected performance is likely to buoy his campaign and may bolster Brazil’s currency and stock market, which have risen on the prospects of the business-friendly challenger.

Oliver Stuenkel, professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) in San Paulo, Brazil, said Lula was in a difficult position as he could not count on voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates to vote for him in the second round.



“Not only is he behind now after this first round, but the other candidates who received a total of nearly 8 percent are largely centre-right, which means that the people who voted for these other candidates are very unlikely to shift for Lula,” Stuenkel told Al Jazeera.

“So he must change his campaign tactics and above all mobilise a significant part of people who stayed at home,” he added. About 30 million Brazilians – 21 percent of the electorate – did not vote in the first round.

Al Jazeera’s Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Rio de Janeiro, said Lula supporters felt their candidate had not used social media as effectively as the right-wing camp. “This is something they have to work on in the second round,” Yanakiew said.

From a historical perspective, however, such efforts are unlikely to change the outcome. “Unless something very unusual happens in the next three weeks, Flavio Bolsonaro is set to win,” Stuenkel said. “In Brazilian presidential politics, no candidate who came second in the first round ended up winning the presidency since 1989.”

Has the Bolsonaro family taken hold of Brazil?

Several politicians from the Bolsonaro family have won congressional races taking place as part of the broader nationwide general elections.

Michelle Bolsonaro, wife of former President Jair Bolsonaro and stepmother of Flavio, won a Senate seat in the Federal District, home to the capital, Brasilia.

In June, the 44-year-old, who has never held government office, had a public falling out with her stepson, whom she accused of disrespecting her in lengthy videos posted on her social media. The pair later made up.

Ex-leader Bolsonaro’s second son Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, was the second most-voted senatorial candidate in the southern Santa Catarina state and won a seat in the Senate.

The fourth and younger son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of Congress.

Some experts credit “antipetismo” — a trend of hostility against Lula’s PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family’s rise to political power.

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies while Lula’s PT got 70.

What are the implications of a Bolsonaro win?

Brazil’s presidential election carries significant regional and geopolitical implications.

Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman said Lula has been “on a collision course” with United States President Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of the Bolsonaro camp.

“That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman said.



While Bolsonarism is strongly aligned with the US and Israel, Brazil also has a tight economic relationship with China, its largest trade partner. Bolsonaro has portrayed Trump as an ally and is expected to strengthen ties with Washington if elected.

In case of a win, the younger Bolsonaro has pledged to seek a congressional amnesty for his father, who is in prison over his role in a coup plot following his election loss to Lula by 1.8 percentage points in 2022. That would need approval from both houses of Congress, which are currently dominated by conservatives.

Similar to Trump, the Bolsonaros have made rigged election claims. The insurrection that shook Brasilia in January 2023 shared similarities with the storming of the US Capitol two years prior. Like Trump, Bolsonaro has also pledged to release his father’s supporters responsible for the coup.

Concerns about US intervention in Brazil’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign. Lula has accused the Trump administration of using tariffs and other means to interfere with Brazilian affairs.

Vinicius de Carvalho, a lecturer in Brazilian studies at King’s College London, UK, stressed that Latin America has been experiencing a right-wing wave, with the election of US-aligned governments. This includes Ecuador, El Salvador, Panama and Paraguay.

By contrast, Lula was part of the so-called “pink tide” in Latin America, a wave of left-leaning governments that came to power in the late 1990s and early 2000s. With Congress stacked against him, if Lula is re-elected, he will still need to “respond to some demands of the right”, de Carvalho said.

World.title: Lionel Messi to join Argentina for farewell match against Benin
World.content:
The friendly marks a symbolic passing of the torch for a player whose international legacy includes a World Cup title.

Lionel Messi will bring the curtain down on his glittering Argentina career with a farewell friendly against Benin that marks the dawn of a new era for the South American champions.

After more than two decades of service to his country, the 39-year-old superstar will hand over the captain’s armband for good as he makes his final appearance in the Albiceleste jersey on Tuesday at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires.

Messi will be joined for his international swansong by 85,000 spectators and several of the teammates with whom he reached the pinnacle of football at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, alongside members of Argentina’s emerging generation.

The friendly marks a symbolic passing of the torch for a player whose international legacy includes a World Cup title, two Copa America crowns and the Finalissima.

Messi will also bow out as Argentina’s record appearance-maker and leading scorer with 125 goals in 207 games as well as a record 68 assists.

His farewell comes two and a half months after Argentina’s ill-tempered World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression.

“I gave it my all. I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote when announcing his international retirement in August.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028 although after the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Friends reunited

Members of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup-winning squad and their families will join Messi for Tuesday’s farewell against Benin, ranked 93rd in the world.



Veterans of that Doha triumph, such as Angel Di Maria, who retired from international football in 2024, will be there to witness the passing of the torch to a new generation charged with extending the Albiceleste’s golden era.

Several of the newcomers, including Franco Mastantuono and Leonel Flores, were not even born when “La Pulga” (“The Flea”) made his Argentina debut in 2005 for a team whose history had for so long been dominated by Diego Maradona.

“It’s going to be an unforgettable day for everyone. Everyone wants to be at this match, and now it’s just about enjoying it,” Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said.

Argentina’s new generation has already shown what it can do without its captain although nobody is pretending that replacing a man regarded by many as the greatest footballer in history will be straightforward.

“Collectively, we will try to fill the void left by Leo,” said Scaloni, who is negotiating a contract extension after leaving his future unresolved following the World Cup defeat in July.

Scaloni, who mastered the art of building the right supporting cast around Messi, will also say goodbye on Tuesday to 38-year-old vice captain Nicolas Otamendi.

Like Messi and Otamendi, midfielders Rodrigo De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso were called up solely for the Benin game, raising the possibility that neither will represent Argentina again.

New generation

Those certain to be involved, at least from the bench, include other veterans of the 2022 World Cup who will be the standard-bearers for Argentina after Messi: defender Cristian Romero, midfielders Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernandez, and forwards Julian Alvarez and Lautaro Martinez.

Tenacious centre back Romero is set to inherit the captain’s armband, first worn by Messi at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez and Lautaro Martinez are next in the captain hierarchy.

They have already begun to rally around Messi’s heirs, who showed their appetite for success in Argentina’s first game since the World Cup final, against Bolivia in Cordoba on Wednesday.

Argentina swept the Bolivians aside 4-0 with young talents Nico Paz and Jose Manuel Lopez among the scorers.

They followed that victory with a 7-0 rout of Burkina Faso at the Monumental on Saturday with Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni scoring their first international goals.

While Argentina’s future is beginning to take shape, one small but symbolically significant question remains: Who will inherit Messi’s number 10 shirt?



“We won’t give the number 10 to anyone until Leo’s match takes place,” Scaloni said. “After that, we’ll see.”

World.title: In Russia-occupied Oleshky, Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines
World.content:
Ukrainians suffering from food shortages are turning to weeds for sustenance in a town where bodies are reportedly eaten by dogs.

Kyiv, Ukraine – On the day of her 41st wedding anniversary, Vera Gulyaeva recalled her husband’s life and death.

In March, a Russian drone plunged into a bread line in the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky, killing several people and wounding Serhiy Gulyaev, a retired 63-year-old driver.

The town in the Kherson region had already been occupied for more than four years, and its 2,000 remaining residents spent the last two and a half years without electricity, running water, natural gas or healthcare.

The Gulyaevs, who had met at a friends’ wedding in 1985, lived in a small house they had built. They were reluctant to leave even after their children fled to Kyiv-controlled areas.

They had an orchid, a vegetable patch, five hens, a water well and a power generator that ran on the overpriced gas they occasionally bought from middlemen.

“I almost never left the house,” Gulyaeva, a stately 64-year-old retired schoolteacher told Al Jazeera. “The husband occasionally went out to buy bread.”

The bread-line attack left him with deep cranial wounds. She tried to get him to a hospital 80km (50 miles) away in the city of Skadovsk but failed as the ambulance ran over a landmine on the road.

Days later, a second attempt worked – but Gulyaev died in the hospital.

She recovered his remains, had them cremated and returned home with his ashes.

Now, she lives in western Ukraine with her daughter-in-law and two grandchildren while her son fights Russian forces.



Gulyaeva left behind all her family photos, friends and neighbours – several of whom have since died.

“People ate all of the food they’d stashed. People are starving,” Gulyaeva said of the food shortage stalking the town.

After four decades of teaching in the elementary school she had attended as a child, she still cannot fathom “how people can kill other people”.

Some residents survive on what they have farmed, stashed or found in abandoned apartments or houses. Others try to reach the nearest functioning grocery shop in the neighbouring village of Radensk, 20km (12.4 miles) away, to buy food.

But some never return.

A resident who fled the town but remains in contact with some residents told Al Jazeera that people have been killed by Russian drones or landmines. The bodies left out in the open are eaten by feral dogs.

On Thursday alone, there were four casualties. As they tried to get to Radensk, two people were killed and two were injured and brought back on a wheelbarrow and a bike.

“The choice that Russia leaves every day to civilian residents – stay and starve to death, leave and risk getting blown on a landmine,” Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram on Saturday.

European officials said the situation in Oleshky proves that Kyiv should not give in to Moscow’s demands to cede its land.

“When someone says: ‘Why don’t they just give up these territories?’ it sounds so simple. Right? But in reality, this is about the people who will suffer on those territories,” European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said on September 28.

Moscow, which has denied targeting civilians throughout the war, has acknowledged the humanitarian disaster but blamed Kyiv.

“There are, indeed, problems with delivering food and medical drugs [because] the Kyiv regime literally does everything to thwart these deliveries,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed on September 20. “Drones always hover in the air, killing people.”

Pro-Russian figures in occupied areas support his claims.

“Those who wanted to leave have left. No one is being held here,” an anonymous pro-Russian woman who runs a Telegram channel on life in Oleshky wrote on September 28. “Unfortunately, locals are afraid to speak on camera” because they have relatives on the Ukrainian side, she claimed. “The elderly live under Ukrainian shelling but are afraid to talk.”



Her claims are a far cry from what Ukrainian officials say.

‘There’s nothing’

Most Oleshky residents eat once a day, according to Tetiana Khasanenko, Oleshky’s mayor, who fled to the Kyiv-controlled side but maintains constant contact with the remaining residents.

Some have found old, dried macaroni to sustain themselves. Some eat whatever they manage to grow next to their houses. And some resort to common purslane – a watery weed that contains next to no protein and can be eaten raw.

“There’s no flour, no meat, no oil, no sugar, no salt,” Hasanenko told Al Jazeera. “There’s nothing.”

She accused Russia of using the residents as human shields.

Russian soldiers are a constant threat in the town with no functioning civilian administration, she said.

They move into the remaining houses without permission and force the residents to feed them and find alcohol.

“They’re often on drugs,” Hasanenko claimed. “But they’re armed. They threaten.”

Oleshky is about 10km (6 miles) west of the regional capital, Kherson, but Russians blew up the 1,400-metre (1,530-yard) bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Europe’s largest, in November 2022 while retreating from the city.

The delivery of food and drugs is perilous and complicated.

The last attempts to get lifesaving cargo to Oleshky in cars were cut short by landmines and drone attacks.

Ukraine has managed to fly several tonnes of food on drones, but retrieving it is complicated.

Most survivors have left their war-damaged houses and apartment buildings to move to the buildings that are more or less intact.

And even if some people manage to charge their mobile phones and contact the Ukrainian side, they “don’t give exact geolocations because they’re afraid”, Hasanenko said.

“Because if there’s a food drop, Russian soldiers will punish them for it,” she said.

Knowing about the remaining residents’ daily ordeal, those who escaped are tormented with guilt.

“You don’t get any joy from life knowing that something like that is happening in our country,” Gulyeva said. “This is a huge tragedy.”

World.title: No10 insists UK military base RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
World.content:
The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats."

It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year.

But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe.

Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks.

Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday.

World.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.

Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.

The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.

In a televised address on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".

Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for SÃ¡nchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.

"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," SÃ¡nchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".

SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.

Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
World.content:
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.

The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.

The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.

He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.

Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".

World.title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.

The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, FranÃ§ois-Xavier Lauch.

"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.

Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.

There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.

AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.

However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl who it said was near the teenager as saying he did not pick up the grenade.

"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.

When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.

"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.

A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".

The incident took place close to the Auguste BÃ©hal high school, the prefect said.

Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.

"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.

"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."

The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.

"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."

This is not the first time students have been seriously injured during the recent wave of protests in France. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.

The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez has announced an investigation.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".

"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.

"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."

World.title: Nobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain
World.content:
US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.

Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works.

The Nobel Committee, external praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".

In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment.

World.title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
World.content:
For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there.

"Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC.

"Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"

Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments.

"I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.

Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.

US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.

Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.

World.title: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say
World.content:
Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives.

Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state.

The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping.

Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; Â£28,440), which he could not afford.

"There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.

Adewale appealed to the government for help.

Those kidnapped had been travelling from Ibadan in the south-west to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states on Thursday when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state.

The NYSC is a compulsory one-year programme for most Nigerian university and polytechnic graduates. Participants, known as corps members, are posted to different parts of the country to work and take part in community service, as well as to foster a sense of national unity.

World.title: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round of Brazil election
World.content:
Right-wing FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of an outright majority.

There will be a run-off between the two candidates on 25 October.

Bolsonaro is the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election.

Sunday's vote was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With almost all of the votes counted, Bolsonaro has 47% to Lula's 45% of the vote.

Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other candidates knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.

His Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.

The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil â Latin America's largest country and economy â will follow suit.

After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".

Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".

World.title: BNXN’s 16 is quiet reflection on the cost of success
World.content:
BNXN’s “16” is a song about routine, but it is not necessarily a celebration of it. Released as the third track on his six-song EP, Still In Charge, the song finds BNXN looking back at the discipline that has shaped his journey while confronting what years of repetition, ambition and success can do to a person.

Over a restrained Afro-fusion production by Walahisteph, the singer presents himself as both the beneficiary and prisoner of his own routine.

“E don dey my routine, since I was 16 / Never to lose my focus / I dey work like machine / But since na my routine / I just dey move like robot,” he sings on the chorus.

It is a simple refrain, but it carries much of the song’s weight. BNXN isn’t merely saying he’s worked hard since he was 16. The comparison to a machine, followed by “I just dey move like robot,” introduces a subtle tension: the same discipline that has helped him remain focused may also have made his life increasingly mechanical.

That is where “16” becomes more interesting than a straightforward hustle anthem.

Sound of repetition

Walahisteph keeps the production deliberately uncluttered. Rather than building toward a huge instrumental moment, the producer creates a steady pocket that keeps BNXN’s vocals at the centre of attention.

The guitar work, credited to Fiokee, adds warmth to the arrangement, while the understated production gives the song a late-night quality. There is movement, but very little urgency.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

That choice works because it mirrors the subject matter. The beat itself feels routine. It moves forward without rushing, almost as though it knows exactly where it is going.

BNXN’s vocal performance complements this approach. He sounds comfortable, occasionally weary, but never overly dramatic.

Ambition to isolation

The song becomes more personal when BNXN shifts from his work ethic to relationships.

“Give me soft landing o / We don’t need no surveyors / You don fly go Paris / You don leave me for Lagos,” he sings.

Here, BNXN asks whether a relationship can survive when one person keeps moving forward, and the other is left behind.

His reference to fame, “And do you expect me to move on, is it because I’m famous?” gives the song another layer. Fame has changed the circumstances, but it has not necessarily made emotional problems easier.

A distinctly Lagos identity also runs through the song. References to Eko, Bima and the streets prevent “16” from becoming a generic success story. BNXN remains rooted in the environment he emerged from, even as the song acknowledges the distance his career has created.

The line “these streets won’t contain us” is particularly effective because it can be read in more than one way. It can refer to romance, ambition or the limitations of the environment itself. The streets that shaped him may no longer be large enough to accommodate the person he has become.

Where the song works, and where it doesn’t

“16” is strongest when it stays with its central idea of routine.

The chorus is repetitive, but intentionally so. The repetition reinforces what BNXN is describing. He has done this for years, and the listener hears that cycle in the song’s structure.

However, the verses do not always develop that idea with the same depth.

The romantic section introduces interesting possibilities but does not fully explore them. BNXN hints at loneliness, fame, distance and desire, yet moves between those ideas rather quickly. The result is a song with a stronger central concept than narrative development.

There is also little structural evolution. Once “16” settles into its groove, it largely stays there. For listeners who appreciate BNXN’s laid-back melodic style, this is part of the appeal. But for those looking for a dramatic musical or emotional payoff, the song may feel too comfortable.

That comfort, however, may be precisely the point.

“16” does not attempt to reinvent BNXN. Instead, it sounds like an artiste becoming increasingly comfortable with the musical identity he has built.

There is no desperate attempt to manufacture a viral moment or introduce an unfamiliar persona. BNXN trusts his voice, his writing style and the atmosphere he has created over the years.

Rating: 7.5/10

World.title: Our president is ready to kick, ready to work, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
When President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua departed the shores of Nigeria for medical treatment in Saudi Arabia on November 23, 2009, I served as Chairman of the Editorial Board of the National Life newspaper. The publication was owned by then Senator Bola Ahmed Tinubu, national leader of the opposition Action Congress of Nigeria, (ACN) and today the President of Nigeria.

Official releases claimed Yar’Adua suffered from acute pericarditis, compounded by a chronic renal condition. What was framed as a brief consultation stretched into an agonizing, month-long absence. In February 2010, Yar’Adua was clandestinely smuggled back at nocturne, shielded from the citizens he was elected to govern. Barely three months later, on May 5, 2010, his passage came like a rude awakening. He was said to have caved in to the Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma disease.

Former President Olusegun Obasanjo later vehemently denied deliberately imposing a terminally ill candidate. Yet, he conceded a critical truth: he was fully aware of Yar’Adua’s severe health challenges prior to handpicking him. Yar’Adua’s declining health was never a state secret. During the presidential campaign in early March 2007, his health failed dramatically, necessitating an emergency evacuation to Germany.

I recall seeing him in person during that turbulent period, sitting just a few seats away from him. It was on his visit to then governor of Enugu State. Yar’Adua bore the unmistakable visage of a deeply frail man, his left hand bearing cicatrix of an engrafted flesh. He was accompanied by a stockily built aide carrying a shoulder pouch of essential medications. As the man who wore a single lapel of dual attributions as Katsina State governor and PDP presidential candidate spoke, that aide decanted drugs into his palm, handed him water and Yar’Adua swallowed them. Whoever drafted a man in such a fragile state into the grueling marathon of governing a nation of over 200 million people could not possibly have had his best interests – or those of the nation – at heart.

As public anxiety deepened, Obasanjo orchestrated a live, televised telephone conversation, making that famous rhetorical question, “Umoru, are you dead or alive?” From his hospital bed, Yar’Adua offered a feeble response of, “I am not dead, I am alive.” Yet, weeks before his inauguration, he was again flown to Germany for urgent treatment. Aso Rock consistently denied the severity of his condition, while political opportunists and religious charlatans issued passionate calls for national fasting and intercession.

It was amid this cacophony of deceit that I wrote a piece in my National Life column with the title, “Why We Must Neither Fast Nor Pray for Yar’Adua.” In it, I invoked that foundational Yoruba proverb: “A kìí jí apiroro – No one wakes the cunning actor who merely simulates sleep; it is only the person who is genuinely asleep that can be awakened. How could a nation genuinely offer prayers for a leader whose inner circle perpetually lied about his physical condition?

Around that same period, the owner of National Life, Bola Tinubu, joined me in what lawyers call consesus ad idem on the Yar’Adua ailment roulette. He launched a scathing verbal assault on the ailing president. In a press release, he declared that “the country is now drifting and groping in the dark, like a ship without a captain, in a stormy ocean.” Tinubu then demanded that Yar’Adua honour Section 145 of the 1999 Constitution by transmitting a written declaration to the National Assembly, empowering Vice-President Goodluck Jonathan to act as President.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Fast-forward sixteen years later, and President Bola Ahmed Tinubu finds himself embroiled in exact same constitutional transgression he once fiercely condemned. He recently went AWOL from his official duties for 30 consecutive days on an undisclosed European sojourn, grossly violating same Section 145, without transmitting power to his Vice President.

This tragic irony brings to mind the classical Yoruba proverb on historical reciprocity: “Tí o bá máa sin ègbón rẹ ní ìhòhò, rántí mú àwọn àbúrà rẹ l’ówó – If you intend to strip your elder brother naked at his burial, remember to bring your younger siblings along to witness the horrifying spectacle. Its moral imperative is timeless: the standard of fairness, empathy, or constitutional integrity you extend to those ahead of you today sets the exact template for how you will be judged when your turn arrives. Today, Nigerians are roiling in unprecedented hunger; petrol sells at a perilous price and hundreds of Nigerians are in kidnappers’ den, yet Tinubu said he enjoyed himself on his Europe vacation and was kicking.

The precedent of national anxiety over the failing health of Nigerian presidents is deeply rooted in our modern political history. Beyond the Yar’Adua era, similar dark clouds hovered during the military dictatorships of Generals Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida and Sani Abacha. Babangida was eventually forced to admit he was suffering from radiculopathy – a painful nerve root compression in the spine caused by an old shrapnel wound – requiring extended medical treatment in Germany.

Similarly, in the final days preceding General Abacha’s sudden demise in June 1998, the dictator appeared in public looking exceptionally gaunt and hollowed out. Investigative publications, most notably TELL magazine, meticulously documented Abacha’s physical decline, noting his strained posture, ashen complexion, drawn features, and hesitant gait. On 8 June, 1998, Abacha passed on inside the Presidential Villa.

Nearly two decades after Abacha’s death, Nigeria entered yet another debilitating cycle of presidential health secrecy under President Muhammadu Buhari. Between 2015 and 2021, Buhari spent hundreds of days in London hospitals undergoing treatments for undisclosed ailments, while his media aides churned out euphemistic press statements that insulted the intelligence of the electorate.

In African political culture, the physical health of a sitting president is almost universally treated with the paranoid secrecy of an Ilédì – the sacred, highly restricted conclave of the traditional Ogboni fraternity. In mature constitutional democracies, however, executive health is recognized as a foundational pillar of political and economic stability. When a leader is incapacitated, executive decision-making stalls, creating dangerous power vacuums, administrative paralysis and governance by unelected cliques.

Modern financial markets thrive on predictability. When a president is incapacitated or shrouded in health rumours, national economies face immediate headwinds: currency volatility, capital flight and stock market declines. Furthermore, in a constitutional democracy, fitness for office is a public trust, not a private matter. When an elected leader lacks the stamina required for daily governance, the presidency devolves into a hollow symbol and the president, a figurine.

Scholars have noted that the instinct of presidential minders to conceal illness stems from traditional African concepts of royalty. In Yoruba traditional political philosophy, it is a deeply rooted taboo to publicly associate a reigning king (Ọba) with human frailty, bodily infirmity or physical decay. The very cognomen of imperial power – Kábíyèsí (K’á bi ó ò sí) – “He who cannot be questioned” – derives from the premise that the king, as Aláṣẹ Èkejì Òrìṣà, embodies the collective vitality of the realm. To publicly admit that an Ọba is sick is to suggest spiritual vulnerability, implying that the kingdom itself is exposed to harm.

Because direct reference to a king’s illness is prohibited, Yoruba culture developed sophisticated euphemisms. To describe a king’s ill health, they say, “Ara Ọba ò dájú” – ” The King’s body is not completely firm”. To announce his passing, one never says he died; rather, Ọba wàjà – “The King has ascended into the vault, the arctic” or, Erin wó, Àjànàkú sùn bí òkè! – “The mighty Elephant has fallen, sprawling endlessly like a huge mountain!”

In two previous essays I did: “The President is a Sick Man: Buhari’s Secret Therapy Inside the ‘Oneida’” (April 4, 2021) and “The President is a Sick Man” (October 20, 2024) I drew a direct historical arc from 19th century American presidential health cover-ups, to modern Africa. I argued that stealth medical trips disguised as “working vacations” mirror the Yoruba idiomatic phrase of “Ó jọ gáté, kò jọ gàté, ó fi ẹsè méjì tiro gáte-gàte.” This descriptive phrase captures an awkward attempt to conceal an obvious impairment, where the effort to hide a physical limp only makes the uncoordinated gait more conspicuous to onlookers.

Nigeria’s Fourth Republic has suffered from a long lineage of presidential medical secrecy, mirroring global precedents of leaders attempting to govern behind a veil of deception: Grover Cleveland (United States, 1893) underwent secret surgery aboard a private yacht to remove a cancerous tumor; Woodrow Wilson (United States, 1919) suffered a stroke hidden by his wife and physician, who functionally ran the executive branch for over a year; Franklin D. Roosevelt (United States, 1944–1945) concealed advanced congestive heart failure during World War II; Winston Churchill (United Kingdom, 1953) kept a severe stroke quiet during his second term; Georges Pompidou (France, 1974) hid terminal blood cancer until his death in office; and François Mitterrand (France, 1981–1995) falsified routine medical reports for a decade to hide prostate cancer.

Across the African continent, this imperial Kábíyèsí mentality was mirrored by figures such as Malawi’s Peter Mutharika, Gabon’s Ali Bongo, Angola’s José Eduardo dos Santos, and Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe. Save for rare exceptions like President Patrice Talon of the Republic of Benin, who chose absolute transparency by publicly issuing medical bulletins when undergoing surgeries in Paris, African leaders routinely cling to power while foreign medical teams manage their failing bodies.

Upon landing in Lagos from France, a period of absence his press office characterized as a “working vacation” – a phrase alien to the letter and spirit of the Nigerian Constitution, Tinubu declared to reporters that he was “ready to kick, ready to work; nothing wrong.” As he uttered those words, I imagine foreign medical specialists who might have spent (I have no evidence of this) the preceding month treating him, must have marveled at the mendacity of Third World political elites. As Yoruba elders wisely observe: A kìí mọ Òṣó ju ìyá Òṣó lọ – no one can claim to know the secrets of Ọṣọ better than Ọṣọ’s own mother. It remains entirely futile to try to awaken someone who is actively simulating sleep.

In situations characterised by such deliberate obfuscation, the Yoruba offer another sobering principle – three people cannot sit simultaneously in twos. Tinubu’s trip follows an established pattern of unannounced stopovers, unrecorded medical stays, and evasive PR spins. The dangerous precedent of imperial power arrogance has not been broken; it has been perfected, supported by a legislature that functions like a rubber stamp.

Unbeknownst to the powerful, the pendulum of human health swings to a rhythm that no sovereign decree can alter. Over the last century, international standards have shifted away from feudal secrecy, toward openness. In 1967, the US 25th Amendment established clear legal mechanisms for the temporary transfer of authority during medical procedures. This was used seamlessly by Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush. Other world leaders, such as Hugo Chávez of Venezuela, Fernando Lugo of Paraguay and Hage Geingob of Namibia openly disclosed their diagnoses and treatments, treating their citizens with respect and honesty.

Why do leaders today, especially Third World leaders, go to such lengths to hide their health struggles? Historically, political minders have viewed illness as a sign of vulnerability, operating under the delusion that hiding an illness preserves an image of strength. The fundamental error in this reasoning is the belief that health is an earned privilege guaranteed by high office.

No, they are wrong! Good health is neither static nor subject to executive command. It is a divine trust, entirely independent of human power. When our bodies enjoy vigour, it is an unearned gift from the Creator, who classical philosophers call the Uncaused Causer. We operate under a temporary mercy that can be recalled at any moment. Humankind may construct vast medical institutions, yet we remain unable to command a single cell in our bodies or halt the gradual decay of our mortal frames.

Among the Yoruba, there is an understanding of diseases (Àrùn) from two perspectives. One is from the metaphysical point. Àrùn, they say, is a malevolent being and one of the eight prominent warlords (Ajogun) who war against human flesh. Second, they say that diseases can be provoked by an individual’s moral shortcomings. These include human refusal to adhere to instructions or declining to offer required sacrifices prescribed through divination.

They also hold the holistic view that good health (Ìlera) is the ultimate earthly treasure and, rather than being seen as an absence of disease, it encompasses a state of total equilibrium between the physical, communal and spiritual realms. To them, when someone maintains a fractured relationship with divine creators (Olódùmarè), the deities (Òrìṣà), the ancestors and their community, they are afflicted with illness (àìsàn). The people also hold that health or its reverse is destiny (àyànmó) and sudden ill health, a conflict with one’s destiny.

The general truth is however that, neither power nor wealth can purchase immunity from bodily frailty. Executive office offers no exemption from illness. In the divine ledger, the high and mighty share the exact same vulnerability as the weak and destitute. Performing artificial strength in the face of bodily weakness as Third World leaders do is an exercise in futility. When they do, they are not hiding their physical condition, they merely expose their arrogance.

To demonstrate that it is foolish for any mortal to mock another at their point of physical vulnerability, Sakara music legend, Yesufu Olatunji, once serenaded his close friend, patron, and prominent socialite, Raimi Ishola. In what came out as one of his classic compositions, Olatunji sang in defence of Ishola whose detractors were secretly praying for his demise. I want to substitute Ishola with President Tinubu’s native praise name, Àkànbí, so that that lyric can echo through time. Yusuff’s line runs thus:“Who is seeking your harm, Àkànbí?/Who wishes you ill?”

In another line, he sang, “No one kills the dog simply because it barks incessant warnings/Nor does anyone slaughter the ram merely because it head-butts/No one destroys the he-goat on account of its unruly nature.” Its raw rendition is: “Taa ló ń pe’rí ẹ o?/Èmi ò pe’rí ẹ, Àkànbí” and “A kìí t’oríi gbígbó, k’á pa ajá o…/A kìí t’oríí kíkàn k’á pa àgbò…/A kìí t’oríí wérewère pa òbúkọ…”

The Ishola serenade ended with another classic statement about how Nigerians may be battling masters of deception in their presidents’ health. He sang: “No one plays the Ikoto game with a crafty master – “A kìí b’ọlọgbọn ta ìkòto.” Okoto or ikoto is a traditional children’s game played with discarded battery head, plastic bottle caps, or a snail shell with a spiral, spinning-top shape.

If President Tinubu were to come clean with the Nigerian people regarding his health challenges, he would find a compassionate public ready to offer supplications to the Creator for redemption. Such candour would signify a mature admission that he is neither a deity nor a superhuman.

No human being is. Many of us have such human battles. Tinubu and Donald Trump shit like all of us and their poo-poo smells like all perishable humanity’s. Every single one of us carries the weight of human frailty and we will all eventually drop this decaying outer garment – this temporary àgó called mortality, just as flowers shed their petals as their season ends.

Akpabio and Obono-Obla’s bala-bala

When your speech appears to contain gibberish or is empty, a famous Yoruba slang gives such talk the moniker, bala-bala or in another context, pala-pala. None of the two has a formal linguistic translation or meaning but have existed long enough to gain individual notoriety. Last week, two Nigerians, both of the APC, spat such nonsensical talks that they could jolly well qualify for the slangs above.

Last week, Senate President Godswill Akpabio mounted the gibberish podium. Give it to him: Akpabio is a professor of gibberish. Sometimes, many wonder if Nigeria’s senate president first talks before engaging his thinking cap. At a senate plenary last week, like an illusionist or magician who Yoruba call the pidan-pidan, Akpabio stunned an unshockable Nigerian people by heaving out a bag of magical statement: He has never truly been a member of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

“My spirit might be there, but my heart was never there,” the senator, who deserves to be garlanded “the most loquacious parliamentarian in Nigerian history,” said.

That pala-pala came when a motion to beatify late former Kogi State governor, Ibrahim Idris, came at plenary. And Senator Jibrin Isah went nostalgic of a time when all of them belonged to the PDP. Akpabio then jumped into the fray anddenounced the label, saying he had always rejected the label, describing himself as a “progressive” who was never a true member of the party.

Now, what can pass as bala-bala more than this? Sometimes when a talk verges on the idiotic, Yoruba call it pala-pala ilu apala (as inchoate as Apala music drumming). If you ask me whether Apala music’s symphony is discordant, I will say ‘no’. I however think the authors of that phrase were just having a nice time with the onomatopoeia and assonance in it.

The man who said his “heart was never there” served for eight years as governor of PDP’s Akwa Ibom State from 2007 to 2015. He was nominated by PDP governors to be their chair at the PDP Governors’ Forum. In 2015, he became Senator on the PDP platform and rose to become PDP’s Senate Minority Leader, from 2015 until 2018. If a man occupied such pinnacle of a political party in over a decade, yet felt no qualms in ditching his benefactor by saying his “heart was never there,” then President Bola Tinubu must be wary of Akpabio. I do not think Judas Iscariot did worse thing to our Lord Jesus Christ.

The spit of Akpabio’s bala-bala had hardly dried when Okoi Obono-Obla, APC founding member, mounted the saddle. He was on a national television last week. Ordinarily in Yorubaland, when you wake up early in the morning to be confronted by a messy and unpleasant scene, of the texture I found strung to Obono-Obla’s mouth that morning, the day is totally fouled up. Nothing good could come out of it. You are advised by our forefathers to go back to bed for a remedial of a metaphysically damaged day. Upon listening to Obono-Obla, I did the needful and re-hugged my pillow.

Listen to the bala-bala: There is nothing wrong with the Rainbow Coalition being championed by FCT minister, Nyesom Wike. “Such is not knew in Nigeria”, he further went on and cited a Kenyan coalition and what he said was an alliance of the ruling NPN of Shehu Shagari government of the Second Republic with the PRP. Yet another, he said: “Reverend Jesse Jackson formed a coalition (that) was a mixed bag of Republicans, Democrats, African Americans, Asian Americans, Latinos, conservatives, and socialists.”

Then he veered into what seemed to vex him most. APC governors had marginalised and alienated original party members like him. He then justified Wike’s interloping role by saying “APC governors are responsible for the circumstances under which Minister Wike is trying to draw people into his coalition.” Not done, when asked about the present state of the PDP, he said, “I don’t think the PDP is scattered.” He justified that cant by saying Wike’s PDP had “candidates nominated to INEC, the PDP has candidates in almost all parts of the country, unlike the NNPP or ADC. The PDP is still there, largely thanks to the efforts of Wike. That is good for the country’s democracy.”

First, in that interview, Obono-Obla committed what is called the fallacy of false analogy. What the ruling NPN did in 1979 was to form a working legislative and political coalition with the NPP shortly after the 1979 elections. Their aim was to secure a working majority in the National Assembly. The alliance however collapsed in 1981, three years after, due to mutual political discordant tunes. The other analogies Obono-Obla gave were what they were: “bala-bala” and “pala-pala ilu apala”!

While all the examples he gave were institutional, involving political parties in alliance, what we have with Wike’s solo romp in the APC has a flavour similar only to what Chief Bola Ige did under Olusegun Obasanjo in 1999. The man of honour that the Immortal Ige was, he retraced his steps out of the bind when he found out that it was like tying one’s legs to a spot with the Yoruba rope called “okun agba.”

I think, between Obono-Obla and Godswill Akpabio, last week was laced with enough gibberish to last a lifetime.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Court sentences man to death by hanging for murder
World.content:
The Anambra State High Court in Idemili Judicial Division on Monday sentenced a man, Ikechukwu Okoye, to death by hanging for murdering his family friend’s wife and stealing her property.

Judge A.O. Okuma convicted Mr Okoye of murder and theft.

Delivering the judgement, the judge dismissed the convict’s claim of self-defence.

The court, however, held that the charge of armed robbery could not be sustained because the defendant had killed the deceased before forming the intention to steal her property.

Earlier, the prosecution, led by Victoria Ononye-Ekwerekwu, a chief state counsel, and including Florence Abadom-Igweike and Nkiru Nzekwu, both principal state counsel, told the court that Mr Okoye went to the residence of the victim, Blessing Mba, at Abime Village, Oba, on 22 February 2024, to steal a multi-purpose grinding machine.

The prosecution stated that an argument ensued between Mr Okoye and the deceased, during which Mr Okoye struck Mrs Mba on the head with a pestle, causing her death.

The prosecution said Mr Okoye dragged the deceased’s body into her children’s room, covered it with their clothes and took away her grinding machine and generator.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It said Mr Okoye then boarded a commercial motorcycle to Afor Oba Market with the stolen items.

According to the prosecution, the deceased’s husband, who had earlier taken their children to school, spotted Mr Okoye on the motorcycle with his wife’s grinding machine and generator.

It said the husband, upon returning home, discovered his wife’s lifeless body in the children’s room and alerted security operatives, who later arrested Okoye at Afor Oba Market with the stolen items.

Mr Okoye, in his defence, denied the offence, disowned his extra-judicial statement in which he admitted committing the offence and pleaded self-defence.

(NAN)

World.title: Zamfara govt approves contract for 53km Gusau-Jauri-Dogon-Kade-Nasarawar Mailayi-Nasarawar Godel road
World.content:
The Zamfara State Executive Council presided over by Governor Dauda Lawal, has approved the award of contract for the construction of the 53-kilometre Gusau–Jauri–Dogon Kade–Nasarawar Mailayi–Nasarawar Godel Road.

The approval was given at the Council meeting held on 5th October, 2026, following consideration of a memorandum presented by the Commissioner for Works and Infrastructure. The Council also ratified the earlier approval granted by His Excellency, the Executive Governor.

Following the evaluation conducted by the Technical and Financial Evaluation Committee, CCECC Nigeria Limited emerged as the Lowest Evaluated Responsive Bidder, with an evaluated contract sum of ₦70,896,387,618.50. The recommendation was subsequently approved by the Ministry’s Tenders Board.

The project has an 18-month completion period and comprises a 7.3-metre-wide carriageway with 1.5-metre shoulders on each side, a 40mm wearing course, three major bridges, box, pipe and triple-cell culverts, road furniture, traffic signs and road markings, as well as all ancillary works required for the completion and commissioning of the road.

Upon completion, the road is expected to:

– Improve road connectivity between Gusau and communities along the corridor;

– Facilitate the movement of agricultural produce and other goods to markets;

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

– Improve access to healthcare, education and other essential services;

– Support security operations and enhance mobility and response within the corridor;

– Stimulate commercial and economic activities in the benefiting communities; and

– Reduce travel time and vehicle operating costs.

The approval underscores Governor Dauda Lawal’s commitment to the Rescue Mission of Zamfara State by improving road infrastructure, strengthening connectivity, securing lives and opening up markets and opportunities for the people.

The State Government calls on the contractor to deliver the project to the required quality standards and within the agreed timeframe, while assuring the public that the project will be closely supervised to ensure compliance with specifications and value for money.
