World.title: Liberia: No Indictment After 47 Days as Justice Minister Denies Offering US$500K to Star Witness in Former Vice President Case
World.content:
Monrovia – When the Government of Liberia charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor in August, officials spoke with confidence. The state said it had the evidence. It said the case was strong.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Forty-seven days later, there is still no indictment.



Howard-Taylor was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19 before she could board a flight to Accra, where she was due to speak at a forum. She was charged with drug trafficking, money laundering and conspiracy linked to an alleged transnational narcotics network. She has denied every charge. Her bail request was denied, and she has since been moved from Monrovia Central Prison to house arrest.

Now, a question is circulating in legal and political circles in Monrovia: is the state’s case stuck because its most important witness won’t take the stand without being paid?

The man at the center

Almost every road in the state’s case runs through one man: Sheikh Bashiru Kante.

During the preliminary examination at the Monrovia City Court, the state’s first witness, acting Crime Services Commissioner Raphael A. Wilson, testified that Kante, himself an alleged co-conspirator, voluntarily surrendered his cellphone, and that forensic analysis found WhatsApp messages and audio recordings linking him to Howard-Taylor.

According to Wilson, the alleged cartel was led by a man identified as “Nicholas,” who met Kante in Dubai in 2021, and Kante later connected the group to Howard-Taylor. The charging documents say she received US$135,000 from people linked to the cartel, including US$75,000 allegedly channeled through Kante for her Jewel Star Fish Foundation.

In other words, the alleged introduction, the alleged money and the alleged recordings all come from Kante.

The US$500,000 claim

Sources close to the defense told FrontPageAfrica that the government, not Kante, initiated contact, and that the state has since built its case so heavily around him that it now cannot proceed without him.

According to those sources, Kante is demanding US$500,000 before he testifies. They say he wants to take the money out of Liberia, deposit it in a bank of his choosing, and only then return to take the stand. He reportedly claims he fears for his life from supporters of the former NPFL, the National Patriotic Party and the Congress for Democratic Change, and that he does not trust the government.

The sources say the government has refused, and the two sides are at a deadlock.

FrontPageAfrica could not independently confirm the claim. The government, through Justice Minister Betty Lamin Blamo has denied offering Kante US$500,000 or any payment to testify against the former vice president.

A witness with a past

Kante’s credibility has been questioned since the case began. A court record shows he was arrested in Maryland in the United States on April 20, 2022, on wire fraud and money laundering charges unrelated to narcotics. His name also surfaced in a 2022 controversy over a Liberian diplomatic passport he held despite having no formal diplomatic role. Then-President George Weah ordered an investigation, and Howard-Taylor’s office at the time denied arranging the passport.

In August, Bong County Representative Marvin Cole openly questioned Kante’s reliability. “You can’t have Sheikh passing all around going to night clubs drinking champagne and trying to blackmail other people by giving information,” Cole said on Sky FM. “How authentic that the information Sheikh is providing can be proven in court?”

“The Grand Jury is not sitting”

The government’s explanation for the delay is that the Grand Jury is not in session. Last month, prosecutors were expected to argue that Howard-Taylor could be held pending the Grand Jury term, which at the time was expected later in September. That term has come and gone without an indictment.

Her defense says the law offers a way around this. They point to Section 15.5 of the Criminal Procedure Law, which allows a Circuit Court judge, on application by the prosecution showing the public interest requires it, to summon fifteen people to serve as a special Grand Jury with the same powers as a regular one.

“If the government truly possesses the ‘overwhelming evidence’ it has repeatedly claimed,” one source close to the defense said, “then the public is entitled to ask a simple question: why has there been no indictment, and why does the entire case appear to depend on one witness?”

Legal experts consulted by The Analyst newspaper last week made a similar point, saying the absence of a Grand Jury indictment after 41 days of restraint was constitutionally significant.

What’s at stake

For the government, the case is a centerpiece of its crackdown on drug trafficking, coming after the seizure of four tonnes of cocaine valued at US$317 million in July.

For Howard-Taylor, a former senator, former vice president and former first lady, every day without an indictment is another day under restraint without formal charges from a Grand Jury.

And for the Liberian public, the question is simple. Either the state has the case it says it has, or it doesn’t. Until a Grand Jury sits, no one will know.

World.title: Liberia: NOCAL, Nigeria’s LADOL Sign Deal to Build Oil Shorebase in Buchanan
World.content:
Monrovia – The last time a major oil company drilled off Liberia’s coast, much of the money never touched Liberian soil.

By Rodney D. Sieh

When ExxonMobil drilled the Mesurado-1 well in late 2016, its operations were based out of Abidjan, in neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire. Supply boats, logistics, waste handling and technical support were all organized from across the border. In the end, the well came up dry and was plugged and abandoned, and Liberia was left with neither oil nor much to show from the drilling itself.



The National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL) now says it does not intend to let that happen again.

On Friday in London, NOCAL signed a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) with the Lagos Deep Offshore Logistics Base (LADOL), a Nigerian company that runs one of Africa’s largest oil and gas shorebases in Lagos. Under the deal, the two will work toward building and operating a logistics base in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County, to serve oil companies drilling offshore.

“We are determined to correct that narrative as we prepare for our next set of drilling programs,” NOCAL President and CEO Fabian M. Lai said. “Our goal is to ensure that the jobs, the contracts, the training, and the ancillary services that support our petroleum operations are performed by Liberian companies and create opportunities for Liberian citizens right here in Liberia.”

What the deal covers

LADOL will serve as technical lead partner, funding and conducting the feasibility study, coordinating engineering design, and partnering with NOCAL to build and run the facility. NOCAL says the study should begin within the next 45 days and run for six months.

It will look at land, waterfront and marine access, utilities, commercial viability, geotechnical and topographical surveys, and the early scoping of an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment.

The agreement also sets up a Joint Steering Committee to oversee progress and commits both sides to negotiating final project agreements. The two companies have also signed confidentiality and non-circumvention clauses.

LADOL Executive Chairman Sir Oladipo Ladi Jadesimi said the company sees itself as more than a financier. “We are not just investors; we are partners in building a sustainable future for Liberia’s oil and gas industry,” he said, adding that the shorebase could help ensure “Liberian businesses and workers are the primary beneficiaries of the country’s natural resources.”

Why now

The timing follows a burst of activity in Liberia’s offshore sector after years of quiet. In September 2025, the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority signed four Production Sharing Contracts with Atlas/Oranto Petroleum for offshore blocks LB-15, LB-16, LB-22 and LB-24, an agreement that followed a recent deal with TotalEnergies.

More blocks are in play. Last month, Australia’s Bounty Oil & Gas agreed to acquire the company holding exclusive rights to the LB-32 offshore block, a right that stems from a letter of commitment issued by NOCAL in October 2025. That contract still has to be negotiated and go before Parliament for approval.

If any of these companies move to drilling, they will need a base on land. NOCAL is betting that if Buchanan is ready, they won’t need to look to Abidjan.

A long wait for oil

Liberia has been chasing an oil discovery for more than a decade. Before Mesurado-1, other companies had drilled off the coast, and Exxon’s well was seen at the time as the latest blow to Liberia’s hopes of emulating the exploration success of Ghana and Senegal. Exxon later pulled out of Block LB-13.

For residents of Buchanan, a port city that has watched iron ore and other resources pass through for decades, the question will be whether this project delivers real jobs for local people or becomes another promise on paper. The feasibility study, due in roughly seven months, will be the first real test.

World.title: Liberia: Bong Filled Pelelei with Praise for Ex-Supt. Jackson, Dead at 74, Yet Never Gave Him the Senate Seat in Four Tries
World.content:
Jackson asked Bong County for a seat four times and did not get it. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, Bong gave him something that no election could: a crowd of people, speaking one after another, telling him that he had mattered. He was 74. He could not hear it. The county, at last, said it anyway

PELELEI, Zota District, Bong County – The women came first, and they came together. Members of the Bong County Women Organization filed into the funeral grounds in Pelelei on Saturday carrying a gratitude that had been years in the making. Behind them came former players, former students, elders, businessmen and young people from Gbarnga, all gathered to bury a man who had asked Bong County for something four times and never received it.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Dr. Ranney Banama Jackson Sr. was 74 when he died. He served as Superintendent of Bong County from 2006 until January 28, 2011, a stretch of years when the county was still finding its feet after the long civil war. He then sought the county’s Senate seat in 2005, 2011, 2014 and 2023, and each time the voters sent someone else to Monrovia. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, the same county that had turned him away filled the program with the words it had held back.



The hall that keeps giving

Madam Olivia Weetol, the former head of the Bong County Women Organization, stood before the mourners and spoke about a building. Jackson, she said, built the county’s first Women Center, a place where the women of Bong gather to hold meetings in the interest of the county.

Then she told them what the hall is doing now. Jackson is no longer around, she said, but the women still rent out the center, and the money they collect goes to needy women of the county who are desperately in need. Somewhere in Bong tonight, a woman who never met him may be eating because of a hall he raised. It was one of the quietest moments of the day, and for many people listening it was the hardest to bear. A man was being lowered into the ground, and something he built was still reaching for the hands of strangers.

The night he slept in the camp

Lincoln Gbaindeh did not come to talk about buildings. He came to talk about a night in 2008. Gbaindeh was a player on the Bong County team that reached the final of the National County Meet that year. He told mourners that Jackson did not stay in Gbarnga waiting for news. According to Gbeinteh, the superintendent literally slept in their camp, sitting among the young men and urging them to fight for the county and win it. That moment, Gbaindeh said, inspired them.

Bong won its first National County Meet soccer trophy that year. People who follow the county’s football say no superintendent has led Bong to that feat since. A county that rarely had anything to celebrate suddenly had a trophy, and a young man who had been afraid of the final had a superintendent beside him. Gbaindeh spoke for a few minutes, but he spoke like someone who had carried the memory for fifteen years, waiting for a place to put it down.

Tributes from every corner of Bong

One by one, others came to the podium, and every voice added something new. A Gbarnga resident, Gormah Flomo, said Jackson understood that the office of superintendent was not about sitting in Gbarnga and waiting for instructions from Monrovia. He believed the superintendent had a duty to bring development closer to the people. Flomo remembered improvements to public facilities, the work around the David Kuyon Sports Stadium and the efforts that helped improve electricity in Gbarnga. Those things may sound ordinary today, the resident said, but at the time they represented meaningful change for Bong County.

A resident of Suakoko District, Clyde Saul, spoke about young people. Jackson invested in them, the resident said, supporting education and scholarships so that many young Bongese could keep studying. More than 600 students reportedly benefited from a county scholarship initiative tied to his leadership, according to a biography from the AREPT organization. For families who could not afford school fees, the resident said, that help meant more than politics. It meant hope for their children.

A former student, Foster Peabody, stood up and made it personal. Some public officials are remembered because they held powerful positions, the former student said, and others because something they did touched ordinary people. When a child gets support to stay in school, that child can grow into a professional who contributes to society. That, Forkpah said, is why Jackson’s education work must remain part of Bong’s history.

A young resident, Jonathan McGill, of Gbarnga said Jackson showed that someone from Bong could rise through public service and still stay connected to home. His scholarship efforts, his development work and his later national service proved that his interest in public affairs went beyond one office. The young man hoped today’s leaders would take the lesson and invest more in education and opportunity for the next generation.

Remembering the ruins he inherited

Several speakers asked the crowd to remember the time Jackson served in. A Gbarnga businessman said Jackson arrived when Bong was trying to recover from the destruction and stagnation of the war years. He understood that development needed government facilities, investment and basic services, the businessman said. Whether people backed his politics or not, it is hard to talk about that chapter of Bong’s history without mentioning what happened under his watch.

The former Chiarman of the Bong Legislative Caucus, Attorney George Mulbah, said Liberia was coming out of a devastating civil war and Bong had enormous challenges. Jackson inherited a county that needed rebuilding, the resident said, and worked to restore public confidence and basic government functions. His contribution was not that everything was perfect, the resident said. His contribution was that he became part of the rebuilding.

Published accounts credit his administration with helping bring electricity to parts of Gbarnga and with renovating the presidential compound and rehabilitating the superintendent’s compound there. They also credit him with work at the David Kuyon Sports Stadium, though accounts differ on whether that was fencing or construction. Jackson himself once told a local radio audience in Gbarnga how he got it done. He clashed with members of the then Bong Legislative Caucus, some of whom opposed the idea, and he fenced the stadium anyway. Before that, residents had cut palm branches to ring the field on match days and big occasions.

A 2026 account says Jackson negotiated two multimillion-dollar rubber-processing plants for Gbarnga in 2008 and helped formalize the Sister States relationship linking Maryland in the United States with Liberia’s Bong and Maryland counties.

Those claims rest on that account and have not been independently verified, but they fit the portrait mourners painted of a man who looked beyond the county line.

The wound he carried

The people who loved him did not pretend he had never been hurt. In 2008, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf suspended Jackson after an audit by the General Auditing Commission examined the management of county funds. Reports said he was accused of irregularities, including the use of US$10,000 of county money for a trip to the United States. He later repaid the money.

People who follow the county’s football say no superintendent has led Bong to that feat since. A county that rarely had anything to celebrate suddenly had a trophy, and a young man who had been afraid of the final had a superintendent beside him. Gbaindeh spoke for a few minutes, but he spoke like someone who had carried the memory for fifteen years, waiting for a place to put it down

Those close to the story say the journey had a purpose. Jackson and then Caucus Chair George Mulbah traveled with money from the Bong Social Development Fund to negotiate the sister-state relationship with Maryland, and one result was a dump truck from the State of Maryland that Bong County kept using. His political rivals, his supporters say, used the trip against him with the president. Sirleaf later explained, at a public forum in Gbarnga reported by FrontPage Africa, that she suspended him because he acted unilaterally, not simply because the money was spent.

A Bong County elder, William Kollie, spoke gently about all of this. Jackson was not perfect, the elder said, and like every public official his administration had controversies. But those controversies, the elder said, should not erase the things he did for the county. He carried Bong with him wherever he went.

Four times he asked

Behind the warmth of Saturday sits a record that is hard to read. In 2005, Jackson ran on the COTOL ticket and received 13,931 votes, or 7.8 percent, finishing fourth. In 2011, running for the Unity Party, he received 29,023 votes, or 25.56 percent, and finished second to Henry Willie Yallah, who received 29,804. The final margin from the National Elections Commission was 781 votes.

Seven hundred and eighty-one. It is a number small enough to fit in a single crowded church. It is the distance between the Senate and a long goodbye.

After that near miss, the support slipped away. In 2014, again as a Unity Party candidate, Jackson received 4,038 votes, or 10.4 percent, and finished third behind Jewel Howard-Taylor, who won with 13,672. In 2023, under the Rainbow Alliance, he received 6,552 votes, or 3.70 percent, and finished fifth in a race won by Johnny K. Kpehe with 78,122 votes. For a man who had once come within a whisper of the Senate, it must have been a lonely thing to watch the numbers shrink.

Bong has always been a difficult county to read. Sirleaf herself once said the people of Bong had been deceitful to her, after the 2011 returns. She received 48,374 votes there in the first round, or 42.9 percent, against 37,787 for Winston Tubman of the Congress for Democratic Change. In the November runoff her support climbed to 52,949 votes, or 83.45 percent, after the CDC declared it would not participate. With 467,561 people according to the 2022 census, Bong is Liberia’s third most populous county, and its voters have never been predictable.

Why gratitude does not always become a vote

Many people at the funeral wondered quietly why the love of Saturday had not appeared on election day. Nobody had a single answer. Elections turn on political alliances, party loyalty, personalities, changing priorities and the arrival of new faces. A politician can oversee projects that serve thousands and still fail to turn that record into votes years later.

But a funeral asks a different question. A ballot asks who should lead next. A funeral asks what a person meant. The woman who sits in the hall Jackson built, the player he encouraged, the student who stayed in school were not choosing between candidates on Saturday. They were answering for a life, and the answers came easily.

What love asks of the living

A community leader said the thing many in Pelelei were thinking. History will eventually judge every public official, the leader said, but Jackson deserves to be remembered for the development work done during his time as superintendent. He helped advance projects that touched public infrastructure, education and basic services. The best way to honor him,

the leader said, is not merely to praise him at his funeral, but to preserve the lessons of his service and keep building a better Bong County.

It is a heavy request, and a fair one. Love that comes late is still love, and the people of Bong showed on Saturday that theirs was real. But a hall that feeds the needy needs hands to keep it open. A scholarship needs someone to remember it. A stadium that no longer needs palm branches needs someone to remember why.

Jackson asked Bong County for a seat four times and did not get it. On Saturday, in the town where he was born, Bong gave him something that no election could: a crowd of people, speaking one after another, telling him that he had mattered. He was 74. He could not hear it. The county, at last, said it anyway.

World.title: Three Liberians Face U.S. Prison, Deportation Over Votes
World.content:
Three Liberians living in Minnesota are among ten immigrants indicted by a U.S. federal grand jury for allegedly voting or registering to vote while not citizens. Prosecutors say most of the votes were cast in the November 2024 presidential election. They face up to five years in prison, and U.S. officials warn deportation could follow.

Monrovia – She is 61. He is 48. The youngest is 43. Somewhere in Minnesota, three Liberians who built lives far from home now face the possibility of losing them, over a ballot.

By Rodney D. Sieh



A federal grand jury in Minneapolis on September 24 indicted Bhator Konah Bryant, Alan Barbu Kargbo and Chis Adam Pettiquoi, along with seven other immigrants, on charges of voting or registering to vote in American elections when they were not American citizens.

Of the ten people charged, from eight different countries, Liberia had the most.

What they are accused of

Prosecutors say Bryant falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen when she registered to vote on October 18, 2024. They do not allege she cast a ballot.

Kargbo and Pettiquoi are each accused of going further. Prosecutors say both falsely claimed citizenship and voted in Minnesota on November 5, 2024, the day Americans chose their president.

All three have already appeared before a federal judge. None has been convicted.

More than prison at stake

On paper, the penalties are heavy: up to five years in prison and a fine of up to US$250,000 for falsely claiming citizenship to vote, and up to one year and US$100,000 for voting as a non-citizen.

But for an immigrant, the harder blow may be the one not written in the charge sheet. U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made sure no one missed it.

“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” he said.

For a 61-year-old woman, that could mean being sent back to a country she may have left decades ago, away from children, grandchildren and everything she has built since.

A community that fought for its place

The charges hit close to home for Minnesota’s Liberian community, one of the largest in the United States, centered in Brooklyn Park and the suburbs around Minneapolis.

Many came running from the civil wars of the 1990s. For years they lived on temporary permission to stay, renewed one deadline at a time, never sure whether the next announcement would send them home. It was not until the Liberian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 2019 that many finally got a path to green cards and, eventually, the right to vote.

For people who waited that long for a ballot, the idea that some Liberians may have cast one without the right to do so is painful. And at a time when the Trump administration is pushing hard against immigrants, many in the diaspora will worry that three names on a federal indictment could cast a shadow over thousands who did everything by the book.

Presumed innocent

The case was investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations, with help from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

U.S. prosecutors were careful to note that an indictment is only an accusation. Bryant, Kargbo and Pettiquoi are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

World.title: Liberia: Sinoe Labour Commissioner Faces Harassment Claims as County Attorney Dispute Deepens
World.content:
GREENVILLE, Sinoe County — New video and photographic evidence obtained by FrontPage Africa has raised questions about the conduct of officials associated with the Sinoe County Labour Commissioner’s Office, amid competing accounts over the handcuffing of a Chinese national and a separate confrontation involving the County Attorney and county officials.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The controversy comes as questions continue to surround an incident involving Sinoe County Attorney Cllr. Mmonbeydo Nadine Joah, who became involved in a dispute with Labour Commissioner Cleophas Nyantee Mah and County Superintendent Alexander Nah Slewion.



Mah, however, strongly denies allegations that he or members of his team have harassed, intimidated or extorted business operators.

He told FrontPage Africa that neither he nor members of his team have demanded unauthorized payments from investors or subjected them to harassment.

What the Footage Shows

Video obtained by FrontPage Africa appears to show a Chinese businessman seated on a green plastic chair with his hands handcuffed.

A man in plain clothes, holding what appears to be documents and a mobile phone, is seen speaking to the businessman and pointing in his direction.

The incident appears to have occurred inside a container-like office at what sources identified as a mining operation.

Mah acknowledged that the incident occurred but disputed accounts portraying him as responsible for the arrest and handcuffing of the Chinese national.

According to Mah, the incident occurred several months ago and was unrelated to the more recent confrontation involving the County Attorney and Superintendent.

He said he went to the location in his capacity as Labour Commissioner and that the Chinese national was arrested and handcuffed by members of the Liberia National Police who were investigating an incident.

Mah said his office subsequently imposed a fine on the company, but that the County Attorney later revoked the fine.

He also said the County Attorney subsequently accused him of abuse of office and took legal action against him.

Mah maintained that the matter was eventually dismissed by the Magisterial Court.

The County Attorney did not respond to FrontPage Africa’s request for comment on the matter.

Competing Accounts of the Mining-Site Incident

Darius Shajay Nagbeh Sr., Superintendent of Kpanyan Statutory District, disputed Mah’s account of what happened.

Nagbeh told FrontPage Africa that the incident occurred within his district at the Glorious Mining Company operation site following an incident involving the death of a miner.

According to Nagbeh, the County Attorney had established a team, led by him, to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death.

He alleged that Mah arrived at the site accompanied by a Community Police officer and participated in the arrest and handcuffing of the Chinese national.

Nagbeh also disputed the amount of the fine, saying the Labour Commissioner imposed a hefty fine on the company. Mah’s account also referenced a fine, but the parties differ over the circumstances surrounding its imposition and subsequent revocation.

Nagbeh said the County Attorney later revoked the fine and initiated legal proceedings against Mah, accusing him of abuse of office.

Mah maintains that the arrest itself was carried out by the Liberia National Police and that his role was limited to labour enforcement.

Allegations of Extortion

Separate allegations have emerged concerning the treatment of business operators in Greenville.

Sources familiar with the situation allege that members of the Labour Commissioner’s team have visited businesses operated by members of the Fula community and demanded payments allegedly outside Liberia’s established labour and work-permit procedures.

The allegations have not been independently verified.

Mah categorically denied the claims, saying neither he nor his team has engaged in extortion or intimidation.

He said his office recently dispatched the Deputy Labour Commissioner to collect information from businesses as part of its reporting responsibilities.

According to Mah, the dispute escalated after the County Attorney allegedly ordered the Deputy Labour Commissioner arrested while he was carrying out his official duties.

Mah said he resisted the arrest of his deputy after being informed of it and was subsequently accused by the County Attorney of obstructing justice.

Dispute Over County Attorney’s Intervention

The competing accounts have now become intertwined with a separate confrontation involving the County Attorney, the Labour Commissioner and Superintendent Slewion.

Mah said the County Attorney later went to his office with police officers to arrest him and his deputy.

He said they resisted the attempted arrests and that a confrontation followed.

According to Mah, the Superintendent became involved after being called to intervene, and the situation subsequently escalated.

Slewion offered a different account.

He told FrontPage Africa that Mah complained to him that the County Attorney had gone to his office to arrest him and asked for his intervention.

The Superintendent said he invited Joah to his office because the dispute involved officials from different government institutions and he wanted to mediate.

According to Slewion, Cllr. Joah declined to participate in the proposed intervention.

He said that when he later went to the Labour Commissioner’s office, he asked Cllr. Joah to stop recording and sit down for dialogue.

Slewion said Cllr. Joah refused and accused him of obstructing justice.

He further alleged that he was assaulted during the ensuing confrontation and had to be taken away from the scene.

The Superintendent denied knowledge of claims that Cllr. Joah’s phone was seized or that she was assaulted.

He said he has sought the intervention of Senator Augustine Chea, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General over continued misunderstanding between him and the County Attorney but that the dispute remains unresolved.

County Attorney’s Hospitalization

Sources told FrontPage Africa that Joah was later taken to F.J. Grant Hospital following the confrontation.

There are also allegations that a man identified as Cornelius, reportedly associated with the Superintendent, struck the County Attorney during the confrontation.

Those allegations have not been independently established.

Cllr. Joah did not respond to FrontPage Africa’s requests for comment.

FrontPage Africa has gathered that the Ministry of Justice is reviewing aspects of the dispute.

Questions Over Official Conduct

The competing accounts raise broader questions about how labour and other regulatory authorities are exercising enforcement powers in Sinoe County.

Labour inspections, work-permit enforcement and related administrative actions are expected to be carried out under established laws and procedures.

The dispute also raises questions about the boundaries between the Labour Commissioner’s Office, the County Administration, the County Attorney’s Office and law-enforcement authorities when government agencies become involved in the same matter.

The growing controversy has prompted calls for an impartial investigation into the competing allegations.

World.title: Social Media Influencer Prophet Key And US-based Liberian Become Latest Victim of Relationship ‘Deception’
World.content:
Varney and Zoey

MONROVIA – The room was ready. Relatives had contributed money, the food was cooked, and a DJ was waiting for his cue. Uncle Alfred had opened his home. By every outward sign, a Liberian family was about to celebrate an engagement.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Then the groom-to-be, a US-based Liberian known publicly only as Varney, picked up the microphone. He began the way such speeches usually begin, with thanks to the host, the contributors, the cooks and the DJ. Within minutes, the evening belonged to something else entirely.



Scene Two: A Man, a Phone, a Border

Two days later, on the late afternoon of Saturday, October 3, 2026, a different kind of broadcast began. Social media influencer Justin Nayapougma Oldpa Yeazeahn, widely known as “Prophet Key,” went live on Facebook. He was crying, and he did not hide it.

He said he had returned from a business trip to his home county, Nimba, to find a nearly empty house. His fiancée, an Ivorian woman by his description, was gone. So was his only daughter. So, he claimed, was US$33,000.

Together, the two videos made one of the most talked-about weeks on Liberian social media in recent memory.

The Groom’s Long Preamble

Varney’s speech did not start with an accusation. It started with a relationship history, and it was a candid one. He said he had known his girlfriend, Zoey Darblo, since 2021. The four years since, in his telling, had been a cycle of quarrels and silences. She would stop speaking to him for two days, three days, even a week, then return and ask why he had called. He would apologize. He admitted he can be sarcastic.

Plans to formalize the relationship were repeatedly delayed. He said he had been due to travel in July and postponed. He postponed again to August. At that point, he said, she told him it was over. It took Uncle Alfred stepping in as intermediary to bring the two back to the table.

Those details matter because they frame what came next. Varney was not presenting himself as a man blindsided from nowhere. He was describing a couple already on thin ice, who had decided, with family help, to try again.

The Unlocked Phone

The turning point, as Varney described it, came the day before the event. He said he had earlier asked Zoey to open her WhatsApp and that she had not. Then, he claimed, he found it unlocked.

What he said he found was, in his words, a woman in conversation with four different men, two of them actively. He singled out one who he said works at the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) and another he described as married with a child. He told the room she had once insisted she never got involved with married men.

He read portions of the alleged messages aloud. Guests who had come to celebrate heard the contents of a private phone read over a party-hall microphone. The engagement did not go ahead.

Clips of the moment spread fast, and the early response was largely comic. Memes and jokes filled timelines. The laughter was, for a while, the main story.

“Immigration, Don’t Let Her Pass”

There was no comedy in the Prophet’s broadcast, even if some viewers reacted with disbelief. He cried openly and repeated the same sentence like a refrain: she ran away with my daughter.

His appeal was precise and urgent. He believed two Ivorian buses were approaching the border and that his fiancée was aboard one. He addressed Liberian and Ivorian immigration officers directly, asking them to stop the vehicles. The buses, he stressed, had not yet crossed. The window was closing.

Prophet Key and family

He named the woman on air, acknowledging he might have misspelled her name. He also announced a US$1,500 reward for credible information leading to her and the child. With no message left behind, he said he could only presume she had gone to Côte d’Ivoire, a conviction rather than a confirmed fact.

Everything described here comes from his own account. No response from the woman has been published, and no authority has publicly confirmed any investigation, stop or arrest.

A Name Already Known

Prophet Key arrived at this moment with a long public record, and Liberian audiences know it well.

He returned to Liberia after years abroad, a homecoming linked to the government of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the Unity Party. Controversy followed. In 2024, the National Elections Commission blocked him from the Nimba County Senatorial By-election, alleging that he had submitted a fraudulent Biometric Voter Registration card.

He rejected the allegation, saying he had registered on April 27, 2023 and obtained his card legitimately. Fact-checkers countered that the BVR number he presented was invalid, absent from the NEC system and missing from the 2023 Final Registration Roll.

In February 2026, the Supreme Court of Liberia jailed him for contempt over remarks about members of the judiciary. He spent six months in the Monrovia Central Prison and was released after completing the term and meeting the Court’s conditions.

None of that bears on whether his fiancée left with his daughter and his money. But it explains why his latest video found such a ready audience: people were already watching him.

What the Two Men Had in Common

Set side by side, the incidents differ sharply in scale. One involves a missing child and a large sum of cash. The other involves wounded pride and a ruined party. Yet the parallels run deeper than timing.

Both chose the crowd over the closed door. Neither went first to a counselor, or, as far as is publicly known, to a formal process. Facebook was the first stop, whether as a rescue tool or a stage.

Both told their side first. The women in both stories have been described, discussed and judged by thousands of strangers without a published word in reply. That imbalance shapes everything readers think they know.

Both stories hit people who are not on camera. A young girl is at the center of one. Several men, one of them said to be married, were named in the other. Relatives who gave their time and money watched an intimate dispute unfold in front of them.

The Law Is Slower Than the Feed

The Prophet’s appeal highlights a basic mismatch. A live video can reach thousands in seconds. A police report, a custody claim or a cross-border request moves at the speed of paperwork. A parent who believes a child has been taken abroad usually has to go through police, immigration and, where relevant, courts and international channels. Whether any of that has begun in this case is unknown.

Public pleas can occasionally speed things up, but they carry risks. A named woman accused of theft and taking a child can face hostility before any facts are established. If the claims prove incomplete, the damage cannot be undone.

The Cost of the Clip

Varney’s case raises a different problem. The messages he described were private, and the guests who heard them were never asked whether they wanted to. Accusations of infidelity, even if true, are not usually settled in front of a DJ and a room of relatives. And once such a moment is filmed and shared, it follows everyone involved: the woman accused, the men named, the host who offered his home.

It is easy to read the viral moment as a punchline. It is harder to remember that the central figures will still be living with it long after the jokes stop.

When the Scroll Moves On

Public heartbreak is nothing new, but social media has changed its shape. A confession that once lived in gossip now lives in a link. A plea that once went to a village elder now goes to a worldwide audience, with all the sympathy and cruelty that implies.

By next week, other stories will fill the timeline. But a father in Nimba will still be waiting for news, a family in a party hall will still be sorting through what happened, and two women who have yet to be heard will still be at the center of narratives they did not write.

World.title: Liberia: National Traditional Liaison Officer Says CDC Could Win Bong Again as Unity Party Battles Internal Divisions
World.content:
Mr. Kollie further claimed that the Unity Party faces serious internal divisions in Bong, which he believes could open political space for the CDC. He attributed part of the division to disagreements among party actors over political influence and access to county leadership

GBARNGA, Bong County – A senior Liberian government official from Bong County says the opposition Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) has a realistic chance of winning the county in the next presidential election, arguing that divisions inside the governing Unity Party (UP) could prevent it from consolidating support.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

William B. S. Kollie, Liberia’s National Traditional Liaison Officer and a native of Bong, said the CDC cannot be written off in the county,



particularly if it keeps its own house in order and strengthens ties with local political actors. “The CDC still has the potential to win Bong because the party has settled some of the differences that affected its performance. If the Unity Party remains divided, the CDC can take advantage of that situation,” Mr. Kollie said.

A county that changes allegiance

Mr. Kollie’s argument rests on Bong’s voting history over the past two decades, in which the county has moved from being a stronghold of former President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf and the Unity Party to being an important base for former President George Weah and the CDC.

In 2005, Mrs. Johnson-Sirleaf defeated Mr. Weah decisively in Bong in the runoff, despite finishing third in the county in the first round. In 2011, she won 83.45 percent of the county’s runoff vote. In 2017, the pattern reversed, with Mr. Weah taking about 64.2 percent against Joseph Boakai’s 35.8 percent.

In 2023, Mr. Weah carried Bong again, but by a much smaller margin. He received 72,159 votes (52.92 percent) to Mr. Boakai’s 64,194 (47.08 percent), a lead of 7,965 votes, or 5.84 percentage points.

Mr. Kollie said the 2023 result should not be read as the CDC losing relevance in Bong. In his view, it shows the party retains a substantial base that could prove decisive if the Unity Party fails to resolve its differences.

“Bong politics is not permanently owned by any political party. We have seen this county move from the Unity Party to the CDC, and the party that organizes its people and builds stronger local relationships will have an advantage,” he said.

Mr. Kollie said the CDC has addressed some of the internal differences that, in his assessment, contributed to its underperformance in parts of Bong during the 2023 election period.

He pointed to the political importance of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, a Bong native, saying that having a major county figure on the CDC ticket had given the party an important link to voters there. He argued that the party’s ability to settle differences among its actors could make it more competitive going forward.

Funeral turnout as a political signal

Mr. Kollie also cited the funeral of Philip Taylor, son of Mrs. Howard-Taylor, as evidence of continuing ties between the CDC, the National Patriotic Party (NPP) and parts of the Bong population.

He said the ceremony in Gbarnga drew significant public attention even though Mr. Taylor was not a prominent political figure in the county. According to Mr. Kollie, residents, particularly CDC and NPP supporters, turned out along the route from the Old Iron Gate to the Gbarnga Administration Building to pay their respects. He said this showed that structures associated with both parties remain active in Bong.

He contrasted this with the reception for the remains of former Bong Superintendent Dr. Ranney Banama Jackson, which arrived in Gbarnga on Friday ahead of funeral ceremonies. Mr. Kollie described the turnout as relatively poor, given Dr. Jackson’s long association with the county and his former role as superintendent.

He cautioned against reading the difference purely as a measure of the two men’s importance. It could also reflect changing political networks, he said, and the ability of political organizations to mobilize supporters around particular events. He suggested political actors in Bong should reflect on

shifting loyalties and the relationship between leaders and ordinary citizens.

Claims of Unity Party divisions

Mr. Kollie further claimed that the Unity Party faces serious internal divisions in Bong, which he believes could open political space for the CDC. He attributed part of the division to disagreements among party actors over political influence and access to county leadership.

He also pointed to allegations involving Bong County Superintendent Lorleyah Hawa Norris. According to Mr. Kollie, some political actors allege that Superintendent Norris has been empowering or giving political space to individuals associated with the opposition CDC.

Those allegations are contested. They are Mr. Kollie’s account of claims circulating among political actors and could not be independently verified. No response from Superintendent Norris or Unity Party leadership was available at the time of writing.

Mr. Kollie said the controversy could deepen disagreements within the UP if members believe individuals or institutions linked to the government are creating opportunities for opposition actors. He argued that a governing party needs a cohesive county-level structure to defend its support, particularly where presidential elections have produced large swings.

Why he sees an opening for the CDC

Mr. Kollie said the CDC could benefit from what he described as uncertainty within the Unity Party’s Bong structure, because the county’s electorate has shown it will change allegiance when it perceives weakness in a dominant organization.

He said the UP cannot assume its 2023 national victory automatically gives it a lasting advantage in the county. The CDC’s task, he said, is to consolidate its existing support, repair remaining internal differences and maintain relationships with influential communities and political actors across Bong.

Political organizations, he stressed, must do more than rely on national popularity. Clan relationships, personalities, local development records and grassroots organization can all determine how voters behave.

World.title: WEEKEND SCORECARD: Green Eagles soars
World.content:
Green Eagles, led by Coach Perry Mutapa, were the best performers on the opening weekend of the 2026 Transitional Super Division season after posting a huge win away at Mighty Mufulira Wanderers.

Eagles recorded the highest score-line of the ten Week One matches, thumping Wanderers 4-1 at Shinde Stadium in Kantanshi, Mufulira.

The victory sees Eagles take command of Stream B after Red Arrows beat Mutondo Stars 3-1 away in Kitwe to secure second place.

Green Buffaloes and newly promoted Stylish Roan United were the other teams that posted wins on Matchday One.

In the same stream, ZESCO United and Kabwe Warriors have a point each following their 1-1 stalemate in Kabwe.

Nkwazi, Mutondo Stars, Chirundu FC and Wanderers have no points after losing their fixtures.

Reacting to the win, Eagles coach Perry Mutapa demanded more from his players despite the fantastic start.

“I think it was a good fight from the boys. We fought from the first whistle to the last. In the first half we could have scored more goals but it wasn’t to be,” Mutapa said.

“In the second half, I think they were good. Congratulations to the boys. It feels nice to score four goals. It is good that our pre-season training has worked. We could have scored more goals,” he added.

Looking ahead, Eagles face ZESCO United away in Ndola.

“Tough match against ZESCO United. It is not going to be easy, especially that we will be away. We have to improve, especially on scoring. Yes we celebrate the win but this is just Week One,” Mutapa said.

WEEK ONE RESULTS

STREAM A

Saturday, 3 October

Konkola Blades 2-1 Power Dynamos

NAPSA Stars 1-1 FC MUZA

Trident 0-1 Nkana

Nchanga Rangers 0-1 Zanaco

Sunday, 4 October

Makeni All Stars 0-0 Kansanshi Dynamos

STREAM B

Saturday, 3 October

Kabwe Warriors 1-1 ZESCO United

Mufulira Wanderers 1-4 Green Eagles

Nkwazi 1-2 Roan United

Sunday, 4 October

Mutondo Stars 1-3 Red Arrows

Green Buffaloes 2-1 Chirundu United

BACKGROUND

The transitional season is facilitating the change of Zambian football from the August-May calendar back to the old calendar-year format (March to November).

This 2026 season is the bridge to the full 2027 season starting in March 2027. It is the second transitional season since 2019.

The format has 20 clubs divided into Stream A and Stream B, with each team playing 18 games from 3rd October 2026 to January 2027.

The top team from each stream will go to the Championship Playoff Final on 31st January 2027, with the winner to be crowned 2026 Transitional Champion and earn a CAF Champions League spot.

Stream A: Power Dynamos, Nkana, FC MUZA, Kansanshi Dynamos, Konkola Blades, Makeni All Stars, Trident, NAPSA Stars, Zanaco, Nchanga Rangers

Stream B: ZESCO United, Kabwe Warriors, Red Arrows, Roan United, Nkwazi, Mutondo Stars, Chirundu United, Green Eagles, Green Buffaloes, Mufulira Wanderers

There will be no ABSA Cup in this transitional season. Instead, league positions will determine qualification for the 2027 ABSA Cup in the first half of next season.

World.title: “Healing Must Start With Us Leaders”: Silumbe Calls for National Indaba and Urges Hichilema To Embrace Dialogue
World.content:
Leadership Movement (LM) president Dr Richard Silumbe has called for a national indaba on reconciliation, saying Zambia’s healing must begin with its leaders and cannot be put off.

Dr Silumbe said the country has lost its identity as One Zambia One Nation because of the issues surrounding the outcome of the August 13 general election. He said Zambians are living through politics of hate and division, which should not be allowed in a Christian nation.

“We need to heal this nation and we must do it now, not any other day,” he said. “And this healing must start with us leaders. Let us open our hearts to the current situation in the country.”

He warned that delay carries a price. “We need a genuine national indaba for reconciliation because if we don’t do it now, we are building a fertile land for a national crisis,” Dr Silumbe said.

The LM, he said, is ready to push for genuine and earnest reconciliation, but the country cannot move forward while it stays bitter and vengeful. “We cannot move forward if we are still bitter, if we are still a nation of vengeance, if we are vindictive, if we cannot forgive and forget,” he said. The only ground on which healing can take place, he added, is respect for the rule of law.

The LM leader then turned to party cadres, and to the leaders who have kept quiet about them. He said supporters are insulting one another and promoting hatred while those in leadership say nothing.

“We need to call for order; we need to call out these cadres to stop, while we promote unity, national reconciliation, forgiveness and national healing,” he said. “This is very important for this nation.”

His appeal to President Hakainde Hichilema was tied to the Government’s own targets. Dr Silumbe urged the Head of State to look beyond the election and face reality if he wants the Grow Zambia Agenda to yield results and benefit the nation.

He said he has seen Mr Hichilema working towards that agenda, but it cannot be achieved while the nation is polarised. “We cannot achieve the three million metric tonnes of copper production; we shall not achieve the 10 million metric tonnes of maize; we shall not grow the economy,” he said. “We will achieve nothing in that Grow Zambia Agenda in the current state of the nation.”

Dr Silumbe’s request to the President was direct: embrace dialogue and call for reconciliation towards national healing.

He also said the United Party for National Development (UPND) government has exposed itself to many battlefronts against its own citizens, and he pointed first to its relationship with the Church. “We have a government that is not in good books with the Church. For me, this is dangerous,” he said.

He went on to say that the Government is in power while people are still challenging its legitimacy, which he called an eye-opener for reconciliation. He said he accepts that Mr Hichilema is President, but the Head of State should extend an olive branch to a grieving society.

“Let him extend a hand to the Church and talk,” Dr Silumbe said. “Let him do that to civil society and political stakeholders.”

The healing he is asking for, he stressed, is not about a few individuals but the entire nation. The opposition still claims it won the election.

The LM says it is ready to lead the push for reconciliation once the call for an indaba is taken up.

World.title: Hichilema Tells Chiefs To Keep Enough Maize for Homes as Drought Warning Stands
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged traditional leaders to tell their subjects to keep enough maize for their own families, warning that an El Niño-induced drought is coming and that no one should say they were not told.

The Head of State spoke at the 2026 Samu Lya Moomba traditional ceremony in Bweengwa, Monze, his first traditional ceremony since his re-election. He assured the nation that the Government will ensure that no one dies of hunger, but said households must also take responsibility by preserving adequate food stocks.

Mr Hichilema put the request to the chiefs directly. He said traditional leaders could “inform our people to retain as much maize as possible for your own family consumption because we have a drought and don’t say we were not told”.

“Please keep as much maize so that we can protect our children from going hungry,” the President said.

He warned that the drought alert should not be taken lightly. He asked traditional leaders to make sure communities, particularly children and vulnerable people, are protected from hunger.

The President also advised farmers to store their maize in granaries rather than in sacks. Households are more likely to sell grain kept in sacks when they need money, he said.

The Government is already preparing programmes with traditional leaders and other partners to support vulnerable communities. It is also working with the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) to rehabilitate existing storage sheds in communities, a step Mr Hichilema said will cut the cost of moving maize from production areas to storage facilities and back to consuming centres.

He invited private individuals to invest in storage that the FRA can later rent.

“A 30×20 storage shed under the FRA specifications is only costing K1.8 million. You can invest back in your village. K1.8 million and FRA will rent your shed. But it will preserve the crop right at the local communities,” Mr Hichilema said.

The President urged Zambians to increase production and become producers rather than merely consumers. A hungry country cannot be a happy country, he said.

Farmers in Chief Choongo‘s area were encouraged to venture into wheat and soya beans, two crops the Government has marked for higher output under the Grow Zambia Agenda. Mr Hichilema said he has shown what wheat can do by cultivating 400 hectares in the area, with the crop sold to a customer at US$550 per tonne.

On water, he said the Government will allocate substantial resources to drought-prone areas to protect communities and support economic activity. Funds have already been allocated, and additional funding is expected in the 2027 national budget.

He asked Members of Parliament and other elected leaders to direct a large share of Constituency Development Fund resources to water harvesting.

Livestock was also on his list. Mr Hichilema called for stronger disease control to protect the country’s target of earning US$1 billion from livestock exports, and said the Government will support communities with additional dip tanks in areas targeted for increased livestock production.

On payments to farmers, he said the Government remains committed to making sure the FRA pays them. The agency has performed better this year than last year, he added.

Mr Hichilema urged Zambians to preserve their cultural heritage, noting that the Samu Lya Moomba site is historically important because it was used to mobilise resources during the struggle for independence.

Chief Choongo pledged to support the Government’s efforts to reduce the effects of El Niño. The chief congratulated the President on his re-election, thanked him for declaring the Samu Lya Moomba ceremonial site a national heritage site, and said the country was in safe hands.

Mr Hichilema, for his part, pledged to donate a pontoon to the chiefdom to improve connectivity and support community needs.

Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde said the province is preparing to limit the effects of the expected weather on people, livestock and crops. He urged farmers not to sell their entire harvest and to make sure household food needs are adequately covered.

Mr Monde also asked traditional leaders and communities to safeguard food security and protect livestock from foot-and-mouth disease. He encouraged partnerships in sustainable forest management and carbon trading as an alternative source of income for communities.

Programmes for vulnerable communities are already being prepared, and additional funding for water provision in drought-prone areas is expected in the 2027 national budget.

World.title: Sympathy Abroad, Deafening Silence Home: Why Sishuwa Sishuwa is Not Getting Support from Zambian Academics
World.content:
Sympathy Abroad, Deafening Silence Home: Why Sishuwa Sishuwa is Not Getting Support from Zambian Academics

There have been several statements of solidarity with Sishuwa Sishuwa by foreign academics following the cancellation of his passport by the Zambian government. The most recent of these is a short statement by Jeremy Seeking claiming that the decision by the government is in response to Sishuwa’s trenchant criticism of HH and his government and, therefore, undermines Sishuwa’s academic freedom.

Surprisingly, however, there has been a deafening silence from the Zambian academia on Sishuwa’s predicament. There is no string of statements of solidarity. No outpouring of sympathy. No grieving over his fate. No defence of his academic freedom. Silence. What could be the reason for this dichotomy? I argue that the people who live in the context in which his “activism” has a bearing have a better understanding of Sishuwa’s “activism” and are better placed to judge his actions.

The local academics have a better understanding that Sishuwa had gone rogue and acted in a territory beyond academic freedom as many of his commentaries cannot be defended on the basis of academic freedom. He had crossed the line of academic integrity into the world of conspiracy and alternative reality, personalised attack, fake news, misinformation, disinformation and hate speech, and possibly cyber bullying and cyber harassment.

This is not to argue that the action by government to revoke is passport is justified. I don’t have sufficient information of the basis on which the government acted and would not like to make assumptions for or against.

Let us start with academic freedom and responsibilities of academics. Principle 1 of the Human Rights Council’s Principles for Implementing the Right to Academic Freedom (2024) defines academic freedom as “the human right to acquire, develop, transmit, apply, and engage with a diversity of knowledge and ideas through research, teaching, learning, and discourse.” Similarly, the Dar es Salaam Declaration on Academic Freedom and Social Responsibilities (1990) defines academic freedom as “the freedom of members of the academic community, individually or collectively, in the pursuit, development and transmission of knowledge, through research, study, discussion, documentation, production, creation, teaching, lecturing and writing.”

Academic freedom, like any other right, is not an open cheque to abuse others, to denigrate those with divergent views, to fabricate lies, spread misinformation, defame others and engage in conspiracy theories and belittle others. Academic freedom comes with responsibilities and academic ethics. As the Dar es Salaam Declaration noted, these include the need for academics to “perform their academic functions in accordance with ethical and highest scientific standards,” perform their role “without prejudice to the rights of others and the needs of our society,” and to engage in academics with “spirit of tolerance towards differing views and positions and enhance democratic debate and discussion.” Academic freedom is not unlimited. As Judge Oliver Wendell Holmes famously stated, “The right to swing my fist ends where the other man’s nose begins.”

Sishuwa’s social and political commentaries have not always respected the responsibilities that come with academic freedom. He often fabricates facts, demeans those with contrary views, makes wild and unsubstantiated claims and often makes claims that border on hate speech, purveys false/fake documents. He has often called academics who have exposed some of his falsehoods or hold different views from his as simply driven by their stomachs and not principle. He has made unsubstantiated claims and personalised attacks against some diplomats, such as the British High Commissioner and the UN Country Coordinator for simply holding views that do not align with his.

If reality does not fit into his political views, he manufactures his own set of facts and tries to fit reality into his manufactured facts using conspiracy theories. For example, in the lead to the 2026 election, Sishuwa came up with totally fake outline of what he called a government strategy for re-election, that the government planned to burn markets and then offer support to affected individuals as a campaign strategy (https://x.com/ssishuwa/status/1986112642763923764 ). In shock at such a baseless claim, for example, Tarcisius Mukuka, a respected senior retired academic posted: “I must have missed the memo in which Sishuwa Sishuwa mutated from government critic to conspiracy theorist evident in his tweeter feed.

Should he not provide evidence of UPND market burning campaign strategy.” Even where Sishuwa has the right like anyone to comment on public affairs, he had crossed the academic line of dispassionate and objective commentary and moved into the realm of toxic emotional, personalised venom and toxic vitriol. For example, when making his prediction for the 2026 election outcome, Sishuwa posted: “Hichilema will lose the election on 13 August. The only thing that can save him from defeat is pre-ballot death or industrial scale vote-rigging. Never again should Zambia elect a lying, tribal, corrupt, unpatriotic, vindictive, hypocritical, lawless, and undemocratic scumbag.”

By the time his passport was revoked, many media houses had long stopped entertaining or publishing his commentaries or giving him space to engage with the public as they were seen as not enlightening but deleterious. In his own post in June 2026, Sishuwa indicated that News Diggers, Radio Phoenix, Lusaka Times and the Mail and Guardian of South African had blacklisted him, but speculated that these media houses had colluded with the government to block him. No evidence of this collusion was furnished.

An impression should not be created that academic freedom is unlimited or that whatever proceeds from an academic, no matter how unethical or unprofessional, should be entertained as academic freedom. History is full of academics who crossed the line and committed atrocious crimes for which they were held accountable. For example, Bilijana Plavsic, a biology professor, was convicted by the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) based on her hate speech and propaganda that led to atrocities and killings of innocent people, while Augustin Ngirabatware, an economics professor and government official, was convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) for his propaganda that incited violence and genocide.

Given this context, it is not surprising that there is hardly any public discourse among local academics about the Sishuwa fate. Claims of a clamp down on academics do not resonate with what is on the ground in Zambia. It seems there is a nuance the foreign academics have missed, demonstrating their costly naivety and ignorance of the context. Sishuwa is not one thing and his academic life must be separated from his social or political commentaries where he often goes rogue and makes claims that are not driven by any evidence or are simply fake.

Sishuwa himself has personally acknowledged this. When asked why he was spreading fake or unsubstantiated news, Sishuwa responded in a post on X in September 2025: “There is a difference between Sishuwa the public intellectual or political commentator, and Sishuwa the scholar.

The former draws inspiration from the world of public debate, the latter from that of scholarship. The former can proudly take a partisan position in the service of a social cause, the latter almost always claims objectivity as an observer.” It is this dichotomy in Sishuwa that the international scholars have not appreciated as they are removed from the context and have given flesh to the ugly stereotype of a concubine who mourns louder than the bereaved wife.

By O’Brien Kaaba

World.title: Sisters of the Child Jesus celebrate 100 years of existence in Kasama
World.content:
Apostolic Nuncio to Zambia and Malawi, Gian Luca Perici, has described the 100 years of existence of the Sisters of the Child Jesus (SCJ), as a testimony of God’s faithfulness and unwavering dedication to serving humanity.

Most Reverend Perici says the congregation’s journey from a humble beginning a century ago to its current position is a story of courage, sacrifice and total trust in God.

The Vatican Ambassador to Zambia and Malawi said this during the centenary celebration of the Sisters of the Child Jesus at Chilubula Mission in Kasama yesterday.

“We are here to celebrate a great milestone. 100 years ago, this congregation began from a humble beginning. Throughout this period, the Lord has guided your journey which has not been easy,” Archbishop Perici said.

The Nuncio disclosed that despite numerous challenges over the decades, the Sisters have remained steadfast and have continued to be a visible sign of God’s love, especially to the most vulnerable people in society.

“Despite numerous challenges, you have continued to show God’s love,” he said.

The Nuncio, who is the Pope’s representative, paid special tribute to the founding members of the congregation, describing them as brave women whose vision and faith laid a strong foundation for the works being seen today.

“We thank God for the brave women who started this mission. We thank the women who have stood firm for this organisation. Your work in health and education is commendable, you have always remembered the poor, giving them comfort,” he said.

He added that the centenary celebration is not only a moment to look back at the past with gratitude, but also an opportunity to look at the present with joy and to the future with hope.

“As we celebrate the present, we see how God continues to bless your congregation. God has sustained you and He is still doing great things through you. I encourage you to stay united. Continue to live out your calling with love, serve the people with total dedication, do not be afraid of what lies ahead,” he said.

Meanwhile, Archbishop of Kasama Archdiocese, Ignatius Chama, called on members of the Sisters of the Child Jesus to continue supporting and appreciating one another as they fulfill God’s work.

Archbishop Chama urged the Sisters to rediscover their vocation of love and to remain true to their identity.

“To find your vocation of love, look, it is who you are,” Archbishop Chama said.

He said the Sisters should remain rooted in love, unity and service which defines their congregation.

Archbishop Chama also thanked the Apostolic Nuncio for accepting to celebrate the milestone with the Sisters of the Child Jesus.

The Sisters of the Child Jesus are a diocesan congregation founded in Chilubula, in the Archdiocese of Kasama in 1926 by Bishop Étienne Larue, a Missionary of Africa.

World.title: President Hichilema reiterates call to preserve culture
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has reaffirmed the government’s recognition of the importance of traditional ceremonies in preserving Zambia’s cultural heritage, national identity, unity and social cohesion.

President Hichilema said traditional ceremonies such as the Lukwakwa, provide an important platform for communities to preserve and showcase their culture and heritage.

He said this in a speech read on his behalf by Northwestern Province Permanent Secretary, Grandson Katambi at the 2026 Lukwakwa traditional ceremony of the Mbunda- people of Manyinga and Kabompo Districts.

President Hichilema said the government will continue supporting the hosting of traditional ceremonies and working with traditional leaders to preserve cultural heritage.

He said the government will also continue working with traditional leadership to accelerate development in their chiefdoms.

“Government has supported various developmental projects in the chiefdom, including the drilling of boreholes, construction of health facilities, classroom blocks and science laboratories, provision of desks and construction of a local court,” he said.

He explained the projects were aimed at improving service delivery to the people of Manyinga district.

He has since called on traditional leaders, Members of Parliament and Ward Development Committees to work together in identifying and planning developmental projects which should be financed through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

The Head of State has meanwhile cautioned Ward Development Committees against frustrating government’s development efforts, saying successful implementation of projects required cooperation among stakeholders.

President Hichilema said Ward Development Committees should be scrutinised and strengthened to ensure that projects are successfully implemented.

He said partnerships among traditional leaders, local authorities, government and communities were important in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President has therefore appealed to traditional and local leaders to encourage young people to participate in skills training, particularly entrepreneurship programmes.

He said the responsibility of empowering young people required all stakeholders to come on board.

The Head of State has further encouraged young people to be proud of their identity, tribes and origins and advised them not to be ashamed of speaking their traditional languages.

And speaking at the same event, Lukwakwa Traditional Ceremony Organising Committee National Chairperson, Ndandula Livingi, has called for the protection and promotion of Mbunda cultural heritage.

Mr Livingi said culture should not be reduced to dancing but must instead encompass the broader values, traditions, language, history and practices of the Mbunda people.

He has since called on organisers and participants to reduce dances that were not part of Mbunda heritage in order to give prominence to authentic Mbunda cultural practices.

Mr Livingi also urged the people to support efforts aimed at transforming the Lukwakwa traditional ceremony into a major cultural and tourism event.

He said the ceremony had great potential to attract tourists and contribute to the promotion of the Mbunda culture.

“Lukwakwa is a big ceremony which, unfortunately, has been a sleeping lion, but eventually we will start seeing tourists coming to the ceremony,” Mr Livingi said.

He said the people belonging to the Mbunda tribe should take ownership of their culture and ensure that cultural materials and practices showcased during Lukwakwa reflected their heritage.

Mr Livingi said the transformation of the ceremony required collective support from traditional leaders, government, local communities and other stakeholders.

He further urged the people to embrace and promote the Mbunda culture so that it could be preserved for future generations.

The Lukwakwa traditional ceremony is an annual gathering of the Mbunda people of Manyinga and Kabompo districts aimed at showcasing and preserving their cultural heritage.

World.title: Heads of departments urged to prioritise Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande, has urged provincial heads of government departments under head 88 in Muchinga to plan and budget deliberately to support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Sichande noted that it is imperative for the Heads of Departments to identify practical interventions within their respective mandates that will enable them to contribute to national aspirations of the Grow Zambia production targets.

He further advised them to ensure that they also align the identified targets to National Development Plan and provincial priorities.

Mr Sichande said this when he addressed Heads of Department during the planning and budgeting meeting to prepare for the 2027-2029 medium term budget plan held in Chinsali district.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary disclosed that the Muchinga Province Administration Head 88 has been given an indicative budget ceiling of K124 million for the 2027 budget.

He added that with the constrained fiscal requirements given, the ceiling requires discipline in prioritisation in order to obtain maximum value from every Kwacha allocated.

Mr Sichande further said departmental submissions should prioritise statutory and legal obligations, realistic costing of tasks and operations, and provision for operational costs of key programmes.

World.title: ECZ trains DVEC, VEFs in Kanchibiya ahead of by-election
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commenced training for the District Voter Education Committee (DVEC) and Voter Education Facilitators (VEFs) in Kanchibiya district ahead of a by-election in Lubaleshi Ward.

The by-election was caused by the death of United Party for National Development (UPND) aspiring Councilor for Lubaleshi Ward in the August 2026 general election, Evans Chileshe, who passed away immediately after filing his nominations.

The training workshop for DVEC and VEFs is being held at Kanchibiya Town Council’s new Civic Centre.

Kanchibiya District Electoral Officer, Julius Katuka, urged participants not to be complacent but proactive in their approach to voter education ahead of the by-election.

Mr. Katuka acknowledged that the district’s vast terrain often proves to be a challenge for Voter Education Facilitators hence the need for them to devise effective strategies for undertaking the voter education exercise.

“A lot of things happen in the field and we must strive to ensure we are professional as we carry out activities that will help facilitate the coming by-election,” Mr Katuka said.

He said every member of the committee has a part to play and must play it well.

Meanwhile, DVEC Coordinator, Chrispin Chishimba urged members to participate fully in the workshop so as to be well equipped for the coming by-election.

Mr Chishimba thanked members for attending the meeting promptly and urged them to demonstrate the same zeal towards the by-election that they have shown in previous electoral exercises.

And DVEC member, Ernest Kambindi, said the committee stands ready to carry out activities for the by-election.

Mr Kambindi said the by-election is of great importance to Kanchibiya district as Lubaleshi Ward is the district’s largest ward.
