This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Hardship Exemption and Its Limits

The only legal way to pay less than the minimum is an exemption, the same route open to any struggling employer. Section 15 of the National Minimum Wage Act lets an employer apply online to the labour department.

Applicants must first consult unions or, where there are none, the affected workers, the department said in June 2023. The LWO Employers Organisation adds that they must pass financial tests on profitability, liquidity and solvency.

The department has said an exemption can cut the minimum wage by no more than 10%. An exemption lasts no longer than 12 months, according to the LWO.

Why Namibia Raised the Question

Namibia confirmed FMD on a commercial farm in its Karasburg veterinary district, in the south of the country, on Wednesday 23 September. The farm lies inside the disease-free zone that Namibia’s beef exports rely on, as reported on 25 September.

On Sunday 4 October, The Namibian quoted Maria Hedimbi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice and Labour Relations. “There are currently no discussions to exempt employers in the agricultural sector,” she said.

She added that all employers must keep paying the national minimum wage unless the government officially announces otherwise. Namibian farm workers have earned at least 14 Namibian dollars (US$0.84) an hour since 1 January.

Labour expert Herbert Jauch told the paper that paying below the minimum would “drive those workers into hunger”.

How Far FMD Has Spread in South Africa

South Africa’s internationally recognised FMD-free zone status was suspended in January 2019. The disease has now reached all nine provinces.

President Cyril Ramaphosa announced in his February 2026 State of the Nation Address that FMD had been classified a national disaster. New control rules, gazetted on 7 July, let farmers vaccinate their own animals with official authorisation.

Where South Africa’s FMD Vaccines Come From

Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp told Parliament on Tuesday 22 September that 21 million doses had been imported or produced in 2026. According to GroundUp, 11.5 million came from Turkey’s Dollvet and nine million from Argentina’s Biogénesis Bagó.

By late April, 2.5 million Biogénesis Bagó doses had already been secured and distributed, the government news agency SAnews reported.

South Africa does make some FMD vaccine at home. The Agricultural Research Council (ARC) handed over its first locally made batch in February 2026, after production stopped in 2005.

That pilot batch held 12,900 doses, and Aucamp said on 22 September that the ARC has produced over half a million. It still cannot meet demand, which GroundUp puts at about 25 million doses a year.

The ARC board agreed on Monday 21 September to let private companies make its vaccine under licence, Aucamp said. Onderstepoort Biological Products, a separate vaccine maker, does not produce FMD vaccine.

Imported doses from Turkey and Argentina cost about R45 (US$2.70) each, the minister said.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors in South African farming, the wage floor is a cost that disease rules do not suspend. FMD-hit farmers carry that bill while quarantines limit sales.

For travellers, FMD is an animal disease. The World Organisation for Animal Health says it is not readily transmissible to humans and is not a public health risk.

For policy watchers, South Africa still relies on Argentine and Turkish suppliers for most doses. Exports are the other pressure point for FMD-hit farmers.

A Department of Agriculture mission visited Saudi Arabia, Oman and the United Arab Emirates in late September. Its aim was to help reopen export channels, Agrinews reported on Monday 5 October.

What Is Not Known

It is unclear how many livestock farms have applied for wage exemptions since FMD spread. It is also unclear whether South Africa will offer FMD-hit farmers any support tied to wages.

No start date has been given for private production of the ARC vaccine. The ARC told Farmer’s Weekly on 29 September that procurement, regulatory and biosafety steps must be completed first.

In Namibia, Kharas regional governor Dawid Gertze said there is no agreement yet on how struggling farmers should handle wages.

More: South Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Do FMD-hit farmers in South Africa still have to pay the minimum wage?

Yes. The R30.23 (US$1.81) hourly minimum wage covers farm workers, with no exception for disease losses. A struggling employer can seek a temporary exemption but must still pay at least 90% of it.

Does South Africa make its own FMD vaccine?

Yes, on a small scale. The Agricultural Research Council restarted production in February 2026 and has made over half a million doses. Most supply still comes from Turkey and Argentina.

Is foot-and-mouth disease dangerous to people?

No. The World Organisation for Animal Health says FMD is not a public health risk. The damage is economic, through sick animals, quarantines and lost export sales.

What did Namibia say about farm wages?

Namibia’s labour ministry told The Namibian, in a report published on 4 October, that no wage exemption for farmers is under discussion. Farm workers there earn at least 14 Namibian dollars (US$0.84) an hour.

NIGERIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Nigeria has fought Islamist insurgents for years, mostly in Borno State in the far north-east, near Lake Chad.

— What happened Army, intelligence and Amotekun forces killed Abdussamad Ohida, a senior leader of ISWAP, in Owo forest at the weekend.

— Who he was Security sources say he led the group’s activities in parts of central and southern Nigeria after his superior’s 2023 arrest.

— Why it matters Ondo is in the south-west, at the other end of the country from the group’s Lake Chad base.

— The alleged plot Sources say he planned attacks on civilians over Christmas, aimed at disrupting the 2027 general elections.

— The catch The army has confirmed the Ondo raid only briefly and has not said how many people died.

Nigerian forces have killed a senior commander of Islamic State’s West African branch in an Ondo raid at the weekend. Security sources named him as Abdussamad Ohida, also known as Anwar.

The group, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), is strongest near Lake Chad in the far north-east. Ohida was killed in a forest in the south-west, far from that base.

How the Raid in Owo Forest Unfolded

Three forces took part. The Nigerian Army sent troops, and the Department of State Services (DSS), Nigeria’s domestic security service, sent operatives.

The third was Amotekun, the Western Nigeria Security Network. The governors of Nigeria’s six south-western states launched it in January 2020.

The team raided a hideout in Owo forest, according to security sources quoted by Nigerian newspapers. Several other members of the group were killed alongside Ohida.

The Ondo raid took place at the weekend, reportedly on Sunday 4 October. Owo is a town in Ondo State, whose capital is Akure.

On Monday 5 October, the army confirmed the joint operation, the Nigerian news site Witness NGR reported. Major Innocent Olamale speaks for the army’s 32 Artillery Brigade in Akure.

“Yes, it was a joint operation which intelligently led to the execution of the ISWAP commander,” he said. He gave no further details.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Abdussamad Ohida Was, According to Security Sources

Sources say Ohida was once deputy to Abu Ikrimah, also known as Abu Uwais. Abu Ikrimah led the group’s operations in central Nigeria until the DSS arrested him in 2023.

After that arrest, Ohida reportedly took charge of the group’s activity in parts of north-central and southern Nigeria. Sources say he planned and coordinated attacks there.

Questioning of Abu Uwais helped the DSS uncover a plan to attack civilians over the Christmas season, one source said. The same source said the plot aimed to disrupt the 2027 general elections.

The source linked Ohida to the July 2022 attack on Kuje Correctional Centre, a prison in Abuja, the capital. He also tied him to a 31 December 2025 attack on the police station at Ipele, in Owo.

Attackers took eight AK-47 rifles from that station, according to the source. Other attacks credited to Ohida hit police and military posts in Kogi and Niger states between 2020 and 2022.

These accounts come from unnamed security officials quoted by several Nigerian newspapers.

Why a Raid in Ondo Matters

The Islamic State affiliate split from Boko Haram and has its stronghold in Borno State. Owo lies in the south-west, the region that also includes Lagos.

Owo has suffered before: in June 2022, an attack on St Francis Catholic Church killed at least 40 worshippers. Nigeria’s federal government blamed ISWAP.

In October 2025, the DSS warned in a memo that the group planned attacks on communities in Ondo and Kogi states. The memo, reported by Vanguard, named Owo as a possible target.

A security source called Ohida’s death a very big blow to the group’s efforts to expand in Nigeria. In the north-east, Gombe State’s governor says Boko Haram is weakened but not defeated.

Another Blow After Al-Minuki

The Ondo raid follows the killing of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, a senior Islamic State figure, in May 2026. Nigeria’s presidency called it a joint Nigerian-American operation.

One source said British intelligence partners corroborated the information on Ohida and supported the operation. The source gave no details of the British role.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department rates Nigeria at Level 3, “Reconsider travel”, citing crime, terrorism, unrest, kidnapping and uneven access to health care. Its advisory was issued on 12 June 2026.

Ondo is not on the Level 4 “Do Not Travel” list, but neighbouring Kogi State is. The advisory warns that terrorists may attack with little or no warning, including places of worship, markets and hotels.

For policy readers, the raid follows a joint Nigerian-American operation in May and, one source says, used British intelligence. It fits Nigeria’s wider security ties with Western powers.

For investors, the alleged target of the plot stands out. Sources say it was meant to disrupt the 2027 general elections.

What Is Not Known

The army’s brief confirmation did not say how many people died in the Ondo raid. It also did not say what was recovered or how Ohida was identified.

Many details of the Ondo raid rest on unnamed sources, including the list of past attacks and the Christmas plot. It is also unclear whether the group will name a successor in the region.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What is ISWAP?

ISWAP stands for Islamic State West Africa Province, the Islamic State group’s branch in the region. It split from Boko Haram and is strongest in Borno State, near Lake Chad.

Who was Abdussamad Ohida?

Security sources describe him as a senior ISWAP leader, also known as Anwar. They say he led the group’s activities in parts of central and southern Nigeria after his superior’s arrest in 2023.

What are the DSS and Amotekun?

The DSS, or Department of State Services, is Nigeria’s domestic security service. Amotekun is a regional security corps that the six south-western states launched in 2020.

Did the army confirm the Ondo raid?

Yes, briefly. A spokesman for the army’s brigade in Akure confirmed the joint operation on Monday 5 October, Witness NGR reported. He gave no casualty figures.

Is Ondo State on the US Do Not Travel list?

No. The US State Department advises Americans to reconsider travel to Nigeria as a whole. Neighbouring Kogi State is on its Level 4 Do Not Travel list.

Sources: The Guardian Nigeria, 5 October 2026; Vanguard, 5 October 2026; Punch, 5 October 2026; Witness NGR, 5 October 2026; Vanguard (DSS memo), 21 October 2025; State House, Abuja, 16 May 2026; US State Department, 12 June 2026.

LIBERIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Liberia is a West African republic of about 5.4 million people, where mining now drives much of the growth.

— What happened On Monday 28 September 2026, the IMF board completed two reviews and cleared an IMF disbursement of about US$50.16 million.

— How it splits About US$26.2 million comes from a low-cost IMF loan programme and US$23.96 million from a climate-linked facility.

— Where it goes Liberia’s government says the cash is not direct budget support and will mostly strengthen central bank reserves.

— The numbers The IMF expects growth of 5.5% in 2026.

— The catch Efforts to recapitalise banks are running slower than planned, and new banknotes are an immediate priority amid shortages.

— What comes next Liberia plans a value-added tax in 2027 and intends to spread a one-off mining windfall over 2026 and 2027.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has cleared about US$50.16 million for Liberia after two reviews on Monday 28 September 2026. The IMF disbursement rewards the West African country for sticking to a reform programme the Fund has backed since 2024.

Liberia’s government says the money is not direct budget support and will mostly strengthen reserves at the Central Bank of Liberia. For investors and visitors abroad, the review is a useful check on how stable the country’s money and public finances are.

What the IMF Board Approved

The board completed the fourth review of Liberia’s 40-month Extended Credit Facility (ECF), a soft IMF loan for poorer countries. It also completed the first review of a 21-month Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF), which funds climate-resilience reforms.

Each completed review releases a new slice of money. This time the ECF pays SDR 19.3 million (about US$26.2 million), and the RSF SDR 17.62 million (about US$23.96 million).

The SDR, or special drawing right, is the IMF’s own unit of account, based on a basket of major currencies. The US dollar values for these SDR amounts are the IMF’s own conversions.

The board approved the ECF on 25 September 2024, with access of SDR 155 million, or 60% of Liberia’s IMF quota. That was about US$210 million at the time.

With this payment, ECF disbursements total SDR 96.5 million (about US$131.67 million), roughly 62% of the arrangement. The climate facility, approved on 27 April 2026, is larger, at SDR 193.8 million (about US$265 million).

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Liberia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Fund Is Satisfied

The IMF disbursement follows a solid run for the economy. According to the IMF, real GDP grew 5.1% in 2025 and should expand 5.5% in 2026.

Strong mining production leads the way, helped by construction and manufacturing. It is the same mining-led growth pattern that carried the economy in 2025.

Deputy Managing Director Bo Li, who chaired the board discussion, said Liberia’s performance “has remained satisfactory” despite “elevated and volatile oil prices”. He added that “fiscal consolidation has continued, supported by strong revenue performance, which has helped to reduce debt vulnerabilities.”

Fiscal consolidation means narrowing the gap between what the state spends and what it collects. Li said capital spending on long-term projects has accelerated, and he wants cuts to unproductive spending to free room for priority infrastructure.

Inflation remains contained, the IMF says. In late July its staff put the first-half 2026 average at 4.5% and expected 6% in the coming months.

What the IMF Wants Next

The Fund lists five priorities. First, Liberia should raise more revenue at home, notably through a value-added tax (VAT) in 2027.

Second, it should manage a one-off mining concession payment prudently and transparently. Li called the plan to spread that windfall over 2026 and 2027 appropriate, given limited capacity to run projects.

The other three are finishing bank restructuring, improving governance and fiscal transparency, and advancing climate reforms under the RSF. Bank recapitalisation is progressing “more slowly than planned”, Li warned.

He wants faster cuts in non-performing loans, meaning loans that borrowers have stopped repaying. That would strengthen banks and help them lend more to private businesses.

“Issuing new banknotes is an immediate priority to alleviate current shortages,” Li said. He also urged Liberia to publish its governance diagnostic report and act on it.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, the IMF disbursement shows the Fund still backs Liberia’s policies. The government says the money will add to central bank reserves.

Mining companies should note that the Fund pairs the VAT with mining tax reform and fewer tax exemptions. Firms that rely on exemptions should watch that process closely.

For travellers, the banknote shortage is the practical point. Liberian and US dollars are both in daily use, as the Liberia Explained 2026 guide sets out.

The IMF says Liberian banknotes are currently in short supply, and it has not given a date for new ones.

For policy watchers, the Fund names declining donor support as a risk to Liberia’s outlook. It also says removing legal barriers to publishing all public officials’ asset declarations would strengthen transparency and accountability.

What Is Not Known

The IMF does not say how large the one-off mining concession payment is or which company made it. Nor does it say how much of this IMF disbursement will stay in the central bank’s reserves.

The IMF gives no figure for the new banknotes, and no exact start date or rate for the VAT.

It also leaves open whether the central bank will need to tighten monetary policy. The bank stands ready to do so if oil prices push inflation up, the IMF says.

What Comes Next

About SDR 58.5 million (roughly US$80 million at the IMF’s conversion rate used above) of the ECF remains to be drawn. Each further IMF disbursement depends on Liberia passing future reviews.

Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan called the approval “a vote of confidence” in President Joseph Boakai’s leadership. “We will make sure that there will be no reversals in the gains that have been made,” he said.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

How much money did the IMF release for Liberia?

About US$50.16 million in total. The IMF disbursement combines about US$26.2 million from the Extended Credit Facility and US$23.96 million from the Resilience and Sustainability Facility.

When was the IMF disbursement for Liberia approved?

The IMF Executive Board completed the two reviews on Monday 28 September 2026. That made the money available immediately.

Is the money budget support for Liberia’s government?

No, according to the Liberian government. It says the IMF disbursement will mostly strengthen international reserves at the Central Bank of Liberia.

How fast is Liberia’s economy growing?

The IMF says real GDP grew 5.1% in 2025 and projects 5.5% for 2026. Mining production is the main driver, helped by construction and manufacturing.

What does the IMF want Liberia to do next?

Introduce a value-added tax in 2027, manage a one-off mining payment transparently and finish restructuring weak banks. It also wants stronger governance, climate reforms and new banknotes to ease shortages.

Sources: IMF, Press Release No. 26/309, Executive Board completes fourth ECF review and first RSF review for Liberia, 28 September 2026; IMF, Press Release No. 24/342, Executive Board approves forty-month US$210 million Extended Credit Facility arrangement for Liberia, 25 September 2024; IMF, staff-level agreement statement on Liberia’s fourth ECF review and first RSF review (via APO Group), 29 July 2026; The New Dawn, IMF Approves US$50.16M for Liberia, 2 October 2026; Liberian Observer, report on the US$50.16 million IMF approval, 2 October 2026.

World.title: Brazil Runoff on October 25, Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula
World.content:
BRAZIL ELECTIONS 2026 · RUNOFF GUIDE

Runoff · Sunday, 25 October Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula: what happens next The official first-round results from the electoral court (TSE), state by state. See the first-round results →

Key Facts — The date Brazil chooses its president in a runoff on Sunday, 25 October 2026, with polls open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time (7 a.m. to 4 p.m. US Eastern Time).

— The first round On 4 October, Flávio Bolsonaro won 47.03% of valid votes and President Lula 45.16%, according to the electoral court (TSE).

— The candidates Flávio Bolsonaro is a conservative senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro; Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the left-wing Workers’ Party is the sitting president.

— How it is decided The candidate with more valid votes wins; blank and spoiled ballots do not count.

— The next steps Free campaign airtime on television and radio runs from 9 to 23 October, and the winner takes office on 5 January 2027.

— Prediction markets Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 85% and Kalshi at 83% (Lula: 15% and 18% ), as of 5 October, 10:40 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— What it means for you The dollar fell more than 4% against the real on 5 October as markets priced a stronger conservative Congress, so the runoff is a market event for anyone holding Brazilian assets.

The Brazil runoff in 2026 pits Flávio Bolsonaro against President Lula on Sunday, 25 October, after a first round that the conservative challenger won by about 2.2 million votes. For readers in the United States, the outcome will decide the direction of Latin America’s largest economy, its currency and its relations with Washington.

This guide explains where the race stands, how the runoff works, the dates that matter until the inauguration, who the two candidates are and what to watch. We update it until the result; the official count is on our Brazil election results page.

Brazilian electronic voting machines. Voters choose a candidate by typing his number and confirming on the keypad. (File photo)

RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only â every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Where the Race Stands After the First Round

Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) finished first on 4 October with 47.03% of valid votes, about 56.1 million votes. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party (PT) received 45.16%, about 53.9 million votes. Those are the electoral court’s final figures.

Because neither candidate passed 50% of valid votes, the two leaders meet again three weeks later. The other candidates are out. Augusto Cury of Avante came third with 2.89%, Renan Santos of Missão fourth with 2.24% and Ronaldo Caiado of the PSD fifth with 2.18%.

The result surprised Lula’s camp. Lula himself called the result unexpected and said the race had gone into extra time, the business site InfoMoney reported. Abstention reached a record of about 21%, with more than 33 million registered voters staying away, the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Brazil runoff set: Flávio 47%, Lula 45%, 25 October” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The right also did well in Congress. The PL elected 19 senators and will hold the largest group in the Senate, with 28 of 81 seats, according to g1 and Folha.

How Brazil’s Runoff Works

Brazil elects its president in up to two rounds. A candidate who wins more than half of the valid votes in the first round is elected outright. Otherwise, the top two meet in a runoff, and the one with more valid votes wins. Blank and spoiled ballots are not counted as valid votes.

Voting is compulsory for literate citizens aged 18 to 70. It is optional for 16- and 17-year-olds, for people over 70 and for voters who cannot read. Polls open at 8 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. Brasília time across the country.

Brazilians vote on electronic voting machines run by the electoral courts, and results usually arrive on the same evening. Citizens registered abroad vote only for president. In states where no candidate for governor won a majority on 4 October, voters also choose their governor on 25 October.

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), who led the first round with 47.03% of valid votes. Foto: Ton Molina/Agência Senado

The Calendar Until October 25 and Beyond

The runoff campaign began on Monday, 5 October, the day after the first round. These are the dates that matter:

Friday, 9 October: free campaign airtime on television and radio begins for the two candidates.

Sunday, 11 October: first television debate of the runoff, hosted by Band and the newspaper Estadão at 8 p.m. Brasília time.

Friday, 23 October: last day of free campaign airtime.

Sunday, 25 October: runoff vote from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time, with the count starting when polls close.

Tuesday, 5 January 2027: the winner is sworn in for a four-year term.

The inauguration date is new. A 2021 constitutional amendment moved it from 1 January to 5 January, starting with the president elected in 2026.

Who Is Flávio Bolsonaro

Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, has been a senator for the state of Rio de Janeiro since 2019. He is the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, the conservative president from 2019 to 2022. His father cannot run. The electoral court declared him ineligible until 2030 in a 2023 ruling, and in 2025 the Supreme Federal Court convicted him over a plot to overturn the 2022 election, which he denies; that conviction adds a further bar of eight years after he serves his sentence.

Flávio stands for his father’s political base: tougher policing and sentences, lower taxes and a smaller state, and conservative social values. His supporters see him as a calmer, more negotiable version of that agenda. His critics on the left argue that his victory would put the Bolsonaro family back in power and strain relations with the courts.

Foreign allies of the right reacted quickly. Argentina’s President Javier Milei and Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated him on his first-round lead, g1 reported.

Who Is Lula

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, is a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the Workers’ Party. He was president from 2003 to 2010 and returned to office in January 2023. He is now seeking a fourth term.

Lula stands for social programmes such as the Bolsa Família cash transfer, state-led investment, income-tax relief for low earners and an active role in climate diplomacy. His supporters credit him with lower poverty and a stable democracy after the 2022 election. His critics on the right blame his government for high public spending, high interest rates and soft policing.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) at a news conference in June 2026. He is seeking a fourth term. Photo: Lula Oficial, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Endorsements and the Race for the Centre

With a gap of about 2.2 million votes, both camps now court the roughly 9 million voters who backed the eliminated candidates and the millions who stayed home. Flávio met São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas of the Republicanos party and other allies on 5 October to plan his runoff strategy, g1 reported. Tarcísio, a former infrastructure minister under Jair Bolsonaro, leads Brazil’s richest state.

Formal endorsements from the third- to fifth-placed candidates had not been announced by the evening of 5 October. Lula’s campaign must win back centrist voters, many of whom rejected his party in the first round, while Flávio must reassure moderates who worry about his father’s legacy.

What Markets Are Pricing

Investors read the first round as a shift toward business-friendly policies. On 5 October the US dollar fell more than 4% and traded below R$5, according to g1. The move reflects bets that a conservative Congress, and possibly a conservative president, would cut spending and lower interest rates over time.

The repricing is a bet, not a result. A Lula win on 25 October could reverse part of it, while a Flávio win would put the focus on his economic team and his first budget. The international echo was immediate as well: US President Donald Trump cited Brazil’s same-day count to criticise slow vote counting in the United States, g1 reported.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets let traders buy contracts that pay US$1 if an outcome happens, so a price of 80 cents implies an 80% chance in the market’s view. Two of them list Brazil’s presidential race: Polymarket and Kalshi, which the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates in the United States.

After the first round, traders made Flávio Bolsonaro the clear favourite. On 5 October, Polymarket priced his chance of winning at about 85% and Kalshi at about 83%. The card below shows the latest prices and updates every 20 minutes.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 84.6% · Lula 14.5% (US$172 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 83% · Lula 18% As of 5 October, 10:40 am ET (15:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Markets are not polls. They show where money is placed, they can swing on a single debate or endorsement, and a favourite at 85% still loses about one time in seven.

What It Means for You

For US investors, the real, Brazilian stocks and US-listed Brazilian companies are likely to stay volatile until the runoff result. For companies doing business in Brazil, the new Congress matters as much as the president, because no Brazilian president governs without a coalition.

For travellers and expats, daily life continues as normal during the campaign. On voting day, expect closed schools used as polling stations, restrictions on alcohol sales in some states and busy roads in the evening.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet known which eliminated candidates will endorse whom, or how their voters will split. It is not known how the polls will move after the surprise of the first round. Nor is it known whether the market rally of 5 October will hold over three weeks of campaigning.

What to Watch

Watch for endorsements in the coming days, the first runoff polls, the free campaign airtime from 9 October and the first television debate on 11 October. Watch the real and Brazilian stocks as a running verdict on the race. On the evening of 25 October, follow the official count on our results page; in 2022 the runoff winner was clear within about three hours of polls closing.

Related reading: Brazil Election Explained After Flávio and Lula Advance; Brazil Election: Betting Markets Favour Flávio Bolsonaro, Polls Show a Tie; Brazil presidential polls diverge sharply 17 days before the vote; more from Brazil Elections 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Brazil runoff in 2026?

The runoff is on Sunday, 25 October 2026. Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time, which is 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. US Eastern Time.

What were the first-round results in Brazil?

Flávio Bolsonaro won 47.03% of valid votes and President Lula 45.16%, according to the electoral court. Because neither passed 50%, they meet in a runoff.

Who is Flávio Bolsonaro?

Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is a conservative senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. He runs for the Liberal Party (PL).

How does Brazil’s runoff work?

The two leading candidates of the first round face each other, and the one with more valid votes wins. Blank and spoiled ballots are not counted.

When does Brazil’s next president take office?

The winner is sworn in on 5 January 2027. A 2021 constitutional amendment moved the inauguration from 1 January.

How did markets react to the first round?

On 5 October the US dollar fell more than 4% and traded below R$5, according to g1, as investors priced a more business-friendly Congress.

What do prediction markets say about Brazil’s runoff?

On 5 October, Polymarket priced Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at about 85% and Kalshi at about 83%. Prices are traders’ bets, not polls, and they move quickly.

Sources: TSE official results, g1, Folha de S.Paulo, InfoMoney, Estadão and Band debate, Constitutional Amendment 111/2021. As of 5 October 2026.

World.content:

NIGERIA · OIL AND POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Nigeria, Africa’s most populous nation, holds its oil and gas stakes through NNPC Ltd, the national oil company.

— What happened On Sunday 4 October, presidential challenger Atiku Abubakar asked NNPC to itemise N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion) it says the state owes it.

— What the figure is The NNPC receivable sits in the company’s 2025 accounts as money owed to NNPC by the Nigerian state.

— The wider question Atiku also asked whether firms holding big federal contracts are helping fund President Bola Tinubu’s re-election campaign.

— The catch The N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion) is a balance NNPC says the state owes it; the accounts do not show what was paid to contractors.

— Still open Atiku offered no evidence linking contract payments to Tinubu’s campaign, and the accounts do not split security costs from advances.

Nigerian opposition presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar wants a detailed breakdown of NNPC receivables worth N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion). NNPC Ltd, the national oil company, books the sum in its 2025 accounts as money owed to it by the Nigerian state.

Atiku, a former vice-president, made the demand in a campaign statement on Sunday 4 October. He also asked whether companies holding large federal contracts are helping to fund President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid.

Who Atiku Is and What NNPC Does

Atiku Abubakar was Nigeria’s vice-president from 1999 to 2007 under President Olusegun Obasanjo. He lost the 2023 presidential election to Tinubu as the candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

In 2025 he moved to the African Democratic Congress (ADC), and he is now its candidate for the 2027 presidential race. Tinubu, of the governing All Progressives Congress (APC), is seeking a second term.

NNPC Ltd is Nigeria’s national oil company. Since the Petroleum Industry Act of 2021, it runs commercially and holds the state’s oil and gas stakes.

Its accounts call the Nigerian state “the Federation”. Amounts here are converted at about 1,331 naira to the US dollar on 5 October 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on NNPC (Nigeria) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the NNPC Receivable Actually Is

Note 24.2 of NNPC’s 2025 financial statements lists N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion) as “other receivables from Federation” for the group. A receivable is money a company expects to collect from someone else.

The note says this NNPC receivable covers advance payments to the government and the cost of protecting oil and gas assets. Under a framework agreed between the government and NNPC, the company can pay for that security and charge it to the state.

The figure is the balance on 31 December 2025, an amount NNPC says the state owes it. The accounts do not say how much of it is security costs and how much is advances.

A year earlier, receivables from the Federation stood at N17.5 trillion (US$13.2 billion). That total combined N8.67 trillion (US$6.5 billion) in energy-security costs with N8.84 trillion (US$6.6 billion) in other receivables.

The older N8.67 trillion (US$6.5 billion) balance was netted against royalties, taxes and dividends due to the Federation.

That reconciliation was completed in September 2025. In plain terms, the claim was netted against sums due to the state rather than settled in cash.

What Atiku Is Asking For

Atiku wants NNPC to say how much of the sum relates to protecting oil and gas infrastructure. He also wants to know what was paid, who received it and what services were delivered.

“Nigerians cannot tell from these totals what was spent on pipeline surveillance,” he said. The statement was issued by Phrank Shaibu, strategic communication director of Atiku’s ADC campaign council.

Atiku also set the NNPC receivable against roughly N3.1 trillion (US$2.3 billion) allocated to the Ministry of Defence in 2025. He acknowledged that the two figures belong to different accounting categories.

The Campaign Funding Question

Atiku pointed to Tantita Security Services, which the federal government engages for oil pipeline surveillance in the Niger Delta. Government Ekpemupolo, known as Tompolo, is associated with the firm.

Ekpemupolo also founded and sponsors the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, which campaigns for Tinubu’s re-election. On Saturday 3 October the group donated 25 campaign vehicles, generators and electronic speakers in Taraba State.

“Tantita holds a pipeline security contract while its founder sends campaign vehicles out to seek another term for the President,” Atiku said. He presented no evidence that payments under Tantita’s contract funded the movement.

He also questioned the award of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to Hitech Construction Company, owned by the Chagoury family. He asked the government to publish the firms invited, the bids, their evaluation and the final contract.

The statement offered no evidence that Hitech or the Chagoury family financed Tinubu’s re-election activities.

What NNPC and the Government Have Said

In April, NNPC said its pipeline-security programme helped lift crude output to an average of 1.71 million barrels a day in 2025. That compared with 960,000 barrels a day in 2022.

Also in April, more than 300 federal lawmakers backed keeping Tantita on pipeline surveillance after a National Assembly roundtable on pipeline security.

When NNPC presented its 2025 results, Group Chief Executive Bayo Ojulari credited community surveillance and the armed forces. “Most of those pipelines have retained 100 per cent availability,” he said, according to Punch.

On the highway, the federal government has said it used restricted bidding. NNPC and the Presidency had not publicly responded to Atiku’s statement by Monday 5 October.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors in Nigerian bonds or oil partnerships, the NNPC receivable shows how closely the company’s books and state finances overlap. The earlier N8.67 trillion (US$6.5 billion) security balance was settled by offset, not in cash.

The breakdown Atiku seeks is not in the published accounts, so any detail NNPC releases would be new information. For policy watchers, oil money and contract awards are now campaign issues before the 2027 vote.

What Is Not Known

The accounts do not split the N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion) between security spending and advances. Nor do they name the companies paid for pipeline protection or what each received.

There is no public evidence that money from Tantita’s contract or from Hitech reached Tinubu’s campaign. It is also unclear whether NNPC will publish the detail, and how the current NNPC receivable will be settled.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What is the NNPC receivable Atiku is asking about?

It is money NNPC Ltd records as owed to it by the Nigerian government: N11.2 trillion (US$8.4 billion) on 31 December 2025. The accounts say it covers advance payments to the government and the cost of protecting oil and gas assets.

Who is Atiku Abubakar?

He was Nigeria’s vice-president from 1999 to 2007 and is the African Democratic Congress candidate for the 2027 presidential election. He lost the 2023 election to Bola Tinubu as the Peoples Democratic Party candidate.

Was the money paid to pipeline-security contractors?

Not as such: the NNPC receivable is a debt the government owes the company. The accounts do not say how much of it relates to security work.

Is there evidence that contractors funded Tinubu’s campaign?

Atiku asked the question but presented no evidence. He cited Tantita’s pipeline contract and the coastal highway award to Hitech Construction.

How was the earlier energy-security claim settled?

NNPC’s accounts say the N8.67 trillion (US$6.5 billion) energy-security balance was offset against royalties, taxes and dividends owed to the state. That reconciliation ended in September 2025.

SOUTH AFRICA · BUSINESS

Key Facts — The country South Africa co-hosts the 2027 Men’s Cricket World Cup with Zimbabwe and Namibia: 57 matches across 12 venues, eight of them in South Africa.

— What happened In the Ticketpro deal, a women-owned empowerment consortium bought Cricket South Africa’s official ticket seller from Blu Label in May 2026.

— The McKenzie link Sport Minister Gayton McKenzie’s former chief of staff became Ticketpro’s chief executive in June; two new shareholders have ties to his party.

— The 4% cut Ticketpro would earn about 4% of general-access World Cup ticket sales, roughly R4.1 million (US$246,000), Daily Maverick reported.

— The catch Daily Maverick found no evidence that McKenzie intervened, and he, his party and the new owners deny any impropriety.

— What comes next The free ticket ballot closes on 21 November 2026, and the tournament runs from 2 October to 21 November 2027.

After South Africa’s Ticketpro deal, a former aide to Sport Minister Gayton McKenzie now runs Cricket South Africa’s ticket seller. Two of the company’s new shareholders also have ties to his Patriotic Alliance party.

On Monday 5 October 2026, South African news site Daily Maverick said Ticketpro looks set to sell 2027 Cricket World Cup tickets. The outlet found no evidence that McKenzie intervened, and he, his party and the new owners deny any impropriety.

How the Ticketpro Deal Came Together

Blu Label, a telecoms group listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, sold Ticketpro in May 2026. It said the buyer, a “women-owned broad-based black economic empowerment consortium”, had approached it with an “unsolicited bid”.

Broad-based black economic empowerment is South Africa’s policy for raising black people’s participation in the economy. Blu Label called the Ticketpro deal “an arm’s length disposal” but keeps the price confidential.

Dollar figures here use 16.66 rand to the US dollar, the rate on 5 October 2026.

In June 2026, three Blu Label executives resigned as Ticketpro directors. A new company, Ticketpro Group, was founded in August; its directors are Astrid Harrison, Omphemetse Mokgosi and marketing professional Zanele Dube.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on South Africa Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Gayton McKenzie Is and How the Links Run

Gayton McKenzie is South Africa’s Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture. He also leads the Patriotic Alliance (PA), one of the country’s political parties.

Ticketpro is the official ticket seller for Cricket South Africa, the national cricket body, and the South African Football Association. Both fall within McKenzie’s oversight reach, Daily Maverick noted.

Bakang Lethoko was McKenzie’s chief of staff from August to November 2024. She then chaired his department’s Formula One bid steering committee and became Ticketpro’s chief executive in June 2026.

McKenzie appointed Mokgosi to the boards of the National Film and Video Foundation and the National Arts Council in 2024 and 2025. Harrison has described herself on social media as a “proud, disciplined member” of his party.

Speaking for Ticketpro Group, Harrison confirmed that she, Mokgosi and Dube are now Ticketpro shareholders.

The Cricket World Cup Ticketing Question

The International Cricket Council (ICC), the sport’s global governing body, unveiled the 2027 schedule in Cape Town on Thursday 1 October 2026. McKenzie attended the launch, according to Daily Maverick.

The 14-team tournament runs from 2 October to 21 November 2027, with 57 matches in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. The final is in Johannesburg on 21 November.

The ICC also opened a free ticket ballot at tickets.cricketworldcup.com. The ballot’s privacy notice names Ticketpro Group as the “official ticketing provider” that runs the platform.

The local organising committee told Daily Maverick it would announce “ticketing and all matters related thereto” in the coming weeks. By Daily Maverick’s press time, neither the committee nor Cricket South Africa had publicly confirmed Ticketpro as the World Cup’s ticket seller.

The 4% Commission and the Money at Stake

As Cricket South Africa’s official vendor, Ticketpro would be entitled to “a small percentage-based cut” of ticket sales. For the World Cup’s general-access tickets, Daily Maverick put that cut at about 4%.

A BDO consultancy study for Cricket South Africa forecasts about 409,000 general-access tickets at an average of about R250 (US$15). That would bring in about R102 million (US$6.1 million), of which 4% is roughly R4.1 million (US$246,000).

Ticketpro also sells tickets for the Proteas, South Africa’s national cricket team, including the current series against Australia. Its yearly turnover is about R100 million (US$6 million), a source told Daily Maverick.

What McKenzie and the New Owners Say

McKenzie rejected any suggestion that he might influence commercial decisions that benefit Ticketpro. “The Minister himself is limited from exercising direct procurement decisions,” his spokesperson said.

On Lethoko’s appointment, the spokesperson said: “There was no involvement.” PA spokesperson Steven Motale said the party “played no part in her appointment, formal or informal”.

Ticketpro Group said its decisions are “made on commercial merit and through the appropriate governance processes”. Lethoko said her role as chief of staff ended well before she joined Ticketpro.

Daily Maverick said it found no evidence that McKenzie intervened in the Ticketpro deal or in the company’s deals with sports bodies. The developments have nonetheless “raised eyebrows” among industry insiders, the outlet wrote.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors in South African companies, the sale is a reminder to ask who stands behind a buyer. Blu Label said it had no knowledge of the buyers’ political affiliations.

Daily Maverick said it was unclear whether Blu Label checked the buyers for links to public office before the sale.

For cricket fans in the United States, the World Cup ballot is free and open worldwide. It closes on 21 November 2026, and the ICC prices tickets from about US$9.50 to US$30.

What Is Not Known

The price the consortium paid in the Ticketpro deal, and where its money came from, have not been disclosed. It is also unclear whether Ticketpro Group owns all of Ticketpro’s shares or whether other investors are involved.

Organisers have not said how the World Cup ticket seller was chosen or how many bidders took part. Daily Maverick calls its report the first in a series named “Caught Out”, with more on the Ticketpro deal to come.

More: South Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What is the Ticketpro deal in South Africa?

In the Ticketpro deal, Blu Label sold Cricket South Africa’s official ticket seller to a women-owned empowerment consortium in May 2026. Ticketpro also sells tickets for the South African Football Association.

Who is Gayton McKenzie?

Gayton McKenzie is South Africa’s Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture. He also leads the Patriotic Alliance, a political party.

How is McKenzie linked to the Ticketpro deal?

His former chief of staff became Ticketpro’s chief executive in June 2026, and two shareholders have ties to his party. He denies any role, and Daily Maverick found no evidence that he intervened.

How much could Ticketpro earn from the 2027 Cricket World Cup?

Daily Maverick put Ticketpro’s cut at about 4% of general-access ticket sales, roughly R4.1 million (US$246,000). The terms of its cricket contracts have not been disclosed.

Can fans outside South Africa get 2027 Cricket World Cup tickets?

Yes. The free ICC ballot at tickets.cricketworldcup.com is open worldwide until 21 November 2026. The tournament itself runs from 2 October to 21 November 2027.

SOUTH AFRICA · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — The country Cape Town is South Africa’s second-largest city, a busy port wedged between Table Mountain and the Atlantic Ocean.

— What happened On Friday 2 October 2026, Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis unveiled a plan to replace the city’s unfinished highways.

— Why it matters The 1970s stubs cut the city centre off from its harbour; the plan would free about 15 hectares for a new neighbourhood.

— What starts first Only phase one, a new link bridge plus two extra inbound lanes, is pencilled in for the next council term.

— The catch There is no cost estimate or published funding model, and the tunnel needs land owned by the state port authority.

— What it means for you No tenders, land prices or housing targets have been published; the second phase is scheduled to run until 2040.

— What comes next The City says public consultation starts with the release of the drawings; road-scheme and heritage processes follow.

Cape Town has unveiled a plan to replace its unfinished highways, freeway ends left hanging in mid-air for about half a century. Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis presented it on Friday 2 October 2026, standing on one of the unfinished bridges.

A new link bridge would come first, with a tunnel and a new neighbourhood on about 15 hectares to follow. The City has given no cost or funding model, and only the first phase has a target start date.

What the City Has Proposed for Phase One

The City of Cape Town wants to build in two halves so that traffic keeps flowing on the old freeways. Phase one would widen the inbound freeway by two lanes and add a new link bridge over Buitengracht Street.

That bridge would carry inbound traffic straight onto Helen Suzman Boulevard. Drivers heading for Green Point, Sea Point and the Atlantic Seaboard would bypass the central business district (CBD).

Phase one also adds bus lanes, a park beneath the bridge and a new canal joining the V&A Canal. That waterway leads to the V&A Waterfront harbour and shopping district.

Three plots would open up for housing, and the City wants this phase to start in the next council term.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Phase Two Brings a Tunnel and a New Neighbourhood

The larger second phase would only begin once phase one is finished. A new outbound bridge would lead into a tunnel near the port, running beside Duncan Road to two national highways.

The existing outbound viaduct would then be demolished to make room for a harbour promenade, parks and more building plots. The City says this phase would run until 2040.

The City is in talks with Transnet, the state-owned freight and ports company, over port land the tunnel needs.

Why the Bridges Were Never Finished

Work on the freeway began in the early 1970s and stopped in 1977. A shortage of money is among the reasons cited.

Capetonians call the unfinished highways “Solly’s Folly”, after Solly Morris, the city engineer of that era.

Who Pays, and Why the Timing Is Political

Hill-Lewis would not give a cost estimate. “It will obviously be a very large project, many billions of rands,” he said, according to the Cape Argus.

According to Eyewitness News, the mayor said the City would fund the first phase. He said national government and Transnet were expected to help with the second, but no funding agreement has been announced.

At the launch, Transnet chief executive Michelle Phillips said: “We are always going to be supportive of the cities in which we operate.” No deal on the port land has been made public.

Hill-Lewis’s Democratic Alliance (DA), which runs the city, faces municipal elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026. Brett Herron, mayoral candidate for the opposition GOOD party, called the announcement “hollow election-linked puffery” without figures on cost, funding and housing.

What It Means for US Readers

For travellers, the Foreshore is where major routes enter and leave Cape Town, between the city centre and the V&A Waterfront. Nothing changes on the road for now, but the mayor expects several years of construction once work begins.

For investors, the unfinished highways are a long-dated story about scarce city-centre land, not a deal on offer today. No tenders, land prices or housing targets have been published.

For policy readers, Herron cited Boston’s Big Dig, where costs rose from an initial estimate of about US$2.8 billion to US$14.8 billion. Housing pressure is already shaping city politics, as in Cape Town Moves to Charge Airbnb Hosts Hotel Rates.

What Is Not Known

The total cost is unknown, and the mayor says an accurate figure will only come after detailed design and procurement. It is also unclear how the second phase would be shared between the City, national government and Transnet.

The City says the plan includes affordable housing but has not said how many homes. Nor is it clear whether Transnet will release the port land, or how much the drawings will change.

What Comes Next

The City says the public-facing phase began on 2 October, when it released the drawings to start public consultation, with updates on the project website, foreshore.capetown. Public participation will include road-scheme amendments and heritage impact assessments, both statutory steps.

Only then come detailed engineering and procurement. Work on the unfinished highways is not imminent, and the existing outbound viaduct is due to be torn down rather than finished.

More: South Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What is Cape Town’s Foreshore Precinct Project?

It is the City of Cape Town’s plan to replace the unfinished highways with a new link bridge and a tunnel. It would also free about 15 hectares of city-centre land for homes, offices and parks.

When will construction start on Cape Town’s unfinished highways?

Only phase one has a target start, during the next city council term after the November 2026 elections. The City says the second phase, including the tunnel, would run until 2040.

How much will the Foreshore project cost, and who pays?

No cost has been published; the mayor would only say it will run to many billions of rands. He said the City would fund phase one, and that national government and Transnet were expected to help with phase two.

Why were Cape Town’s highways never finished?

Work began in the early 1970s and stopped in 1977, with a lack of money among the reasons cited. The concrete ends have stood in mid-air ever since.
