World.title: Leader of Opposition says “Belizean families cannot afford more increases”
World.content:
Leader of Opposition says “Belizean families cannot afford more increases”

By Zoila Palma: Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton says that data from the Statistical Institute of Belize shows how Belize’s economy grew by just 1.4% in the second quarter of 2026 while the primary sector contracted by 6.1%, the secondary sector by 6.4%, and manufacturing by 9.9%.

“These figures expose the failure to strengthen the productive base that sustains livelihoods and generates export earnings.

Meanwhile, consumer prices rose 4.4% in August. Transport costs jumped 11.7%, food and non-alcoholic beverages increased 2.5%, and housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels rose 4.4%. Belizean families are paying more for groceries, transportation and basic utilities. Belizean families cannot afford more increases, more uncertainty and more excuses,” Panton expressed.

Panton says that Belize’s trade figures are “alarming.”

“Tourism stakeholders have reported declines of as much as 30–40%. The Government must investigate these reports and engage the sector immediately. Tropic Air’s decision to close its Punta Gorda station effective November 1, 2026, citing sustained losses and uncertainty surrounding domestic aviation, is another serious warning that has caused much concern for workers, businesses, tourism partners and Toledo’s connectivity,” she added.

The Leader of the Opposition further called on the Government to answer for the widening gap between its promises of prosperity, “todos ganamos” and the reality facing Belizean families who are being forced to make impossible decisions every day.

World.title: Leader of Opposition says “UDP ready” for 2027 Municipal elections
World.content:
Leader of Opposition says “UDP ready” for 2027 Municipal elections

By Zoila Palma: Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton says that the UDP is ready for the 2027 municipal elections.

“We are proud of our Belize City Municipal Team who joined us and we are grateful for the opportunity to share our plans and commitment to serving our communities with humility, integrity and compassion,” Panton said this morning.

“The UDP is Ready to Lead and We are Ready to Serve,” she added.

The UDP recently introduced its municipal slates for all municipalities across Belize.

World.title: National Biodiversity Office participates in Belize Birding Festival 2026
World.content:
National Biodiversity Office participates in Belize Birding Festival 2026

By Zoila Palma: The National Biodiversity Office (NBIO) participated in the Belize Birding Festival 2026 on October 3, engaging with more than 90 members of the public and sharing information about its work, projects and mandate. The event provided an opportunity for the office to raise awareness about Belize’s biodiversity and the importance of conservation.

The Belize Birding Festival, organized by the Belize Audubon Society and Belize Tourism Industry Association, brought together birders, tour guides, conservationists, tourism businesses, local communities and visitors. The festival celebrated Belize’s diverse birdlife while encouraging greater appreciation for the country’s natural heritage.

NBIO highlighted the important role birds play within Belize’s ecosystems, with many species relying on habitats found within the country’s protected areas.

Through protected areas management, biodiversity policy coordination and public awareness initiatives, the office supports national efforts to conserve Belize’s ecosystems and species.

The National Biodiversity Office said events such as the Belize Birding Festival are important in connecting people with nature and strengthening appreciation for Belize’s rich biodiversity.

World.title: Join the World Mental Health Day walkathon!
World.content:
Join the World Mental Health Day walkathon!

By Zoila Palma: As World Mental Health Day approaches on October 10, 2026, this year’s observance is being held under the theme, “Lived experiences heard: Real voices, real change.”

The Ministry of Health and Wellness is inviting everyone to join a mental health awareness walk through the streets of Belize City on Wednesday, October 7, beginning at 5:15 p.m. at the ITVET campus.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says this year’s campaign aims to meaningfully engage people with lived experience (PWLE) of mental health conditions and recognize their experiences and knowledge as a vital form of expertise.

WHO says people with lived experience are too often asked to share their stories but are excluded from decisions involving policies, services and systems that directly affect their lives.

WHO noted that meaningful engagement must go beyond simply giving people an opportunity to speak. It should create opportunities for people with lived experience to influence decisions, co-design mental health services, strengthen peer-led approaches, challenge stigma and improve accountability. WHO says when these voices are meaningfully included, mental health systems can become more person-centred, rights-based and responsive to people’s needs.

This year, WHO is also launching practical guidance on deinstitutionalization, emphasizing the need for careful planning and investment in community services and support.

World.title: Jealousy over supper ends with three people injured in Trial Farm
World.content:
Jealousy over supper ends with three people injured in Trial Farm

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 20 year old man has been detained after three people were injured in an alleged attack in the Black Water Area of Trial Farm Village, Orange Walk District.

Police say a 26 year old domestic reported that on Saturday, October 3, she had invited a 21 year old male friend, a construction worker, to her home for supper. A 16 year old girl who lives at the house was also there.

Her former common law husband arrived, became upset at seeing the friend and accused her of having an affair with him.

The man allegedly tried to punch the friend, then used what appeared to be a broken glass to inflict cuts to the left side of his face and abdomen. The friend fled on his bicycle.

The man is then accused of punching the woman in the face and striking the teenager in the face and abdomen.

The suspect has been detained pending charges.

World.title: Man says shotgun was pointed at him after money dispute in Orange Walk
World.content:
Man says shotgun was pointed at him after money dispute in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk are investigating a report of aggravated assault involving what appeared to be a shotgun.

A 35 year old mason and welder of Santa Familia Street, Orange Walk Town, told police that around 7:00pm on Sunday, October 4, he was at his cousin’s house on Audinett Alley.

He said a man arrived and got into an argument with his cousin over money before leaving. About ten minutes later, the man returned in a green vehicle, with a grey taxi in front.

The complainant said a man in the taxi called for his cousin. When he went over instead, the man allegedly pointed what looked like a shotgun at him and told him, in Kriol, to talk to his cousin so he would know what the deal is.

The taxi then drove off. No one was hurt.

World.title: Expired licence and no insurance land August Pine Ridge man in trouble
World.content:
Expired licence and no insurance land August Pine Ridge man in trouble

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 38 year old laborer of August Pine Ridge Village, Orange Walk District, has been charged with traffic offences after a police stop on Saturday night.

He is Silverio Perez.

Police say Corridor Police officers on motorcycle patrol in August Pine Ridge around 10:30pm noticed Perez riding a white motorcycle.

When officers stopped him and asked for his driver’s licence, Perez allegedly said he had one but it was expired. Checks also showed no licence sticker on the motorcycle, and Perez reportedly admitted he had no insurance.

He was charged with driving a motor vehicle not covered by third party risk insurance and driving without a valid Belize driving licence.

His 2023 white Honda 150L was impounded at the Orange Walk Police Station.

World.title: America goes all in on super intelligence. Where is Belize?
World.content:
America goes all in on super intelligence. Where is Belize?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP) : The world’s biggest economy just made AI a matter of national priority.

President Donald Trump has formed a Super Intelligence Force to coordinate the US Government’s push to lead the world in advanced artificial intelligence. Top officials will steer it, tech giants have signed on, and it reports straight to the White House.

The message is clear. AI is not the future. It is now.

Which raises a big question at home: what is the Government of Belize doing?

Is there a national AI strategy? Who in Government is responsible for it? Are our schools preparing students for an AI driven job market? Are our public services, businesses and BPO workers ready for the changes AI will bring? And what protections are in place for Belizeans’ data and privacy?

Small countries cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. AI will shape jobs, education, healthcare, tourism and security, whether we plan for it or not.

The US is moving fast. Belize needs to move too.

BBN invites the Government of Belize to tell Belizeans what its plan is for artificial intelligence.

What do you think, Belize? Is our country ready for the AI age?

World.title: GET SLAVERY HISTORY RIGHT
World.content:
Warmington

THE Global Afrikan Congress (GAC) has pointedly told Government Member of Parliament Everald Warmington that he has a “misinformed understanding” of history in relation to the transatlantic slave trade and has urged him to apologise for his recent comments on the issue in the legislature.

Additionally, the organisation recommended that he undertake a process of what it calls “historical self-repair” and directed him to the works of historians, scholars and writers who have examined the history of Africa, the Caribbean, European expansion, slavery, colonialism, and resistance.

In an open letter to the St Catherine South Western Member of Parliament, the GAC, described as an international umbrella organisation created by and for Africans and people of African descent, challenged Warmington’s comments relating to Jamaica’s petition to King Charles III and the King’s referral of the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

The petition asks the Privy Council to make determinations on Britain’s seizure, transportation, chattelisation, and enslavement of Jamaica’s ancestors from the mid-17th century to 1834. On September 22, after Culture Minister Olivia Grange — who led a delegation that delivered the petition to Buckingham Palace on September 7 — informed Parliament that King Charles has referred the petition to the Privy Council, Warmington said he found the delegation’s visit to London embarrassing.

“I’m embarrassed at the spectacle of the photo ops in London. We went there and [it] remind me of this nursery rhyme: Pussycat, Pussycat where have you been? I’ve been to London to see the king.

Pussycat, Pussycat what did you do there? I left a petition on the empty chair,” Warmington declared in the House.

“We keep on speaking of the buyers of the slaves, but nobody speaks of the sellers of the slave. The white man didn’t go to Africa and pick up enslaved people and take them across here.

They were caught by black people who sold them to the white man to come here,” he added. In response, the GAC said Warmington displayed a “subjective and derisive formulation of history”.

“We respect your right to your own interpretation of history, though it is a colonial formulation and historically falsified to justify their crimes.

However, we vigorously assert that you don’t have the right to rewrite history based on your obviously misinformed understanding of it,” the organisation said in the letter signed by its Ambassador General Cikiah Thomas.

“The problem is not that you have raised the question of African involvement in the history of the slave trade.

The problem is that you have presented an extraordinarily complex historical system of European invasion, military coercion, commercial expansion, warfare, forced transportation, plantation enslavement, colonial law, and racial ideology as though a simple distinction between African sellers and European buyers can adequately explain it,” the GAC said.

The group argued that there was no market for buying and selling free Africans. “On the contrary, there was coercion at bayonet point by Europeans to forcibly coerce Africans to round up other Africans, not for sale but for European appeasement; and forcible capture for the enslaved person awaiting ships.

Hence, your depiction of a market in Africans is not only based on misinformation, but it is also an example of how many of us have internationalised racism.”

The GAC insisted that the history of the transatlantic slave trade cannot properly be understood by asking only who physically captured a particular African and who purchased that person.

Rather, much larger and more insightful questions needed to be asked, such as who created the enormous transatlantic demand for enslaved labour; who organised the Atlantic commercial system for African labour; who financed and insured the voyages of European ships and their cargoes; who controlled the ships and shipping networks; who established and protected the plantation economy; who developed colonial laws defining Africans and their descendants as property; who accumulated wealth from the system, and where is the wealth; who defended the enslavement of Africans through colonial governments and legislatures; and who maintained the system through military and imperial power?

“Unfortunately, contrary to your simplistic and infantile responses in our country’s Parliament, the cited questions cannot be answered by simply saying that Africans sold Africans,” the GAC told Warmington.

It said that the colonial miseducation and misconception that Warmington demonstrated as an MP requires clarification for him and “other black folks who may think, like you, that the existing African communities did not resist the massive European invasion and encroachment on those communities.

Thus, it must be underscored that African societies fought against the capture and enslavement of their peoples.”

The GAC said that had Warmington taken some time to inform himself about the vicious history of the European invasion of Africa he would have learned that Africans resisted that invasion and that limitless numbers of Africans were slaughtered.

In relation to Jamaica’s petition to King Charles, the GAC said it was unclear what Warmington found embarrassing about a legitimate action regarding reparation. “Are you embarrassed about asking legal questions and holding white power structures accountable? Are you embarrassed about asking questions that make white people uncomfortable?” the GAC asked the MP.

“Specifically, the legal questions raised in the petition concern whether the seizure, transportation, and enslavement of Africans in Jamaica under British rule were lawful under English law; whether those practices breached relevant international obligations; and whether the United Kingdom has a legal obligation to provide a reparatory remedy to Jamaica.

What is there to be embarrassed about these fundamental questions of justice regarding African humanity?” the GAC said. It noted that the petition has now become a legal matter, and told Warmington that the least he could and should do “is allow due process of the law and the historical evidence to be examined”.

World.title: Not true
World.content:
TULLOCH-NEIL…it may be useful to determine what should constitute a formal complaint on the issue

NEW YORK, United States — Diaspora leaders here have rubbished a claim by permanent secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Sheila Sealy Monteith that there are no complaints among Jamaicans abroad about unspent Hurricane Melissa donations.

“We have been hearing voices of concern about how the donations have been or is being spent,” Irwine Clare Sr, a leading Diaspora advocate told the Jamaica Observer.

“There are many who believe that there is a serious trust issue when it comes to how donations from the Diaspora are handled by Government. We are not seeking to cast blame, but we believe we have a vested interest in seeking accountability and transparency in this matter.

We had a vested interested in what is considered as the most massive mobilisation of donations to help those who were affected by the hurricane, and we will do it again, but we must have clarity,” Clare Sr said.

On Thursday, September 30, 2026, Sealy Monteith told Parliament’s Internal and External Affairs Committee that the foreign ministry “had many opportunities to receive feedback from the Diaspora” but had not received any indication of concern.

She was responding to a question from Opposition Member of Parliament for St Ann South Eastern Dr Kenneth Russell as to whether the ministry has received any feedback from members of the Diaspora and donors about the slow use of their contributions. Jamaicans abroad and at home, as well as other groups and individuals, had donated millions of dollars to help the country recover from the ravages of Hurricane Melissa, which hit sections of the island last October.

But questions have been raised about the slow pace of utilising the funds, after the auditor general found that only about 1.7 per cent of the donated funds had been used months after the contributions were made.

Last Thursday, Sealy Monteith said that the ministry had not seen evidence of a decline in confidence in Jamaica’s ability to handle international support.

“We have used the strength of our diplomacy to ensure that countries who wish to contribute are enabled to contribute, that we are able to record it. We are providing direction for them, and we pass them on to the relevant authorities. We have not received any indication to date that there has been a loss of confidence in our abilities to use it,” she told the committee.

However, there was unanimity among Diaspora leaders who spoke to the Observer that there is widespread concern about the handling of the millions of dollars in donations made by members of the Diaspora. Former Global Jamaica Diaspora Council (GJDC) representative for the Northeast United States Dr Karren Dunkley cautioned against “interpreting the absence of formal complaints as an absence of concern”.

She said that she has “personally heard from Diaspora leaders and members across the globe who are deeply concerned about the pace of recovery”.

“Most importantly, there are also concerns about Jamaicans who still need meaningful assistance.

The reported utilisation of only 1.7 per cent of the donated Hurricane Melissa funds, understandably, raises serious questions about urgency, transparency, accountability, and our collective capacity to translate generosity into tangible relief for those who need it most,” Dunkley said.

“The Jamaica Diaspora remains deeply committed to our homeland, but generosity must be matched by timely action and clear communication about what was received, what has been spent, where resources have gone, what barriers may be slowing development, and when those waiting can expect assistance,” Dunkley added.

Dr Allan Cunningham, a university lecturer and leading Diaspora advocate in Florida, also alluded to what he argued is a trust issue some people within the Diaspora have when it comes to donating money to be used for relief efforts in Jamaica.

While he was careful not to blame the Government, Cunningham related a matter in which he said he was instrumental in raising US$800,000 to assist with COVID-19 relief efforts in Jamaica but never got any response on how the funds were used.

He said he is not surprised by the present concerns about the Melissa relief funds. “While the permanent secretary is reporting that there have been no complaints from the Diaspora regarding the slow response of the recovery spending, it would have been useful if mechanisms were put in place to inform us, and the general public, about the recovery programme,” said Cunningham.

Current GJDC representative for the Northeast United States Michelle Tulloch-Neil, while acknowledging that there are concerns among several members of the Diaspora over the issue, believes that it may be useful to determine what should constitute a formal complaint on the issue.

She believes that with the matter now in the open it might be the right time for it to be dealt with by the Diaspora. Another Diaspora leader, Peter Gracey, said it is unfortunate that the ministry has not received any complaints about the slow pace of the recovery effort and how financial donations are being used.

World.title: Designing Resilience
World.content:
“WHO knew that within a few weeks of Design Week Ja 2025, held under the theme ‘Creative Resilience’, Jamaica would be confronted with the devastating impact of Hurricane Melissa?” asked Jamaica Observer Design Week Ja conceptualiser Novia McDonald- Whyte at Sunday’s launch event for the 2026 edition.

Back again with aplomb and renewed purpose — powered by Tile City & Home Centre and KOHLER — this year’s edition is aptly themed ‘Restoration & Resilience’.

The S Hotel Kingston-hosted launch featured presentations from industry players and partners all on board with fervour for the continued mission.

“We wanted a slate of presenters who understood the magnitude of Hurricane Melissa — people who had survived it, lived through it, and were now considering what they could contribute to the wider conversation around Restoration & Resilience,” shared McDonald-Whyte.

Here, pictured at the Sunday, October 4 kick-off are McDonald-Whyte (centre) with presenters and partners (from left) Marsha Parchment, Nastassia Morrison, Joelle Smith, Michelle Arroyave, Annaliesa Lindsay, and Dwayne Berbick.

Donnielle Robe, marketing manager, Tile City & Home Centre, who announced that as her team works on expanding offerings to build back Jamaica even better, they will soon open a signature showroom.

World.title: Sandals Island Challenge hits £100,000 fund-raising target
World.content:
Participants pose before competing in a 21km run through the town of Falmouth in Trelawny and into the hills of the Good Hope Eco Park, hosted by Chukka Caribbean Adventures, on Saturday as part of the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge Jamaica has reached its £100,000 fund-raising target, paving the way for the purchase of critical equipment to help restore neonatal and paediatric services at Falmouth Public General Hospital nearly one year after Hurricane Melissa devastated the facility.

The milestone was reached on Sunday as participants took on day three of the four-day endurance challenge, completing a 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth, with the route taking them past the hospital that has been at the heart of this year’s fund-raising effort.

The achievement represents a major boost for the hospital which suffered extensive damage when the record-breaking Hurricane Melissa struck sections of Jamaica as a Category 5 system on October 28, 2025. Falmouth Public General Hospital lost much of its roofing and, consequently, critical medical equipment, furniture and appliances.

Sunday’s half-marathon brought the purpose of the Island Challenge into sharp focus as participants made their way through the historic town. Workers from the hospital gathered outside the facility to cheer on the runners as they passed. Nurse/midwife Monique McKenzie-Matherson was among those who welcomed the initiative.

“I am super excited about this initiative. We are really in need — the babies at the hospital and the wider community. “Melissa came and she did a number on us, and we are grateful that somebody saw the need and is willing to assist,” she said. Psychiatric nursing aide Shawn Daley shared similar sentiments, stressing the importance of assistance as the hospital continues its recovery.

“It is something I think we should do early. The devastation was very bad so the help is very crucial for the staff, community and the parish,” Daley said.

For the hospital’s administration, the £100,000 will allow attention to be placed on replacing the equipment that was lost when the hurricane ripped through the facility. Falmouth Public General Hospital CEO Carlington McLennon said the extent of the losses went beyond the visible structural damage.

“While a lot of persons focus on the infrastructural impact we had, what they fail to realise is that the equipment, furniture and appliances were also destroyed as a result of us losing the roof,” McLennon said. “With Sandals Foundation we can now focus on the equipment and appliances.”

Head of the hospital’s paediatric department, Dr Kerri-Ann McKenzie, said the funding will help to replace several pieces of essential equipment while also allowing the department to acquire resources it did not have before the hurricane.

For McKenzie, the support represents a significant step towards restoring the hospital’s ability to adequately care for some of its most vulnerable patients. “Words cannot express how grateful I am. This is a significant contribution, and I just want to say thanks to Sandals Foundation and to the athletes,” she said.

The Sandals Foundation Island Challenge is being staged in Jamaica for the first time, bringing together approximately 30 participants from the United Kingdom — including athletes, travel industry figures and other supporters — for four days of physically demanding activities across the island.

The challenge began last Friday with participants completing a 10-kilometre run from Rio Nuevo Fishing Beach in St Mary to Sandals Ochi Beach Club in St Ann, followed by a five-kilometre kayak journey along the White River Fish Sanctuary.

On Saturday the group climbed the world-famous Dunn’s River Falls before heading to the Bogue Forest Reserve where participants completed a rainforest trek and joined a reforestation effort which saw 300 West Indian cedar trees being planted as part of continued recovery efforts following Hurricane Melissa.

Sunday’s 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth marked the third and one of the most symbolic legs of the challenge, allowing participants to see first-hand the hospital and community that will benefit from the funds raised.

The challenge concludes on Monday in St Andrew, where participants are scheduled to face a military-style endurance challenge in Newcastle before embarking on a partial hike of the Blue Mountains, reaching approximately 4,500 feet above sea level. Jamaica is the fourth Caribbean country to host the Island Challenge, following Antigua and Barbuda in 2023, St Vincent and the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025.

Previous stagings collectively raised more than £300,000 and benefited approximately 1,800 babies across the region.

World.title: Wet Music Festival paints waterfront
World.content:
Soca artise Lyrikal takes control of the Wet crowd.

DOWNTOWN Kingston’s waterfront became a playground of paint, foam, and water as hundreds of revellers welcomed daylight in a spectacularly colourful fashion at the Xodus Wet Music Festival on Saturday.

Staged at Port Spectrum, the cooler-friendly event brought rum, food, and infectious Caribbean rhythms together for a morning in which where drenched was part of the pleasure and leaving spotless was practically impossible. The venue was already full by 4:00 am, with patrons ready to surrender to the music.

As dawn gave way to daylight, the party revealed its full palette — paint-covered bodies, foam-flecked hair, and smiling faces that wore the evidence of a thoroughly good time.

Some revellers were so completely coated in blue that they could have passed for a delegation from the Smurfs’ village; although this crew had swapped mushroom houses for coolers and came armed with considerably more waistline action. DJs Zess, Rico the DJ, Nocturnal, Fatalic, Banka, and Tonio kept the waterfront moving, supplying the soundtrack for hours of dancing as water, paint, and foam added fresh excitement to the festivities.

A mini dance-off between two women, one Jamaican and the other Trinidadian, brought a playful dose of island rivalry to the celebration. Their friendly showdown added to the vibes, capturing the Caribbean camaraderie running through the event. “Between the music, the paint, and the water, I had the best time.

I came to enjoy myself, and Xodus gave me every reason to stay until the very end,” one female patron told the Jamaica Observer. There was plenty to keep appetites satisfied, too. Foska, Elle & Vire, KFC, and Pizza Hut provided complimentary food, while Janga’s sold meals of jerk, allowing patrons to refuel before returning to the revelry.

“The vibes were strong from early, and they never dropped. Good music, food, and everybody enjoying themselves. That is what made the morning for me,” a male patron added. At exactly 10:21 am, soca artiste Lyrikal stepped onstage, joining a party that was already in full swing.

His arrival gave fans another reason to keep the energy flowing. His performance included favourites Look Back, Judgmental, Happy Place, and Dip and Roll, bringing a live dimension to the morning’s musical offerings. Amid the celebration, Lyrikal also paid tribute to late soca star Ricardo Drue, performing selections from his catalogue, including Professional.

The tribute made room for remembrance while keeping Drue’s music woven into the Carnival spirit he helped shape. Even the advertised 11:00 am finish could not quite contain the festivities.

The party continued for approximately another halfhour, with Fatalic keeping the momentum going and ensuring female patrons had ample opportunity to enjoy themselves during the closing stretch.

The event came just days after Xodus launched its 2027 costumes under the theme Reign, carrying that excitement from the costume unveiling into a waterfront celebration bursting with colour and Caribbean flavour. The morning ended perfectly with a downpour, giving the paint-splashed revellers one final soaking, and the event a cooling finish.

World.title: Bartlett moves to plug tourism import leak
World.content:
Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett (right) making a point, last Friday, to Damine Sinanan, chief executive officer of the Caribbean Export Development Agency, following the plenary session on ‘Practical Building Blocks for Export Expansion’. It was held during the final day of the six-day Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Warning that the region is losing billions of dollars in potential earnings by failing to adequately connect its farmers and agro-processors with the tourism industry, portfolio minister Edmund Bartlett is calling for a major overhaul with the establishment of a Caribbean Tourism Agricultural Logistics Centre among a raft of proposed initiatives.

He made the call last Friday, the final for the six-day Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

His comments came during the plenary session on ‘Practical Building Blocks for Export Expansion’.

The proposed Caribbean Tourism Agricultural Logistics Centre, Bartlett said, should go beyond conventional storage.

“It’s not a warehouse we’re looking for here, but what we’re seeking is a repository of all the supplies from within the Caribbean area, [for example] what Barbados provides, what Guyana provides, what Jamaica provides,” he said.

The facility, he explained, would accommodate fresh agricultural commodities as well as processed products — including juices, nectars, jams, and jellies — and facilitate their distribution throughout the region.

Other measures he proposed include establishing a dedicated tourism agricultural loan programme for small farmers, and harmonising food and agricultural standards across the Caribbean.

Bartlett also wants Jamaica’s Agri- Linkages Exchange (ALEX) platform, which links farmers with tourism buyers, expanded into a Caribbeanwide system. “We know the example we’ve had in four years — over $2 billion of trade between small farmers and hoteliers,” he said of ALEX.

Under the proposed regional platform, farmers in one Caribbean country could access buyers in another, with information on prices, quantities, availability, and delivery schedules made accessible to facilitate transactions.

Meanwhile, Bartlett said the tourism agricultural loan programme would be specifically designed to help small farmers achieve the consistency, quantity and quality required by hotels, while continuing to produce distinctive crops that can enhance the visitor experience.

He pointed to Jamaica’s experience, saying the Government placed $1 billion in EXIM Bank to support a lending programme, offering up to $25 million to smalland medium-size businesses at a 4.5 per cent interest rate, repayable over five years.

Bartlett said 443 small entities had benefited, with about $3 billion already re-lent through the revolving scheme and another $750 million available.

Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Floyd Green welcomed the tourism minister’s proposals. “I support a regional ALEX,” Green said, while calling for hotels to provide real-time information on their requirements so farmers can better match production with demand.

He also backed adapting Jamaica’s tourism lending experience to agriculture. “The experience of having pioneered the loan scheme that focuses on tourism enterprises clearly can be remodelled for our small farmers,” Green said.

Bartlett further called for the harmonisation of food safety and agricultural standards across the Caribbean, arguing that common protocols would remove barriers to regional trade and make it easier for major hotel brands to source from Caribbean producers.

His proposals, he said, are aimed at creating a Caribbean tourism economy in which a greater share of the money generated by visitors remains within the region — turning the relationship between the Caribbean’s “oil” and “soil” into a stronger engine of economic growth.

Bartlett argued that tourism, the Caribbean’s major economic driver, must be deliberately used to create a larger and more reliable market for regional agriculture.

“Tourism is our oil in the Caribbean…thanks to Guyana. Yes, and agriculture is our soil. The effort, therefore, is to bring our oil in consonance with our soil, and to create a Caribbean outcome that feeds the Caribbean, and then invite the world to come and taste it, and pay for it,” the tourism minister argued.

He said the region needs a comprehensive policy framework linking production, financing, infrastructure, marketing, and distribution, while eliminating leakages from the tourism economy.

Noting that agriculture accounts for about 42 per cent of visitor consumption requirements, he questioned how much of that demand is being met by Caribbean producers. “Where does the food come from?

Whose food are they consuming? Is it the Caribbean food, or is it imported food?” he asked. The minister argued that the scale of imports represents a major opportunity for local producers, insisting that the region must move away from an overly extractive tourism model.

“We have been concerned because, for us, tourism is the driving economic force of the region but it has been a very extractive industry — and that requires a paradigm shift,” Bartlett said.

World.title: HOT SEAT!
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Diaz (right) tackles Jamaica’s Bailey Cadamarteri during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match at Cuscatlan Stadium in San Salvador on October 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

ALTHOUGH Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz are in pole position to qualify for the Concacaf Nations League knockout stage, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says they will take nothing for granted ahead of tonight’s rematch against host Honduras at Chelato Uclés National Stadium in Tegucigalpa.

Kick-off is at 9:00. The national senior men’s team currently sit second in Group B on six points, a point behind leaders Suriname, with a game remaining. The top two teams will advance to the knockout stage and the Jamaicans can guarantee their spot with a win.

However, their lone defeat of the competition was a 0-1 loss to Honduras at the National Stadium recently, which ended Jamaica’s 13-year unbeaten streak against the Central American team.

A win for the Hondurans, who sit fourth on three points, could also see them overtake the Boyz in the standings, if they win by two goals. Speid says he’s expecting another tough contest from the hosts, with a spot in the next round on the line.

“They are a good team, a dangerous team, and that is something that the Jamaican contingent will have to contend with in these games,” he said. “They are very skillful, fastpaced, resolute, tenacious.

Even when they went down to 10 men, they were able to hold us off and get a famous victory, so we are mindful and aware of their strengths.” Striker Javon East, who scored Jamaica’s two goals in their win over El Salvador on Friday, also spoke of the difficulty ahead for the Boyz.

“We know they have good qualities, technical players, so we expect a difficult match with many fans supporting them and on a complicated pitch,” he said.

“We can’t rule out the Honduran team because they’re a good team and have a good coach, so we expect a great battle. We just have to go there and follow the coach’s instructions.” A win for the Boyz is the safest option as three teams, including Honduras, can overtake them if they drop points.

A Jamaica defeat would see Guatemala advance with a win over Suriname. If Guatemala fail to win, Martinique could still move ahead of Jamaica by beating El Salvador by two or three goals.

Speid says his main focus is getting all three points against Honduras. “We could still lose and continue the competition but we know that the safest way is to get a victory and another way is to probably get a draw, so we are aware of all the permutations,” he said.

“We understand and we see that Honduras are really a good team.

I know what has been happening — all the teams in our zone have been able to defeat each other at some point or not so I think all the teams are even, and that’s where we have to start.”

Winger Kaheim Dixon believes a win for Jamaica could help to soften the blow of missing out on last summer’s FIFA World Cup. “For the whole country it would mean everything.

We missed out on a chance in the World Cup qualifiers but now we have a chance to make it right,” he said. “It’s not just about me, but for the whole country at this point.”

After losing Renaldo Cephas, Rumarn Burrell, Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer and Tayvon Gray following the Honduras loss, Speid will now also be without defender Joel Latibeaudiere (injury) and striker Bailey Cadamarteri (suspended), who both started in the 2-0 win over El Salvador.

Goalkeepers — Andre Blake, Amal Knight, Shaquan Davis

Defenders — Damion Lowe, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Kyle Ming, Christopher Ainsworth, Miguel Freckleton

Midfielders — Dwayne Atkinson, Karoy Anderson, Brandon Cover, Courtney Clarke, Ramone Howell

Forwards — Kaheim Dixon, Tyreece Campbell, Javon East, Jahmarie Nolan, Jamone Lyle, Tajay Grant

World.title: Caribbean trade chief paints grim outlook for region’s food exports
World.content:
SINANAN…we’re going to face more challenges in the year (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Caribbean Export Development Agency Chief Executive Officer Damine Sinanan has warned that Caribbean countries will have to pay more to feed their populations for the rest of the year as rising energy and shipping costs, tighter export regulations, and disruptions to global trade threaten to deepen the region’s dependence on imported food.

“We’re going to face more challenges in the year 2026,” Sinanan said, pointing to disruptions in international shipping and escalating commodity prices. “Ship traffic has collapsed from 160 ships to six ships per day.

That’s going to impact our value chains,” he added. Sinanan was addressing delegates last Friday, ahead of the plenary session ‘Practical Building Blocks for Export Expansion’, on the final day of Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

His warning comes against the backdrop of a widening food import bill across the region. Agricultural imports, he noted, have surpassed US$5 billion, representing a 20 per cent increase from 2022, while Caribbean food and agriculture exports contracted by seven per cent in 2025 after reaching a peak the previous year.

The situation, Sinanan said, leaves the region vulnerable to developments beyond its control.

“Sugar alone has gone up 11 per cent in one month,” he said, warning that higher costs would be passed on to countries already relying heavily on imported food and agricultural products.

He warned that new requirements in major export markets, including European Union deforestation regulations and United States food traceability rules, are now also additional threats.

“All of this is going to impact our costs of doing business in the Caribbean region,” Sinanan said.

He identified transportation and logistics as a major weakness in the regional food trade, with inefficient shipping routes, limited cold storage capacity, small cargo volumes, and border delays adding to the cost of moving agricultural products.

Climate shocks are another threat to supply chains. “We have to bear in mind that these climate shocks can really disrupt our value chains and our supply chains, which can only impact the cost of doing business in the Caribbean region,” he said, pointing to the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa.

Sinanan also warned that fragmented sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) systems are restricting the region’s ability to expand trade.

The Caribbean Export Development Agency CEO argued that multiple agencies, outdated legislation, weak enforcement, and limited financing have resulted in differing requirements across Caribbean countries, making it more difficult and expensive for exporters to access markets.

“We don’t have a regional code for SPS, so everybody has their own rules in the Caribbean region,” he said.

He proposed the adoption and implementation of 10 regional SPS standards, as well as a shared network of accredited laboratories, to harmonise requirements and reduce testing costs.

Sinanan said support is also needed for small and medium-size enterprises through group certification, export- anchored supply schemes, shared pack houses, and cool rooms.

But he argued that the region must also change what it sells, moving from primary commodities towards higher- value goods and services.

“Can we encourage investment into the Caribbean region that can stimulate these value-added services and bring more money and more efficiency to the Caribbean region?” he questioned.

Sinanan identified agri-tech and nutraceuticals as promising areas, citing digital irrigation, water management, protected agriculture, testing, traceability, and drone technology.

He also pointed to turmeric, ginger, sea moss, gels, powders, and premium cocoa as products with growth potential, while suggesting that sargassum could be transformed from an environmental nuisance into a commercial opportunity.

He also urged the region to diversify its markets, including through Caribbean tourism, the United States, Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Latin America, which he described as an underrepresented market for Caribbean exporters.

World.title: Sánchez bets it all on housing ahead of Spain’s snap election
World.content:
But critics have questioned the wisdom of the prime minister casting himself as a champion of housing rights when his time in power has coincided with a deepening of the current crisis.

Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Spanish Tenants’ Union, which has spearheaded the housing protests, said Sánchez had “no track record to boast about” and called his Socialist Party “a party of landlords.”

“We’re done with these politicians,” she added. “We’re not falling for their nonsense anymore.”

Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, thinks the prime minister’s electoral bet made sense.

“The current outlook for Sánchez is dire,” he said. “Even if you ignore the migrant crisis in Ceuta — which isn’t going to be solved anytime soon — and the ongoing corruption cases, he’s still leading a minority government that can’t pass any legislation, with negative inflation steadily undermining his claim that Spain is doing great in economic terms.”

By making the election about housing, Simón added, the prime minister is seeking to shift the conversation away from corruption in his inner circle and the national defense issues surrounding Spain’s North African exclaves, and toward the social issues championed by the left.

World.title: Merz and Macron want the EU to hit back harder — and faster — against trade threats
World.content:
“Without delaying the full use of the existing set of instruments, we need a comprehensive framework to complement our toolbox with new legal instruments — in a lean and non-bureaucratic way,” they wrote.

The leaders of the EU’s two largest economies want a new tool that would empower Brussels to exclude imports from certain countries.

The proposal arrives before Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič flies to Beijing for talks on Thursday, the final round of a four-month process in which Brussels hopes to rebalance its trading relationship with China.

The Anti-Coercion Instrument, also known as the EU’s trade “bazooka,” in theory gives the Commission enormous powers to restrict imports in response to actions that are considered economic coercion.

But in practice, activating it would require months of investigation and the support of a qualified majority of EU governments. Divisions among capitals have previously complicated efforts to agree on trade measures targeting China.

The new instrument would make it much harder for member countries to block swift action. Commission measures would stand unless a “reverse” qualified majority of countries voted to block them, a senior German official explained.

World.title: Emmanuel Macron is most impressive world leader on AI, says Sam Altman
World.content:
The recognition is notable because Macron has sought to use his leadership to push AI safety on the global stage, and because the French president is months away from leaving office.

After two terms as president, Macron is barred from running in the next election in April 2027. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, is advocating a policy of deregulation on AI, three senior party officials told POLITICO.

Le Pen's National Rally party also wants to become less dependent on foreign tech companies and is considering reviving a proposal for a sovereign wealth fund to channel money toward French tech leaders such as OVH or Mistral, as well as favoring French companies in public contracts.

Some party figures have even threatened to repatriate French capital invested in American tech — €80 billion, according to party official Alexandre Loubet — without specifying how.

Macron himself has been a major champion of the French AI lab Mistral. Next month he’ll host the annual Paris Peace Forum — one of his pet diplomatic projects — to focus on AI safety and the risks technology poses to children and teenagers.

The Altman interview appears in Monday’s debut edition of Decoded by POLITICO and its accompanying daily podcast, covering global technology and focused on the personalities, political shifts and policy battles shaping the future of the world.

Read the full Decoded newsletter for more.

Also check out the full interview on YouTube and listen to the podcast here.

World.title: Germany risks being drawn into ‘violent conflict’ with Russia, spy chief warns
World.content:
“Russia is determined to bring Ukraine to its knees this coming winter,” Jäger said. “We must expect Russian attacks of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen on this scale. The war in Ukraine is entering a new and extremely dangerous phase.”

Jäger’s comments come a day after a politically weakened Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv in what appeared to be an attempt to show resolve following two first-place finishes by the Kremlin-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in regional elections last month. Those AfD victories, blamed in large part on the chancellor’s historically low domestic approval ratings, raised concerns in Ukraine and across the EU that German support for Ukraine might waver due to the chancellor’s troubles at home.

With his highly symbolic visit to Kyiv on Sunday, Merz sought to illustrate that he remains firmly at the helm and unflinching in his support for Ukraine.

“Mr. Putin, put an end to this senseless war,” Merz said during the visit, echoing one of his political heroes, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and his famous Cold War speech at the Brandenburg Gate alongside the Berlin Wall in 1987: “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.”

In his comments Monday, Jäger suggested Russia’s escalation was in part driven by the fact that Putin had been backed into a corner as Moscow faces rising economic pressure and burns through resources to wage its war on Ukraine.

Putin, he said, has “passed the point where he could simply call off the attack on Ukraine without jeopardizing his domestic power base,” adding, “He must demonstrate a success in Ukraine that, from Russia’s perspective, justifies the immense sacrifices made so far.”

Jäger also said he currently sees “no evidence” for a large-scale Russian attack on a NATO member country. Yet “we consider it entirely possible that Russia might carry out targeted, smaller-scale operations” like the “little green men” who spearheaded the annexation of Crimea in 2014.

Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

World.title: Suspected plague in Russia puts EU on alert
World.content:
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s consumer watchdog, has not confirmed the exact cause of death, saying only that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology.” More than 200 people have been placed under observation following her death.

“The sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable,” Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement, adding that “a special set of measures was organized and carried out” in connection with the death.



It added that no microorganisms associated with her professional activities were identified in the sample from the deceased patient.



Igor Kobzev, governor of the Irkutsk region, where the institute is located, said authorities had identified, examined, and placed under medical supervision all the people who had come into contact with the patient. No other employee at the anti-plague institute has visited the doctor over the past few days, he added.

Information sharing

U.S. officials have told Radio Free Europe that they are monitoring the situation, and urged Russian authorities to "share accurate information quickly and openly.”

A spokesperson for the World Health Organization said the United Nations health agency was aware of the “reports” of the death and attempting to verify the details.

In accordance with International Health Regulations, “WHO is in contact with the Russian health authorities to verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results, the rationale for contact-tracing and the health status of contacts, as well as any potential international public health implication,” a WHO spokesperson told POLITICO.

“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” the spokesperson said, adding that the risk assessment will be updated once more information is available.

World.title: Is Kemi Badenoch abandoning the Red Wall?
World.content:
Is Andy Burnham an easier opponent for the Conservatives than Sir Keir Starmer?

At the Tory conference in Birmingham, Kemi Badenoch’s team sniff a chance to attack the prime minister – with a particular chance to seize on and attack his economic argument.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy pore over Badenoch’s “The Right Way” pamphlet and how she plans to take the fight to Reform UK in the north and the Liberal Democrats in the southeast.

Elsewhere, Anne has been speaking to shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately – who has a couple of blunt messages for Burnham.

Plus, are the Conservatives truly over Robert Jenrick after his defection to Reform?

World.title: Europe’s last socialist heavyweight Sánchez calls snap Spanish elections for Nov. 29
World.content:
Lawmakers on Friday rejected two bills intended to address a housing crisis that has ignited major protests across the country since last week over the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived since 1956.

Although Sánchez has established a reputation as a master of the political bounce-back, he faces a steep climb to turn this latest crisis to his advantage.

Polls overwhelmingly suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, currently supported by 34% of the electorate, compared with 26% backing the Socialist Party. The PP would likely partner with the far-right Vox party, which is projected to score 18%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

In calling for an election, Sánchez warned of the surge of the far right.

“You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play,” he said in his address to the nation.

“You must decide whether to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he added.

World.title: The race for the EU’s plum diplomatic jobs begins
World.content:
The race for some of the EU’s most coveted diplomatic jobs is under way.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur unpack why this year’s routine EEAS rotation is attracting unusually strong interest from senior Commission officials — and what it says about the mood in Brussels.

Then, we head to France, where a wave of student protests is spilling into the presidential campaign, sharpening the contrast between Jean-Luc Mélenchon and Marine Le Pen and adding to what one government adviser called a “maxi merde” moment for French politics.

Plus, Brussels’ revamped Schuman roundabout is becoming a new protest hotspot — close enough for the noise to reach the upper floors of the Berlaymont.

World.title: Germany and France agree new trade tool to counter China
World.content:
France and Germany have proposed new powers for the European Commission to counter market distortions as the EU confronts mounting trade pressure from China.

 

In a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday, accompanied by a policy paper on global economic imbalances, Paris and Berlin called for tools to restrict access to the EU market, diversify supplies and prepare for possible retaliation.

Brussels describes its economic relationship with Beijing as unsustainable, with the EU’s trade deficit reaching an estimated €1 billion a day in 2025. It has given China until this month to offer concessions.

The issue is due to come before EU leaders at next week’s European Council summit, where France and Germany will press for urgent action.

"We need a comprehensive framework to complement our toolbox with new legal instruments – in a lean and non-bureaucratic way," reads the letter, signed by President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The accompanying paper warns that “a massive industrial shock” is hitting sectors central to Europe’s economic model, including pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, industrial machinery and chemicals.

New powers

The letter calls for a new instrument to be activated "where third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions by political or economic means, leading to severe and systematic distortions."

The tool would restrict access to the European single market, which Paris and Berlin see as the EU’s main leverage in negotiations with China.

They want decisions taken swiftly through a procedure known as comitology, in which member state representatives scrutinise Commission measures.

Crucially, the instrument would be activated “unless a qualified majority is opposed”, making it easier for the Commission to act.

The tool should also be "country agnostic, capture all market distortions, from a single production to a whole sector, from subsidies to currency manipulation," the policy paper says.

The aim is to enable the Commission to devise tailor-made solutions that reflect the EU's interests and do not place obligations solely on European companies.

Diversifying supplies

The letter also calls for a diversification instrument, which von der Leyen already announced at the last European Council in June.

According to the paper, it should "reduce European dependencies, resolve existing supply chain concentration and prevent emerging concentration risks – taking into account import concentrations from a given country, company or stakeholder nationality, market share at the global level."

In other words, Berlin and Paris want a comprehensive framework that serves diversification goals in line with the economic security agenda and covers distortions beyond trade.

Preparing for retaliation

The paper acknowledges that retaliatory measures are likely to test the EU's political unity, and that a united front will be crucial in any trade war with China.

"The EU must be prepared and factor in international reactions and potential retaliations to its policies, instruments and measures. Understanding the extent and variety of coercion is essential," it continues.

The proposal calls for an inventory of possible retaliatory measures and an assessment of their impact on each member state, alongside coordination among EU leaders.

Strengthening trade defences

The paper also calls for measures to reduce risks and sever dependencies, urging the Commission to make greater use of trade defence instruments by launching more investigations on its own initiative and reallocating staff and resources to support them.

It also advocates a broader approach to sector-wide trade disputes, when "protection for narrow categories of goods is now insufficient in the face of more systemic distortions and the global dominance of third countries on the whole value chain of specific sectors."

Paris and Berlin also propose targeted changes to anti-dumping, anti-subsidy and safeguard rules to make it harder to circumvent EU trade measures.

World.title: Female AI agents would get paid 10% less than male ones, study finds
World.content:
A new study on how people interact with AI agents in the workplace has found that those with a female appearance or presenting as female would get paid less than their male-presenting counterparts for the same work, revealing that gender can influence interactions with artificial intelligence.

 

The findings come just as AI agents are entering the mainstream, with almost 79% of companies reporting the use of AI agents this year and a further 40% of applications using them too, according to IT consulting firm Accelirate.

This means that if you are not already working with an AI agent, you probably will be soon.

The study, conducted by the University of Limerick and called ‘Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR' aimed to see how humans interact with AI agent co-workers.

Researchers placed 189 human workers in a virtual reality office and tasked them with completing workplace tasks with four different AI assistants.

Among their options were a text-based chatbot, a desk robot, and two human-like agents presented with male and female appearances: Johan and Johanna.

All the assistants had the same background functionality and used the same underlying model, OpenAI’s gpt-4-1106-preview.

Human participants were then asked to rate the AI agents’ work and given real money to pay them for completing tasks, with the aim of recreating a real-world scenario to see how much people were willing to pay AI agents for their work.

Overall, participants rated both human-like agents Johan and Johanna similarly for their work, with Johan trusted marginally more but not by any statistically significant margin.

However, both men and women paid the female-presenting AI agent Johanna significantly less than Johan (10%), despite her having the same capabilities. Johan was also seen as more human-like than Johanna.

This is despite most participants telling researchers in interviews that they would not treat male and female-presenting AI agents differently.

Fortunately for Johan and Johanna, they were both paid more for their work than the other AI agents, with women in particular scoring and rewarding the human-presenting agents more than men did.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, participants also saw both human-presenting AI agents as much more human-like than the chatbot and robot.

Not only that, workers trusted and credited Johan and Johanna more than the other AI agents, with women in particular trusting them more than men.

“Having Johanna next to me made me more prone to credit her more again because I felt there was a person, a colleague sitting next to me that I had a conversation with and that was giving me her own input,” said one participant.

The study also found that people preferred AI agents that were either human-presenting or clearly non-human presenting, rejecting the robot design that appeared to be “in between” the two options.

Outside of the gender dynamics, those who took part in the study said that “AI assistants should integrate seamlessly into every knowledge work to be useful”.

World.title: What does Spain's snap election mean for European politics?
World.content:
A defeat for Pedro Sánchez could reshape the balance of power inside the EU institutions and further weaken the centrist majority that has traditionally underpinned European integration.

 

The loss of the last centre-left government in a major member state could strengthen conservative forces and make progressive lawmakers less willing to cooperate across the aisle.

On Monday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November, after parliament rejected two housing decrees on Friday.

His government, widely seen as the last major bastion of progressive policies in Europe, was already under pressure from corruption scandals, the unresolved migration crisis in Ceuta and protests over the housing shortage.

A defeat could have significant repercussions in Brussels. Several EU officials told Euronews, on condition of anonymity, that the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group in the European Parliament would likely adopt a more confrontational stance.

Destabilisation

Sánchez's supporters say it is too early to write him off. He defied expectations after the 2023 election, remaining in power at the head of a minority government backed by Catalan and Basque pro-independence parties.

Current polls, however, suggest the centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox could secure a majority, making another Sánchez-led minority government harder to assemble.

EU officials with direct knowledge of the matter said the campaign itself was unlikely to have a major impact on European politics, beyond some symbolic votes in the European Parliament.

One immediate test is the re-election of Sánchez ally Iratxe García Pérez (Spain/S&D) as head of the S&D group, the Parliament's second-largest political group. No challenger has emerged, although the deadline for nominations is 13 October.

The bigger consequences could come after the election, particularly if Sánchez loses office. The S&D would then have fewer incentives to compromise with the European People's Party (EPP), EU officials said.

"The group would be more sharply critical towards [Commission President] von der Leyen's agenda," one EU official told Euronews, adding that centre-left lawmakers would face fewer political constraints with Sánchez in opposition in Madrid.

Another EU official said the links between Madrid and Brussels had become unusually close, with Sánchez at times appearing to set the tone for the wider S&D group.

Shaking majority

The European Commission, led by President Ursula von der Leyen, currently relies on a parliamentary majority made up of the centre-right EPP, centrist Renew Europe and the centre-left S&D. The Greens/EFA also broadly support the Commission, despite not being part of the coalition agreement.

Those centrist forces have traditionally formed the political backbone of European integration. But the rise of parties on the far left and far right could prevent them from securing a majority in the next European Parliament.

With one of the EU's largest socialist delegations potentially leaving government in Madrid, progressive MEPs could face greater pressure to challenge deals with the EPP.

"Sánchez was a huge stabilising factor. He was the main guarantor of von der Leyen, always pushing to find a compromise with the European People's Party," an EU lawmaker told Euronews, asking not to be named.

The first institutional test could come with the mid-term reshuffle, which was planned on the assumption that socialist António Costa and Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) would remain presidents of the European Council and European Parliament respectively.

Without the Spanish Socialists in government, the S&D could find it harder to resist a symbolic challenge to Metsola, potentially from Katarina Barley (Germany/S&D).

The EPP is backing a third mandate for Metsola, who is popular among MEPs. Under an informal agreement reached by centrist political groups at the start of the legislature, the S&D is due to hold the Parliament presidency.

But the shift in Madrid could have wider consequences. With Sánchez, a key sponsor of Costa, gone, the EPP could also seek to claim the European Council presidency.

Right-wing shift

"If Spain's Prime Minister were to come from the centre-right PP (EPP) in the future, S&D's influence would be diminished in the European Council in a way that we haven't seen since at least the early 1990s," Tobias Gerhard Schminke, founder of the election observatory Europe Elects, told Euronews.

Only Denmark, Lithuania and Malta would then have centre-left governments. Sweden's September election could add another centre-left prime minister, Magdalena Andersson, who has so far failed to form a government.

With Sánchez out of office, Denmark's Mette Frederiksen would become the senior progressive leader. Her migration policy, which is closer to the right, has already put her at odds with Sánchez and caused tensions within the S&D.

Sánchez has also become a prominent dissenting voice on issues including migration, Israel, US President Donald Trump, defence spending and the green agenda.

Critics say von der Leyen's majority is already showing signs of strain, with the EPP regularly forming alternative majorities with right-wing lawmakers on issues including deforestation, corporate sustainability and migration.

At the same time, some socialists fear that bringing down von der Leyen could produce an outcome even less favourable to the centre-left as more EU member states shift to the right.

"It is an extremely risky situation. The EU without its social democratic pillar changes fundamentally. That alters the historic balance for decision-making in the European Parliament," another EU lawmaker said.

World.title: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ dethrones 'Avatar' once more as highest-grossing movie in history
World.content:
Endgame is on top once more.

 

Prior to their upcoming team-up adventure, Avengers: Doomsday, Marvel rereleased 2019’s Avengers: Endgame with four new post-credits scenes.

After a second weekend in theatres, the blockbuster has brought its worldwide box office total to $2.925 billion, making it the Number 1 film on the all-time box office chart.

The previous record holder was James Cameron’s Avatar, which has earned $2.923 billion worldwide.

The two films have traded the top spot on the all-time chart since 2019. Endgame dethroned Avatar seven years ago, but then James Cameron’s film was rereleased in 2022 in the run-up to Avatar: The Way of Water, when it grossed enough to reclaim the #1 title.

The standings are as follows:

Avengers: Endgame (2019) - $2.925 billion Avatar (2009) - $2.923 billion Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) - $2.505 billion Avatar: The Way of Water (2022) - $2.334 billion Titanic (1997) - $2.257 billion Ne Zha 2 (2025) - $2.217 billion Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) - $2.068 billion Avengers: Infinity War (2018) - $2.048 billion Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021) - $1.922 billion Zootopia 2 (2025) - $1.866 billion

While the rerelease of Avengers: Endgame has delighted most fans, some have called out Marvel for retconning the original film, accusing Marvel of cheaply rewriting the end of the film to fit the narrative of Doomsday. Others have simply called foul and deemed that Marvel is “cheating” when it comes to box office gross...

Wherever you stand on the issue, Endgame is projected to finish its rerelease with $2.95 billion worldwide, according to Global Box Office.

As for all Avatar fans out there feeling sore, both franchises are now controlled by Disney, so whoever’s on top just means that the House of Mouse remains the undisputed box office titan.

Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on 18 December – the same day as Dune: Part Three – leading to Barbenheimer-like double-bill aspirations under the moniker Dunesday.

The question is now: Will Doomsday top Endgame and Avatar? Considering how this year’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day broke box office records to shoot up the chart and become the third highest-grossing film of all time, who’s to say Marvel can’t shake things up once more?

World.title: This new Japanese walking trail connects six cities across 320 kilometres
World.content:
If you’re heading to Japan for an active holiday you should lace up your walking boots and tackle a 320km-long hiking trail that is now fully open.

 

The Hitachinokuni Long Trail, Japan’s longest loop trail, has been in the works for seven years since first announced in 2019 by the Ibaraki Prefecture and the Hitachi Province Trail Club.

Now having opened in September, the hiking destination links six cities and towns across the northern Ibaraki Prefecture, less than a two-hour train ride away from Tokyo.

Connecting Kitaibaraki, Takahagi, Hitachi, Hitachi Ota, Hitachi Omiya and Daigo, the route takes hikers through landscapes known as “satoyama”, which are rural spaces where communities have lived alongside mountains, meadows, ponds and rice fields.

The trail is not high in elevation, nor easily impacted by heavy snowfall due to its geography, making it an experience that can be enjoyed year-round. However, there aren’t many refuelling points, while some areas are rocky and others include steep slopes.

Where to start?

Due to its design, hikers can choose where to tackle the circular trail, which is roughly divided into five areas.

The Central Area is one of the more challenging sections of the trail, featuring continuous steep ascents and descents for especially skilled hikers. Located in the Yazimo mountain range, on the northern edge of the Japanese town of Daigo, the Central Area rewards hikers with views including the Fukuroda Falls, the rocky peaks of Okukuji Nantaiyama as well as the Ryujinkyo Gorge valley.

The Northeastern portion of the trail covers mountains, like the high peaks of Eizomuro and Hanazono Yama, as well as coastal destinations, including the Kohama and Sasaki beaches. The area also takes hikers through history, including the Salt Road, which is an ancient trade route, and the Jikkoku Canal, which has been in use dating back to the Edo period from 1603 to 1868.

Within the Southeastern area, which first opened in 2024, the hike begins at Hananuki Valley with a climb up Mount Tsuchidake, which offers sweeping views of the surrounding scenery. The area is also marked by waterfalls, historic sites like the Kitadaimon Castle ruins before ending at the Kuji River.

The Southwest area is in Hitachiomiya City and takes hikers through mountains that are home to diverse flora and fauna, including Iwauchiwa flowering plants. This area also features a once thriving gold mining region.

Mt. Yamizo is just one of the stops along the Northwest area. Here, visitors can explore sacred sites steeped in history, such as the Yamizomine Shrine, which is thought to date as far back as the 1st century. At the summit of the mountain, there is also a castle-shaped observation deck that offers panoramic views of Fukushima and Tochigi's mountains.

World.title: VAT hike: Canal+ threatens to cut its support for cinema
World.content:
Tensions are rising between Canal+ and the government. As the executive prepares its 2027 budget, Maxime Saada is openly opposing plans to scrap the reduced VAT rate enjoyed by pay television. The Canal+ chief executive considers the measure "political" and "absurd", and says it would mean an extra cost of around 200 million euros a year for the group.

 

Raising VAT from 10% to 20% could, in his view, lead to higher subscription prices, but also internal cost-cutting and job losses.

"We cannot absorb 200 million euros", says the executive, speaking to RTL, warning that Canal+ will have to rethink its spending.

Cinema as a pressure tactic

Canal+ plays a central role in financing French cinema. In 2025, the group invested 155.6 million euros in French films and helped fund 148 productions. It thus accounts for almost half of the investments made by traditional private broadcasters. Any reduction in its spending could therefore have a direct impact on production.

This is precisely where the threat is taking shape. Canal+ was due to invest 980 million euros in French and European cinema between 2028 and 2032. But Maxime Saada warns that if VAT is doubled, these commitments could be scaled back. He even raises the possibility of funding "perhaps three-quarters fewer films".

This stand-off comes in a context of already heightened tensions around Canal+. In May, Saada announced that the group no longer wished to work with the signatories of an op-ed criticising the influence of conservative billionaire Vincent Bolloré, who controls Canal+.

The Human Rights League and the CGT-Spectacle union have since taken legal action, denouncing discrimination based on opinion.

With its 2027 budget, the government is seeking to bring the public deficit down from 5.4% to 5% of GDP. The VAT rise for Canal+ is part of this hunt for additional revenue, but opens up a new front with a group determined to defend its margins and its role in French creative industries.

World.title: Australia, New Zealand probe Flydubai pilot's time there
World.content:
The Flydubai pilot from Oman suspected of trying to crash a plane in Israel spent time in Oceania as a young man. Police in both Australia and New Zealand said they would investigate his links to the countries.

Security agencies in Australia and New Zealand on Monday said they were investigating the time that the co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073 spent in the countries in his youth

The Omani national is in custody in the United Arab Emirates. He is suspected of attacking his pilot Smit Machchhar with the emergency ax in the cockpit, and attempting to hijack the plane and crash it intentionally in Israel.

The pilot and passengers combined to thwart his attempts and restrain him. After a near-vertical dive lasting around 30 seconds during the fight for control, the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

What did Australian and New Zealand authorities say about the case?

The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) said on Monday that the man had enrolled at the Melbourne university in the state of Victoria, but said that he did not successfully complete an engineering qualification.

A spokesman for the Australian Federal Police said that the Victorian Counter Terrorism Team — comprising federal poice, Victorian state police, and the ASIO intelligence agency — was "investigating the man's links to Australia."

Based on Australian media reports, the man arrived on an Australian student visa in 2014, enrolled in 2015, left in 2017, and had his visa canceled in 2019.

Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Similarly, police in New Zealand said on Monday that the suspect spent time there, without specifying exactly where or when.

"We are looking into the time he spent here, alongside other agencies where appropriate," New Zealand Police assistant commissioner Micahel Johnson told the RNZ news outlet, issuing similar comments elsewhere. "We are unable to comment further at this time."

Flight FZ1073's pilot, Indian national Machchhar, also spent some of his formative years in New Zealand. He completed his early flight training some 18 years ago with the Mainland Air carrier.

"I was really pleased to read how he handled the situation," the airline's chief executive Philip Kean told RNZ. "He got through and he got the door open so the other people could save the airplane, because if he hadn't done that, it would have been a disaster."
