See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

After almost 11 years, people can again travel by train from Groningen to the German city of Leer.

Services were suspended in 2015 after a cargo ship crashed into the Friesenbrücke, the rail bridge over the Ems on the German side of the border.

At Groningen central station, travelers lined up at 5:30am to catch the first train in over a decade.

The rebuilt Friesenbrücke is 335 metres long and is Europe’s largest lift-swing rail bridge. Its 145-metre central section lifts and turns to let ships pass.

The new bridge was opened in 2024, but needed additional testing before rail service could resume.

Regional Director Gerrit de Groot of Arriva, which maintains the rail service, told RTV Noord he was “delighted” with the reopening. “It is fantastic that, as a regional carrier, we are making international transport possible in this way. It is a wonderful moment,” he said.

The journey takes around 90 minutes. Arriva expects that they will see peaks of travel during the holiday season when people want to visit the Christmas markets across the border.

World.title: Minister seeks inquiry into benefit fines for non-Dutch surnames
World.content:
People with non-Dutch surnames get fined more often and more harshly by the benefits agency UWV’s fraud unit, according to an internal analysis the agency’s board has had since December, AD and current affairs programme EenVandaag reported on Monday.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief said he wants the claims thoroughly investigated and the UWV to take appropriate measures. “Your surname or background must play no role at all in whether you get a fine or how high that fine is,” he told AD.

The two outlets based their joint investigation on confidential documents and interviews with more than 10 current and former staff, including managers, at the fraud unit, which employs around 600 people.

The analysis divided 1,682 case files into Dutch and non-Dutch surnames. In the region covering Alkmaar, Amsterdam and Utrecht, 44% of the people in the files had a non-Dutch surname, but they received 74% of the fines.

In the southern district, which includes Heerlen and Eindhoven, the figures were 36% and 71%. Because their fines were also higher, that group paid 98% of the total there, although fewer files were examined in that district.

The authors recommended further research, but this was never carried out, according to EenVandaag.

Country of origin

A 2015 work instruction for detecting fake employment contracts also listed the applicant’s “country of origin” as a possible risk characteristic. When a court asked about the document, the UWV denied in an official letter that it used risk characteristics at all, AD said.

After 2020, a thin line was drawn through the criterion, but it remained legible until at least mid-2026. “I have never seen such clear evidence that it happens as in this document,” lawyer Ayhan Kara, who obtained the uncensored version, told AD. He is considering filing a criminal complaint with the public prosecution service.

The UWV says the criterion was never used, was officially removed in 2020 and has now been taken out of all documents.

Current and former staff also described racist remarks in the fraud unit. Managers born outside the Netherlands were referred to as the “Arab League”, and during a case meeting someone said the solution was “to kick all Moroccans out of the country”.

Political reaction

MPs from both coalition and opposition parties reacted angrily. Stephan Neijenhuis of the centrist D66 told AD there was possibly “institutional racism” at the agency.

Mariëtte Patijn of the opposition party Pro said the revelations reminded her of the childcare benefits scandal, in which thousands of parents were wrongly labelled fraudsters by the tax office. “It is not systems selecting wrongly by accident, it is the UWV’s own people,” she told AD.

Dogukan Ergin of the left-wing, multicultural party Denk said it fitted a pattern. “First it was the tax office, then [student finance agency] DUO, now the UWV again: if you have a migration background, you are distrusted and dealt with more harshly,” he said.

According to AD, the minister was only informed of the analysis after the paper put questions to the ministry. The UWV told broadcaster NOS it had informed the ministry in January.

Apologies issued

Abdeluheb Choho, who became the UWV’s chairman on September 1, said in a statement that it was reprehensible that some staff still made discriminatory remarks to one another. “We apologise to everyone who feels discriminated against or has been treated in a racist way,” he said.

However, the agency said in a statement that the analysis was not scientific research, and that its data and method were not suitable for drawing conclusions about structural unequal treatment. A separate external study into equal treatment is due later this year.

The UWV has asked anyone who has experienced discrimination by or within the agency to report it to integriteit@uwv.nl.

In 2024, a reader who took part in a DutchNews survey on discrimination said UWV staff had told them to go back to their own country when they applied for unemployment benefits.

World.title: Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
World.content:
US prediction platform Polymarket has gone to court in The Hague to overturn a Dutch ban on its services, arguing that it sells financial products, rather than bets.

The company confirmed the case to the Financieele Dagblad. The judges will reportedly be asked to decide whether betting on real-world events counts as gambling, which the Dutch gambling regulator Ksa says that it is.

Polymarket argues that it is more like trading in derivatives, which should be supervised by financial markets regulator AFM.

Polymarket users buy contracts that pay out in USDC, a type of cryptocurrency whose value is equal to the US dollar, if a particular event does or does not happen. The company says this is comparable to futures contracts traded on financial markets.

Fines and bans

The Ksa ordered Polymarket to stop serving Dutch users in an order dated January 20 and made public on February 17. It said the platform was offering games of chance without a licence and threatened a penalty of €420,000 a week, up to a maximum of €840,000.

Polymarket stopped Dutch users from placing bets later in February, but the regulator ruled it had acted too late and in May demanded €420,000, and rejected the company’s objection in June.

The platform drew widespread attention in the Netherlands after users staked millions of dollars on the outcome of the October 2025 general election.

Only sport

According to the Ksa, Dutch law only allows betting on sport, so a licence would not be an option for Polymarket either.

“Prediction markets are on the rise, in the Netherlands too,” Ksa director Ella Seijsener said in a statement in February. “These types of companies offer bets which are not allowed on our market under any circumstances, not even by licence holders.”

Last week, MPs voted down a motion from the far-right Forum for Democracy (FvD) asking the government to look into regulating prediction markets as a separate category within gambling law.

Gambling lawyer Micha Schimmel told the FD he gives Polymarket’s case little chance. He pointed to a 2015 ruling which found that a service can be a financial product and still count as gambling. Polymarket is also banned in France and Germany.

World.title: School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Consumer watchdog ACM has criticised educational publishers for pricey and poor-quality textbooks, calling on the industry to change its practices.

The ACM says that for the past seven years, prices for educational materials have been rising faster than those of other products and schools say the publications are not meeting their needs.

In a statement, the watchdog said it “calls on educational publishers to stop mandatory tied selling of licences and textbooks, and to better align product supply with demand.”

One major problem the organisation highlighted is that textbooks and the licences for e-materials are bundled together, which drives up costs. The ACM wants them to be sold separately.

The organisation also calls on schools to do more research into the textbooks they purchase.

“Pressure on publishers starts with schools’ willingness to switch to other learning materials,” board member Martijn Snoep said in a statement.

Secondary schools buy around €280 million worth of learning materials every year.

The Netherlands men’s football team beat Serbia 2-1 in the Nations League in Eindhoven on Sunday, marking Xavi Hernández’s second win in four games as head coach.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored the winning goal in the 71st minute in a game that also marked captain Virgil van Dijk’s 100th cap, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Teun Koopmeiners put the home side ahead in the first half with a free kick. Serbia equalised soon afterwards by a goal from 19-year-old Anderlecht striker Mihajlo Cvetkovic.

Zirkzee tapped in the winner from close range after Crysencio Summerville’s cross was laid back by Tijjani Reijnders. The Dutch finished with 10 men after Micky van de Ven went off with a hand injury, as Xavi had already used all his substitutes.

Xavi, who was appointed in August, has now won twice and drawn twice in his first four games. Germany and Greece drew 0-0 on Sunday, which leaves the Netherlands joint top of their group.

The next round of international matches is in November.

Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest. As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight. „Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka." Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6 — Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026 The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest. They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position. The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so. The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday. On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist. However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony. Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”. News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage. 🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026 After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression. Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal. But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m. Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026 Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal. “We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule. The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020. However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040. “This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.” Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱 To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️ ✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych; ✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026 Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors. The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway. The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030 In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025 Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned. Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation. Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year. Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government. That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications. The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026 The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU. Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity. World.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year

We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002. World.title: Leading Polish business owners invest in small nuclear reactor venture
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow. Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm. The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK. As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us. We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG — SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026 The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland. Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe. “They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity. In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland. The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030. Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK. It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”. Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector. SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living. Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025. Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036. Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland. OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites. Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR). It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025 The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen. “I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said. Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects. At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator. World.title: Activists launch world’s first abortion pill delivery locker in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted. They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world. The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group. They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills. Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located. The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws. Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year. However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills. But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered. Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal. However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025 “The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.” They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe. Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable. “The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025 Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced. In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation. In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue. World.title: Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria. Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations. Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry. Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego. Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group. However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown. In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”. The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid. ❗️Sąd Okręgowy Warszawie wydał @RomanowskiPL list żelazny, uchylając środek zapobiegawczy w postaci tymczasowego aresztowania od momentu uprawomocnienia się orzeczenia❗️ Mój Klient na terytorium Polski nie będzie mógł być zatrzymany i tymczasowo aresztowany, a ENA „upada”, jeśli… — Bartosz Lewandowski (@BartoszLewand20) September 30, 2026 In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”. Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him. The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies. The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”. The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low. The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law. “These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity. Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis. In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case. Prokurator ocenia dzisiejsze postanowienie Sądu o wydaniu podejrzanemu Marcinowi Romanowskiemu listu żelaznego jako niezasadne. Na postanowienie to prokurator złoży zażalenie. Sąd może wydać list żelazny, jeżeli podejrzany przebywający za granicą złoży oświadczenie, że stawi… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office. Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years. Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
