World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Designblok 2026 to Take Over Six Prague Venues This Week
World.content:
The 28th edition of Designblok, Prague’s international design festival, will take place from October 6 to 11, 2026, across six locations in the city.

The professional program and conference begin on Tuesday, October 6, while the main festival opens to the public on Wednesday, October 7. This year’s theme is “Light,” with exhibitions and installations exploring both the practical and symbolic role of light in design.



The program will look at design as a tool for addressing social and economic challenges and examine its role in everyday life. Curated exhibitions, exhibitor installations, discussions on the Designblok Stage and the Designblok Talks conference will explore themes including knowledge, truth, hope and sustainability.

The Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) will serve as the festival’s main venue. It will bring together hundreds of presentations by designers, brands, schools and emerging talents, alongside curated exhibitions, lectures and workshops. The venue will also host activities for children and adults.

At the Prague Castle Riding School, Designblok will present two curated exhibitions connecting contemporary design and craftsmanship with Czech cultural history.

The Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague will host one of the festival’s main exhibitions, as well as dozens of design presentations and a special project marking the 100th anniversary of the creation of the popular Czech puppet character Hurvínek.

The Industrial Palace will host much of the festival’s conference and social program, including Designblok Talks, a live edition of the Czech quiz show AZ-kvíz focused on design, and the Designblok Awards Gala. The venue is reopening following its recent reconstruction.

Saturday will also bring fashion shows featuring finalists from the international Diploma Selection competition, which highlights emerging designers from around the world.

Other Designblok venues include the Chapel of the Holy Cross in the Second Courtyard of Prague Castle and the UMPRUM Technology Centre on Mikulandská Street. The latter provides facilities for student projects and workshops.

World.title: Bollywood and Beyond: Prague Indian Film Festival Returns for Its 23rd Edition
World.content:
The Prague Indian Film Festival will return for its 23rd edition from October 8 to 10, bringing a selection of recent Indian films to Kino Světozor.

The festival will open with a historical drama and feature Bollywood, arthouse cinema, a Sundance-winning film and a vampire comedy.

The festival opens on Thursday, October 8, in the presence of the Ambassador of India with Main Vaapas Aaunga, directed by Imtiaz Ali.

Set against the Partition of British India in 1947, the film follows a young Sikh man and his Muslim girlfriend whose lives are transformed by the political upheaval of the period.



Friday’s program will offer two very different takes on contemporary Indian cinema. Bollywood fans can see Cocktail 2, a romantic comedy about a love triangle starring Shahid Kapoor, Kriti Sanon and Rashmika Mandanna. The film follows the successful 2012 movie Cocktail.

The festival will also screen Cactus Pears, an arthouse drama set in a remote village in Maharashtra. The story follows a man who returns home after his father’s death and, while observing traditional mourning rituals, reconnects with a childhood friend.

The film won the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival, where it drew attention for its portrayal of a relationship that goes beyond friendship.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Indian Film Festival 🎥🇮🇳 (@pragueindianfilmfestival)

Saturday afternoon will once again be dedicated to popular Indian films from the 1990s and 2000s. This year’s selection is Rang De Basanti, the 2006 film starring Aamir Khan.

The film has also gained renewed attention in India in connection with recent student protests. Festival art director Radim Špaček said he followed the demonstrations online and saw Rang De Basanti become one of the films associated with the movement.

Saturday evening will take a turn toward horror with Thamma, which combines comedy, horror and vampire folklore. The film stars Ayushmann Khurrana and Rashmika Mandanna, who also appears in Cocktail 2. It is directed by Aditya Sarpotdar.

Dance will also be a major part of the festival program. The accompanying Indian Dance Festival will feature workshops and masterclasses with instructors from around the world, culminating in the Bollywood Fiesta dance gala at Prague’s Rokoko Theatre on Sunday, October 11.

The festival will also feature Indian food, cinema decorations by Sanu Babu and a Bollywood dance party on Saturday night. DJ Dance Sandeep will perform at Theatro Music Club at the Karlín Music Theatre.

World.title: Prague’s Oldest Nightclub Lávka is Closing After 36 years
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known nightlife venues is closing after more than three decades beside the Charles Bridge.

Lávka, which opened in 1990 on the banks of the Vltava, held its final farewell party on September 30. The club will leave its historic premises by October 8 as the City of Prague prepares to renovate the building.



For 36 years, Lávka was more than a nightclub. Its programme included concerts, theater, exhibitions, fashion shows and other cultural events. Its visitors included former president Václav Havel, politician Karel Schwarzenberg and singer Karel Gott.

The venue also hosted Czech acts including Lucie and Lunetic, as well as international performers such as Supertramp and R.E.M.

The first version of the venue was modest. It began as a theater bar in the Bedřich Smetana Museum, replacing the building’s cloakroom. With little money available, co-founder Boris Gaydečka and his partners constructed the bar themselves using scaffolding and wooden boards found on the site.

Advertising on the newly launched Radio Evropa 2 helped attract customers, and the business soon outgrew its original space.

Over the years, Lávka became a regular stop for performers from very different parts of Prague’s cultural scene. Its stage hosted the avant-garde Opera Mozart, the Semafor theater and the Spejbl and Hurvínek Theatre.

During the catastrophic floods of 2002, water eventually reached the ceiling despite efforts to protect the premises.

The damage was extensive. Seating was destroyed, a piano borrowed from the museum was swept away and doors were torn from their hinges.

The building is now being cleared

The end of Lávka’s original premises is linked to a wider renovation of the historic building.

The former Old Town Waterworks building belongs to the City of Prague and has been associated with the Bedřich Smetana Museum since 1936. The museum will also leave the building as part of the planned renovation.

Lávka will continue operating a canteen and café in the neighboring building owned by the Czech Association of Scientific and Technical Societies.

World.title: Only 29 Percent of Czechs Have a Higher Education Degree, OECD Finds
World.content:
Only 29 percent of people aged 25 to 64 in Czechia have completed higher education, according to the latest data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The figures highlight a persistent difference in the country’s education profile compared with other developed economies. While university-level education remains less common in Czechia, upper secondary education is far more widespread.

Around two-thirds of Czech adults have completed upper secondary education, compared with an OECD average of 39 percent. Vocational secondary education remains particularly common, although its share is gradually declining, as younger generations attain higher levels of education.



The change is most visible when comparing age groups. Vocational secondary education is the highest level of education for around 70 percent of Czech residents aged 55 to 64. Among people aged 25 to 34, the figure has fallen to 52 percent.

Across the OECD, the proportion of younger adults completing higher education has continued to increase. Czechia, however, is also facing a less positive trend at the lower end of the education scale.

Among 25- to 34-year-olds, the share of people who have not completed upper secondary education increased from 6 percent in 2015 to 7 percent in 2025. The trend is moving in the opposite direction across the OECD as a whole, where the average fell to 12 percent last year.

Young Czechs have relatively low unemployment

Despite the country’s comparatively low share of university graduates, Czechia performs well on several employment indicators.

In 2025, just 7 percent of people aged 18 to 24 were neither in education nor employment. The OECD average was twice as high, at 14 percent.

The unemployment rate among recent graduates has also declined over the past decade. In Czechia, it fell from 3 percent in 2015 to 2 percent in 2025. The corresponding OECD average was 5 percent.

Education is reflected in Czech wages

The OECD data also show a clear relationship between educational attainment and earnings in Czechia.

People whose highest qualification is general secondary education, including graduates of gymnasiums, earn an average of 8 percent less than the national average wage.

The difference is larger for people with vocational secondary education, whose earnings are 16 percent below the national average. Those who have not completed secondary education earn 33 percent less on average.

Higher education is also associated with greater access to remote work. Around 31 percent of Czech employees with a university education work remotely at least occasionally. Among workers with secondary education, the proportion is approximately 10 percent.

Czech education spending remains below OECD average

The OECD report also points to differences in public investment.

In 2023, public expenditure on education from primary schools through universities amounted to 3.6 percent of GDP in Czechia. The average across OECD countries was 4 percent.

Czechia also spent less per student than the OECD average. Annual expenditure stood at $11,861 per student, compared with $13,601 across OECD countries.

The figures are included in the OECD’s latest assessment of education systems in member countries, covering education levels, employment outcomes, earnings and public spending.

World.title: Rising Number of Czech Families Struggle to Afford School Lunches
World.content:
A growing number of Czech parents are unable to cover the cost of school lunches for their children.

The non-profit initiative Lunches for Children (Obědy pro děti), run by Women for Women, cites divorce, job loss, or serious illness as the primary causes driving families to apply for help. Even state food subsidies are proving insufficient.



At the start of this school year, demand for support is especially steep. Between January and September, the program aided nearly 16,000 pupils through cooperation with more than 1,150 schools and cafeterias nationwide.

Participation rose by about 15 percent compared with the same period last year, with sharp increases in Prague and the Ústí nad Labem region. A typical lunch costs 30–50 crowns, but for older students, monthly totals can exceed 1,000 crowns.

Under Women for Women’s rules, schools help identify children in need. Class teachers, principals, and canteen managers evaluate applications based on factors such as low income, single-parent status, or sudden financial crisis. Schools apply on behalf of families; funding is granted under donation agreements and routed directly to the schools (not to parents).

The heaviest wave of applications arrives each September, when the new school year begins. In more strained regions, quota limits have already been reached. The Ministry of Education endorses the project as a model of effective public–nonprofit partnership.

Marta Hekl, the organization’s director, emphasizes that the school lunch is more than nourishment: “Children feel part of a community, gain confidence, and receive the energy they need for learning.” Nejedlá adds that even in Prague, the country’s wealthiest region, applications have risen by 20 percent, as living costs outpace wages.

Historically, need is greatest in regions burdened by high unemployment and social difficulties—especially Ústí nad Labem and Karlovy Vary.

Some corporate donors also back the program. For instance, ADM Olomouc offered a significant grant to the Lunches for Children project, helping nearly 100 children eat lunch with their peers all year.

World.title: Lego to Open New Prague Store on Na Příkopě Street on October 22
World.content:
Lego will open its second Czech store on Na Příkopě Street in central Prague on October 22.

The Lego Store Prague City Center will open to the public at 10 a.m. The 496-square-meter shop will carry the full Lego range, including sets available exclusively through Lego stores.



The interior will incorporate references to Prague and Czech history.

Among the models on display will be Lego versions of the Prague Astronomical Clock, Charles Bridge, Charles IV and the Czech double-tailed lion. A model of a Prague tram will also be part of the store’s design.

Visitors will have access to several interactive features, including a station where they can create their own minifigures and a Pick & Build area.

Prague-wide Lego Game

The opening campaign will begin earlier in October with a series of Saturday challenges. During the first three Saturdays of the month, families will be able to follow clues published on social media and search different parts of Prague for project ambassadors.

The ambassadors will be carrying Lego models representing Prague landmarks, including a tram, the Astronomical Clock and Charles IV. Participants who find the correct location will have to give the ambassador a specific password revealed through the published clues.

The campaign will involve content creators and public figures including Bára and Ondřej Havel, Janek Rubeš and Honza Mikulka, known for their Kluci z Prahy project, as well as influencer Karel “Kovy” Kovář.

Three families will win the opportunity to attend the new store’s opening ceremony. As part of the event, they will assemble a large golden key from Lego bricks outside the store, which will be used to symbolically open the new shop.

The store will also host a special activity in November. On November 4 and 5, visitors will be able to build their own Lego model of a Prague tram and take it home.

World.title: Discovering Debrecen: Hungarian hospitality beyond the language barrier – Video
World.content:
American creator Ray of Magyar Minute travelled from Budapest to Debrecen with Hungarian food journalists on a hosted press trip arranged with help from Daily News Hungary’s Alpár Kató. At Next Bistro, a waiter’s goulash recommendation, owner Albert István’s “fine bistro” approach and conversations across a language gap became a personal introduction to the city. His short video captures the visit, while the accompanying article explores the history behind Debrecen’s trade, independence-era role and university.

For an American living in Budapest, a trip to Debrecen can feel like a small journey into another side of Hungary. The language may be the same, but the city has its own character, history and traditions — and sometimes the easiest way to discover them is through a plate of food and a conversation with a stranger.

Ray, the American creator behind Magyar Minute, recently travelled from Budapest to Debrecen with Hungarian food journalists on a hosted press trip arranged with the help of Daily News Hungary’s Alpár Kató. At Next Bistro, a waiter’s recommendation of goulash, conversations that moved between Hungarian and English, and the warm welcome of owner Albert István offered a personal introduction to the city.

The restaurant visit became more than a meal. It showed how hospitality can bridge a language gap, and how food can open the door to discovering a place.

When the language barrier becomes part of the experience

At Next Bistro, communication did not always happen in one language. Staff members switched to English when necessary, while conversations continued with the help of translations and gestures.

For a foreign visitor, these small moments can make a significant difference. Rather than feeling like an outsider struggling to navigate an unfamiliar environment, Ray found himself drawn into the atmosphere around the table.

The waiter’s recommendation was suitably Hungarian: goulash. The dish offered a straightforward introduction to the country’s culinary traditions, while the conversation around it revealed something less tangible about Debrecen — the people who live and work there.

That welcoming atmosphere is also central to Albert István’s approach to Next Bistro. He describes the restaurant as a “fine bistro”, combining a relaxed dining experience with attention to quality and presentation.

The restaurant also offers a more hands-on experience for guests interested in steak. Next has a steak-selection concept involving dry-aged meat, while its separate yakiniku experience features bite-size Wagyu and Angus cooked on a tabletop charcoal grill. The two experiences should not be understood as interchangeable, however, as the cuts and preparation options depend on the particular offering available.

(The following 5 subtitles may be selected above: English, Hungarian, Italian, German and Chinese.)

A city shaped by trade

The story of Debrecen cannot be separated from trade. For centuries, the city developed as an important commercial centre on the Great Plain. Its location helped connect agricultural production and livestock farming with markets farther afield.

One particularly important part of this history was the cattle trade. Long-distance cattle drovers were known as gulyás in Hungarian, a word that has since become famous around the world through the dish goulash. Historical accounts also associate the long-distance cattle-driving network with the hajdúk.

Cattle from the Great Plain were driven toward major markets, including Vienna, Nuremberg and Venice. Debrecen was one important trading centre within this wider network, rather than the single point from which all cattle left for Western European markets.

It is a fitting historical connection for a city where a visitor can still encounter Hungarian food traditions centuries after livestock trading helped shape the region’s economy.

The terrace at Next Bistro, beside Debrecen’s Nagyerdő. Still from Ray’s visit on 1 October 2026. Credit: Magyar Minute

More than a trading town

Debrecen’s significance goes well beyond commerce. The city occupies an important place in Hungary’s political history. During the 1848–49 revolution and War of Independence, Debrecen became a centre of the Hungarian national movement. In 1849, after the Hungarian government left Pest-Buda, the city briefly served as the country’s political centre.

The Great Reformed Church became one of the defining locations of this period. It was here that the Hungarian National Assembly declared the dethronement of the Habsburg dynasty and the independence of Hungary in April 1849.

Education is another part of Debrecen’s long-standing identity. The city’s Reformed educational tradition stretches back centuries, and the institution that developed into today’s University of Debrecen has helped establish the city as one of Hungary’s major university centres.

For visitors arriving from Budapest, this provides another perspective on Debrecen. It is not simply Hungary’s second-largest city or a destination on the other side of the country. It is a place whose identity has been shaped by commerce, religion, education and the country’s turbulent political history.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Is Budapest really that far away?

For Albert, one of the challenges is getting people from the capital to make the journey. In the video, he estimates that 90 percent of people in Budapest will not make the drive to Debrecen. That figure is his personal estimate rather than the result of a verified survey, but it points to a genuine challenge for destinations outside the capital: convincing visitors to spend time exploring another part of the country.

Owner Albert István during the hosted press visit to Next Bistro on 1 October 2026. Still from Ray’s footage. Credit: Magyar Minute

Ray’s own journey illustrates the point. The trip from Budapest to Debrecen took roughly two and a half hours each way during the press visit, while comparisons made in the video describe the journey as approximately two hours. Exact travel times naturally vary depending on the route and traffic.

Yet the distance is also part of what makes the experience worthwhile. Leaving Budapest behind offers the chance to see a different Hungarian city, encounter a different rhythm of life and discover stories that cannot be reduced to the country’s capital.

If you missed it: Refused or terminated? What one missed appointment taught an American about Hungarian residency

Discovering Debrecen, one conversation at a time

Ray’s visit to Next Bistro ultimately provides a simple entry point into a much larger story. There is the food: goulash, steak and the restaurant’s contemporary interpretation of Hungarian hospitality. There is the language barrier, softened when people switch to English or help translate. And there is the city itself, with a history stretching from cattle trading and the Great Plain to the events of 1849 and a centuries-old educational tradition.

For an American visitor, perhaps the most memorable part is not a particular historical date or dish, but the experience of being welcomed despite not speaking Hungarian fluently. That is one of the pleasures of travelling beyond the familiar tourist route. Sometimes discovering a city begins not with a landmark, but with someone recommending what you should eat.

Editorial disclosure: Ray of Magyar Minute’s visit to Debrecen was part of a hosted press trip on 1 October 2026, arranged with the help of Daily News Hungary’s Alpár Kató.

Featured image: Ray Brown – Magyar Minute

World.title: Business Meets Rugby brings business leaders together in Budapest
World.content:
Business meets Rugby brought together senior executives, business leaders and figures from professional rugby in Budapest, exploring how lessons from elite sport can be applied to leadership, teamwork and communication in the corporate world. Daily News Hungary attended the event at the invitation of Confindustria Ungheria, an official partner of DNH.

The Executive Rugby Leadership Experience – Business meets Rugby was held on 24 September at the Novotel City & Budapest Congress Center. The programme combined discussions, interactive workshops and team exercises, bringing together members of Hungary’s international business community and representatives of Benetton Rugby.

According to Confindustria Ungheria, the event was designed primarily for CEOs and senior executives, with a focus on leadership, teamwork and performance.

Business Meets Rugby connects business leaders in Budapest

Business meets Rugby connects sport and corporate leadership

Rather than concentrating on rugby as a sport, the programme used situations familiar from the pitch to examine challenges that also appear in business environments.

The afternoon was structured around three main themes: leadership, supporting the team and effective communication. Participants discussed what it means to lead from the front, why collective performance often matters more than individual achievement, and how rapid and reliable communication can influence results.

The programme also included an Executive Challenge, in which mixed teams of managers took part in activities inspired by rugby. No previous rugby experience was required, with the exercises instead focusing on cooperation and decision-making. What’s more, participants were able to practise the basic movements at an off-site venue.

A panel discussion later turned to the question of how principles developed in professional sport can be transferred from the playing field to the boardroom.

If you missed it: Legendary Milanese pastry house Cova opens first confectionery in Hungary – video

Benetton Rugby representatives share their experience

Among the guests were Antonio Pavanello, president of Benetton Rugby and a former captain of the Italian national team, as well as the club’s marketing manager Fabio Rigoletto.

Former Italian internationals and coaches Tommaso Benvenuti, Tommaso Iannone, Marco Lazzaroni and Ezio Galon also participated in the programme, sharing perspectives from professional rugby and discussing the importance of trust, clearly defined roles and collective responsibility.

During the discussion, I asked what they see as the defining difference between rugby and other team sports. Their answer focused on one of the game’s most distinctive rules: the ball can only be passed backwards. This means that the player carrying the ball must always have teammates positioned behind them, fundamentally shaping how the team moves, supports each other and builds an attack. It creates a very different strategic dynamic from sports where the ball can be passed or kicked forward, making coordination, positioning and collective support especially important.

The formal programme concluded with a networking dinner, providing participants with an opportunity to continue discussions and establish new professional contacts.

Daily News Hungary participated in Business meets Rugby at the invitation of Confindustria Ungheria as part of the official partnership between the two organisations.

Business Meets Rugby connects business leaders in Budapest

Beyond its sporting theme, the Budapest event provided another meeting point for Hungary’s international business community and highlighted how experiences from elite sport can offer practical perspectives on leadership and organisational culture.

World.title: Motorists watch out: 10 new speed cameras installed on Hungary’s busiest motorway
World.content:
Drivers using Hungary’s busiest motorway are being urged to stay below the speed limit as ten new speed cameras have been installed along sections affected by the motorway’s major expansion project.

Ten new speed cameras installed

The new cameras were installed along the M1 motorway by MKIF Hungarian Concession Infrastructure Development Plc in consultation with the Hungarian police. While MKIF purchased and installed the equipment, the cameras will be operated by the police, who are responsible for actual speed enforcement.

The new speed cameras are designed to do more than simply display or record a vehicle’s speed. Equipped with microwave radar, they can immediately show motorists how fast they are travelling through so-called “SMILE” displays.

According to MKIF, the equipment is also capable of authenticated, VÉDA-compatible speed enforcement. Technically, it can additionally be used to monitor average speed over a section of road and measure the distance between vehicles.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Cameras powered by solar panels

The new speed cameras can operate without a conventional electricity connection. Solar panels and batteries provide their power, allowing the devices to be deployed at locations where mains electricity is unavailable. MKIF says the main purpose of installing the cameras is to improve safety around construction zones.

The M1 expansion means motorists face narrower lanes, diversions and changing traffic arrangements, while construction machinery, equipment and materials may be operating close to live traffic. Maintaining an appropriate speed and safe following distance is therefore intended not only to prevent fines but also to reduce the risk of accidents and help traffic flow more smoothly.

The new speed cameras when drivers are exceeding the speed limit. Screenshot from Medirlab/YouTube The new TraffiPack when drivers are below the speed limit. Screenshot from Medirlab/YouTube

More on traffic in Hungary: Budapest transport and parking could change dramatically from 2027 under new government-city deal

Major traffic changes ahead

Further changes are expected in the autumn, when a 2+2 lane traffic arrangement is planned as part of the motorway works. Drivers will need to adapt to a traffic layout that differs significantly from normal motorway conditions.

With construction continuing and ten new speed-monitoring devices now in place, motorists on the M1 have another reason to pay close attention to speed limits, road signs and changing lane arrangements — and, of course, to ease off the accelerator.

World.title: Hungarian FM: Viktor Orbán’s influence still entrenched as government dismantles former system
World.content:
Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán says Hungary is undergoing a profound transformation, but the legacy of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán remains deeply rooted in the economy, institutions and society.

FM Orbán gave an interview

Hungary is undergoing a major political transformation, but dismantling the system built during Viktor Orbán’s years in power will take time, Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán told Estonian security and defence journal The Baltic Sentinel in an extensive interview at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Budapest.

Anita Orbán said the new government was working to restore the rule of law, strengthen independent institutions and pursue money allegedly stolen under the previous government. She also said Hungary needed more time to reduce its dependence on Russian oil and natural gas, while outlining the government’s ambition to meet the Maastricht criteria and adopt the euro by the end of its term.

‘The entire system has to be dismantled’

Asked how much of Viktor Orbán’s political system remained in place, Anita Orbán said that changing the government alone was not enough. “A great deal,” she said, arguing that the government needed to dismantle the broader system built under the previous administration.

According to the foreign minister, the government has introduced a “very busy legislative agenda” aimed at reversing what she described as state capture and restoring the independence of institutions, including the Constitutional Court and government agencies.

She highlighted Hungary’s decision to join the European Public Prosecutor’s Office and the establishment of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which she said is tasked with pursuing stolen public money, recovering it and returning it to public use.

The government has also abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office, which Anita Orbán accused of harassing civil society and journalists. But she stressed that the former prime minister’s influence extends beyond institutions.

“His influence is also entrenched in the economy and, unfortunately, to some extent in people’s mindsets.”

Could Viktor Orbán face arrest?

The interview also touched on the recent detention of two ministers who served under the former government. Asked directly whether Viktor Orbán himself could eventually end up in handcuffs, Anita Orbán did not rule it out.

“We’ll see,” she replied.

She said the government was committed to pursuing stolen public funds and that Hungary needed to become a country “where actions have consequences”. The foreign minister said the recent detentions were symbolic, describing them as part of the government’s effort to establish new standards of integrity and political conduct.

Hungary still heavily dependent on Russian energy

Anita Orbán also acknowledged that Hungary remains significantly dependent on Russian energy. Hungary continues to purchase a large share of its oil and natural gas from Russia, while its current exemption from sanctions runs until November 21, according to the foreign minister. Hungary has asked the United States to extend the exemption.

Asked whether the country simply needed more time to end its dependence on Russia, Anita Orbán replied: “We simply need more time.” She argued that the government had inherited an economy and an energy system heavily dependent on Russian supplies, which provide the heating and electricity on which people rely. At the same time, she said Hungary was working on diversifying its energy supplies and strengthening energy security.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Government targets euro adoption

The government also faces a difficult fiscal situation, with Anita Orbán saying the budget deficit had initially stood at 8.3% before falling to 7.5%. She attributed part of the improvement to EU funding recovered by the new government.

The minister said the government had sought savings without introducing austerity measures or new burdens. Instead, it had cut what she described as unnecessary and luxury spending, including travel expenses and politicians’ allowances.

“Our goal is to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of our term so that we can adopt the euro,” she said. The government therefore intends to combine tighter control of public spending with efforts to generate economic growth.

About the joining the euro area: When could Hungary adopt the euro? Central banker gives earliest possible date

Hungary says Ukraine must follow the normal EU accession path

On Ukraine’s EU membership ambitions, Anita Orbán reiterated that Hungary supports a merit-based enlargement process but opposes any fast-track accession. She said two of the six EU negotiating clusters had already been opened for Ukraine and stressed that Hungary had participated in the consensus behind those decisions.

However, she said Ukraine should undergo the same reform process as previous EU candidates. “We support a merit-based approach,” she said, adding that Hungary does not support “fast-track membership or any shortcuts around the normal process”. Hungary plans to hold a referendum on Ukraine’s EU membership at the end of the accession process, according to the minister.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian foreign minister Anita Orbán speaks to CNN about changes under new government

‘Hungary is returning to Europe’

Anita Orbán also portrayed the political changes of recent months as a return to Hungary’s European democratic traditions. She said Hungary was returning to its “cultural heritage” and its place “in Europe, in the heart of Europe, in the European Union and in NATO”.

According to the minister, the country is returning to democracy, the rule of law, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. She acknowledged that the transformation would take time, particularly given that the previous government had been in power for 16 years.

Anita Orbán also highlighted the symbolic importance of 2026, which marks the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 revolution. She said the government wants the October 23 commemoration to underline the idea that Hungarians have the courage to defend freedom, human rights and democracy.

World.title: 250kg Second World War-era bomb found in Budapest’s agglomeration
World.content:
A 250-kilogram German bomb from the Second World War has been discovered at a construction site in Vecsés, just outside Budapest, alongside a smaller 50-kilogram bomb.

Two German bombs discovered from the Second World War

The explosives were found recently on the outskirts of Vecsés, in Pest County, after police received a report about suspected unexploded ordnance at a construction site. A bomb disposal patrol from the Hungarian Defence Forces identified the devices as a German-made 50-kilogram bomb and a 250-kilogram German demolition bomb.

According to the MH 1st Explosive Ordnance Disposal and River Flotilla Regiment, the condition of the bombs allowed them to be moved safely. Specialists transported both devices to the Hungarian Defence Forces’ central collection facility, where they will later be destroyed.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Historic military significance

The discovery is not considered unusual in the area, according to the bomb disposal unit. During the Second World War, the area around Vecsés formed part of the immediate logistical and approach zone of Ferihegy Airport, which was used by the German Luftwaffe.

The region also saw heavy military activity towards the end of 1944, when German and Hungarian forces conducted prolonged defensive operations in front of the Attila Line, a defensive system established around Budapest.

With unexploded wartime ordnance still occasionally emerging during construction and excavation work, bomb disposal experts continue to play an important role in ensuring such discoveries are handled safely. The latest find appeared more than eight decades after the Second World War, but many are found every year.

World.title: New discount giant enters Hungary: Budapest store revealed as expansion plans take shape
World.content:
Malaysian discount retailer MR.DIY is preparing to open its first Hungarian store at Budapest’s KÖKI shopping centre, with recruitment already underway. The rapidly expanding chain has entered several European markets in recent years, and industry sources say hundreds of stores could eventually be possible in some countries.

MR.DIY prepares first Hungarian store

A new international player is entering Hungary’s discount household goods market. Work is already underway on the first Hungarian MR.DIY store at KÖKI Terminal in Budapest, where the chain has also started recruiting staff, according to signage at the site.

The Malaysian retailer is not a newcomer to Europe. Over the past five years, it has expanded from Turkey and Spain to Poland and Romania, with further expansion into Central Europe now underway.

The Hungarian launch comes after industry analysts had already identified MR.DIY as a potential new entrant to the Hungarian market alongside brands such as Uniqlo and Miniso. The exact opening date of the KÖKI store has not yet been announced, however.

What is MR.DIY and what does it sell?

Founded in Kuala Lumpur in 2005, MR.DIY has grown into one of Asia’s largest retailers of home improvement and household goods. The company’s business model is built around its “Always Low Prices” concept, putting it firmly in the discount segment.

A typical MR.DIY store covers around 900 square metres and carries between 15,000 and 17,000 products. Its range includes tools, household goods, home decoration, electrical accessories, stationery, toys and sporting goods.

The retailer therefore combines elements of a DIY shop, household discount store and homeware retailer. The company has recently reported having around 5,700–6,000 stores across 15–16 countries, depending on the period and corporate reporting used.

From Istanbul to Budapest: MR.DIY’s European expansion

MR.DIY opened its first European store in Istanbul in November 2021. It entered the European Union in 2022, opening its first Spanish shop in Talavera de la Reina in Toledo province. Expansion accelerated considerably over the past two years.

Poland joined the chain’s European network in late 2024, while Romania opened its first store in March 2026. The chain is also preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first store planned at the Forum Nová Karolina shopping centre in Ostrava.

Spain has continued to see new openings, including a store of almost 600 square metres at Madrid’s Xanadú shopping centre in September. MR.DIY is reportedly planning another 20–30 Spanish stores in 2027. In Germany, the company has so far progressed to establishing a local corporate entity: MR. D.I.Y. Germany GmbH was registered in Berlin in January 2026.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Poland offers a glimpse of what could come next

Poland has become one of the main drivers of MR.DIY’s Central European expansion. The first Polish store opened in Zabrze on 15 November 2024. By July 2026, the chain had already reached 35 stores in the country, with 19 new locations opened during the first half of the year alone.

Romania has seen similarly rapid growth. Seven stores have opened in the seven months since the chain’s debut in Pitești, with at least 11 expected by the end of the year. In both countries, MR.DIY has focused on shopping centres and retail parks rather than limiting its expansion to major cities.

Whether Hungary will see a similar pace of growth remains unclear. The company has not announced a specific Hungarian expansion target.

Who will MR.DIY compete with in Hungary?

Industry sources cited by Pénzcentrum identify TEDi and KiK as two of MR.DIY’s most obvious Hungarian competitors, while JYSK could also overlap with the chain in certain product categories. In the Czech Republic, local media have primarily described MR.DIY as a challenger to discount chains such as Pepco and Action.

The extent of the price competition will only become clear once the Hungarian store opens, as the retailer’s Hungarian pricing has not yet been disclosed.

MR.DIY wants to cover Europe

Magdalena Nazarewicz, MR.DIY’s European business development director, told Czech business newspaper E15 in July that the company’s ambition is to cover the whole of Europe and become a leading player in every market it enters, while acknowledging that conditions differ from country to country.

Polish media have reported that the company sees at least 1,000 stores in Poland as a long-term ambition. The figure is a strategic goal rather than a commitment tied to a specific deadline.

In Romania, MR.DIY’s local business development manager, Cătălin Secăreanu, has also referred to an ambition of around 500 stores. Again, this is a long-term objective rather than a promise to reach that number within a particular year. There is currently no equivalent public target for Hungary.

When will the Budapest store open?

The exact opening date of the KÖKI store is not yet known. Recruitment has already begun, however, suggesting that preparations are well underway. If the Budapest location performs well, MR.DIY could potentially accelerate its Hungarian expansion, following the pattern seen in Poland and Romania. For now, though, there is no confirmed plan for hundreds or thousands of Hungarian stores.

World.title: Train derails at busy Budapest railway station, services disrupted
World.content:
A shunting locomotive derailed at Budapest’s Southern Railway Station (Déli pályaudvar) on Monday morning, disrupting several services and causing changes for passengers travelling towards Lake Balaton and Pécs.

Several trains affected after locomotive derailment

A shunting locomotive derailed in the points area of Budapest’s Déli railway station, temporarily blocking tracks 1–5, according to MÁVINFORM.

Several trains were left stranded on the affected tracks, forcing MÁV-csoport to reorganise services. As a result, some trains are only running to and from Budapest-Kelenföld, while some suburban services have been cancelled.

Passengers travelling towards Lake Balaton and Pécs should expect further changes and different train formations as the disruption continues.

If you missed it: Budapest–Belgrade railway runs at 160 km/h in final test before passenger launch

Suburban trains cancelled

Among the affected suburban services are:

The Z30 trains to Martonvásár are not running.

The S40 trains to Százhalombatta are not running.

Balaton and Pécs services also affected

The Mecsek InterCity services to Pécs are currently only running between Budapest-Kelenföld and Pécs, rather than serving Déli railway station.

The disruption is also affecting several Balaton services:

The 7:35 AM Tópart InterCity (IC 842) from Déli to Nagykanizsa has been cancelled. Passengers can instead take the Balaton InterCity (IC 862) one hour later. After the train arrives in Balatonszentgyörgy, a replacement bus will continue to Nagykanizsa.

A replacement bus will also leave Balatonszentgyörgy at 10:01 AM, following the original train’s departure time, and will stop at intermediate stations.

The 9:05 AM fast train to Tapolca (9792) only runs from Budapest-Kelenföld and is expected to depart with a 15–20-minute delay. Passengers can travel from Déli to Kelenföld on the 9:10 AM Z30 train to Székesfehérvár, with a connection provided.

Meanwhile, the 5:51 AM fast train from Tapolca to Déli (9709) will terminate at Budapest-Kelenföld instead of continuing to the Southern Railway Station.

Train tickets accepted on several Budapest public transport services

Passengers affected by the disruption can use their valid train tickets on several BKK services until the disruption is resolved. These include:

M2 metro between Déli railway station and Keleti railway station

The entire M4 metro line

Bus routes 140, 140A and 139, recommended for passengers travelling between Déli and Kelenföld

Tram routes 56, 56A, 17 and 61 towards Móricz Zsigmond körtér

The entire length of tram routes 19 and 49

World.title: Budapest–Belgrade railway runs at 160 km/h in final test before passenger launch
World.content:
The Budapest–Belgrade railway has completed its most extensive test yet, with trains running at speeds of up to 160 km/h under conditions designed to simulate a normal peak-hour timetable. The test brings the long-awaited launch of passenger services another step closer.

The latest test on the Hungarian section of the Budapest–Belgrade railway was successfully completed over the weekend, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced on Sunday.

During the overnight trial, trains operated for several hours according to the timetable planned for daytime peak periods. The main difference from normal passenger operations was that there were no passengers on board. Engineers also simulated various disruptions and examined how the railway’s systems would respond to unexpected traffic situations.

One of the most important elements under examination was the European Train Control System, or ETCS, which is essential for ensuring safe passenger operations at speeds of up to 160 kilometres per hour.

According to Vitézy, the system performed well during the test, marking another important milestone before passenger trains can begin operating on the route.

Passenger information system still needs work

The tests did, however, reveal problems with the passenger information systems, which did not perform at the required level. These will still have to be corrected before the railway can fully enter service.

Photo: MTI/Péter Lakatos

MÁV, Hungary’s state-owned railway company, has previously stressed that there is no fixed political deadline for the launch of passenger services. According to the company, operations will only begin once the ETCS testing programme has been successfully completed and the required safety checks have been carried out.

Budapest–Belgrade journey could take just three and a half hours

Once passenger services begin along the full route, the new railway is expected to significantly shorten journey times between the Hungarian and Serbian capitals.

According to MÁV, the journey between Budapest and Belgrade could fall from around eight hours to approximately three and a half hours.

Domestic passengers are also expected to benefit. Long-distance journeys between Budapest and Kelebia could become around an hour shorter, while commuters travelling towards the capital from the southern suburbs could save as much as 20 minutes.

The project involved rebuilding the existing Hungarian railway line, constructing a second track and installing new signalling, safety and station infrastructure.

If you missed it: Budapest to get more police officers as public safety moves up the agenda

Trains could run every 15 minutes on part of the line

MÁV plans significantly more frequent suburban services once the upgraded line is fully operational. Trains between Budapest and Kunszentmiklós-Tass could run every 30 minutes, while services from Délegyháza could operate as frequently as every 15 minutes.

The railway company estimates that passenger numbers on the line could eventually rise to as much as four times the levels recorded in recent years.

The upgraded railway is also expected to increase freight capacity and strengthen rail connections between Central Europe, Serbia and transport routes further south.

The latest successful test does not yet mean passengers can board trains between Budapest and Belgrade immediately. However, with trains now operating at 160 km/h under conditions closely resembling a real peak-hour timetable, the project has moved considerably closer to its long-awaited passenger launch.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Moves Towards Changing Law to Curb Hague Special Court
World.content:
The first reading of the special court law amendment at the Kosovo parliament, October 5, 2026. Photo: Antigone Isufi/BIRN.

Kosovo MPs on Monday voted to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers so the Hague-based court, part of Kosovo’s justice system, may not impose a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 15 years. The amendment has not been adopted yet, as it must undergo a parliamentary committee review and return for a second reading.

Outside parliament, protesters who had staged an all-night vigil in front of the legislature chanted: “Vote [for] the law.”

The vote comes amid anger in Kosovo after the court sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes on September 16.

The four were found guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and several locations in Albania.

Critics have, among others, claimed that the court did not apply the “lex mitior” principle, which allows defendants to be sentenced under the most favourable law of the time that the crime was committed. According to the applicable law of former Yugoslavia, the maximum prison sentence is 15 years.

The amendments include for the sentences to be served in Kosovo. Based on the current law, “the Specialist Chambers may order the transfer of a convicted person to a third country for service of his or her sentence of imprisonment”.

The amendments also grant Kosovo’s President power to grant pardons, the work of the court to be subjected to monitoring by international organisations, and for a constitutional review of the law to be conducted by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo.

It is not certain whether a second reading will take place on Monday.

Bedri Hamza, chair of the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which Thaci founded, and which proposed the amendments, said before the vote that the law does not belong to his party, even if it “is a PDK initiative”.

The verdict, which is to be appealed, caused outrage in Kosovo and people have been protesting daily ever since.

It also led to the initiative to change the law on the court. The court is a hybrid tribunal – although it is part of Kosovo’s judiciary, it is staffed with internationals and located in The Hague.

It was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies because of concern of potential witness intimidation if the processes were to be held domestically in Kosovo.

The court has a mandate to try crimes committed from January 1, 1998, to December 31, 2000, based on a Council of Europe report by Swiss Senator Dick Marty, which made allegations of war crimes and organ trafficking by KLA fighters.

An EU Special Investigative Task Force, led by former US prosecutor Clint Williamson, concluded that there was enough evidence to indict suspects for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but not enough to bring charges for organ trafficking.

The amendments of the law aim to change the mandate of the court to only cover crimes allegedly committed after the Kosovo war, from July 1, 1999 until December 31, 2000. The draft amendment says that the court will not have jurisdiction over acts that were not committed in relation to the allegations of organ-trafficking in the Dick Marty report – for which it has already been established that there is not enough evidence for trials.

On Monday, before the law was put to a vote, Prime Minister Albin Kurti reminded MPs that the country faces another crisis, over the election of a President.

“A law regarding the Hague court is necessary, but so is a President of Kosovo. Proceeding with one without the other could be highly detrimental. We cannot claim to be defending Kosovo’s interests in The Hague while allowing an institutional vacuum to develop within Kosovo,” he said.

Tuesday is the constitutional deadline for Kosovo to elect a President and finalise the formation of institutions deriving from the June 7 elections. If a President is not elected, the country faces its fourth parliamentary elections in less than two years.

Even if the law amendments pass the second reading, they will be enforced only after the appeals panel at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers issues a verdict for Thaci and the three others.

World.title: Serbs Abroad May Have to Vote Overnight Under New Election Rule
World.content:
Serbs voting abroad in upcoming elections will have to follow polling hours based on Central European Time under a new decision adopted in the early hours of Monday morning by the Republic Electoral Commission, RIK, which has set standardised voting hours of 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

The decision means that while some polling stations abroad will operate simultaneously with those in Serbia if they are in the same time zone, voters in some countries, including the United States, Australia and Indonesia, may have to cast ballots during local nighttime hours.

The proposal was passed by 20 RIK members in favour, while seven voted against. Several RIK members criticised the move, arguing it could make it harder for Serbian citizens abroad to exercise their right to vote. They also questioned why the Foreign Ministry, which initiated the proposal, had become involved in determining polling hours.

RIK member Ivan Sebek said such an arrangement had never been introduced since Serbia began organising voting abroad, and no previously reported problem justified it. “You are further restricting voters’ rights and effectively cutting the time available to exercise their right to vote in half,” Sebek said.

Other RIK members raised concerns about voters’ safety when voting at night. Vladimir Dragas called it “completely illegal” and warned it could anger some diaspora voters, forced to cast their ballots in the middle of the night.

The decision comes as the governing Serbian Progressive Party faces its strongest challenge since it came to power in 2012, from the recently-established opposition Student List, which grew out of the student-led protest movement. Some commentators have suggested there is strong support for the students’ cause among diaspora Serbians.

The change in voting times has worried some Serbian voters around the world.

Marija, who lives in China, speaking to BIRN on condition of anonymity, said the opening hours of the Serbian embassy on election day would be inconvenient, lasting from 2 p.m. until 3 a.m. Another issue is that, for the whole of China, only one polling station has been approved, in Beijing.

“Considering that China is a huge territory, the travelling distance we are talking about is huge … Don’t forget families who need to add two hours per flight, book accommodation, eat in Beijing, and come back home the same day. Also, local laws are very strict when it comes to people gathering, especially around the San Li Tun area [where most of the embassies are],” she explained.

Marija said diaspora voters had already faced various difficulties since the elections were announced.

“When we initially contacted the authorities about our request to vote abroad, we did not receive timely responses to our emails. In some cases, we had to wait a day or two for an answer. There were also significant delays concerning the documents we were supposed to receive from our local authorities in Serbia confirming we were eligible to vote outside the country, particularly here in China,” she said.

She said they had been expecting polling stations to be opened wherever at least 100 citizens had registered. However, only one polling station, in Beijing, was ultimately approved.

The same issue has emerged in Australia, where polling stations were approved only in Melbourne and Sydney, even though more than 100 Serbian voters have registered also in Perth and Brisbane.

Nemanja Djurovic told BIRN that voters from Brisbane have been directed to vote in Melbourne, even though Sydney is closer.

He added that the decision to open polling stations in only these two cities would result in many people not voting, as travel is a financial burden, and some citizens, like pregnant women, will not be able to take the flights that are necessary.

“The state is effectively slapping Serbian citizens living in Brisbane and Perth in the face. We are deeply disappointed and feel like second-class citizens because our rights are being openly ignored. The state is sending us a clear message that it does not want the diaspora to vote,” Nemanja said.

He added that the voting hours could significantly affect turnout in Australia, as polling there would take place from 5 p.m. on Sunday until 6 a.m. on Monday, when many people would already be preparing for work.

“Public transport stops running around midnight, while some bus services stop even earlier. This will significantly reduce turnout,” he predicted.

“The authorities want to prevent the first results coming from diaspora polling stations in the east from being negative for them,” he added.

World.title: In Montenegro, Whistleblower Reports Rise, But Convictions Remain Rare
World.content:
A growing number of Montenegrins are blowing the whistle on irregularities, abuse or corruption in their workplaces, but rarely do those behind the wrongdoing end up in court.

According to data from the Agency for Prevention of Corruption, ASK, the rate of whistleblowing has shot up since 2020, when the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, left office after three decades of uninterrupted rule.

Between 2016 and 2025, a total of 1,259 whistleblower reports were filed, according to the ASK. Seventy-two per-cent of those reports came after 2020.

Yet since 2016, indictments have been raised by prosecutors in only four cases based on whistleblower reports. Two of those resulted in convictions, though the ASK said it did not know whether those verdicts were final.

The rise in reports is evident in the ASK data, which 110 were submitted in 2019 compared to 142 in 2021, 188 in 2022 and 190 in 2023.

World.title: Bosnian Election Sees Record Low Turnout, Dodik Triumphant, Presidency Reshaped
World.content:
Republika Srpska Prime Minister Savo Minic (L) and Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) President, Milorad Dodik (R) celebrate after the announcement of the early results in Banja Luka, 04 October 2026. Photo: EPA/NIDAL SALJIC.

With more than 90 per cent of votes counted in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s general elections, preliminary results on Monday morning indicated a new composition for the country’s three-member presidency – amid a turnout that plummeted 9.5 per cent compared to the previous nationwide elections in 2022.

The presidency looks set to comprise Denis Becirovic of the United for Bosnia and Herzegovina coalition as the Bosniak member, Darijana Filipovic of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, HDZ BiH as the Croat member, and Zeljka Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD as the Serb member.

Becirovic won a second term as the Bosniak member of the presidency with 38.12 per cent, ahead of Party of Democratic Action, SDA leader Bakir Izetbegovic on 33.98 per cent and Semir Efendic of the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina on 25.75 per cent.

HDZ BiH candidate Filipovic won the race for the Croat seat with 46.55 per cent, ahead of Democratic Front candidate Slaven Kovacevic on 30.57 per cent and independent candidate Zdenko Lucic on 22.88 per cent.

The SNSD’s Cvijanovic won the Serb seat with 55.37 per cent, securing a second term. Serb Democratic Party, SDS candidate Marinko Bozovic received 26.54 per cent, while Nebojsa Vukanovic won 18.08 per cent.

Turnout nationwide was just 42 per cent. The Central Election Commission has stressed that the results remain preliminary as counting continues.

Voters on Sunday cast ballots for the members of the state presidency, the state parliament, the president of Republika Srpska, entity parliaments and cantonal assemblies in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The results secure the continued political influence of Bosnian Serb nationalist leader Milorad Dodik, the head of the SNSD, even though he has been barred from standing for public office due to a conviction.

“I declare victory at all levels. Thank you to everyone,” Dodik said after the vote.

In the Republika Srpska entity, the SNSD was leading the race for the entity’s National Assembly with 38.93 per cent of the vote, based on almost 87 per cent of counted ballots. The SNSD’s Savo Minic, Dodik’s close all who is currently the entity’s prime minister, also looks set to position of the president of Republika Srpska.

Dodik attributed part of the party’s success to what he described as a changed political environment in the United States. Amid intensive lobbying by the Bosnian Serbs, US sanctions against Dodik and SNSD allies imposed for corruption and secessionist activities have been dropped by the Trump administration.

“If there had not been Trump’s magnificent victory, we would probably be politically dead today, but thanks to the new environment, we are now political winners,” Dodik said. He also thanked Vladimir Putin, who had declared his support.

The SDA was leading the race for the House of Representatives of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to results from 93.48 per cent of polling stations. The SDA was on 30.58 per cent, the Social Democratic Party, SDP second on 15.39 per cent, with the coalition led by the HDZ BiH third with 13.61 per cent.

SDP leader Nermin Niksic said the party was satisfied with its performance, highlighting Becirovic’s win in the presidency race and Ivan Begic’s expected victory as vice-president of Republika Srpska, coming second behind Minic.

“It is not usual for governments to perform well in elections, but the SDP has received confirmation that it has a better electoral result, more votes and two individual positions – the candidate for the presidency and, as things stand now, the vice-president of Republika Srpska,” Niksic said.

He said the SDP expects to gain two or three additional seats in the Federation parliament compared with the 2022 elections. He also expects the party to retain its five seats in the state-level House of Representatives.

The CEC is expected to continue publishing updated preliminary results as ballots are processed.

Besides expected smaller issues with new election technologies, including biometric voter identification and ballot scanners, which were introduced for these polls, the voting process went off without major issues.

According to BIRN’s contacts at the Central Election Commission, over 80 per cent of the polling stations in the country filed election results in the first 15 minutes after polls closed.

World.title: Hungary’s New Government Haunted by Orban’s House of Terror
World.content:
Controversial from the off

The exhibition, although an indisputable commercial success attracting 200,000 to 300,000 people from Hungary and abroad each year, has been controversial from the very outset.

Orban opened the museum during the campaign for the 2002 election, which his Fidesz party ultimately lost, and it was designed to paint his socialist-liberal rivals as the heirs-apparent of the communists. The fathers of two prominent liberal politicians even featured on the museum’s Wall of Perpetrators as members of the brutal communist secret police.

Critics accuse the museum of offering a biased and one-sided version of Hungary’s past. The very beginning of the exhibition sets the tone: from 1944 to 1990, it says, Hungary was oppressed by two dictatorships, Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union – even though the country in 1940 formally joined the Tripartite Pact, becoming an ally of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. “This is an attempt to absolve Hungarians from all their historical responsibilities,” Peter Csunderlik, a historian, tells BIRN.

Csunderlik also says the concept of drawing clear parallels between communism and fascism as two totalitarian regimes is outdated.

Perhaps the biggest weakness of the exhibition, however, is its staggering imbalance: while it seeks to put Nazism and communism on an equal footing, it dedicates only one room to the victims of fascism in Hungary, while the rest of the exhibition deals with the atrocities committed under the communist regime.

“It portrays the Arrow Cross Party as if it had no antecedents in Hungary’s history, as if they had been a byproduct of German occupation,” Csunderlik says, referring to Hungary’s main fascist and Nazi party founded in the 1930s.

The exhibition also fails to mention that Hungary was one of the first countries to pass anti-Jewish laws already in the 1920s.

Despite establishing a parallel between fascism and communism, the museum has no room dedicated to the Holocaust, which claimed the lives of 600,000 Hungarian Jews. Instead, it focuses on the fate of the 700,000 Hungarians deported to Soviet labour camps. It also blurs the distinction between the early 1950s and the late 1980s, suggesting that Hungary lived under the same brutal communist regime for several decades.

“It tries to divide the society into victims and perpetrators, but history is more complicated,” Csunderlik explains.

In Hungary’s case, you could be both. Among the victims mourned in the House of Terror, there are several who were implicated in violent crimes previously. And among the perpetrators, there are many who had earlier been persecuted and tortured, perhaps by their own party comrades (for example, Imre Nagy, Hungary’s martyred prime minister executed after the 1956 uprising, was actually a Communist Party leader). But those complexities are left without explanation.

World.title: Norwegian Charged in Greece Rues Trial’s ‘Chilling’ Effect on Migrants’ Rights Defenders
World.content:
It was just before dusk, and Tommy Olsen, from Norway, was waiting to collect his rental car at the airport on Lesvos in September 2015 when he saw a boat that had capsized just off the shore.

He and a German tourist waded into the water to help the passengers, some of them children, reach land.

“That was my baptism,” said Olsen, who had flown to the Greek island to help with the humanitarian crisis unfolding on its shores. According to the United Nations refugee agency, UNHRC, more than 850,000 refugees and migrants arrived by boat to Greece that year.

“It was an intense moment… the first of many, unfortunately,” he said.

World.title: Biljana Plavsic, Bosnian Serb War Criminal Who Withdrew Her Remorse
World.content:
The Serb political elites do not recognise the legitimacy of the ICTY and believe, as Plavsic did, that the court was set up “to prosecute Serbs”. Lack of recognition of the court as a legitimate, bipartisan institution has led to many high-ranking war criminals returning to Serbia and being welcomed as heroes, and/or buried with the highest state honours.

Plavsic never changed her convictions. In her now infamous statement of guilt at the ICTY, she apologised for the persecution of “thousands of non-Serbs” during her sentencing hearing in 2002. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organised, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said.

“Although I was repeatedly informed of allegations of cruel and inhuman conduct against non-Serbs, I refused to accept them or even to investigate. The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she added.

But, two years later, in an interview from her prison cell in Sweden, Plavsic withdrew her expression of remorse, saying she had done “nothing wrong”. Her denial of any responsibility for the crimes she was convicted of was met with outrage on behalf of victims’ organisations and the international community.

Although Plavsic may be buried with honours in Republika Srpska, she remains a controversial figure among some Serbs because she was the only high-ranking Serb leader who expressed remorse. Some have not forgiven her for this move.

“She should have never apologised and admitted that Serbs committed crimes,” I was told by some of Plavsic’s close acquaintances during my research. I think the backlash Plavsic received from Serbs after her infamous statement of guilt made her adamant in denying it and ultimately withdrawing her remorse. My impression was that she had a strong urge to go down in history as unrepentant.

To regain the image she had lost because of her unpopular expression of remorse, she repeatedly insisted that she did not regret anything she was accused of. On the contrary, she told me on many occasions, “I would do the same again. I had to protect my people. If I contributed anything in establishing Republika Srpska, our Serb state, and I know I did, there is nothing to regret.”

But although she has been called one of the “founders of Republika Srpska”, Plavsic is no longer a household name for the post-war generations of Serbs like her compatriots Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic – who never apologised for their crimes.

Olivera Simic is a professor at Griffith Law School, Griffith University, Australia. She is the author of the book ‘Madam War Criminal: Biljana Plavsic, Serbia’s Iron Lady’, published by Hurst, 2025.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Croatia Ranks 3rd in EU for Renewable Energy
World.content:
October the 5th, 2026 – Croatia has ranked an impressive 3rd in the EU for its renewable energy, with solar energy being the most important source in 2026’s second quarter.

Renewable energy sources produced more than half of the electricity in the European Union in the second quarter of 2026. Marin Penavic reports for Poslovni that according to Eurostat data, their share in total production reached 54.1 percent, which is still slightly less than in the same period last year, when it stood at 54.3 percent.

Differences among EU Member States are very pronounced, at the top is Latvia, where as much as 97.7 percent of the electricity produced came from renewable sources. Denmark follows with a share of 94.3 percent, while Croatia ranks third with 92.2 percent. In Latvia the largest contribution comes from hydro power and solar, in Denmark wind energy dominates, while Croatia’s result relies primarily on hydro power plants.

Infographic shows the ten European Union Member States with the highest share of electricity produced from renewable sources in total electricity produced. At the top are Latvia with 97.7 percent of electricity, Denmark with 94.3 percent and Croatia with 92.2 percent. At the bottom of the list is Germany with 63.8 percent.

Among the countries with the highest shares of renewable electricity are also Austria, Estonia, Portugal and Lithuania, which means that countries with large hydro power potential, but also those that have strongly developed wind farms and solar energy, particularly stand out at the top of the European ranking. At the level of the entire EU, solar energy was the most important renewable source in the second quarter, with 41.6 percent of total renewable production. It was followed by wind with 27.7 percent and hydro power with 22.6 percent, while other renewable sources had a significantly smaller share.

At the same time, the data show that the transition towards renewable sources is not equally fast in all parts of the Union. While in Latvia their share almost reached 100 percent, at the bottom are Slovakia with 19.8 percent, Czechia with 20.9 percent and Malta with 24.5 percent. Eurostat notes that this indicator refers to the share of renewable sources in net electricity production and should not be equated with the share of renewable energy in gross final consumption, which is calculated according to a different methodology.
