That progression provides the context for the 403-seat announcement. Chirag Paswan now has five Lok Sabha MPs, 19 MLAs in Bihar and a Union cabinet position.

The question is whether that political weight can be extended beyond Bihar.

The 403-seat gamble

The latest phase of the UP push took shape in September, when Paswan launched his party's youth outreach in Prayagraj. At the "Youth Bole Toh" programme, he spoke about education, employment, skills and greater youth participation in politics, and announced plans for a National Youth Commission.

On September 28, he made the electoral plan explicit: "There is no doubt that LJP (Ram Vilas) will contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."

The following day, he said the response in Prayagraj had strengthened his confidence in the UP plan. LJP(RV) MP Rajesh Verma subsequently said the party was preparing for all 403 seats, while making clear that the eventual alliance arrangement would be decided later.

Chirag Paswan on law and order in Bihar.

The 2020 flashback

The 2020 Bihar assembly election was the debut test of Chirag Paswan's leadership. His father,

, had just died a few days ago.

The LJP won only one seat but emerged as a significant factor in 54 constituencies where its vote total was greater than the victory margin.

In 25 seats where JD(U) finished second, LJP's vote exceeded the winning margin. Chirag was explicit about the objective, saying after the election: "My main idea in the election was to make the BJP stronger. I am happy with the impact I have had in this election."

The BJP finished with 74 seats in that election, ahead of JD(U)'s 43 for the first time. The episode demonstrated that LJP did not need to win seats itself to affect the relative strength of its larger alliance partner.

The 2025 Bihar election showed the other side of the equation. LJP(RV) was no longer operating as a spoiler outside the alliance. It contested 29 seats as an NDA partner and won 19, converting its electoral relevance into representation inside the alliance.

UP could now test both models: LJP(RV) as an alliance partner with an electoral base of its own, and LJP(RV) as a potential vote-splitter in constituencies where even a few thousand votes can decide the outcome.

The Dalit arithmetic

The potential constituency is significant, but far from straightforward.

The BSP won no seats in the 2024 Lok Sabha election in UP and polled around 9.4%. At the same time, the SP expanded its support among Dalit voters as part of its broader PDA coalition. A Lokniti-CSDS post-poll analysis showed a sharp difference between Jatav and non-Jatav Dalit voting patterns, with the BSP retaining much stronger support among Jatavs than among non-Jatav Dalits.

For Chirag Paswan, the challenge is therefore larger than taking the Paswan identity from Bihar to UP. Pasis, Valmikis, Khatiks and other non-Jatav communities have distinct political histories and local calculations. Whether LJP(RV) can persuade sections of these voters that it is a credible political vehicle will determine whether its UP expansion produces votes or merely an organisational footprint.

The impact could also vary by constituency. A modest LJP(RV) vote could matter in a close BJP-SP contest if it draws disproportionately from one side's potential support base.

But unlike Bihar in 2020, there is no single obvious target. The BJP, SP, BSP and Congress have overlapping social coalitions, making the direction of any vote transfer harder to predict.

Why UP and why now?

The UP expansion also fits Paswan's attempt to establish LJP(RV) beyond its Bihar base. The party has already demonstrated that it can operate outside the state: in the 2023 Nagaland assembly election, it contested 16 seats, won two and finished runner-up in eight, securing more than 8.6% of the vote.

But UP is on a different scale. A credible organisation here would give Chiag Paswan a political presence in the country's largest state and potentially strengthen his position in future NDA negotiations.

Chirag Paswan asked CEC to address recent SIR controversy.

His recent conduct suggests that maintaining an independent identity is part of that calculation. He has criticised the Bihar government's handling of law and order while remaining part of the NDA, and questioned the Election Commission over concerns surrounding SIR before welcoming its subsequent clarification.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The UP experiment, therefore, would not simply be about how many seats LJP(RV) could win. It would be abot whether Chirag Paswan can build an influence outside Bihar to make his party a more consequential NDA partner, while retaining the political independence he summed up in his own words: "I am in the alliance but I am not the BJP."

World.title: Amma Unavagam workers stage protest demanding regularisation of job in Virudhunagar
World.content:
Workers of Amma Unavagam, affiliated to the CITU, staged a protest here on Monday, demanding regularisation of their jobs.

Inaugurating the protest, CITU district general secretary (Rural Development Local Administration Department Employees) Balasubramanian said that Amma Unavagam was started in Tamil Nadu in March 2013.

After having worked for 12 to 13 years in the same job, the workers were being paid meagre daily wages of ₹250 to ₹340. “The wages differ from one Amma Unavagam to another. Though the daily wage fixed by the Virudhunagar District Collector is ₹578 with effect from April 2026, they have not been paid as per the order. However, even six months after it came into effect, the workers were not given the revised salary,” he said.

Stating that the TVK had promised to regularise the jobs of temporary and contract workers who had completed five years, the CITU demanded that the Government fulfil its election promise.

State general secretary R. Balasubramanian addressed the gathering.

World.title: SIR: NDA defends bulk Form-7 filings, accuses Congress of ‘unlawful’ interference
World.content:
Days after at least four FIRs were registered against BJP workers for seeking deletion of names, mostly of Muslim voters, through Form-7, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) accused the Congress-led State government of “unlawfully” interfering in and influencing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and using the police machinery to intimidate people filing Form-7 objections.

The alliance met Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) V. Anbu Kumar and submitted a complaint against the State government on Monday (October 5).

BJP and JD(S) leaders, including Union Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy, Union Minister Shobha Karandlaje and Leader of Opposition in the Karnataka Legislative Assembly R. Ashok, said that members of the ruling Congress and Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) workers were “extensively and unduly influencing and interfering” in the process.

Defending the filing of Form-7 objections, including in bulk, as a legitimate statutory right, the NDA cited the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, under which an objection to the inclusion of a name in the electoral roll has to be filed in Form-7 by a person whose name is already included in the roll “for corrections”. The NDA said Form-7 objections were subject to scrutiny, with the ERO required to issue notices and conduct an inquiry before taking a decision.

The party members also pointed to the appellate mechanism, saying that a person dissatisfied with the ERO/AERO’s decision can appeal, with a further appeal before the CEO.

Citing these provisions, the NDA alleged that the State government was using the police to target people filing Form-7 objections, particularly BJP workers and those sympathetic to the party. It alleged that, instead of restricting action to Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which deals with false statements and declarations, the police were registering cases invoking offences such as cheating, forgery, intimidation and breach of peace.

Pointing further to the protest held by Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and his cabinet colleagues at the CEO office on October 1, NDA said it amounted to pressure on the CEO’s office, stating that the CEO appeared to have “succumbed” to pressure from the State government.

The parties said the CM’s protest and the CEO’s circular issued on the same day directing EROs to take action against anyone knowingly filing false statements, had created apprehension among people who had filed Form-7 applications, who now feared criminal cases.

World.title: Electric shock from DJ equipment kills engineering student during celebrations at Coimbatore hostel
World.content:
An engineering student was electrocuted after suffering electric shock from DJ equipment during the annual day celebrations at his college hostel near Coimbatore on October 3.

The police said A. Amilthan, a resident of Kambainallur and a final year BE EEE student at a private college at Vattamalaipalayam, died during the celebrations on the night of October 3. Another student Saran, who tried to rescue Amilthan, also suffered electric shock.

Amilthan’s father complained to the police that the persons who arranged for the DJ equipment, the hostel warden, and the college management failed to ensure safety and acted negligently, resulting in his son’s death.

The Thudiyalur police booked DJ organisers, identified as C. Ranjith (32) and Kanishkaran Kumar (23) of Vellakinar near Coimbatore and M. Jayasurya (27) of Ambasamudram.

Further investigation is on.

World.title: Congress nominee Limbikai files nomination after procession, student leader Kanthakumar too in fray
World.content:
On the penultimate day of filing nomination papers for the election to the Karnataka West Graduates’ Constituency of the Karnataka Legislative Council, five candidates, including Congress nominee Mohan Limbikai and students’ leader Kanthakumar, filed their nomination papers on Monday. With one more day to go before the deadline ends, there are now eight candidates who have entered the fray.

Those who filed their nominations on Monday were Congress candidate Mohan Limbikai, independents Basavaraj Kotagi and Jishan Shirsangi, Karnataka Rashtra Samithi candidate Nishanth Bankapur, and All-Karnataka Students’ Association president Kanthakumar, who is contesting as an independent candidate.

Returning Officer and Belagavi Regional Commissioner K.M. Janaki said that eight candidates had filed 14 sets of nomination papers.

While the independent candidates arrived at the office of the Returning Officer at the Dharwad Deputy Commissioner’s office with their proposers, Mr. Limbikai took out a procession from Kadapa Maidan in an open vehicle before filing his nomination.

He was accompanied by Cooperation Minister Laxman Savadi, Labour Minister Santosh Lad, former Minister H.K. Patil, legislators N.H. Konaraddi, Srinivas Mane, Prakash Koliwad, U.B. Banakar, F.H. Jakkappanavar, former MLA D.R. Patil and others.

Speaking to presspersons after filing his nomination papers, Mr. Limbikai said he would effectively represent the interests of graduates in the Legislative Council. He said the State government’s decision to fill vacant posts in various departments would benefit graduates and claimed that government employees, who constitute a sizeable section of voters in the four districts, would support the government.

S.V. Sankanur, the BJP nominee and two-time MLC, is set to file his nomination papers on the last day to file nomination papers, Tuesday (October 6).

The constituency has 88,087 voters, including 51,599 men and 36,488 women. 2,540 voters have further been added during the continuous revision of the electoral roll, bringing the total number of voters to 90,627.

The last date for filing nominations is Tuesday, October 6. Scrutiny will be held on October 7, while candidates can withdraw their nominations until October 9. Polling will be held on October 23, and counting will be held on October 27 at the University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad. The election process will conclude on October 31.

A total of 128 polling stations have been set up across the constituency, including 54 in Dharwad district, 23 in Gadag, 28 in Haveri and 23 in the Uttara Kannada district. The voting will be through ballot papers, and there will be no NOTA option.

World.title: Fire breaks out in Mumbai’s Film City
World.content:
A fire broke out at a temporary production unit at Goregaon Film City in Mumbai on Monday (October 5, 2026), sending a large plume of smoke into the air. No injuries have been reported.

According to the Mumbai Fire Brigade, a Level-I fire was reported at 4:02 p.m. behind Reliance Media Works and Prime Focus in Film City, Goregaon (East). The blaze was confined to a 100 ft × 20 ft Production Control Room (PCR) unit set up at a temporary location behind Prime Focus Studio.

#Watch | A fire broke out at a temporary production unit at Goregaon Film City in Mumbai on Monday (October 5, 2026), sending a large plume of smoke into the air. No injuries have been reported. Video: Special arrangement https://t.co/6nPUjqqHpF https://t.co/oqksqQZjZ9 — The Hindu (@the_hindu) October 5, 2026

The fire affected electrical wiring, cables, installations, wooden planks, AC units, bamboo, plastic, sound systems and shooting equipment inside the unit. The Mumbai Fire Brigade, local police, BMC Ward Control and a 108 Ambulance team were mobilised, and the blaze was brought under control by 4:55 p.m. More details are awaited.

World.title: Plea to preserve, protect Onankaradu
World.content:
The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Monday ordered notice to the State government on the public interest litigation petition that sought a direction to preserve and protect Onankaradu/Perumal Malai in Peraiyur in Madurai district and restrain stone quarry operations.

A Division Bench of Justices P. Velmurugan and K.K. Ramakrishnan was hearing the petition filed by Nammalvar Eyarkkai Pathukapu Sangam represented by its president G. Pethanan of Peraiyur in Madurai district.

The petitioner said the hill has considerable ecological and biodiversity significance. During field study and documentation undertaken by persons associated with the association, 47 different species of birds were observed and documented.

He said the importance of the hill was not confined to its ecological and hydrological significance. Various features of potential historical and archaeological significance had been noticed.

Among the materials reported and documented were ancient stone remains, structural remains, carved stones/sculptures, inscription-like markings, an ancient smelting furnace, burial urns/Muthumakkal Thazhis pottery, nadukal and other artefacts, he said.

Water resources connected with the hill were utilised by the local people for drinking and agricultural purposes. The surrounding agricultural lands depended substantially on the availability of groundwater and surface water replenished through the natural catchment of the hill, he said.

The petitioner said the hill was a common natural resource serving multiple villages. Its protection was a matter of public importance. He sought a direction to authorities to preserve and protect Onankaradu/Perumal Malai and restrain stone quarry operations. The court adjourned the hearing in the case by four weeks.

World.title: Dharapuram bypoll: industries in Tiruppur told to provide paid holiday on October 6
World.content:
Industries, construction companies and public sector establishments in Tiruppur district have been instructed to provide a paid holiday to workers eligible to vote in the Dharapuram (Reserved) Assembly constituency byelection to be held on October 6 (Tuesday).

The directive applies to daily-wage, temporary and contract workers employed in the district who are registered voters in the 101-Dharapuram (Reserved) Constituency. The establishments have been asked to enable such workers to travel to their respective constituencies and exercise their franchise.

The paid holiday is mandatory under Section 25 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, read with a June 8, 1957 notification of the Union Ministry of Home Affairs. Establishments failing to grant the holiday will face appropriate action, the Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health said.

A district-level control room has been set up by the Tiruppur office of the Directorate to receive complaints from eligible workers who are denied paid leave.

Workers can contact C. Karthikeyan (9865072749), G. Vadivel (9629702695) or S. Muruganandam (9715274119) to lodge complaints, said N. Sabina, Joint Director-II, Industrial Safety and Health, Tiruppur.

World.title: Tusker Pallattu Brahmadathan, who died in a lightning strike, cremated in Keralam
World.content:
The premises of the Pallattu house at Melambara near Pala witnessed a large gathering on Monday as people from different parts of the State arrived to pay their last respects to Pallattu Brahmadathan, a 54-year-old tusker who died after being struck by lightning on Sunday evening.

People had poured in to the house here since Sunday to catch a final glimpse of the elephant, which had been a familiar presence at temple festivals across Keralam for nearly three decades. After the Forest department completed the post-mortem examination by noon, the animal was cremated on a plot near the house.

The tusker, brought to Keralam around 1999, had been initially owned by Pothen Varghese of Puthuppally and was known as Puthuppally Brahmadathan. He was later bought by Rajesh Pallattu, State president of the Kerala Festival Coordination Committee, and came to be known as Pallattu Brahmadathan.

The elephant had been under observation for musth and was resting at a shed on the premises of the house when lightning struck on Sunday evening. The tusker was slated to be released from the shed within a week after the musth period ended. The post-mortem report is expected to establish the exact cause of death.

Official sources said a similar incident was reported in Pala 12 years ago, when a tusker named Thiruvappallil Krishnan Kutty died at Kadapattur near Pala after being struck by lightning.

World.title: After breakdown of talks with govt, PTI says reconciliation not possible without including Imran
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: PTI leaders on Monday declared that reconciliation between their party and the government was not possible without including incarcerated party founder Imran Khan in the dialogue process.

Narrating the opposition’s stance on why the talks with the government failed over the weekend, PTI’s secretary general, Salman Akram Raja, presented his party’s demand that Imran be included in any future political dialogue.

“Only [Imran] has the capability to bridge the gulf that has developed between the state and the nation,” Raja said during the press conference held at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad.

“Imran Khan is very important for us and we had every right to seek his opinion, but it was not allowed,” Raja said.

The PTI leader said that another reason for the failure of the talks was that the government was not willing to pursue a collective strategy against terrorism. Raja told the media that the PTI had entered into the negotiations with sincerity and was serious about addressing the issues.

“Even on the second day, we were hoping that another round of talks would streamline things,” he said.

Describing the reasons for talks failing, Raja said: “We were being pushed to support the government over every action being taken regarding terrorism in KP.”

He added that the PTI had demanded that the government respect the recommendations and opinions of a jirga held by the KP Assembly, in which political parties and stakeholders had participated.

The jirga had recommended solutions to the problem, the opposition delegation had told the government, according to Raja.

The delegation had also asked the government to consider the opinions of tribal leaders, Raja said.

He said the PTI had suggested the agreement should mention that a collective decision would be made regarding terrorism, but the government had said it would not put it down on paper.

“We were told that a unanimous strategy against terrorism would not be developed and it would not be included in the agreement,” he said. Raja said that the government had deliberately complicated the situation.

“It is a fact that the current issues can only be addressed by Imran Khan.

“We had demanded that Imran Khan and his opinion should be included in all issues, which is why we demanded a meeting of party leaders with him,” Raja said.

The two rounds of talks between the government and the opposition held on Friday and Saturday did not yield positive results, with counterterrorism policies and access to Imran emerging as two major sticking points.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who was part of the process, on Sunday singled out KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi for the failure of talks, saying that he changed the agreement.

Separately, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the PTI representatives came for talks but were unwilling to abandon their “double standards and hypocrisy”.

For its part, the PTI said it wanted immediate access to party founder Imran for consultations, and even agreed to forgo other demands for this. However, the government declined to make access to Imran part of the proposed agreement, the opposition party claimed.

Addressing the failed talks, Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam said on Monday that the government’s delegation had suggested that both sides “be on the same page” about terrorism.

Following the failed talks, the PTI went ahead with its protest march on Sunday despite warnings from the federal government.

KP Assembly speaker to summon security committee meeting

Against this backdrop, KP Assembly Speaker Babar Swati said he was going to summon another meeting of a special committee on security, which was constituted after a peace jirga in the assembly in November last year.

“I am again summoning a meeting of the special committee. I wish for the relevant authorities and institutions to sit together on this important matter,” he posted on X.

He emphasised that it was important to consider this process initiated by the KP Assembly before the Centre held the former responsible for the law and order situation in the province.

Swati recalled that political parties had issued a joint statement after the Nov peace jirga, in light of which the assembly had constituted a special committee on security. The committee, he said, was briefed by the provincial police chief, the Counterterrorism Department, the KP home additional chief secretary, the Home Department, the KP chief secretary and other relevant provincial institutions.

“We also informed the leadership in the Centre about this process and sent letters to the prime minister, the Senate chairman, the National Assembly speaker and the interior minister, informing them that the assembly was moving towards [formulating] comprehensive parliamentary recommendations,” he said.

Swati said just one important official, the Peshawar corps commander, was left to brief the committee.

“I had spoken to the Peshawar corps commander and he had assured me of his participation. However, the meeting has yet to take place,” he added.

“I am again summoning a meeting of the special committee. I wish for the relevant authorities and institutions to sit together on this important matter.

“Whatever we have heard, seen, and whatever facts have come before the committee — they will present their stance; the relevant institutions will present theirs,” Swati said.

Following that, he continued, the committee would formulate its recommendations, which would be presented before the assembly.

“After the assembly’s approval, the recommendations will be forwarded to the provincial and federal governments so that responsibility, policy and practical measures are clearly [stated].”

The speaker said the people of KP wanted peace and called for the relevant parties to play their respective roles in moving towards a collective solution.

“We have to find a way while collectively implementing the National Action Plan, clarifying the responsibilities of relevant institutions,” he added.

World.title: At Moscow moot, Pakistan says terrorism remains core of Afghanistan's problems
World.content:
Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan Mohammad Sadiq on Monday said that terrorism remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems, reaffirming that Pakistan would continue to take “all appropriate measures” for ensuring the safety of its citizens, in accordance with international law.

Sadiq made these remarks at the eighth meeting of Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan in the Russian capital.

The moot brought together Afghanistan and other countries of the region to discuss the situation in Afghanistan and issues of regional concern, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement.

Separately, Sadiq posted a transcript of his address at the meeting, according to which he told the moot that the roots of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan were in a “nexus between the Taliban regime and terrorist groups […] that operate with impunity on Afghan soil”.

“The situation is worsened by external actors and spoilers who support proxies inside Afghanistan to target Pakistan and other countries in the region,” he added.

Sadiq highlighted that five years into the Taliban rule in Afghanistan, “Pakistan faces the most serious security threat.”

Over the last three years alone, he said, more than 4,700 Pakistanis had been killed due to terrorism emanating from Afghanistan.

“No country would tolerate such a situation,” he remarked. “Thousands of innocent Pakistani civilians and security personnel have been martyred in the last few years. A result of terrorist attacks planned, financed, supported and carried out from Afghan soil. The Taliban regime is complicit in this. No responsible state can remain passive when its security is repeatedly undermined. and its people are viciously targeted.”

The special representative said Pakistan’s counterterrorism operations were conducted in response to the terrorist attacks being perpetrated from Afghan soil.

“These operations are precise, intelligence-based and defensive in nature. Pakistan’s actions are in exercise of its right to self-defence, to ensure the safety and security of its citizens. These actions are directed solely against the terrorist outfits based in Afghanistan that pose a threat to the region and beyond.”

Sadiq continued that Pakistan had been, and would continue to take “all appropriate measures to uphold the safety and security of its citizens in accordance accordance with with international law, and based on the principles of necessity and as a measure of last resort”.

“All measures taken by Pakistan constitute legitimate defensive actions against sanctuaries and bases used for planning, training and launching terrorist attacks inside Pakistan.

“The scale and scope of our actions represent restraint, particularly in light of the severity of the challenge we face.”

Sadiq said Islamabad desired peace in the region and had “remained patiently engaged” in political and diplomatic efforts aimed at addressing terrorism emanating from Afghan soil.

“It is unfortunate that Pakistan’s numerous goodwill gestures and highly responsible approach were misconstrued, resulting in increased terrorist attacks from Afghan soil, with the active support and backing of the Taliban regime.

“Pakistan reiterates its strong resolve and determination to uproot the menace of terrorism emanating from across the border. We call upon the Afghan authorities to end the impunity with which terrorist groups continue to operate from their soil,” he said.

Sadiq also expressed hope that “countries in the region will work together to address the sources of instability in our immediate neighbourhood, with a view to achieving our collective objectives of regional peace, stability and prosperity”.

“We expected the Taliban regime would take concrete and verifiable actions against those terrorist groups. Regrettably, they failed to act in complete disregard for the legitimate security concerns of Pakistan and other countries. We hope that the Taliban will honour their commitments made to the international community,” he said.

Sadiq said Pakistan and Afghanistan were immediate neighbours having historical relations and fraternal bonds.

“Peace and stability in Afghanistan is in the national interest of Pakistan.”

Earlier in his address, Sadiq noted that the meeting was taking place at a “time of immense turmoil”.

“The regional and global environment is fraught with challenges. Proliferating crises across the world, the ongoing conflict in West Asia, and disruptions in global energy markets have put unprecedented strain on our region and beyond.

“At the same time, regional countries remain highly vulnerable to destabilising threats caused by terrorism, drug smuggling, illegal migration, and human trafficking,” he said.

He noted that it had been five years since the transition in Afghanistan, with the Afghan Taliban taking the reins in Kabul in August 2021.

This represented a “critical milestone” to assess the situation on the ground, he said.

In the period after August 2021, Pakistan joined the regional countries in the efforts to help stabilise the situation in Afghanistan and address the humanitarian needs of people of Afghanistan, the special representative continued.

“As a close neighbour, Pakistan engaged at the highest level, facilitated humanitarian relief efforts, and provided visas to vulnerable Afghans. Pakistan also extended trade and transit incentives to support Afghan economy, participated in regional initiatives and connectivity projects, and remained at the forefront of the efforts to facilitate Afghanistan’s integration into the international community.”

These endeavours, he said, were driven by “our shared commitment to a peaceful, stable and prosperous Afghanistan”.

“Our regional engagement had been central to assisting the Afghan authorities as they worked towards rebuilding their country.”

However, he said, despite these efforts, Afghanistan stood at a critical juncture.

“The country faces a deteriorating humanitarian crisis, and is grappling with multiple challenges driven by severe food insecurity, extreme climate shocks, water scarcity, and recurrent natural disasters and [a] permissive environment allowing terrorism to grow.”

While it remained essential to call for sustained support, it was equally imperative to assess the progress towards resolving the legitimate concerns of regional states and the wider international community, Sadiq emphasised.

“Nowhere is the lack of progress more evident than on the issue of counterterrorism, ensuring women’s rights and girls’ education, and promoting inclusivity. Continuing restrictions on women and girls, absence of any meaningful efforts to ensure broad-based governance, and the lack of progress on counterterrorism commitments not only impede Afghanistan’s long-term development and stability, they also threaten regional security and undermine our collective efforts towards regional peace and prosperity,” he said.

Sadiq said the situation required careful reflection.

“There is a need to ask whether the Taliban regime’s policies have advanced the collective objective of helping ordinary Afghans, and whether these policies have helped Afghanistan in responding to the legitimate concerns of the immediate neighbours,” he said.

According to the FO statement, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov also attended the session and addressed the participating delegations.

The consultations at the meeting focused on regional peace and security, counterterrorism, economic cooperation and connectivity, as well as continued engagement with Afghanistan, the FO said.

It added that apart from Sadiq, the delegation from Islamabad included Ambassador to Russia Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, Ambassador to Afghanistan Ubaidur Rehman Nizamani and other senior officials.

The Moscow Format is a Russia-led regional consultation mechanism that was initiated in December 2016.

Cross-border terrorism and fraught Pak-Afghan ties

As its eighth meeting takes place, Islamabad continues to urge the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say these repeated appeals have gone unheeded.

According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group.

The report also points to growing operational and facilitation linkages among TTP, Al Qaeda, ISKP and BLA.

Ties between the two neighbours have been strained in the past few years amid Islamabad’s concern over cross-border terrorism.

On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts.

September witnessed another bout of conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

On Sept 21, in response to recent major terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts, with the government saying more than 28 terrorists were killed.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the action as part of Operation Ghazab lil Haq, which was launched on the night of Feb 26 in response to unprovoked cross-border firing by the Afghan Taliban.

Days later, Pakistan shot down eight drones launched from across the border that had entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan.

In retaliation to the drone incursion, Pakistan conducted “precision aerial and drone strikes” in 10 locations across Afghanistan.

The Foreign Office (FO) said a demarche was also delivered to the Afghan side on account of an airspace violation by drones on Sept 23. The demarche was delivered on Sept 26, the FO spokesperson said in a statement.

On Sept 25, the information ministry had also dismissed claims by the Afghan defence ministry of a Pakistani post having been destroyed near the Spin Boldak border — the frontier between Balochistan and Kandahar.

World.title: PTI long march: After Karak address, KP CM's convoy departs for Kohat
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Monday resumed PTI’s march as he addressed supporters in Karak, from where his convoy will depart for Kohat.

The opposition has gone ahead with its march despite warnings from the Centre, which has vowed to prevent any gatherings in Islamabad. The protest aims to demand the release of jailed party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan.

PTI decided to embark on the march after weekend talks with the federal government to bridge their differences failed for multiple reasons, particularly over the counterterrorism policy.

As per an update by PTI after 6pm on Monday, the Afridi-led march was advancing from Karak towards Kohat.

Addressing party supporters at Karak’s Jail Chowk in the afternoon, the chief minister again railed against the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and criticised past military operations and drone attacks.

Afridi also referred to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s remarks from a day earlier, wherein the latter called him “immature”.

He went on to recall Punjab CM Maryam Nawaz’s remarks on the terrorism threat to her province, adding: “Suppose, I say that [my province] does not have a threat from India, but from the other three provinces, will you consider me mature?”

The KP CM said, “If you deem it immature to speak about one’s province and people, then I have shown this immaturity yesterday, still do and will keep doing so.”

Afridi contended that “wrong policies drafted behind closed doors were impacting all institutions”.

Expressing his patriotism for Pakistan, the PTI leader said, “We also chant Pakistan zindabad, we stand up for the national anthem as well.”

But he added that future generations might not do so as there were attempts to “divide Pakistan and spread hatred”.

Insisting that his party was democratically presenting the public’s demands, Afridi warned that if the situation crossed all limits, neither would he be able to control the public “nor will anyone’s father have the courage” to do so.

He asserted that only those policies would be implemented that the people and the youth desire, and which were in the interests of the nation.

“We will not accept any decision taken behind closed doors that is against us, our province or Pakistan,” the KP CM added.

He argued that Imran could secure his release if he wanted but was choosing to remain behind bars for the nation’s “freedom”. “He is free even in jail, and we are slaves even when free,” he quipped.

The chief minister urged people to reach Swabi, adding that no one could even imagine or think of the next plan of action.

Earlier, Afridi’s focal person for digital media Yar Muhammad Khan Niazi shared a video on X of PTI supporters welcoming the KP CM at Karak’s Jail Chowk.

According to a post by CM Afridi, the people of Karak were to join the convoy at 12pm, with the departure set for 12:30pm, which faced a delay.

The convoy plans to stay overnight in Kohat, and then resume the journey towards Peshawar at noon on Oct 6. It will spend the night near Mattani.

On the afternoon of Oct 7, the caravan will depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar and spend the night near Charsadda Interchange.

The protesters will then move forward the next afternoon and spend the night of Oct 8 at Khairabad.

Notably, the KP CM has refrained from detailing the final leg of the trip to the federal capital and said the plan for the next phase would be announced at Khairabad.

This screengrab from Google Maps shows the planned route of the PTI convoy from Lakki Marwat to Khairabad, where it is scheduled to reach on Oct 8.

The march so far

After launching the already-postponed march from Lakki Marwat on Sunday afternoon, the KP CM’s caravan reached Karak at night, where Afridi addressed supporters at Jail Chowk.

Ahead of the march, movement on several roads in KP’s Dera Ismail Khan, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Tank and Hangu was restricted under Section 144 for varying periods.

On Monday, former KP CM Ali Amin Gandapur, who was leading PTI workers from DI Khan to Lakki Marwat, took a U-turn from Yarik because of road blockades and the prevailing law and order situation.

Noting that Section 144 had been imposed in the area for three days, Gandapur stressed that the party leadership had clearly directed workers not to damage public property or engage in any activity that could worsen the situation.

Nevertheless, he contended that the return should not be viewed as a withdrawal from the protest movement, but as a temporary decision.

In Karachi, a planned protest campaign in different areas was disrupted after police deployed personnel at several locations, blocked roads and detained several party workers and leaders.

The PTI claimed that police detained more than 75 of its leaders and workers, including women, from different parts of Karachi. It further alleged that arrests made in other parts of Sindh, including Sukkur, put the total number of detained PTI workers across the province at more than 100.

On Saturday night, an opposition delegation comprising PTI and Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), and a joint team of the government and PPP held hours-long negotiations , which ended in a deadlock.

While the federal government blamed CM Afridi for the failure of negotiations, PTI denied the allegations and claimed that access to Imran, his medical treatment and the federal government’s counterterrorism policy were the key reasons.

According to PTI, the government agreed to restore meetings between Imran and his family members and lawyers from Tuesday, but “declined to make access to Imran Khan part of the proposed agreement”.

World.title: Sahibzada Farhan to lead Pakistan T20I side against Sri Lanka; Shaheen Afridi retains ODI captaincy
World.content:
Sahibzada Farhan will lead Pakistan in the three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, while Shaheen Shah Afridi has retained the ODI captaincy for the subsequent tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) announced on Monday.

The T20Is will be played at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Oct 9, 11 and 13 before Pakistan host England and Sri Lanka in a seven-match ODI tri-series.

The first three matches of the tri-series will be played in Rawalpindi, with the tournament then moving to Lahore for the remaining league matches and the final.

Farhan, who captained Pakistan at the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan, takes over the T20I captaincy from Salman Ali Agha, who has been omitted from the shortest format. Salman, however, remains part of the ODI squad.

The T20I squad also does not include Babar Azam and Shaheen, with the two retained for the ODI assignment.

The 15-member squad includes uncapped all-rounders Razaullah and Mohammad Imran Randhawa. Razaullah recently made an impact on his Test debut against England, scoring 81 off 63 balls with nine sixes and taking four wickets.

Randhawa, who also made his Test debut during the England series, has been included as a medium-pace bowling all-rounder.

Maaz Sadaqat has retained his place after featuring prominently Pakistan’s Asian Games campaign, while Abdul Samad returns to the T20I side after last representing Pakistan in the format in March 2025.

Hasan Nawaz has also been rewarded for his performances at the Asian Games, where he was Pakistan’s leading batter and finished the tournament as its highest run-scorer with 123 runs.

He made 96 off 51 balls, including five fours and seven sixes, in Pakistan’s defeat by India in the final as the team settled for the silver medal.

Fast bowler Naseem Shah returns to the T20I squad after last playing the format for Pakistan against Sri Lanka in February 2026.

Shadab Khan, Fakhar Zaman, Saim Ayub and Abrar Ahmed are among the other established players in the squad.

The 16-member ODI squad, meanwhile, retains a more experienced core under Shaheen, with Babar, Salman, Haris Rauf and Faheem Ashraf included.

Hasan also returns to the ODI setup, and so does Razaullah.

Wicket-keeper-batter Saad Baig, the former Pakistan Under-19 captain who scored more than 1,000 runs in the 2025-26 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, has earned his maiden ODI call-up.

Left-arm wrist-spinner Sufiyan Moqim is the other notable addition, while Mohammad Ghazi Ghori is also included as a wicket-keeper-batter.

The PCB also announced a change to the coaching staff, with former Australia fast bowler Shaun Tait returning as bowling coach in a consultancy capacity.

Tait previously served as Pakistan’s bowling coach during 2022-23 and will replace Ashley Noffke, who stepped down following the Asian Games to take up the head coach’s position with the Netherlands.

World.title: Upper parts of country likely to see rainy, windy conditions from Oct 6-7
World.content:
The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) on Monday predicted heavy rains, strong winds and thunderstorms, with isolated hailstorms, in the upper parts of the country over the next two days.

In a press release, the Met Office said a westerly wave was likely to enter the upper parts of the country tonight and was expected to persist until Oct 7 (Wednesday).

Under the influence of this weather system, the PMD predicted rain, windstorms and thunderstorms, with isolated hailstorms, in various locations in Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Punjab as well as the Islamabad region.

In KP, “rain-windstorm/thunderstorm” were expected to begin from Monday night in Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Shangla, Battagram, Mansehra, Abbottabad, Haripur, Buner, Malakand, Bajaur, Mohmand, Kohat, Peshawar, Charsadda, Nowshera, Mardan, Swabi, Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, Hangu, Lakki Marwat, Karak, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan and Waziristan.

They are predicted to last until Oct 7 (Wednesday), the PMD said.

In Kashmir, rain and hail were expected to fall during the next two days in isolated places, including Neelum Valley, Muzaffarabad, Rawalakot, Poonch, Hattian, Bagh, Haveli, Sudhanoti, Kotli, Bhimber and Mirpur.

In GB, they were likely in Diamer, Astore, Ghizer, Skardu, Hunza, Gilgit, Ghanche and Shigar during the same period.

For Punjab, the PMD forecast “rain-windstorm/thunderstorm” on Oct 6 and Oct 7 at isolated places in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Murree, Galliyat, Attock, Chakwal, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad, Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Narowal, Mianwali, Khushab, Sargodha, Jhang, Toba Tek Singh and Faisalabad.

While “mainly hot and dry weather” was likely to prevail in Sindh and Balochistan, the PMD noted that rain-windstorms and thunderstorms were also expected at isolated places in Balochistan’s Zhob, Barkhan and Musakhel on Tuesday evening and night.

The Met Office warned that windstorms, hail and lightning could damage weak structures such as roofs and walls of kutcha houses, electric poles, billboards, vehicles and solar panels.

It also noted that daytime temperatures were likely to drop by two to four degrees Celsius during the forecast period.

“Farmers are advised to manage their crop activities keeping in view the weather conditions,” the press release stated, also calling on all relevant authorities to remain vigilant and take the necessary measures to avoid untoward situations.

A fresh spell of rain hit the country last month, particularly affecting Rawalpindi as inundated roads and knee-deep water at certain points exposed the city’s poor drainage system.

Islamabad and Rawalpindi received another burst of heavy rain at the end of September, with civic departments in the garrison city placed on high alert.

Earlier that month, KP also witnessed rain as heavy downpours lashed Mohmand, damaging and flooding roads and creating difficulties for residents. Rain coupled with strong winds and dust had also damaged vegetable and maize crops in Bajaur district, but no casualties were reported.

World.title: US withdraws all bomber aircraft from UK airbase used during Iran war
World.content:
The United States confirmed that it had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from the British airbase of RAF Fairford, reportedly due to “new threats”, with Britain’s government insisting on Monday that the site is safe.

Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.

The scare prompted a counter-terrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the US to launch strikes on Iran.

Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but “a quantity of petrol was recovered”, according to counter-terrorism police.

A statement from a Pentagon official on Sunday said, “We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”

The statement noted that “operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday expressed “confidence in the security of all of our bases”.

US facilities “theoretically could be threatened at any moment, and that’s why there’s so much security built around them”, Rubio said, adding that Washington had worked with London on the investigation and “they couldn’t be more cooperative”.

An unidentified US official told CNN that the bombers were moved after “an unspecified new threat”, with the source calling the latest threat a “real world incident”.

It was unusual to move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official reportedly said.

Two US officials told the New York Times that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an alleged Iran-backed plot against the base.

One American official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours, NYT reported.

Asked whether the base was safe, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesman said: “Yes.”

“We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world,” he told reporters.

Heightened security

Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.

Burnham has said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.

Six London-based Britons arrested in the September incident, including a UK-Iranian dual national, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.

“I wouldn’t have done that,” US President Donald Trump told reporters, while Rubio alleged a “foreign actor” was involved.

Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved.

Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects, but police have not commented on the reports.

Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.

Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran”, and US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing at the base.

Fairford is the only airbase on Britain’s mainland used for this purpose.

The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.

Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.

World.title: Remaining 3 Pakistanis rescued from hijacked vessel in Somalia expected to fly home on Wednesday
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Monday that the three remaining Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25, an oil tanker that was hijacked off the coast of Somalia in April, are expected to be flown back to Pakistan on Wednesday.

The maritime police force of Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland said last week that it had recovered the MT Honour 25, a Palau-flagged oil tanker with 19 crew members on board, including 10 Pakistanis, which had been hijacked by Somali pirates in April.

The Foreign Office subsequently confirmed that three Pakistanis had died and several others were injured during the operation, later identifying the deceased as Rafiullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmed Ansari. Four Pakistanis injured in the operation had arrived in Karachi on Sunday, with the remains of those killed.

In a post on the social media platform X, Dar said three crew members, Imran Ali, Muhammad Yasin and Syed Husain Yousuf, have been “successfully rescued” and flown to Addis Ababa — the capital of Ethiopia — accompanied by a team from the Pakistan embassy in Djibouti.

“The three crew members will be received in Addis Ababa and depart for Pakistan on the first available Ethiopian Airlines flight to Karachi,” Dar said, adding that this flight would be expected on Oct 7 (Wednesday).

He expressed his gratitude to the government of Somalia and the European Union Naval Force Operation Atalanta for their assistance and cooperation in securing the crew’s release.

“Pakistan remains firmly committed to strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation to combat maritime piracy and safeguard the security and freedom of international maritime routes,” he added.

Apart from Pakistanis, the vessel’s crew also included seven Indonesians, an Indian and a Sri Lankan. After the hijacking, months passed with no progress either in negotiations or the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages.

The hostages were said to be victims of an “ ownership crisis ”, as it was not clearly established who owned the ship — the man previously thought to be an owner was later revealed to be more likely a middleman who hired them.

Since its hijacking, the crew had made several emotional videos and audio appeals , reporting that they had run out of clean water, food and medicine. Meanwhile, their families launched an international appeal, calling on foreign governments, the United Nations (UN) and the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to take coordinated action to help secure the release of their loved ones.

For its part, FO maintained that it remained “actively engaged” to secure the release of the sailors.

World.title: Makkah defence pact meeting to be held today in Riyadh, confirms FO
World.content:
A meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement will be held on Monday in Riyadh and will focus on regional developments and ongoing cooperation among the member states, the Foreign Office (FO) confirmed.

In a statement on social media platform X, the FO said Pakistan’s delegation to the meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) will include Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Defence Minister Khawaja Asif.

“The meeting will also be attended by the respective ministers of foreign affairs, ministers of defence, as well as chiefs of general staff of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the Republic of Türkiye,” FO added.

It said that the member states will discuss “latest developments in the region and review ongoing cooperation under the framework of the Makkah Agreement”.

The FO added that Pakistan’s participation signified its “resolve to continue contributing towards regional peace and stability”.

In another post, the FO said Dar arrived in Riyadh for the meeting and was received by Major General Othman Al-Zahrani of the Saudi military and Pakistan’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Ahmad Farooq.

An earlier post said Dar had arrived in Madina ahead of the meeting, where he paid his respects at the Prophet’s (PBUH) Mosque and offered prayers.

Last week, Dar confirmed the meeting while addressing a press briefing. He said the “emergency meeting” would focus on recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The development comes as Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition government launched a major military campaign on Sunday to recapture territory held by the Houthis.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis showed no signs of abating over the weekend, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on Yemen’s capital Sanaa, after which they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones south of Riyadh.

The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait in a lightning offensive.

Meanwhile, the defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

The first meeting of the SPDC was held in Istanbul on Aug 31 , during which it was decided that the alliance’s secretariat will be initially headed by Pakistan for three years. Retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood has been appointed as the first secretary general of the alliance.

On Sept 25, the military chiefs of Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh for urgently convened talks under the pact in light of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

On Sept 18, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry had expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn.
