World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yu Mingrui at his studio in Shanghai, August 2026. Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.



Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A participant tries to catch a caterpillar at Beijing Wildlife Park, September 2026. From @北京野生动物园 on Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

(Header image: Tourists take photos at Yuyuan Garden in Shanghai, Sept. 27, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.title: The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.content:
This summer, “All Wishes Come True!” took in more than 1.8 billion yuan ($268 million) at the Chinese box office, becoming the latest in a string of hit animated films inspired by traditional Chinese myths and legends. The movie reimagines the Eight Immortals, a group of legendary figures in Chinese mythology and Taoism, as ordinary mortals who pose as immortals and venture into the celestial realm of Penglai. There, the mismatched group finds itself caught up in a conflict involving powerful gods, including the warrior deity Erlang Shen.

Despite the film’s widespread acclaim, some Taoist friends of mine were far from impressed. They believe it trivializes important figures in Taoist tradition, completely reimagining their stories while simply borrowing the names of Chinese immortals as a gimmick. But how fixed are the stories of the Eight Immortals in the first place?

Firstly, what makes the Eight Immortals — one of the best-known groups of immortals in Chinese culture — so special? And how exactly are they understood within Taoism?

Let’s start with why there are eight. In traditional Chinese culture, the number eight has long been associated with completeness and balance. The “Zhou Yi” (or “Book of Changes”), for example, describes the eight trigrams; traditional cosmology divides space into eight directions; and ancient people worshipped eight agricultural deities collectively associated with the harvest.

Then there are the “immortals” themselves. The Chinese word xian, or “immortal,” has long been associated with hermits who withdraw into the mountains in pursuit of spiritual cultivation. In Taoism, immortals are distinct from shen, or deities, in that ordinary humans can attain immortality through cultivation. Immortals thus occupy a space between the human and sacred worlds, embodying the Tao in the human realm.

Before the Eight Immortals became established as a group, several individual members had already appeared in historical writings and paintings from the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) dynasties, each associated with their own supernatural feats.

Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin practiced neidan, a Taoist tradition of spiritual cultivation sometimes called “internal alchemy,” and frequently interacted with the influential Taoist priest Chen Tuan. Zhang Guolao once demonstrated various miraculous Taoist arts before Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Han Xiangzi could make flowers bloom instantly. Lan Caihe was a beggar who wore a shoe on one foot while leaving the other bare, often singing and dancing while intoxicated and carrying a large clapper.

Once they had formed into a group, however, the Eight Immortals did not simply retreat into the mountains or ascend to heaven. Instead, they remained closely connected to the human world. The most representative figure in this respect is Lü Dongbin, who chooses to remain among mortals and save them. He assumes various guises, including those of a fisherman, an ink and paper peddler, a sick beggar, and even a pregnant nun. Stories and images of Lü spread across China, with saving and enlightening ordinary people becoming a central theme in legends surrounding him.

The Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) mural “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” at Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, in northern China’s Shanxi province, shows that the Eight Immortals had by then become an established subject in Taoist art. But closer inspection reveals that the only female member of today’s group, He Xiangu, is missing. In her place is Xu Shenweng, a Taoist figure associated with the Northern Song period (960–1127) who once ranked among the Eight Immortals. In other words, the Eight Immortals were originally an all-male group.

So, when did He Xiangu become one of the Eight Immortals? One early appearance of her as part of the group comes in the Yuan dynasty drama “Chen Jiqing Mistakenly Boards a Bamboo Leaf Boat” by Fan Kang. By the time Wu Yuantai wrote the mythological novel “Journey to the East” during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), she had become a permanent member of the group.

This change came amid the flourishing of women’s literary and religious activity during the mid-to-late Ming. Like male scholars, educated women participated in religious and intellectual life and produced literary works of their own. In “Journey to the East,” He Xiangu’s defining supernatural ability is her power to foresee good and bad fortune. Born into a family that ran an herbal medicine shop, she possesses medical knowledge and uses encounters with people seeking treatment as opportunities to encourage them to do good.

With the addition of He Xiangu, the lineup familiar today became fixed and increasingly popular. The Eight Immortals eventually became influential enough to attract the attention of European missionaries studying Chinese religion and folklore. French Jesuit Henri Doré (1859–1931), for example, compiled stories about them in “Researches into Chinese Superstitions,” his multivolume study of Chinese popular religion, folklore, and customs.

The Chinese Jesuit priest Pierre Hoang (1830–1909), also known as Huang Bolu, meanwhile, described the Eight Immortals as representing a cross-section of society: the old and young, men and women, the rich and poor, the noble and lowly. In another interpretation, Zhang Guolao represents old age; Lan Caihe and Han Xiangzi, youth; Zhongli Quan, the military; Lü Dongbin, the scholar; Cao Guojiu, the nobility; Li Tieguai, the sick; and He Xiangu, women.

The Eight Immortals thus came to encompass a broad range of social identities and experiences. They had, collectively, seen many sides of the human world, allowing people from different backgrounds to recognize something of themselves in the group. Their differences also created a kind of balance, recalling a passage in Chapter 2 of the “Tao Te Ching,” which states: “Thus existence and non-existence produce each other; the difficult and the easy bring about each other; the long and the short impart form to each other; the high and the low comply [or change places] with each other; sounds and voices harmonize with each other; priority and sequence alternate with each other.”

From the mid-to-late Ming dynasty onward, the Eight Immortals also became a popular decorative motif on ceramics produced in both imperial and private kilns. They often appeared more subtly on everyday objects, including furniture, utensils, clothing, and architectural decorations. Rather than depicting the immortals themselves, artisans represented them through eight objects associated with the group: Li Tieguai’s gourd, Zhongli Quan’s fan, Zhang Guolao’s fish drum, Lan Caihe’s flower basket, Cao Guojiu’s jade tablet, Han Xiangzi’s flute, He Xiangu’s lotus, and Lü Dongbin’s sword. Craftsmen combined these symbols with scrollwork, bats, clouds, and waves to create decorative compositions that also conveyed wishes for longevity, good fortune, and wealth.

Stories about the Eight Immortals were similarly adaptable. Among commoners, plays such as “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” and “The Eight Immortals Assembly Celebrate Longevity” were widely performed. By the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns (1736–1820) of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), such stories were increasingly associated with birthday celebrations, with gatherings of the Eight Immortals symbolizing longevity, joy, and good fortune.

Among intellectuals, meanwhile, the Eight Immortals served as a source of creative inspiration. One example is “The Record of Handan,” the last of the “Four Dreams of Linchuan” by the great Ming playwright Tang Xianzu. Rather than focusing on reunion, the play uses Lü Dongbin to explore the illusory nature of worldly ambition.

In the play, Lü meets a poor scholar obsessed with achieving fame and gives him a porcelain pillow. After putting on a pot of rice to boil, the scholar falls asleep and dreams that he marries, places first in the imperial examinations, and spends decades navigating political machinations before becoming a powerful and honored official, only to eventually die from overindulgence. Waking to find his pot of rice still cooking, the scholar realizes his entire lifetime of ambition was merely a brief dream. Lü then begins the process of enlightening him, introducing him to the other immortals, who appear one by one to admonish him until he finally awakens to the emptiness of his desires.

All this shows just how adaptable the stories of the Eight Immortals have always been. Taoist traditions and popular folklore have continually shaped and reshaped one another, producing new versions of the group for different audiences and eras.

In that sense, what is happening to the Eight Immortals today is nothing new.

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: An Eight Immortals room screen at a museum in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. VCG)

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Rainy season over for 2026 as southwest monsoon ends
World.content:
BAD WEATHER. Pedestrians wait at the corner of Taft Avenue and UN Avenue in Manila on September 9, 2026, amid heavy rain brought by the southwest monsoon.

Now, the Philippines is transitioning to the period of the northeast monsoon. But El Niño is also expected to cause hotter-than-usual conditions in the coming months.

MANILA, Philippines – The southwest monsoon or habagat is over, marking the end of the 2026 rainy season in the western portions of Luzon and the Visayas.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Monday, October 5, that it has observed “a gradual shift in the prevailing weather pattern” over the past days.

PAGASA noted the weakening of winds and reduced rainfall linked to the southwest monsoon, as well as the strengthening of a high pressure system over East Asia and the “southward migration” of the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ).

The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet. So far, it is the only weather system currently affecting the country, bringing scattered rain showers and thunderstorms to the Visayas, Mindanao, and Palawan.

The southwest monsoon had begun in late May, and monsoon rain subsequently triggered the onset of the rainy season in early June.

Now, the Philippines is transitioning to the period of the northeast monsoon or amihan, which is also called the cool and dry season.

The northeast monsoon typically lasts from October to February or March, causing surges of cool temperatures.

But PAGASA has warned that the strong El Niño currently active in the tropical Pacific Ocean may become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026, and persist until the first half of 2027.

That would mean hotter-than-usual conditions and below-normal rainfall in most parts of the Philippines, according to the weather bureau. Droughts and dry spells are likely to spread in the coming months.

However, tropical cyclones can still develop within or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility, and possibly affect the country, even during El Niño. These are PAGASA’s estimates for the next six months:

October 2026 – 1 or 2

November 2026 – 1 or 2

December 2026 – 1 or 2

January 2027 – 0 or 1

February 2027 – slim chance

March 2027 – slim chance

Other weather systems that may bring rain in the next six months include the ITCZ, shear line, low pressure areas, easterlies, and localized thunderstorms. – Rappler.com

World.title: German and US scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on optogenetics
World.content:
NOBEL PRIZE. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, as announced during a press conference at the Nobel Forum at Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, October 5, 2026.

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were selected for their 'discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics'

STOCKHOLM, Sweden – American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday, October 5, for their discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works.

The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were selected for their “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.”

Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” said Thomas Perlmann, Secretary-General of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet.

“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” Perlmann said.

In clinical trials, researchers are restoring vision to people blinded by a condition called retinitis pigmentosa by inserting a light-sensitive protein in the retina.

Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlea implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.

The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days.

Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel will share a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

Recipients surprised and delighted

In the early 1990s, Hegemann investigated how the alga Chlamydomonas reacts to light in half a millisecond. He hypothesised that a single protein captured light and acted as an ion channel. Nagel tested this by injecting Chlamydomonas genes into frog eggs, discovering channelrhodopsin-2—an ion channel that opens when exposed to light.

In 2003, they published that this protein could be introduced into human and hamster cells to generate electrical impulses using light. In 2005, Deisseroth at Stanford demonstrated the technique in rat nerve cells and the method was named optogenetics a year later.

Perlmann said he had talked to all three laureates this morning, and that they were surprised and delighted.

“All three said the same thing, that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two and they call them my friends. That it’s such an honor to receive them together. So that’s something they conveyed,” Perlmann said.

Nobel prizes awarded since 1901

The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel’s will and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited interruptions, chiefly during World War One and World War Two.

A sixth award, the economics prize, was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, the Riksbank.

The medicine prize has honored some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past century, including Alexander Fleming’s work on penicillin, recognised in 1945, and Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups.

Last year, American scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan’s Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer.

Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in Oslo, a tradition often linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel’s lifetime.

More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their longstanding traditions.

The celebrations culminate on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honor. – Rappler.com

World.title: On Teachers’ Day, they still don’t hear what they want to hear from Marcos
World.content:
TEACHERS' DAY. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers a speech during the Department of Education's National Teachers' Day Celebration at the Smart Araneta Coliseum in Quezon City on October 5, 2026.

Quezon City has good news for its public school teachers on Monday, October 5, but others are left wishing 'sana all'

Teachers could only say “Sana all (I wish I had the same experience)!” after learning that their peers in Quezon City would have a higher monthly allowance in 2027.

Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said their city government is set to increase the supplemental allowance for teachers and non-teaching personnel to P2,000 next year, up from the previous P1,500.

Belmonte made the announcement during the 2026 National Teachers’ Day celebration of the Department of Education (DepEd) on Monday, October 5, saying that they recognize the dedication of public school workers.

The crowd of 10,500 Luzon-based public school teachers at the Smart Araneta Coliseum, located in Belmonte’s turf, cheered.

But what about other teachers all over the Philippines?

In his speech at the same event, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said other mayors may now have to raise allowances for teachers after Belmonte’s announcement.

“Mayayaman naman kayong mga city eh (Your cities are rich),” Marcos quipped.

Just as September ended, the Caloocan City Council approved an increase in the additional augmentation allowance of its teachers and staff to P2,555.56, effective October this year.

But on Monday, even the President might have felt the pressure. “Mayor Joy, kasama ako do’n sa [napasubo], dahil ako kaagad ang nilapitan. ‘Pahingi ng pondo para makapagbigay din kami ng allowance.’” (Mayor Joy, I’m among those who were put on the spot, because some mayors immediately approached me. “Please give us funds so that we can also provide allowance.”)

Not every local government unit provides a separate allowance for their teachers.

“Sana gano’n din ‘yong sa buong Pilipinas…. ‘Yong monthly allowance, napakalaking tulong ‘yon (I hope it’s the same experience across the Philippines. A monthly allowance would be a big help for us),” said Ronald Ventura, a teacher from Batac City, Ilocos Norte. He said their province — the Marcoses’ bailiwick — does not provide the same allowance.

Under the Kabalikat sa Pagtuturo Act, the government provides teachers with an annual tax-free teaching allowance of P10,000. The national budget also includes a P1,000 World Teachers’ Day incentive benefit.

Marcos mentioned this incentive in his speech, along with teaching and medical allowances, updates on the over 82,000 teachers and school heads who have been promoted under the Expanded Career Progression System, and the expedited process for the still-unreleased 2024 performance-based bonus.

Missing from the speech?

But some teachers wanted to hear more from the President, such as a higher World Teachers’ Day incentive. Someone also shouted “Sahod!” (wage).

Play Video

“Parang pahaging lang ‘yong nangyari (It’s like he just dropped indirect hints),” said Noliver Viray, a public school teacher from Valenzuela City.

Viray, who has over two decades of teaching experience, told Rappler that teachers who attended the DepEd event wanted to hear good news. “Wala kasing nailatag kung ano ba ‘yong dapat na benepisyo na mabibigay sa mga teacher, ‘yong mga increase,” he added. (The benefits that teachers truly need, including salary increases, were not outlined.)

The Teachers’ Day celebration highlighted Marcos’ seeming silence on calls for a salary increase for teachers. Even during his recent State of the Nation Address, the topic was left untouched.

“I was hoping he would make a public announcement in front of all the teachers,” Novie Ann Varias, a public school teacher from Cardona, Rizal, said in a mix of Filipino and English.

She believes that there should be a P15,000 across-the-board wage hike, which is the same plea of the Teachers’ Dignity Coalition.

In the streets, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers, along with other progressive groups, marched toward Mendiola in Manila on Monday, in a bid to bring close to Malacañang their call for a P50,000 starting salary for teachers.

In his written message, Marcos said the government recognizes the sacrifices of teachers, and reaffirms its “shared responsibility to cherish and uplift those who shape our lives.” For many, however, those words may remain empty unless their requests for higher wages are granted. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte’s flagged transactions ‘linked’ to flood control, drugs – AMLC
World.content:
SARA DUTERTE. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.

'To be fair to the AMLC, they simply received this report from a covered institution.... They are merely mirroring the report submitted to them by a covered institution,' Escudero clarifies

MANILA, Philippines – The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) has flagged financial transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte allegedly related to the flood control issue and illegal drugs, the House prosecution team said on Monday, October 5.

During his direct examination, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified on AMLC’s Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) related to the couple’s financial transactions.

Play Video

Asked by prosecutor Mae Divinagracia, Buenaventura read the reason cited in an STR dated November 15, 2019: “Based on records, as reported by the covered person, the reason indicated is graft and corrupt practices” related to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) flood control issue. Another STR for Duterte, dated August 1, 2024, mentioned alleged “shabu (metampethamine) importation.”

The AMLC is the Philippine government’s financial intelligence unit tasked to implement Republic Act No. 9160 or the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA). AMLC specifically looks into two types of transactions and issues corresponding reports: covered transaction reports (CTRs) and STRs.

CTRs are automatically triggered if a financial transaction reaches P500,000 within a single day. Meanwhile, STRs are triggered not because of amount threshold, but because of certain conditions.

The law lists down the circumstances that include cases where customer cannot be properly identified; the amount is inconsistent with the person’s financial capacity; transactions appear structured to avoid reporting requirements, and the transaction appears connected to an unlawful activity, among other reasons.

However, it must be noted that transactions flagged or reported by AMLC do not automatically mean that money was illegal or if a crime has been committed. The reporting is just part of the AMLC’s mandate to monitor financial transactions and implement the AMLA.

Based on the summary of reports submitted by the AMLC to the Senate impeachment court, Duterte has 373 CTRs and 34 STRs, while her husband has 363 CTRs and 30 STRs. When combined, the transactions amount to P4.4 billion, based on the summary.

Screenshot/Senate impeachment court

During the presentation of the STRs, some senators interjected and raised concerns on the context behind the STRs. Specifically, why covered persons or bodies — like financial institutions — use media reports for the STRs.

“We don’t even know the context of that. We don’t even know. Honestly, we don’t even know that banks do that,” Senator-judge Pia Cayetano said.

Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano raised the same concern.

“To be fair to the AMLC, they simply received this report from a covered institution. As earlier asked by the Chair, this did not come from them. They are merely mirroring the report submitted to them by a covered institution. And that covert institutions at times do submit it based on available information, whether from news or media reports or other information,” presiding officer Chiz Escudero clarified.

Play Video

Cale88 in spotlight

Divinagracia also asked Buenaventura about the CTRs related to Cale88, a firm allegedly connected to Carpio. The prosecution alleged that there were inward remittances to Cale88 from China and other countries.

Based on the summary, there were 141 CTRs and 3 STRs involving China remittances. The total remittance reached P319 million, including remittances from Hong Kong.

On Friday, October 2, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV claimed that Cale88 allegedly got P319 million from “Chinese government and corporations.” Trillanes made this allegation the same week the prosecution dropped him from its list of witnesses.

But during the Monday hearing, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan, during his cross-examination of Buenaventura, reiterated that the issuance of CTRs do not necessarily mean that the transactions were illegal per se.

“For the record, transaction that is reported as a covered transaction is not necessarily an illegal transaction, correct?” Vinluan asked.

“Tama po (Correct),” Buenaventura replied. – Rappler.com

World.title: AMRO further cuts PH growth outlook as flood control issue slows investment
World.content:
HAZE. Metro Manila experienced hazy air conditions on September 1, 2026, due to smoke from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, blanketing the sky. The Manila local government advised residents to take precautions and wear face masks when going outdoors.

‘The Philippines also had some domestic issues that they need to deal with. Remember, there was this flood control-related issue, and that's significantly slowed down public investment,’ AMRO chief economist Dong He says

MANILA, Philippines – The ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) cut its Philippine growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027, pointing to the combined negative impacts from the Middle East energy shock and a slowdown in public investment linked to the flood control controversy.

AMRO now expects the Philippine economy to grow by only 3.3% in 2026, down from its 4.1% forecast in July. Its 2027 growth forecast was cut to 4.6% from 5.5%. In contrast, the wider ASEAN+3 region is expected to grow 4.1% in both years, with Vietnam showing particularly strong growth at 8.0% in 2026 and 7.6% in 2027.

NEW OUTLOOK. The table shows that AMRO has cut the Philippines’ growth outlook for 2026 and 2027. Photo from AMRO briefing.

The October update is yet another downgrade from AMRO’s assessment after its annual consultation with Philippine authorities in August, when it expected growth of 3.4% this year and 4.8% next year. At the time, it already flagged weaker private consumption due to higher prices alongside subdued investment.

In its latest update, AMRO also pointed to persistent high global oil prices and its effect on energy.

“The Philippines is one of the economies that was hit harder by the energy shock,” AMRO chief economist Dong He said during a briefing on Monday, October 5. “Growth did slow down significantly and the inflation went up very quickly.” (READ: DOE sees ‘no signs’ oil prices will fall as excise tax relief goes on table)

But AMRO said the slowdown cannot be blamed on external conditions alone.

“The Philippines also had some domestic issues that they need to deal with. Remember, there was this flood control-related issue, and that’s significantly slowed down public investment,” He said.

“So the growth outlook is very dependent on how fast public investment and construction-related activities can pick up,” he added.

In a July analysis, AMRO said infrastructure projects had been delayed or cancelled following corruption allegations that emerged in mid-2025. It estimated that public construction contracted 31.5% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026.

The financial stability report similarly said foreign investors had pulled money out of Philippine equities, reflecting what AMRO said were “investor concerns over the Philippines’ widening current account deficit, delayed infrastructure implementation, and the potential implications for growth and corporate earnings.”

There are still buffers. He pointed to remittances and the country’s IT-BPM industry, while saying the Philippines has clear monetary and fiscal policy frameworks. But he stressed that the recovery would also depend on the quality and pace of government spending.

Authorities should ensure that “public investment, well-governed public investment, can pick up speed,” He said, calling this important for the economy to return to its potential growth rate.

The World Bank likewise warned that the fallout from the flood control corruption controversy was weighing on the economy through weaker investment. In August, the World Bank said heightened scrutiny and audits of infrastructure projects had delayed spending and made private investors more hesitant, contributing to its decision to cut its 2026 Philippine growth forecast to 3.7% from 5.3%. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No, Malabon congressman Oreta did not slam Sara Duterte’s travels
World.content:
Malabon City Lone District Representative Lenlen Oreta did not make such a statement, according to his office’s email response to Rappler. It added that public conversations should be based on verified information and reliable sources.

Claim: Malabon City Lone District Representative Antolin “Lenlen” Oreta III pointed out Vice President Sara Duterte’s multiple travels to The Hague, Netherlands while bringing up President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s modernization plan for the Philippines.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The quote attributed to the congressman was posted on Facebook on August 5 by Malabon Standard, which has 10,000 followers.

The post has already garnered more than 43,000 reactions, more than 14,000 comments, and 376 shares as of this writing, alleging that Oreta said: “Puro kasi pagpunta sa the Hague ang inaatupag ni VP Sara habang si PBBM gumagawa ng paraan para sa modernization ng bansa.”

(VP Sara is busy flying to The Hague while PBBM is doing the work for the country’s modernization.)

The quote has also been reposted across various social media platforms, including Instagram.

The facts: Oreta did not issue such a statement as confirmed by his office in an email to Rappler on September 30.

“We would just like to clarify that the statement currently being attributed to Rep. Lenlen Oreta is not supported by any verified source or official record. Rep. Oreta has not made such a statement in any interview, speech, Facebook Live, or other official recording,” his office said.

“We believe that public conversations should be based on verified information and reliable sources, especially when statements are being attributed to a public official,” it added.

Rappler previously fact checked a false statement attributed to the congressman from the same Facebook page. In such a post, Oreta allegedly wished for Sara Duterte’s death. This has since been labeled by Meta and Oreta himself as false information.

As of this writing, Oreta still has not flagged the August 5 post as false information.

Oreta was one of the 257 lawmakers who voted for Duterte’s second impeachment. In 2019, he was threatened with arrest by Sara’s father then-president Rodrigo Duterte over the drug problem in Malabon.

Personal trip: While Oreta did not criticize the vice president’s trips abroad, another lawmaker has expressed statements relating to this.

On July 22, Manila 6th District Representative Bienvenido Abante Jr. criticized Duterte’s personal trip to five countries Qatar, Germany, United Kingdom, Northern Ireland, and The Netherlands from July 16 to July 31, amid her impeachment trial. Abante added that Duterte’s travel abroad is “betrayal of public trust.”

The Vice President is on trial for her alleged death threats against high-ranking Philippine officials, including Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House speaker Martin Romualdez, alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and alleged bribery of public officials. – Eunicito Barreno/Rappler.com

Eunicito Barreno is a 2026 Aries Rufo Fellow. He is a senior journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he is also a news staffer at the Philippine Collegian, the university’s official student publication.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Gasoline, kerosene prices rise on October 6, diesel gets slight rollback
World.content:
NOT AVAILABLE. Signs are posted on fuel dispensers at a gas station in Quezon City due fuel shortages, on March 26, 2026.

The mixed adjustment comes after price cuts last week, while China’s suspension of refined fuel exports threatens to tighten Asian supply further

MANILA, Philippines – Gasoline and kerosene prices are going up again starting Tuesday, October 6, while diesel prices are set to fall slightly, as fuel markets remain volatile after the previous week’s rollback.

The Department of Energy announced the following fuel price adjustments for the week of October 6 to 12:

Gasoline – increase of P1.93 per liter

Diesel – rollback of P1.30 per liter

Kerosene – increase of P3.30 per liter

Before the latest adjustment, the Department of Energy’s price monitoring showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P94.10 per liter for gasoline RON95, P87.20 per liter for gasoline RON91, P95.70 per liter for diesel, and P125 per liter for kerosene for the week of September 29 to October 5.

The mixed movement follows last week’s rollback, which saw gasoline, diesel, and kerosene prices finally fall after three consecutive weeks of steep increases.

“Gasoline prices increased due to a combination of regional supply constraints, refinery operating

conditions, and sustained demand in key consuming countries. In particular, Chinese gasoline

exports were expected to decline during the October 1–7 Golden Week holiday due to the late

release of export quotas, while South Korea was expected to reduce gasoline output for four to five

days,” the DOE said in a press release on Monday.

The diesel rollback is still a carry-over from the previous week’s drop in international diesel prices, so it does not yet fully capture the more recent developments pushing fuel costs higher again.

“Diesel prices in the region were affected by changing supply and shipping conditions. Asian diesel

prices remained generally high but were volatile as shipping costs stayed elevated and price

differences between regional markets changed. These developments contributed to the decrease

in diesel prices during the monitoring period,” the DOE said.

Worryingly, however, those pressures are building as China suspends refined fuel exports, while disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab continue to threaten major oil and fuel shipping routes.

Chinese refiners have temporarily suspended exports of petroleum products outside Hong Kong and Macau as Beijing seeks to rebuild domestic fuel inventories.

At the same time, China has also stepped up its purchases of crude oil as refiners seek to replenish supplies and replace disrupted Iranian and other Middle Eastern barrels. Chinese independent refiners have snapped up cargoes from Russia, West Africa, Canada, and South America in recent weeks, adding competition and supporting even higher spot premiums.

The combination of China buying more crude while withholding more of its refined fuel output from overseas buyers could add further upward pressure on Asian fuel markets in the coming weeks.

China is the world’s largest oil refining market by capacity and an important source of fuel for the Philippines. In 2025, it supplied 3.78 billion liters, or about 20% of the country’s imported finished petroleum products, second only to South Korea.

Local pump prices also remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Orders Defense Reforms After Inspection Finds Systemic Failures
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev ordered reforms in Kazakhstan’s Armed Forces after a commission investigating a military incident in the Mangystau Region revealed serious shortcomings in planning, oversight and personal safety, reported the presidential press service on Oct. 5.

Tokayev held a meeting with members of the commission on Oct. 5, where its chair Aida Balayeva, who also serves as a deputy chair of the Security Council, presented the results of the work carried out across the main areas of the inspection.

The meeting noted that the events in the Mangystau Region exposed systemic problems within the Armed Forces. Preliminary findings indicate serious shortcomings in the planning of military activities and inadequate oversight by the previous leadership. The investigation into the circumstances of the tragedy identified deficiencies in the preparation and planning of exercises, risk assessment, organization of troop deployment and ensuring the safety of military personnel.

A pre-trial investigation into alleged criminal negligence by commanders is ongoing. Five officials have been arrested, while a final legal assessment of their actions will be made upon completion of the investigation.

Thirteen criminal cases launched

Law enforcement authorities opened 13 criminal cases during the first stage of the inspection over suspected embezzlement of state property and other alleged violations involving the Ministry of Defense and military units.

The inspection also uncovered lapses in military discipline and preventive work, including reported violence against service members that prompted criminal investigations.

Tokayev stressed that initial personnel decisions have been made and that all officials found responsible for the deaths of military personnel must face legal accountability. He stressed that the incident remains under his personal control.

Defense reforms to focus on modernizing the army

Tokayev instructed the commission and the Defense Ministry to draft proposals to address the shortcomings identified by the inspection. He said the findings should also be taken into account in preparing a broader reform plan for the Armed Forces.

Particular emphasis was placed on building a new-model army capable of effectively responding to modern challenges and threats, including stronger military discipline, improved safety standards and better conditions for service members.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Population Tops 20.6 Million as Astana Passes 1.7 Million
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s population reached 20.62 million as of Sept. 1, while Astana surpassed 1.7 million residents, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The capital’s population increased by 9,780 people in August alone and has grown by 61,209 people since the start of the year. Kazakhstan’s total population stood at 20,618,796 people as of Sept. 1, up from 20,499,822 at the beginning of 2026.

Almaty remains the country’s most populous city, with 2,387,896 residents. The population of the city increased by more than 8,000 people in August.

The Turkistan Region ranks second among the country’s most populous regions, with 2,142,709 residents. Unlike Almaty, however, its population declined by more than 2,000 people over the month.

Several other regions and cities also have populations exceeding one million. The Almaty Region had 1,615,631 residents as of Sept. 1, while Shymkent recorded 1,316,888. The Zhambyl Region had 1,210,084 residents and the Karagandy Region 1,130,123.

The country’s least populated region is the Ulytau Region, with 217,274 residents. The North Kazakhstan Region had 510,756 people, while the Abai Region recorded 590,702.

World.title: Tokayev Says Teachers Matter More Than Ever in AI Era
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said teachers are more important than ever as artificial intelligence and digital technologies reshape education, urging Kazakhstan to strengthen human capital and adapting its schools to a rapidly changing world.

“A teacher is a key figure in every person’s life. I believe everyone would agree with this. Deep respect for educators is an important sign that determines the maturity of a civilized society,” Tokayev said at an Oct. 5 ceremony in Akorda marking Teachers’ Day in the country.

“Today, in an era of rapid development of advanced technologies and enormous information flows, the role of the teacher has become more important than ever. This is an undeniable fact,” Tokayev added.

Expanding access to quality education

More than four million schoolchildren make up nearly one-fifth of Kazakhstan’s population, Tokayev said. He stressed that children should have the opportunity to grow up in a safe, developed society.

According to him, the quality of human capital is what determines the strength of an advanced and civilized state. The country’s position in the world and its economic potential, he added, depend directly on the level of education and science.

“I always emphasize in my speeches: both villages and cities should have modern schools that provide children with equal access to quality education,” he said.

Over the past seven years, 1,342 schools have been built in Kazakhstan, providing more than one million student places.

AI to become part of school education

Tokayev said Kazakhstan is implementing a program to introduce AI-based lessons in secondary schools.

“The government should pay particular attention to this extremely important area of work,” he said, stressing that the introduction of new technologies should be carried out systematically.

He said AI could help reduce the administrative burden on teachers and allow them to devote more time to students.

“When used properly, new technologies will significantly facilitate teachers’ work and become a reliable tool that eliminates routine tasks. Teachers should have more time for mentoring and direct work with students,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev said he makes strengthening partnerships with leading universities a priority during his foreign visits. At least 30 branches of foreign universities now operate in the country, including Cardiff University, Coventry University, and universities from the United States, South Korea, Italy, Russia, China and France.

World.title: US Report Sees Progress in Kazakhstan’s Investment Climate, Flags Tax and Regulatory Risks
World.content:
