World.title: Armenia’s environmental activities pose transboundary risks - EPP
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. Armenia’s environmental activities pose transboundary risks to the region, the statement from the briefing held at the office of the Forum of National Non-Governmental Organizations of Azerbaijan, part of the “Environmental Protection First” coalition, says, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

The event focused on issues related to Armenia’s mining industry, water resource use, the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, the Amulsar gold mine, and the environmental damage inflicted on Azerbaijani territories during the occupation.

At the briefing, it was noted that the activities of the mining industry in Armenia raise concerns not only from the country’s perspective but also in terms of the environmental safety of the region as a whole. It was pointed out that mining waste can enter transboundary rivers via groundwater and thus affect the territories of other countries. In this regard, the impact of mines located in Alaverdi and Syunik, in particular, on groundwater pollution was highlighted.

Coalition representatives also drew attention to the situation regarding Armenia’s water resources. During the briefing, World Bank data was cited, indicating that Armenia is one of the countries experiencing water scarcity. It was noted that the use of groundwater in the Ararat Valley for commercial fishing and irrigation has exceeded the annual rate of natural recharge. The World Bank’s 2024 report on climate and development also indicates that groundwater extraction in the Ararat Valley has exceeded the annual rate of recharge, and that water discharge from Lake Sevan has significantly exceeded historical levels of natural outflow.

In addition, it was noted that increased water withdrawal from Lake Sevan could have an impact on the lake’s ecosystem and biodiversity. Speakers emphasized that, given Armenia’s position as a downstream country in the Caucasus, transboundary water issues arising on its territory are also significant for Azerbaijan. Attention was also given to the issue of assessing transboundary environmental impacts under the Espoo Convention.

The briefing included a separate discussion of the Amulsar gold mine project, located near the city of Jermuk. It was noted that the project’s location in an area connected to the Arpa and Vorotan river basins raises concerns regarding potential impacts on water resources, biodiversity, and ecosystems associated with Lake Sevan.

Speakers noted that in 2018, residents of Jermuk and environmental activists blocked the roads leading to the Amulsar mine in protest against the project, effectively suspending operations at the mine for several years. Subsequently, efforts to resume the project were restarted.

In addition, it was reported that on August 31, 2026, an agreement on community development was signed between the Government of Armenia, Lydian Armenia, and the communities of Jermuk, Vayk, and Sisian. The agreement provides for the allocation of $7 million annually to the communities affected by the Amulsar project during the construction phase, and $7 million or $9 million during the production phase, depending on the average price of gold.

Coalition representatives believe that the practical implementation of the project is continuing, despite concerns about its potential environmental impact. Given the connection between the Arpa and Vorotan rivers and the Araz River basin, it was emphasized that it is important to bear in mind the potential transboundary environmental impact of the “Amulsar” project.

The briefing also mentioned the operations of the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant in Armenia among potential environmental risks. It was noted that the problems include the aging equipment of the second power unit, which has been in operation since 1980, and the extension of its service life. According to information from Armenia and the International Atomic Energy Agency, a program is underway to extend the service life of the second power unit until 2036.

Speakers noted that in the event of a potential serious accident or damage to safety systems, there is a likelihood of transboundary release of radioactive substances into the environment, including surface and groundwater.

The briefing also extensively covered the damage inflicted on the environment and biodiversity in Azerbaijan’s sovereign territories during the Armenian occupation.

Moreover, it was noted that during the occupation, forests on Azerbaijani territory were destroyed and degraded. It was recorded that approximately 8,900 hectares of forest were lost, and a total of more than 50,000 hectares were destroyed. Damage was also inflicted on specially protected areas and rare plant species, including the destruction of rare oriental sycamores located in the Basitchay State Nature Reserve.

The reports also noted a serious deterioration in the condition of agricultural land. It was noted that between 1995 and 2015, approximately 54,544 hectares of agricultural land were taken out of productive use. Furthermore, it was emphasized that irrigation infrastructure was destroyed during the occupation.

Regarding the Sarsang Reservoir, it was noted that the lack of proper management of the reservoir and changes in water use patterns affected access to water for the population of adjacent regions and for agriculture.

The report also addressed the issue of the illegal exploitation of natural resources, particularly mineral deposits, on the territory of Azerbaijan during the occupation. It was noted that deposits such as Gizilbulag, Demirli, Soyudlu, Aghduzdag, Tutkhum, Vejnali, Mehmana, Shorbulag, Saribulag, Aghhyatag, Levchay, Gamishli, Aghgaya, Chilgazchay, and Narzanli were being mined or were in the process of being mined at various times.

The speakers also drew attention to the impact of mining activities on land and water resources, noting that revenues generated by mines in Azerbaijani territories during the occupation were used to fund economic activities in Armenia and by certain individuals. In this context, the activities of Ruben Vardanyan were also mentioned.

Regarding the pollution of transboundary water resources, special attention was paid to the example of the Okhchuchay River. It was noted that the river’s ecosystem had suffered serious damage as a result of pollution from waste generated by mining facilities located in Armenia. Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources reported that, during monitoring, samples taken from the Okhchuchay River showed levels of heavy metals such as copper, molybdenum, manganese, iron, zinc, and chromium that exceeded established standards by several times. In addition, the deaths of more than 500 trout and other fish species were reported.

At the conclusion of the briefing, it was noted that the potential transboundary environmental consequences of mining, water management, and other economic activities carried out on the territory of Armenia must be a focus of attention from the perspective of environmental and water security for the countries of the region, including Azerbaijan.

World.title: Germany at risk of 'violent conflict' with Russia, intelligence chief warns
World.content:
Germany is at risk of entering a violent conflict as Moscow steps up an increasingly aggressive "shadow war" against European democracies, its head of foreign intelligence has warned.

The ongoing war between Ukraine and Russia is now in its fifth year, with Ukraine and allies increasingly concerned about the tactics Russia may employ to gain an advantage.

"The confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension," Martin Jaeger, head of Germany's Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), told the annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs in parliament.

"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia — the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example," he said.

Russia calls Leipzig drone attack accusations 'start of real war' The German government concluded last week that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month.

He described Russia as "waging a shadow war" with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining "real and imminent".

German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber attacks, and have blamed it for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in August.

President Vladimir Putin last week said Russia had "no intention of attacking anyone … but if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond".

Mr Jaeger, however, said Moscow was prepared to use force to achieve its goals, and that Russian intelligence services' operations in and against Germany were "increasingly aggressive".

"Russia is putting us to the test and closely watching how we handle this situation. From the perspective of the Kremlin leadership, any sign of wavering invites them to further increase the pressure on Germany."

Mr Jaeger's confronting assessment came as Russia continued to carry out strikes on targets in Ukraine and the Black Sea.

A Russian air strike hit a Ukrainian sewing factory in Kharkiv on Monday. (Reuters: Sofiia Gatilova)

Three people were killed and 25 injured in an attack in Kharkiv on Monday, in what a local mayor said was a strike on residential buildings and warehouses.

One person was also killed and another wounded after a drone attack on a Turkish-owned civilian vessel in the Black Sea, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye. Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board," he wrote on X.

Reuters

World.title: US moves bombers from UK airbase after suspected Iranian plot
World.content:
The United States has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from a British air base a week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

Police were called to RAF Fairford in south-west England on September 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.

The scare prompted a counter-terrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the air base, where the US planes had been stationed including some used to carry out recent strikes on Iran.

'Strong indications' Iran involved In an interview with the BBC, Andy Burnham says UK authorities "believe Iran to have played a part" in the security incident.

The UK government insists RAF Fairford is safe, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the suspected plot was likely backed by Iran.

"We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," Mr Burnham told reporters.

Security at the base has been heightened since the incident.

A statement from a Pentagon official on Sunday said "we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States".

The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday, local time, expressed "confidence in the security of all of our bases".

US facilities "theoretically could be threatened at any moment, and that's why there's so much security built around them," he said.

He said Washington had worked with London on the investigation and "they couldn't be more cooperative".

Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over British air base incident UK police arrested the 27-year-old in London and a second British man, 26, had also been questioned under caution.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said in late July that the base was a legitimate target but have denied accusations it was involved in any plot.

Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" that speculation.

US bombers are not stationed permanently at RAF Fairford but they have been taking off and landing at the base after Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran".

Some residents have voiced concerns about the RAF Fairford base housing US military assets during the war against Iran. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Fairford is the only air base on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.

Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the short term reduce the US's capacity "to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat".

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Teenager loses hand as French student protests escalate
World.content:
A 15-year-old protesting against France's dilapidated and understaffed schools has had his hand blown off in the northern town of Lens, officials say.

A police union source said the teenager appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police and that it exploded in his hand.

Violent protests in France French students and police have accused each other of violence as protests continue over conditions in education.

The local prefect François-Xavier Lauch said an investigation into the incident, on Monday, local time, had been opened.

A nationwide day of demonstrations is expected on Tuesday.

The protests began in late September at a high school in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages before spreading across France.

"Our priority is to restore order," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said on Monday.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked and that 78 teaching staff had been injured since the beginning of the demonstrations.

Police and students clash, tear gas used

On Monday, the news channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille in northern France, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest and of a fire being lit as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.

Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in the 13th district of Paris, said her school had been attacked by a "very determined" group wearing hoods and masks who tried to break through the school's entrance door and then lit a fire.

Visible damage at Lycee Vauquelin high school with bicycles and bins set on fire by protesters in Paris. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated and classes suspended.

"It was very violent and happened very quickly," she said, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.

"It was terrible for students who witnessed this outburst of violence," she said, adding those behind the attack on her school were not students of the school.

Fires as school protests spread in France Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools.

Since last Monday, around 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested nationwide and dozens injured.

Teachers and members of the public have been attacked, while damage to property is estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

Ms Bregeon said the French government would fast-track a bill in parliament on October 27 to make those found to have damaged property during protests financially liable.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure, in an open letter published on X on Saturday, said those who had launched the protests no longer controlled them and called on students to abandon blockades in favour of peaceful protest.

Student unions have nevertheless called for a national day of demonstrations on Tuesday.

Security officials fear that an organised protest in central Paris in particular could see further violence amid concerns that far-left and anarchist groups could try to take over the protests.

High school students gather outside the Lycee Sophie Germain high school in Paris as part of nationwide protests. (Reuters: Eric Baradat)

CGT union head Sophie Binet said on Monday that union members will attend Tuesday's demonstrations "to protect high school students."

"We've been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students," she said.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Nobel medicine prize awarded to scientists for brain activity research
World.content:
The Nobel Prize in Medicine has been awarded to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.

Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method "is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries".

Professor Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Professor Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Professor Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany, the Nobel Assembly said.

There are six Nobel prize categories: medicine, physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics. (AP Photo: Jacquelyn Martin, File)

The Nobel Assembly said optogenetics opened a new era in neuroscience, unravelling the pathways that lead to behaviour and disease.

The research started with Dr Hegemann exploring how a single-celled type of green algae can swim toward light.

He and Dr Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.

Dr Deisseroth then worked with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.

Nobel Peace Prize won't go to Trump this year, experts say It is often regarded as the most prestigious of all Nobel prizes, which are given to those who have "conferred the greatest benefit to humankind". But the Nobel Peace Prize can also be controversial.

The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, on Monday, kicking off Nobels week.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.718 million).

Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.

Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday, local time.

After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on October 12.

AP

World.title: US accuses California woman of spying on Taiwan president's son for China
World.content:
The FBI says authorities have arrested a California woman and accused her of spying on a son of Taiwan's president at the direction of Chinese officials.

The FBI arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday, local time, before she was due to depart for China, the agency said in a statement.

Authorities charged Ms Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

Ms Zhang surveilled one of the sons of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the FBI said.

The agency did not directly name Ms Zhang's alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.

Taiwan's presidential office described Ms Zhang's actions as a "typical case of transnational repression" and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.

"Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.

Wanying Zhang was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. (X: Bill Essayli, First Assistant US Attorney for the Central District of California)

China's foreign ministry said it was "not familiar" with the situation, and that it had "consistently opposed the sensationalisation of so-called 'Chinese spies' to slander and smear China".

Mr Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan's separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as Chinese territory.

Mr Lai says only the people of Taiwan can decide its future.

The Justice Department said Ms Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and license-plate information about the Taiwanese president's son and his family.

Ms Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection and did not notify Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

It was not immediately clear whether Ms Zhang had a defence lawyer.

She will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday, Mr Essayli said.

Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island's most important international backer and weapons supplier.

Reuters

World.title: Child psychiatrist's good standing enabled patient sex abuse, court told
World.content:
A WA judge has warned a former Perth child psychiatrist who sexually abused his young patients and later filmed boys in public toilets he will be going to prison.

WARNING: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

Benjamin Wen, 52, touched the boys’ genitals on the pretext of conducting “puberty checks” he said were routine, but the WA District Court heard it was not necessary for a psychiatrist to perform such checks.

Wen was found guilty in April of multiple charges, including indecent dealing with a child under 13, and persistent sexual conduct with a child under 16, with the offences occurring more than 10 years ago.

Wen's face was covered when he left court today. (ABC News: David Weber)

In 2017 he was given a suspended sentence for making videos of boys urinating in public toilets.

Wen, who was previously known as Aaron Voon, had made the videos in Canada, the United States, New Zealand and Perth.

Parents of boys who had been Voon's patients contacted WA police following the publicity surrounding that case.

During sentencing submissions on Monday, the court heard Wen had been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis, neuralgia, ASD, PTSD and OCD and his time in prison would be harder than it would be for a "normal prisoner".

'Abuse of trust'

But prosecutor Tracy Tan said Wen used the trust placed in him to "repeatedly" offend against children in his care.

Ms Tan said his "abuse of trust" had impacted on his victims, who were neurodivergent, and their families.

Perth doctor indecently touched 15 boys, court told A former child psychiatrist who changed his name after being convicted of child exploitation touched young neurodivergent boys indecently at his practice, a Perth court hears. WARNING: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

She said Wen did not appear to accept the offending, as he still seemed to maintain his actions were "medically warranted".

This showed he was not remorseful, Ms Tan told the court.

Enabling offending

The prosecutor targeted a defence submission suggesting the judge should consider the good Wen had done in treating more than 500 patients, aside from the victims.

Ms Tan told the court "it was precisely that good standing" that enabled the offending, and "little mitigation" turned on that.

She said the matters to do with Wen's health were the only ones that should be considered in mitigation.

Patti Chong asked the judge not to impose a "crushing sentence". (ABC News: David Weber)

Wen's lawyer Patti Chong said Wen was likely to experience "disproportionately more suffering" and his mobility was "vastly impaired".

She told the court his health issues warranted a significant sentence reduction and called on the judge not to impose a "crushing sentence".

Judge Linda Petrusa said her sentencing remarks were likely to take some time, and the matter was adjourned until Wednesday.

But she warned Wen a term of immediate imprisonment would be imposed.

His bail was continued until Wednesday.

World.title: More than 5,000 pepper spray canisters sold in the NT since start of trial
World.content:
More than a year after it was legalised, data on the personal use of pepper spray across the Northern Territory has found 3,714 people have bought the product so far, with 46 prohibited buyers identified and three non-lawful deployments recorded.

Since September 2025, NT residents have been able to buy and use pepper spray, or oleoresin capsicum (OC) spray, for personal protection, in a trial implemented by the NT government.

The trial was due to finish at the end of August but has been extended until December 31.

A community reference group (CRG) report reviewing the trial's first 12 months has now been submitted to the chief minister's department. It uses data from the NT Police Force, which has also provided the ABC with figures up to date as of this week.

The report includes statistics from NT Police. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The data shows a total of 5,882 canisters have been sold to 3,714 people in the NT since the trial began, and 69 cans have been seized by NT Police.

An NT Police Force spokesperson said since the trial began, there had been nine reported uses of OC spray, three of which were not in self-defence.

They said one of those instances had led to charges for the for unlawful use of OC spray.

According to the CRG report, eight people have been charged with making a false declaration or unlawful possession of OC spray since the start of the trial.

Customers must fill out this declaration form before they can buy OC spray under the NT trial. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

To be eligible to purchase OC spray under the trial, a person must be over 18, and declare no relevant criminal history, police or court orders.

The CRG report said it "did not identify any significant or widespread community concerns" about the trial in its first 12 months.

Woman sentenced for OC spray misuse A Darwin woman is sentenced for attacking someone with OC spray weeks after the NT government announced a trial of the product.

However, it said there was a "need for clear, accessible and consistent public information", particularly around storage and transport of the product, and noted some people "who had previously carried improvised items for self-defence … had instead transitioned to carrying OC spray".

Superintendent Ian Kennon said police were "currently happy" with the trial.

"Over 98 per cent of people purchasing OC spray having done so in alignment to the conditions of the trial," he said.

" We continue to urge everyone who legally purchases OC spray to familiarise themselves with their legal use. "

The trial means people over the age of 18 can legally purchase OC spray from licensed firearms dealers. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

Aside from Western Australia, NT is the only jurisdiction in the country where it is legal for members of the public to buy and use pepper spray.

The start of the NT trial faced community criticism, with more than 20 prominent organisations signing an open letter to the NT government warning its legalisation "risks escalating violent incidents".

Buyers mostly women, retailer says

Warren Smith, a local outdoor and fishing retailer, said he had sold at least 1,000 canisters of OC spray from his shop in the Darwin CBD.

"Ever since it came out, the most people that buy it, would be females," he said.

"I'd say anywhere from 20s, mid-20s, right up to 60s, that would be the main group that buy it.

" Most people, the ladies, say it's just to make them feel safe, when they go for a walk of the evening, or the morning. "

Warren Smith says most OC spray customers at his store have been women. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

Mr Smith said he believed the trial should become permanent, "if it makes people feel safe and it's something they can feel protected with".

OC spray used in recent incident

Just last month, a worker at a business in Palmerston deployed OC spray after she was allegedly assaulted.

Police allege a 34-year-old woman was throwing items in the store, and an accompanying 17-year-old physically assaulted the worker.

After they left the store, the worker allegedly followed them outside and deployed OC spray through the driver's side of the vehicle they were in.

The 17-year-old and the 34-year-old have since been charged over the alleged assaults.

A police spokesperson said the use of OC spray during the incident was still under investigation.

World.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launches legal action over Epstein files arrest
World.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against the police over his arrest in relation to the Epstein files earlier this year.

Britain's judicial office said a court hearing would take place on Thursday ​after the former prince and brother of King Charles requested that a judge examine ‌the lawfulness ⁠of search warrants that preceded his arrest ​in ‌February.

Britain's Thames ‌Valley Police issued a statement confirming they were ⁠engaged in legal proceedings.

"Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court," the brief statement said.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal titles in October 2025. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of leaking government documents to the late ​sex ‌offender Jeffrey Epstein when he was ⁠a special ‌representative for trade ‌between 2001 and 2011.

It is the first time a member of the royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since King Charles I's trial in 1649.

The arrest of the senior royal, eighth in line to the throne, was also unprecedented in modern times.

Ex-prince's emails in Epstein files

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested at his Norfolk home in February this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

King Charles's younger brother was interviewed for almost 12 hours before he was released under investigation.

The focus of the inquiry is the former prince's trade and investment role.

It followed the release of millions of documents by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) relating to Epstein.

In the glut of files was several emails that appeared to show Mr Mountbatten-Windsor forwarded on sensitive materials to Epstein in 2010.

Investigation into King Charles's brother, Andrew, will be lengthy, UK police say The British police investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor will be long and complex, senior officers say, after his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

Being named in the Epstein files is not an indication of misconduct, but trade envoys are required to maintain confidentiality over sensitive, commercial or political information related to their work.

The second son of the late Queen Elizabeth has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein and said he regretted their friendship.

He has made no public statement since his arrest.

In 2011, Mr Mountbatten-Windsor resigned as trade envoy.

Misconduct in public office, which carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, can relate to any serious wrongdoing from sharing confidential information to corruption and sexual misconduct.

In May, Thames Valley Police assistant chief constable Oliver Wright said the force was also assessing reports that a woman was taken to an address in Windsor in 2010 for sexual purposes after a lawyer for the alleged victim told the BBC she had been sent to Britain by Epstein for a sexual encounter with the former prince.

King Charles, who stripped his sibling of his titles and honours last October, said at the time of his brother's arrest that he was deeply concerned about the news.

He said authorities had the royal family's "full and wholehearted support and cooperation".

ABC/Reuters

World.title: The ‘loneliest place on Earth’ is a spectacular NZ spot most Australians miss
World.content:
InspirationCruises The ‘loneliest place on Earth’ is a spectacular NZ spot most Australians miss Craig Tansley October 6, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In 2025, 1.6 million cruise ship passengers visited Norway’s fjords, a record for that country. In the southern hemisphere’s version, New Zealand’s Fiordland, only its northern-most fjord, Milford Sound, garners real interest. Fiordland is made up of 14 fjords in the south-west of the South Island, spread across 12,000 square kilometres of a World Heritage-listed national park and is serviced by a handful of expedition boats. At about 40 kilometres long, Dusky Sound is the largest fjord in Fiordland. Mine is an 18-passenger, 24-metre-long cruising catamaran built for these fjords, and it’s not until day six of a six-night expedition that we actually see any other vessel at all – a lobster boat, with a crew of three. Captain James Cook was the first non-indigenous visitor here. On Cook’s second expedition in 1773, his naturalist, Johann Forster, described Fiordland’s isolation: “Here, was the deepest silence. Nature was hushed, not a breath of wind penetrated to this sheet of water enclosed by high mountains and great forests.”



In the 250 years since, nothing appears to have changed: there are no roads in, no towns, no indication humans were ever here at all. “Fiordland has to be the loneliest place on Earth,” our skipper, Francis Brundell, says. “It’s a beast. God, I love it.” 



Guests land directly on board Fiordland Jewel via its roof helipad. Not only is the helicopter flight convenient – as the pilot threads a path through tall snow-capped mountains, it provides a sense of scale to this wilderness. We emerge a couple of hundred metres above Preservation Inlet where our boat, Fiordland Jewel, sits at anchor, a helipad on its top deck. We will travel north from here through Chalky Inlet, Dusky Sound and Breaksea Sound, finishing in Doubtful Sound. Doubtful Sound, the deepest and second-largest fjord in New Zealand. iStock Though exactly where we go is anyone’s guess, even the skipper’s. “I know the beginning and the end point,” Brundell explains. “Then the rest is set by the weather. You can’t plan a trip in Fiordland, no two trips are the same.”



As we set off, bottlenose dolphins zero in on our bow, riding the waves we generate. These dolphins grow up to four metres long and weigh as much as a horse. I watch them surf from a small deck at the very front of the boat, their faces turn up to gawk at me. There are Fiordland crested penguins here too, and New Zealand fur seals. Both seem curious as we pass. When we anchor for the night, the silence is claustrophobic. Rain, a constant in these fjords, turns the steep slopes of the heavily forested mountains around us into waterfalls as far as I can see. The catamaran’s open-plan dining and lounge area. In the frigid evening air, the best place to observe Fiordland’s cascades (you won’t be able to count them all) is from the hot tub on the top deck. Visiting Fiordland, with its vegetation almost completely untouched over time, is one of the best ways to time travel to the ancient supercontinent Gondwanaland. In this twilight, it’s other-worldly.



This part of New Zealand has the longest European history of anywhere in the country. Once, more people lived here than anywhere else in New Zealand. In 1773, Captain Cook spent five weeks repairing his ship in Dusky Sound, which we reach after a bumpy ride on the Tasman Sea beside migrating humpback whales (the characteristics of fjords are such that they are separated by sea, so pack your sea legs). We retrace Cook’s crew’s foot expeditions. The forest paths take me beneath 1000-year-old beech trees and through thick green rainforest, where the sound of water cascading and running along swollen creeks is deafening. Here there are birds thought extinct; others such as the kakapo, the world’s heaviest parrot, are on the brink of extinction. The Fiordland Jewel’s Captain Cook cabin. One afternoon, we hike along and up a steep forest trail for two hours and are rewarded with the sound of two kakapo squawking in the canopy.



A fellow guest – who says he’s hiked practically every square inch of New Zealand except here – has tears in his eyes when he tells me that these are the first kakapo cries he’s ever heard. Another morning, I kayak across the fjords as inquisitive fur seal pups in the shallows, and dolphins in the deep, pass close by. Guests can take in the scenery from a kayak. After inspecting Cook’s maps of Dusky Sound, sealers and whalers arrived and established the first European settlements in New Zealand. In Preservation Inlet, gold was discovered resulting in a mini-boom and a township called Cromarty. Only the skeletons of these mines and buildings remain. Some days we help the crew drop lobster pots into the water and return the next to haul the pots, full of southern rock lobsters, up. Our chef serves the crustaceans, which can weigh up to nine kilograms, alongside blue cod and hapuku (groper) caught at sea between fjords. With such a small passenger load, meals are communal. Every day brings a new hike, or paddle, or a fishing session off the bottom deck. Though some days I prefer to simply stare at the surroundings, imagining Cook and his men battling their way through these dark tannin-stained waters, where deep-water marine species are tricked into living close to the surface.



Related Article New Zealand NZ’s adventure capital is transforming into something else It comes as a shock when, on day seven, we reach Doubtful Sound and see two small passenger boats. Apart from the lobster boat, we haven’t seen another person, or a building (which wasn’t a wreck), or even a single power line or communication tower. We take a dirt road to Manapouri where a ferry waits to take us across a lake and then we drive back to Queenstown. We mightn’t be far from civilisation as the crow (or helicopter) flies, but as soon as I leave this place it’s difficult to remember it in any detail. Why? That’s likely to be because nothing in the rest of my world is remotely like it. THE DETAILS



FLY

Fly to Queenstown with Virgin Australia, Jetstar or Qantas. See virginaustralia.com; jetstar.com; qantas.com CRUISE

Fiordland Discovery’s six-night Southern Fiords tour includes meals, activities, helicopter ride in and coach out, $NZ8500 ($6893) a person in a Captain Cook cabin that sleeps two. The season runs from May to September. See fiordlanddiscovery.co.nz MORE

World.title: Alex de Minaur books a spot in China Open final after semi-final twist
World.content:
SportTennisAlex de Minaur Alex de Minaur books a spot in China Open final after semi-final twist Trevor Marshallsea October 5, 2026 — 10:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur has won through to the China Open final after his semi-final opponent, Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz, retired injured while trailing in the second set in Beijing. De Minaur was up 6-4, 3-2 with a break of serve when Hurkacz pulled out while down 40-0 in the sixth game of the second set, after showing mobility problems. Alex De Minaur will now play in the final on Tuesday. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim The No. 9-ranked de Minaur will now pursue a 12th career title in the final against the winner out of sixth seed Novak Djokovic and the third-seeded Daniil Medvedev. Passage to Tuesday’s decider continued a strong turnaround for de Minaur after his tournament looked in doubt 24 hours earlier.



On Sunday, the 27-year-old was in dire trouble in his quarter-final against Russia’s Andrey Rublev after winning only one game in the first set, but came back to win 1-6 6-2 6-3. Monday continued the Australian’s sparkling form, though world No. 34 Hurkacz made him earn the win, despite coming in trailing de Minaur 3-1 on career meetings. De Minaur pounced immediately to break a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4-0, and again for 5-1. To his credit, Hurkacz steadied and after breaking back from deuce in the eighth game he held again to make it 5-4. De Minaur steeled himself, however, holding serve to 15 to take the set.



Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3-1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game - surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game - to make it 3-2. De Minaur consoles Hubert Hurkacz after he withdrew from the semi-final. Getty Images But he would see only three more points before withdrawing. In Tokyo, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz overcame early wobbles on his serve ‌to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5-7 6-3 6-1 ‌and reach the Japan Open final, ‌taking another step towards his first singles title after his comeback from a wrist injury.



Alcaraz completed the career grand slam by capturing the ‌Australian Open ‌title ⁠in February but sustained the injury ​two months later. Related Article Analysis

Tennis Australia Lleyton Hewitt says Australian tennis is struggling. Is he right? He came back at the US Open, where a quarter-final run hinted at a swift return to form. The 23-year-old, who ⁠moved through the ‌gears ​during Team Europe’s triumphant Laver Cup campaign in September, was ‌cruising against Munar in Tokyo at 5-4 ​before gifting the opening set to his opponent with two shaky service games. After a ​sluggish ​start to the ​next set - completing a run of 16 straight losing points - Alcaraz raised ‌his level to force a decider and the seven-time major champion wore Munar down with stunning shot-making to set up a title clash ​with either Jiri Lehecka or Valentin Vacherot ​on Tuesday.

World.title: Cat fight has Maylands residents at wits’ end
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAAnimal cruelty Cat fight has Maylands residents at wits’ end Andrew Du October 5, 2026 — 9:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Neighbours of a Maylands property allegedly housing more than a dozen cats claim persistent odours and roaming animals are making life unbearable. Residents on Caledonian Avenue claim cats from the home of 82-year-old Louise Jones regularly enter neighbouring properties and climb onto roofs. Dozens of cats living at a Maylands home are making life difficult for neighbours. “They came over the fence and hang around on our roof,” one neighbour, Lily, told 9News Perth. “The washing on the line, sometimes we have to take it in early so it doesn’t smell like cat.”



Another neighbour, Ryan Quinn, claimed he and his partner had barely used their backyard since moving in two years ago. “Anyone that’s cleaned a cat’s litter tray, it’s like that amplified a thousand-fold,” he said. There are allegedly more than a dozen cats living at the home. Concerns about the property date back about a decade, when more than 30 cats were living there and the City of Bayswater deemed the home unfit for human habitation. The city’s chief executive, Jeremy Edwards, said the council had responded to complaints since 2016 and was now investigating obtaining a warrant to re-enter the property to determine whether the state’s Cat Act has been breached.



He said the city had conducted numerous investigations, issued notices under the Health Act and exercised enforcement powers under its cat local law. Edwards alleged the property owner had repeatedly challenged the city’s actions through the State Administrative Tribunal. Property owners can keep up to three cats, which must be sterilised, microchipped and registered. Jones is also facing 12 animal cruelty charges brought by RSPCA WA. The RSPCA alleges a dozen cats were confined between December 2024 and June 2025 in a way that caused, or was likely to cause, harm.



It also alleges Jones allowed the animals to suffer harm that could have been alleviated by taking reasonable steps. Jones is due in Perth Magistrates Court next week. 9News Perth approached Jones at her Maylands home for comment but received no response.

World.title: Joey starts a movement
World.content:
For Brian Richardson of MacMasters Beach, “A topical celebrity encounter (C8) occurred about 10 years ago, when I was selling copies of Big League magazine for Rotary at Penrith Stadium. Andrew ‘Joey’ Johns approached, and I expected either a sale or some words of wisdom on the game. Alas, all he said was ‘Where are the toilets, mate?’”

Bart Fielden of Avoca Beach attended his sister’s 21st at “the trendiest restaurant in Kings Cross” and “was talking over my shoulder and walked straight into a gentleman, making him trip and fall flat on his arse. As I apologised and started to help him up, I felt I recognised him from somewhere. The penny dropped when I saw his tall red-haired date. As I helped Tom Cruise up, he was staring daggers at me. Thankfully Nicole thought it was hilarious, and as the security detail swooped in, she waved them off, saying ‘Don’t worry, he’s just a kid.’ I’m not sure if I’d have survived if she wasn’t there.”

″Jo Rainbow, I’m not sure if Eine Kleine Nachtmusik would deter bogong moths (C8), but it would certainly deter me,” thinks Greg Oehm of Western Creek (Tas). “I can’t stand the dreadful thing. I’m just grateful bogong moths are a problem we don’t have here in Tasmania!”

Warren Menteith of Bali isn’t sure about music deterring pests but can guarantee that “playing Barry Manilow at shopping centres deters teenagers from hanging out”.

“I have an EV and don’t need to buy anything from a servo,” informs Manbir Singh Kohli of Pemulwuy. “However, I still need to pump up my tyres, a courtesy service that servos provide for their customers. I feel like I am stealing something when I use their air service for free. What’s the protocol?”

World.title: Details of accused hijack co-pilot’s Melbourne studies revealed
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastAviation Details of accused hijack co-pilot’s Melbourne studies revealed Alexander Cornwell and Maayan Lubell Updated October 5, 2026 — 8:49pm ,first published 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jerusalem: The flydubai co-pilot who allegedly stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane last week told interrogators in the United Arab Emirates he planned to do so before being hired by the airline, according to two Israeli officials with knowledge of the probe. A third source briefed on the UAE investigation said the co-pilot, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, planned to crash Wednesday’s flight into Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but chose not to, the source said. Omani pilot Hammam al-Hammami is accused of attacking his colleague on a flydubai flight to Israel. LinkedIn It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although he is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said. The sources all spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did flydubai.



On Monday night, RMIT university confirmed reports that al-Hammami was a student of theirs between 2015 and 2017, though he did not complete his undergraduate mechanical engineering degree. Related Article Aviation Flydubai co-pilot allegedly wielded axe in attempted terrorist attack “RMIT has been [helping] the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team with their investigation and importantly, there is no security threat to RMIT,” acting vice-chancellor Catherine Itsiopoulos wrote in a confidential email to the institution’s leadership team. Al-Hammami, the co-pilot on flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai last Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the UAE prosecutor general has said. The prosecutor called the incident a “terrorist attack”. The airline and Israeli and UAE officials have not named the co-pilot but have said he is from Oman. Two sources have confirmed his identity as Hamam al-Hammami.



Reuters has been unable to independently reach al-Hammami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal charges against him and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident. The two Israeli officials said the co-pilot told interrogators he had applied for a job at Dubai state-owned flydubai after searching for airlines that flew to Tel Aviv. The third source said the UAE was continually updating Israel about the investigation. A disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted when passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot after he allegedly stabbed the pilot. Loading



The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been hailed as a hero for managing to open the cockpit door to allow passengers to subdue the co-pilot. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling ​on the flight took control of ⁠the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and then transferred to the UAE on Thursday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots who are citizens of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with, such as Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is unclear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv, and Netanyahu has since ordered a review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.

World.title: An empire on the edge of a cliff: Inside Sam Wood’s rise to fame and fortune
World.content:
In 2015, Sam Wood was just another personal trainer working at a gym in Melbourne’s south-east. But after a stint on the third season of The Bachelor, his career quickly took off. So much so, that years later he sold his online fitness business to a Melbourne billionaire for $71 million. The father of four also earned a $6 million windfall following the sale of his family home in Elsternwick in May, and recently bought a $7.1 million property in Brighton, and a $2.7 million Mount Martha pad. Bachelor star Sam Wood, pictured with wife Snezana, has been charged with domestic violence offences. Getty Images Though the 46-year-old has shared much of his life on social media over the past 11 years, by Monday morning, commenting was turned off across all his social media accounts, and those linked to his wife, Snezana, and their four daughters. Wood’s empire and fortune are built on the empowerment of women. But all of that is now in danger after he was charged with domestic violence offences in Queensland on Sunday.

World.title: The ‘loneliest place on Earth’ is a spectacular NZ spot most Australians miss
World.content:
InspirationCruises The ‘loneliest place on Earth’ is a spectacular NZ spot most Australians miss Craig Tansley October 6, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In 2025, 1.6 million cruise ship passengers visited Norway’s fjords, a record for that country. In the southern hemisphere’s version, New Zealand’s Fiordland, only its northern-most fjord, Milford Sound, garners real interest. Fiordland is made up of 14 fjords in the south-west of the South Island, spread across 12,000 square kilometres of a World Heritage-listed national park and is serviced by a handful of expedition boats. At about 40 kilometres long, Dusky Sound is the largest fjord in Fiordland. Mine is an 18-passenger, 24-metre-long cruising catamaran built for these fjords, and it’s not until day six of a six-night expedition that we actually see any other vessel at all – a lobster boat, with a crew of three. Captain James Cook was the first non-indigenous visitor here. On Cook’s second expedition in 1773, his naturalist, Johann Forster, described Fiordland’s isolation: “Here, was the deepest silence. Nature was hushed, not a breath of wind penetrated to this sheet of water enclosed by high mountains and great forests.”



In the 250 years since, nothing appears to have changed: there are no roads in, no towns, no indication humans were ever here at all. “Fiordland has to be the loneliest place on Earth,” our skipper, Francis Brundell, says. “It’s a beast. God, I love it.” 



Guests land directly on board Fiordland Jewel via its roof helipad. Not only is the helicopter flight convenient – as the pilot threads a path through tall snow-capped mountains, it provides a sense of scale to this wilderness. We emerge a couple of hundred metres above Preservation Inlet where our boat, Fiordland Jewel, sits at anchor, a helipad on its top deck. We will travel north from here through Chalky Inlet, Dusky Sound and Breaksea Sound, finishing in Doubtful Sound. Doubtful Sound, the deepest and second-largest fjord in New Zealand. iStock Though exactly where we go is anyone’s guess, even the skipper’s. “I know the beginning and the end point,” Brundell explains. “Then the rest is set by the weather. You can’t plan a trip in Fiordland, no two trips are the same.”



As we set off, bottlenose dolphins zero in on our bow, riding the waves we generate. These dolphins grow up to four metres long and weigh as much as a horse. I watch them surf from a small deck at the very front of the boat, their faces turn up to gawk at me. There are Fiordland crested penguins here too, and New Zealand fur seals. Both seem curious as we pass. When we anchor for the night, the silence is claustrophobic. Rain, a constant in these fjords, turns the steep slopes of the heavily forested mountains around us into waterfalls as far as I can see. The catamaran’s open-plan dining and lounge area. In the frigid evening air, the best place to observe Fiordland’s cascades (you won’t be able to count them all) is from the hot tub on the top deck. Visiting Fiordland, with its vegetation almost completely untouched over time, is one of the best ways to time travel to the ancient supercontinent Gondwanaland. In this twilight, it’s other-worldly.



This part of New Zealand has the longest European history of anywhere in the country. Once, more people lived here than anywhere else in New Zealand. In 1773, Captain Cook spent five weeks repairing his ship in Dusky Sound, which we reach after a bumpy ride on the Tasman Sea beside migrating humpback whales (the characteristics of fjords are such that they are separated by sea, so pack your sea legs). We retrace Cook’s crew’s foot expeditions. The forest paths take me beneath 1000-year-old beech trees and through thick green rainforest, where the sound of water cascading and running along swollen creeks is deafening. Here there are birds thought extinct; others such as the kakapo, the world’s heaviest parrot, are on the brink of extinction. The Fiordland Jewel’s Captain Cook cabin. One afternoon, we hike along and up a steep forest trail for two hours and are rewarded with the sound of two kakapo squawking in the canopy.



A fellow guest – who says he’s hiked practically every square inch of New Zealand except here – has tears in his eyes when he tells me that these are the first kakapo cries he’s ever heard. Another morning, I kayak across the fjords as inquisitive fur seal pups in the shallows, and dolphins in the deep, pass close by. Guests can take in the scenery from a kayak. After inspecting Cook’s maps of Dusky Sound, sealers and whalers arrived and established the first European settlements in New Zealand. In Preservation Inlet, gold was discovered resulting in a mini-boom and a township called Cromarty. Only the skeletons of these mines and buildings remain. Some days we help the crew drop lobster pots into the water and return the next to haul the pots, full of southern rock lobsters, up. Our chef serves the crustaceans, which can weigh up to nine kilograms, alongside blue cod and hapuku (groper) caught at sea between fjords. With such a small passenger load, meals are communal. Every day brings a new hike, or paddle, or a fishing session off the bottom deck. Though some days I prefer to simply stare at the surroundings, imagining Cook and his men battling their way through these dark tannin-stained waters, where deep-water marine species are tricked into living close to the surface.



Related Article New Zealand NZ’s adventure capital is transforming into something else It comes as a shock when, on day seven, we reach Doubtful Sound and see two small passenger boats. Apart from the lobster boat, we haven’t seen another person, or a building (which wasn’t a wreck), or even a single power line or communication tower. We take a dirt road to Manapouri where a ferry waits to take us across a lake and then we drive back to Queenstown. We mightn’t be far from civilisation as the crow (or helicopter) flies, but as soon as I leave this place it’s difficult to remember it in any detail. Why? That’s likely to be because nothing in the rest of my world is remotely like it. THE DETAILS



FLY

Fly to Queenstown with Virgin Australia, Jetstar or Qantas. See virginaustralia.com; jetstar.com; qantas.com CRUISE

Fiordland Discovery’s six-night Southern Fiords tour includes meals, activities, helicopter ride in and coach out, $NZ8500 ($6893) a person in a Captain Cook cabin that sleeps two. The season runs from May to September. See fiordlanddiscovery.co.nz MORE

World.content:
SportTennisAlex de Minaur Alex de Minaur books a spot in China Open final after semi-final twist Trevor Marshallsea October 5, 2026 — 10:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur has won through to the China Open final after his semi-final opponent, Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz, retired injured while trailing in the second set in Beijing. De Minaur was up 6-4, 3-2 with a break of serve when Hurkacz pulled out while down 40-0 in the sixth game of the second set, after showing mobility problems. Alex De Minaur will now play in the final on Tuesday. AP Photo/Achmad Ibrahim The No. 9-ranked de Minaur will now pursue a 12th career title in the final against the winner out of sixth seed Novak Djokovic and the third-seeded Daniil Medvedev. Passage to Tuesday’s decider continued a strong turnaround for de Minaur after his tournament looked in doubt 24 hours earlier.



On Sunday, the 27-year-old was in dire trouble in his quarter-final against Russia’s Andrey Rublev after winning only one game in the first set, but came back to win 1-6 6-2 6-3. Monday continued the Australian’s sparkling form, though world No. 34 Hurkacz made him earn the win, despite coming in trailing de Minaur 3-1 on career meetings. De Minaur pounced immediately to break a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4-0, and again for 5-1. To his credit, Hurkacz steadied and after breaking back from deuce in the eighth game he held again to make it 5-4. De Minaur steeled himself, however, holding serve to 15 to take the set.



Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3-1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game - surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game - to make it 3-2. De Minaur consoles Hubert Hurkacz after he withdrew from the semi-final. Getty Images But he would see only three more points before withdrawing. In Tokyo, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz overcame early wobbles on his serve ‌to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5-7 6-3 6-1 ‌and reach the Japan Open final, ‌taking another step towards his first singles title after his comeback from a wrist injury.



Alcaraz completed the career grand slam by capturing the ‌Australian Open ‌title ⁠in February but sustained the injury ​two months later. Related Article Analysis

Tennis Australia Lleyton Hewitt says Australian tennis is struggling. Is he right? He came back at the US Open, where a quarter-final run hinted at a swift return to form. The 23-year-old, who ⁠moved through the ‌gears ​during Team Europe’s triumphant Laver Cup campaign in September, was ‌cruising against Munar in Tokyo at 5-4 ​before gifting the opening set to his opponent with two shaky service games. After a ​sluggish ​start to the ​next set - completing a run of 16 straight losing points - Alcaraz raised ‌his level to force a decider and the seven-time major champion wore Munar down with stunning shot-making to set up a title clash ​with either Jiri Lehecka or Valentin Vacherot ​on Tuesday.

World.title: Cat fight has Maylands residents at wits’ end
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAAnimal cruelty Cat fight has Maylands residents at wits’ end Andrew Du October 5, 2026 — 9:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Neighbours of a Maylands property allegedly housing more than a dozen cats claim persistent odours and roaming animals are making life unbearable. Residents on Caledonian Avenue claim cats from the home of 82-year-old Louise Jones regularly enter neighbouring properties and climb onto roofs. Dozens of cats living at a Maylands home are making life difficult for neighbours. “They came over the fence and hang around on our roof,” one neighbour, Lily, told 9News Perth. “The washing on the line, sometimes we have to take it in early so it doesn’t smell like cat.”



Another neighbour, Ryan Quinn, claimed he and his partner had barely used their backyard since moving in two years ago. “Anyone that’s cleaned a cat’s litter tray, it’s like that amplified a thousand-fold,” he said. There are allegedly more than a dozen cats living at the home. Concerns about the property date back about a decade, when more than 30 cats were living there and the City of Bayswater deemed the home unfit for human habitation. The city’s chief executive, Jeremy Edwards, said the council had responded to complaints since 2016 and was now investigating obtaining a warrant to re-enter the property to determine whether the state’s Cat Act has been breached.



He said the city had conducted numerous investigations, issued notices under the Health Act and exercised enforcement powers under its cat local law. Edwards alleged the property owner had repeatedly challenged the city’s actions through the State Administrative Tribunal. Property owners can keep up to three cats, which must be sterilised, microchipped and registered. Jones is also facing 12 animal cruelty charges brought by RSPCA WA. The RSPCA alleges a dozen cats were confined between December 2024 and June 2025 in a way that caused, or was likely to cause, harm.



It also alleges Jones allowed the animals to suffer harm that could have been alleviated by taking reasonable steps. Jones is due in Perth Magistrates Court next week. 9News Perth approached Jones at her Maylands home for comment but received no response.

World.title: Joey starts a movement
World.content:
For Brian Richardson of MacMasters Beach, “A topical celebrity encounter (C8) occurred about 10 years ago, when I was selling copies of Big League magazine for Rotary at Penrith Stadium. Andrew ‘Joey’ Johns approached, and I expected either a sale or some words of wisdom on the game. Alas, all he said was ‘Where are the toilets, mate?’”

Bart Fielden of Avoca Beach attended his sister’s 21st at “the trendiest restaurant in Kings Cross” and “was talking over my shoulder and walked straight into a gentleman, making him trip and fall flat on his arse. As I apologised and started to help him up, I felt I recognised him from somewhere. The penny dropped when I saw his tall red-haired date. As I helped Tom Cruise up, he was staring daggers at me. Thankfully Nicole thought it was hilarious, and as the security detail swooped in, she waved them off, saying ‘Don’t worry, he’s just a kid.’ I’m not sure if I’d have survived if she wasn’t there.”

″Jo Rainbow, I’m not sure if Eine Kleine Nachtmusik would deter bogong moths (C8), but it would certainly deter me,” thinks Greg Oehm of Western Creek (Tas). “I can’t stand the dreadful thing. I’m just grateful bogong moths are a problem we don’t have here in Tasmania!”

Warren Menteith of Bali isn’t sure about music deterring pests but can guarantee that “playing Barry Manilow at shopping centres deters teenagers from hanging out”.

“I have an EV and don’t need to buy anything from a servo,” informs Manbir Singh Kohli of Pemulwuy. “However, I still need to pump up my tyres, a courtesy service that servos provide for their customers. I feel like I am stealing something when I use their air service for free. What’s the protocol?”

World.title: Details of accused hijack co-pilot’s Melbourne studies revealed
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastAviation Details of accused hijack co-pilot’s Melbourne studies revealed Alexander Cornwell and Maayan Lubell Updated October 5, 2026 — 8:49pm ,first published 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jerusalem: The flydubai co-pilot who allegedly stabbed his captain in a suspected attempt to crash the plane last week told interrogators in the United Arab Emirates he planned to do so before being hired by the airline, according to two Israeli officials with knowledge of the probe. A third source briefed on the UAE investigation said the co-pilot, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, planned to crash Wednesday’s flight into Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but chose not to, the source said. Omani pilot Hammam al-Hammami is accused of attacking his colleague on a flydubai flight to Israel. LinkedIn It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although he is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said. The sources all spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did flydubai.



On Monday night, RMIT university confirmed reports that al-Hammami was a student of theirs between 2015 and 2017, though he did not complete his undergraduate mechanical engineering degree. Related Article Aviation Flydubai co-pilot allegedly wielded axe in attempted terrorist attack “RMIT has been [helping] the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team with their investigation and importantly, there is no security threat to RMIT,” acting vice-chancellor Catherine Itsiopoulos wrote in a confidential email to the institution’s leadership team. Al-Hammami, the co-pilot on flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai last Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the UAE prosecutor general has said. The prosecutor called the incident a “terrorist attack”. The airline and Israeli and UAE officials have not named the co-pilot but have said he is from Oman. Two sources have confirmed his identity as Hamam al-Hammami.



Reuters has been unable to independently reach al-Hammami, who is in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal charges against him and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident. The two Israeli officials said the co-pilot told interrogators he had applied for a job at Dubai state-owned flydubai after searching for airlines that flew to Tel Aviv. The third source said the UAE was continually updating Israel about the investigation. A disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted when passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot after he allegedly stabbed the pilot. Loading



The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been hailed as a hero for managing to open the cockpit door to allow passengers to subdue the co-pilot. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling ​on the flight took control of ⁠the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and then transferred to the UAE on Thursday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said pilots who are citizens of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with, such as Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is unclear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv, and Netanyahu has since ordered a review of foreign airlines flying to Israel.
