World.title: Japan wins Kirin Cup with 2-1 victory over All Whites at Tokyo National Stadium
World.content:
The All Whites have lost the Kirin Cup final against Japan, despite putting on a brave defence.

The host side proved too strong for the New Zealanders at Tokyo National Stadium, with Doan's close-range winner settling the contest after some excellent work from Nakamura down the left.

Like the World Cup, the All Whites were asked to defend for long spells and were largely successful in repelling deliveries into the box. However, once the game became more stretched, Japan proved too dangerous around the area.

New Zealand's international window now comes to a close with the players set to return to their clubs. The All Whites will next be back in action at home in November, taking on India in a two-match series, first at Go Media Stadium before making history with their first-ever match at One New Zealand Stadium in Christchurch.

See how the game unfolded in our blog:

World.title: Two dead, one seriously injured in Dairy Flat crash near Auckland
World.content:
Two people have died after a crash involving a truck and two vehicles in North Auckland this afternoon.

Police were called to the accident on Dairy Flat Highway at 2.30pm on Monday.

They said two people were pronounced dead at the scene, while a third person was taken to hospital in a serious condition.

The road was closed between Postman Road and Horseshoe Bush Road, but has now reopened.

World.title: Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking fellow pilot had spent time in NZ, police confirm
World.content:
The Omani co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a Flydubai flight in a bloody attack last week had spent time in New Zealand, police have confirmed.

Hammam al-Hammami has been named as the co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague Captain Smit Machchhar on board Flight FZ1073 bound for Israel, and trying to seize controls of the flight.

Last week's flight - carrying more than 170 passengers - dropped 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds, according to Reuters.

Machchhar was covered in blood when he managed to release the cockpit door, which allowed passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and regain control of the flight.

International investigators are still working to determine a motive for the attempted hijacking.

NZ Police assistant commissioner Michael Johnson said police were aware that Hammam al-Hammami had spent time in New Zealand.

"We are looking into the time he spent here, alongside other agencies where appropriate.

"We are unable to comment further at this time," he said in a statement to RNZ.

Captain Machchhar completed his early flight training in New Zealand 18 years ago with Mainland Air.

Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean told RNZ he was pleased with how his former student managed the ordeal.

Immigration New Zealand declined to answer RNZ's queries including when Hammam al-Hammami entered NZ; what type of visa he had and whether he had a student visa to undergo pilot training in NZ; and whether INZ identified any security issues during his visa application process.

It said in a statement: "New Zealand Police are the lead agency for this matter. Please direct any further questions to them."

World.title: Demand surges for telehealth ADHD assessments
World.content:
Telehealth services are offering assessments for ADHD, as some people seeking a diagnosis for the condition don't want to wait months for an in-person consultation.

Since February, GPs and nurse practitioners have been able to diagnose ADHD and prescribe medication for it.

It isn't mandatory for GPs and nurse practitioners to specialise in ADHD, meaning many GP practices aren't offering the service.

That means many people are turning to virtual assessments instead. After suspecting for a few years that she may have ADHD, Nikki (who didn't want her surname used) decided to act last year.

She had seen that GPs would soon be offering assessments so, after hearing about the long wait times and high cost of getting diagnosed through a psychiatrist, she thought she'd see her doctor when the rules changed.

But when February rolled around, her Palmerston North GP gave her the news she didn't want to hear.

"So I went to my GP and said 'Hey I'd like to do this, and she was like huh we don't do that here in Palmy, we haven't got a collective of GPs to be able to do that yet, maybe in July we might have one, do you want to wait?' And I was like no."

Frustrated she had waited longer for no reason; she was referred to an online telehealth service.

Her teenage son was also diagnosed through telehealth, and she said for both of them it was pretty much smooth sailing, bar the cost.

"You go to book and it was like $972 and you had to pay upfront, so I kind of prioritised [my son's] one first, and then I did mine a few months later."

Stuart Cowley (left). Supplied

Despite the cost, Nikki said that finally getting a diagnosis was more than worth it.

"It's changed our lives, we can concentrate. My son in particular can sit at the desk I bought him five years ago which is amazing, and for me it just means I can pay attention more in meetings."

After spending his whole life being labelled a 'poster boy' for ADHD, at 53, Stuart Cowley decided it was time to get assessed.

Like Nikki, he'd heard about the GP changes and decided to wait for nearly a year until they were brought in.

"We did some research into looking into getting it done privately and then we held off specifically for the reason that I would have preferred to go to my own GP obviously having that connection already and her understanding me as a person."

But, like Nikki, his GP didn't offer the service.

Cowley ending up choosing a telehealth service and was diagnosed by a psychiatrist.

He said the hour and half online consultation was simple, and two weeks later he received the diagnosis he was expecting, something he said had been a gamechanger.

"If we'd had known the GPs weren't going to be doing it then we could have got it underway a lot quicker."

Stuart Cowley and Nikki are part of a growing number of Kiwis getting assessed for ADHD via telehealth.

One of those services is ADHD Simple, which also operates in the UK and Australia.

Founder Cameron Houston set up the company after struggling to get his own ADHD diagnosis in New Zealand.

Once he had established the service overseas, he decided to launch in New Zealand after hearing about the changes allowing doctors and nurse practitioners to assess for ADHD.

"It's been a bit of a rollercoaster, demand has been very high, very quickly, I think as soon as we established a name for ourselves, and what we stood for and what we were able to deliver, demand has, I'd say that demand in the early stage has outstripped supply."

Not everyone is convinced by the online model, with some clinicians worried about the level of service offered over the phone.

President of the Royal New Zealand College of GPs, Dr Luke Bradford, said while it was a positive for those living rurally, telehealth had its drawbacks.

"They're not able to do the complete job and they're often not following up either, often there's a diagnosis, and 'ok we think they've got it', and starts giving notes back to the GP as opposed to an ongoing treatment plan, and they can't see and examine the patient in person.

"So, I don't think it's the best model for this, but it certainly is an option, given the examination is essentially verbal as opposed to putting your hands on someone to examine."

Psychiatrist Dr Caleb Armstrong has been doing ADHD assessments via telehealth service, Validus, since 2019.

He said telehealth was now a standard part of healthcare, and the level of service and experience clinicians were offering was more important than the form in which it was delivered.

"Whether a service is telehealth or not is not much of a marker of its quality. It's been well established for many years that telepsychiatry for instance is equivalent for outcomes, and much better for access compared to going and having to see a doctor in person."

Dr Bradford said he worried that telehealth providers could be missing out on checking blood pressure and doing echocardiograms, both important checks during an ADHD diagnosis.

World.title: Loafers Lodge blaze: Manslaughter trial begins in Wellington
World.content:
The deaths of five men killed in the 2023 Loafers Lodge blaze in Wellington were avoidable, a jury has been told.

The Crown has opened its case against four people facing manslaughter charges over "layers of failings" in management of the budget accommodation's fire safety system.

Gregory Bruce Mein, 73, Barry Charles Collins, 76, Glenn Brendan McAllister, 59, and Marie Louise Murphy, 71, appeared in the High Court at Wellington on Monday.

Esarona Lologa was last year sentenced to life in prison after being found guilty of murder and arson for deliberately lighting the fire on 16 May 2023 that killed Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings.

According to the Crown, Murphy was the lodge's part-time property manager, while Mein was the director. Both McAllister and Collins were residents who had access to the fire safety system, it said.

The four each face five charges of gross negligence causing death. They also face, in the alternative, five charges of breaching health and safety, thereby committing manslaughter.

A jury of five men and seven women heard the first of the Crown's opening address on Monday.

The fire on 16 May 2023 claimed five lives. Denise Garland

Prosecutor Stephanie Bishop told jurors that while Lologa lit the fatal fire at 12.12am on 16 May, the trial would cover why it took 12 minutes for a 111 call to be made, 13 minutes for the fire safety system to activate, and why an alarm only sounded on the lower floors.

She said minutes and seconds mattered. "Flames move fast, smoke even faster."

That night, firefighters arrived to a chaotic scene, she said, and reports of people trapped on the upper levels of the three-storey building - but after evacuating some residents, they were forced to withdraw for safety reasons.

"The Crown says that if the building's fire safety system was working as it should have been, the five residents who died would have had the opportunity to escape and would have likely survived."

She said alarms were frequent at the building - which housed about 90 people, mainly men of lower socio-economic status - but over the years fire safety systems had degraded.

"Years prior to the fatal fire a practice emerged at Loafers Lodge allowing residents to both silence and also reset the fire alarm system.

"And that was, the Crown says, done in an attempt to save costs."

Bishop said this practice took place under the authority of Murphy, the property manager.

As director of the lodge, she said Mein held overall responsibility and had a duty to ensure the fire safety system worked.

Bishop said the fatal fire in the early hours of 16 May was the second lit by Lologa that night.

She said the first fire activated the fire safety system as it should, sounding alarms and closing fire-proof doors.

Collins - just one of the residents who had access - silenced the alarm but did not investigate the cause, she said.

McAllister, described as the building's fire warden and Murphy's second-in-charge, would reset the system, Bishop said, but did not do so that night, allowing the second fire to spread undetected.

She said when McAllister was finally roused by residents from his room, he called 111.

Bishop said Collins carried out his duties on a voluntary basis, while McAllister did so for cash.

She said there was no evacuation procedure in place at the lodge and it was left up to residents to alert emergency services.

The building's fire alarm system was not connected to automatically alert Fire and Emergency or monitored by an independent company, she said.

"It should have been.

"The Crown says that this is a case of layers of failings of management and those who held a quasi-management and fire warden role.

"These failings were both systemic and long-standing they were also specific on the night of the fire."

The Crown is expected to continue its opening statements on Tuesday, followed by the defence.

World.title: High Court urged to acknowledge Bill of Rights breach in recent electoral changes
World.content:
Courts do not need to declare recent electoral changes breach the Bill of Rights Act (BORA), because any future government would already know, according to the Crown.

But Christopher Carrol - who is seeking a declaration of inconsistency in the High Court regarding the government's controversial 13-day voter enrolment deadline - says given the concession from the Crown the Bill of Rights Act had been breached, there was a need for the court to both acknowledge and respond in some manner.

Justice David Boldt, presiding over the case, said he would not be silent on the "seriousness" of the breach: "The only question is whether that needs to be a declaration, or whether something… a bit lower voltage will do the trick."

Peter Gunn, representing the Attorney-General, said Carrol's argument was "unconvincing".

"What is the court actually going to be telling Parliament, even a new Parliament, that it doesn't already know?" he said.

Justice Boldt also asked what "value" it would add to tell Parliament something it "plainly already knows", given the law was passed knowing it breached the BORA.

Parliament's "eyes were wide open, and it made that decision anyway", he said.

Justice Boldt was concerned about "potential eye rolling" on the part of the Parliament, but indicated he was "certainly not going to remain silent about the breach or the seriousness of it".

The case was heard at the Wellington High Court on Monday and focused on the Electoral Amendment Act, which among other things ends same-day voter enrolment and requires people to enroll at least 13 days before the election.

The legislation was found to be inconsistent with the BORA and the changes to enrolments could prevent 100,000 or more people from voting.

The Government said the bill would improve the timeliness, efficiency and integrity of elections.

The Electoral Commission has said official election results would not be available any sooner based on changes, but Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith argued without any changes, it could get worse.

Carroll, a law student at Waikato University, wanted the declaration to state the 13-day enrolment deadline was inconsistent with the right to vote in the BORA because people will be disenfranchised.

"It's really important that people hear from the court that a right fundamental to our democracy has been breached by Parliament," he told RNZ.

"If the court is essentially saying that Parliament hasn't given due weight to the right to vote, then that's an important finding, and I think New Zealanders will see that as an important finding."

He was concerned for those people most impacted by the change.

Gunn, the Crown lawyer, acknowledged the legislation was not BORA compliant, but noted that did not prevent Parliament from passing laws.

In July 2025, then Attorney-General Judith Collins found the bill to be inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act and indicated 100,000 or more people could be directly or indirectly disenfranchised by the rules banning enrolment in the final 13 days before an election.

"Taking into account these factors, I conclude the proposal for a 13-day registration deadline appears to constitute an unjustified limit on s12 of the NZBORA," she wrote in her report, noting Māori, Asian and Pasifika communities, and younger people would be more affected by the deadline.

Gunn said on Monday the attorney-general's report was accepted by government and formed part of the parliamentary debates on the legislation.

Declarations serve as a formal judicial mechanism to show a law infringes on basic rights in a way that can't be justified in a "free and democratic society".

Carroll argued the declaration would go before a new parliament and to deny it one would deprive a new Parliament of an "authoritative understanding of the inconsistency and demonstrability of the enrolment deadline in relation to the right to vote".

He said he was thinking of the future and how the court's decision informs a future Attorney-General of apparent inconsistency.

Gunn said that argument was "unconvincing", and there was no need.

Justice Boldt said he likely would not reach a decision ahead of the election, and no decision would have an impact on the law itself.
