Tech.title: The Best Gifts Under $25 for Everyone on Your List (2026)
Tech.content:
$25 doesn’t go as far as it used to. As recently as a decade ago, $25 could fill up your gas tank and buy a pretty good gift, with plenty of options for just about every interest and occasion. Nowadays, it’s a struggle to even find a $25 takeout meal for one person and average national gas prices are inching toward $5 a gallon. And we all know wages have not kept up.

Good news: There are still plenty of thoughtful, interesting items out there to be had for $25, which are sure to appeal to everyone from coworkers to neighbors, relatives you don’t know well, and the friend who seems to have everything. All things on this list have been tested and vetted by at least one person on the WIRED Reviews team—often more than one—to ensure it is indeed a good gift you’d be proud to give. Check out more of our gift guides to find something for everyone on your list this year.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

For the Notetaker

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist MoMA Design Store Colorplay Pen & Pencil Cup Holder $15 MoMA Design Store WIRED senior Gear editor Julian Chokkattu recommends this colorful acrylic desk accessory that keeps pencils, scissors, and other large items on top and smaller items like paper clips (or, in Julian’s case as a phone reviewer, SIM ejection pins) on the bottom. Shown is the pink-and-amber color combination, but there’s also a blue-and-green option.

Photograph: Field Notes Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Field Notes National Parks Series (3-Pack) $15 Amazon (Denali, Cuyahoga, Olympic) $15 Amazon (Glacier, Hawai'i Volcanoes, Everglades) $15 Field Notes I’ve used Field Notes for years—they’re lightweight, sturdy, and a perfectly pocketable. The National Parks Series elevates what would otherwise be a utilitarian notebook to its giftable status, with artist-created covers inspired by our nation’s natural wonders—from Acadia to the Hawaii Volcanoes. Courtesy of Muji Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Muji Ballpoint Pens (10 Pack) $19 Muji My city recently got its own brick-and-mortar Muji store, and if you’ve never visited the famed Japanese retailer in person, it’s basically a mecca for stationery and desk accessories. These pens in particular are famous for their smooth ink and precision tips, and make a perfect companion for the Field Notes notebooks at left.

For the Party Person

Photograph: Nena Farrell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Puffin Drinkwear $20 Puffin (The Fleece) $25 Puffin (The Alpine) $25 Puffin (The Resort) These drink cozies are a favored white elephant gift from WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell (“It’s like playing Barbie with your drinks,” she says), but I like them because they remind me of Will Ferrell and his friend Harper Steele in the movie Will & Harper, where they go on a road trip, dress up their drinks in these exact cozies, and come up with ridiculous names for them like Cornelius Danderhoff. It reminds me of road trips I took with friends in college, which reminds me that I’m old, which … makes me want a drink.

Courtesy of Govee Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Govee Smart LED Color-Changing Light Bulb (H6008) $15 $13 (13% off) Amazon Set the right vibe in any room with this WIRED-recommended, Matter-compatible smart light bulb that features millions of colors, scenes, and effects you can control with Alexa, Google Assistant, or the Govee app. You can also sync it to music with the latter, using the microphone on your phone. Photograph: Parker Hall Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Bonaok Karaoke Microphone $21 $18 (14% off) Amazon Let your giftee be heard wherever they go with their very own Bluetooth microphone. Former WIRED A/V editor Parker Hall especially liked this one for its series of playback and mixing controls, in addition to adjustable volume, echo effects, and the ability to play, skip, or pause your backing track.

For the Anti-Party Person

Photograph: Louryn Strampe

Photograph: Louryn Strampe

Courtesy of Quince Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Quince Mulberry Silk Beauty Sleep Mask $20 Quince A sleep mask is a must for proper sleep hygiene, and WIRED reviewer and sleep mask aficionado Louryn Strampe loves the roomy fit of this 22-momme silk model from Quince. It’s half the price of similar 100-percent silk sleep masks, and there’s free shipping to keep things affordable. Choose from among 12 color options, including Eucalyptus, Espresso, Pink, Terra Cotta, and Light Blue.

Courtesy of Amazon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Loop Quiet 2 Ear Plugs $25 Amazon $25 Loop Crowned our best earplugs for sleep, the silicone Loop Quiet 2 are capable of blocking out 24 dB and fit entirely flush with your head, ensuring that they’re perfectly comfortable when you lie on your side. The little handle makes them easy to pull out, and they come in four fun colors with a variety of ear tips to ensure your giftee can get the perfect fit. Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck

Video: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Diveblues Portable Handheld Fan $20 Amazon Help your giftee’s personal space stay cool and fresh with this 4-in-1 fan, the best handheld fan I’ve personally tried. You can set it on a table or desk, hold it in your hand, clip it onto something with the bottom carabiner, or wear it around your neck. It’s plenty quiet enough to hold a conversation over, and it comes in four fun colors.

For the Home Chef

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Jacobsen Salt Co. Salt and Salt Cellar $15 Jacobsen Salt Co. (Salt) $25 Jacobsen Salt Co. (Salt Cellar) My entire family is obsessed with this finishing salt, which is harvested in Netarts Bay, Oregon, just a couple of hours from our house. The large, irregular crystals look (and taste) fantastic on meat, roast vegetables, and desserts, and offer the perfect amount of crunch. Either the salt itself or the stylish arched salt cellar—handmade by Pigeon Toe Ceramics in Portland, Oregon—would make a terrific gift on its own.

Photograph: Louryn Strampe

Courtesy of Kiwi Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Kiwi Brand Chef’s Knife $10 Amazon A sharp, trusty chef’s knife is a staple in any kitchen, and Kiwi knives are beloved by multiple members of the WIRED Reviews team for their ability to hold an edge just as well as knives that cost 10 times as much. I’ve had a Kiwi knife in my own knife drawer for more than 20 years, and it’s still going strong. Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Le Creuset Stoneware Mini Round Cocotte $22 Amazon $22 Le Creuset Who doesn’t love a colorful Le Creuset Dutch oven? The real-deal, enameled cast iron version may not be in your gifting budget, but the 8-ounce stoneware cocotte is perfect as a salt cellar, garlic roaster, or even a bowl to eat out of. Most of the classic colors are available, so you can match your giftee’s kitchen or other Le Creuset pots if they have them.

For the Gardener

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Vanessa Minton How to Grow Medicinal Herbs $20 Target $20 $17 (15% off) Thriftbooks I have a separate gift guide for plant lovers, where I talk about how much I like the usability of this book. Put together by Vanessa Minton of From the Garden, “How to Grow Medicinal Herbs” features clear and complete directions that are perfect for beginners, from growing the plants to how to incorporate them into infused oils, tinctures, teas, and syrups. I actually did give a copy to a friend as a gift, and she liked it so much she took it on a trip and read it cover to cover on the plane.

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Back to the Roots Organic Mini Mushroom Growing Kit $16 Amazon (oyster) I received this dehydrated fruiting block in a box for my birthday a couple of years ago, and I was super impressed with how quickly and abundantly the oyster mushrooms grew—right on my windowsill. Growing mushrooms isn’t always easy, but this is a fun and educational method for kids and adults alike. Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Happy Happy Houseplant Monstera Deliciosa Fruit Salt Water Taffy $15 Happy Happy Houseplant Tropical Monstera deliciosa houseplants are all the rage right now, but many people may not know that they actually bear a fruit. It’s rarely produced outside the monstera’s native climate, so you may not have the opportunity to taste it, but you can get the gist with this one-of-a-kind monstera fruit taffy. (It’s tart!)

For the Well-Organized

Photograph: Kat Merck

Courtesy of Amazon Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Ugreen FineTrack Air Tracker Tags (iOS) $24 $23 (4% off) Amazon Being able to keep track of keys, luggage, and other gear is critical, and these Bluetooth trackers work just as well as AirTags for a quarter of the price. A pack of four with little lanyards and fun stickers retails for $24 but often on sale for even less. They work with Apple’s Find My and take just seconds to sync to your phone. I have four of these in use in my household, and they are truly indistinguishable from AirTags in both tracking and quality. There’s also a rechargeable set that works with both iOS and Android, but we haven’t tried that one.

Photograph: Alexis Berger

Photograph: Alexis Berger

Photograph: Alexis Berger Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist SmartLabels QR Code Organizing System $20 Amazon $20 Walmart $19 SmartLabels WIRED contributing reviewer Alexis Berger organized multiple zones of her house with these QR Code stickers. They come with a free app that will scan and catalog all of a drawer or box’s contents using AI—that way you can just look on your phone for the location of an item instead of spending all day tearing your home and garage apart. Photograph: Kabir Fernandez/Baggu Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Baggu Standard Reusable Bag $16 Baggu I cannot even begin to list all the times I’ve been glad to be carrying a reusable bag, but the ones I usually have in my purse are small and flimsy. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano loved this 25-inch-tall ripstop model that carries up to 50 pounds yet folds into a flat 5-by-5-inch pouch. It’s also machine washable and comes in 35 colors and prints.

For the Coffee Lover

Photograph: Pete Cottell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Barista Basics Triple Spout Shot Glass $11 Espresso Parts WIRED contributing reviewer and former barista Pete Cottell loves this espresso accessory for its durability and design—and can be found in seemingly every coffee shop where I live in the Pacific Northwest. However, even if you don’t have an espresso machine, the uses for a little spouted measuring cup are endless. I have a plastic one and use it for everything from measuring small quantities of liquid ingredients to fertilizing plants.

Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Hydro Flask Mug $28 Amazon (12-Ounce) WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane recommends this Hydro Flask in her guide to the best travel mugs for its stainless steel rim that makes for smooth sipping. I have the tumbler version, but I wish it had a handle like this mug. Mine is not easy to hold when it’s cold outside and I’m wearing gloves. (Mug is hand-wash only.) Photograph: Pete Cottell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Bestinnkits Auto On/Off Gravity-Induction Mug Warmer $22 $21 (5% off) Amazon Though this simple warmer only turns on when you have a mug on it, it was effective and reliable when we tested it, and it makes a great gift for anyone who works from home and ends up having their coffee or tea run cold during meetings. I bought one for my husband for Christmas last year, and it’s still going strong.

For Teens

Photograph: Louryn Strampe Save to wishlist Save to wishlist CRKD Atom Controller $20 $17 (15% off) Amazon $20 $18 (10% off) CRKD WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe has this mini gaming controller, which is compatible with Nintendo Switch, PC, macOS, iOS, and Android devices. It’s tiny, cute, and actually works—she uses it to play Stardew Valley and Bastion on her iPhone. If your teen loves gaming, it would make a great stocking stuffer too. (It gets about 10 hours of battery life per USB-C charge.)

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Kat Merck Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Dr. Squatch Soap $23 Amazon (3-Pack Variety Pack) $24 Amazon (3-Pack Tajin) $24 Amazon (3-Pack FIFA) Dr. Squatch soap is a pretty safe gift for teen boys (source: I have a teen boy), and a three-pack makes it more likely they’ll at least get one scent that’s a favorite. There are always lots of fun collabs each season, too—this year’s include Taijn seasoning and FIFA. Photograph: Kat Merck

Courtesy of Sand + Fog Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Sand + Fog Perfume Bag Charms $26 Sand + Fog Yes, they are $1 over the limit, but these bag charms are worth the extra buck. They include little roller-ball bottles of popular Sand + Fog fragrance oils and come in a ready-made gift box, The charms look great on bags and backpacks, and would be a perfect stocking stuffer or angel-tree gift for teen girls.

For a Laugh

Photograph: Simon Hill Save to wishlist Save to wishlist The Op Games Telestrations $20 Walmart $20 Target WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s family loves this hilarious drawing game that’s based on Telephone. Sketch a visual representation of a word or phrase and then pass it around the table for people to guess what it is. It’s great for parties and can accommodate four to eight people. The recommended minimum age is 12, but Simon’s 9-year-old daughter loves it.

Photograph: Kat Merck Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Prank-O Prank Puzzle $19 Amazon $19 Prank-O These puzzles look like normal landscapes but contain a secret section not pictured on the box, with something jarringly incongruent like a dog pooping or a cat barfing. Remove the red sleeve and your giftee will have no idea anything is amiss until they put it together. I gave one of these to my husband, and the ruse worked flawlessly and was just as hilarious as I’d hoped. Courtesy of Amazon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Prank-O Gift Boxes $10 Amazon (Roto Wipe) $10 Amazon (Baby Influencer Kit) $10 Amazon (Pudding Pouch) $10 Amazon (Earwax Candle) I have given these boxes countless times with either a gift certificate or homemade coupon inside, and they’re always a hit, especially in group settings. Many of the dozen or so designs are toilet-themed, but each one is just serious-looking enough that it usually takes people a few long (and hilarious) minutes to realize it’s not a real item.

For the Outdoorsy

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Epiphany Outdoor Gear Collapsible Pocket Bellows $18 Amazon WIRED reviewer and esteemed outdoorsman Scott Gilbertson swears by this tiny telescoping bellows that will help any fire get going again, whether that’s a campfire or your wood stove at home. It stretches out to be surprisingly long and is a must-have for wet firewood, bug-out bags, or even backyard cookouts.

Courtesy of Amazon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Nalgene Sustain Tritan BPA-Free Water Bottle $17 Amazon I carried a Nalgene all through college in the late ’90s before the brand’s polycarbonate was found to have BPA. Now Nalgenes are back with BPA-free Tritan renew plastic, which makes them lightweight and perfect for both outdoor activities and everyday use. Photograph: Scott Gilbertson Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Opinel No. 8 Folding Knife $23 $16 (30% off) Amazon $22 REI I’m a Leatherman kind of person myself, but sometimes you just need a bigger knife. In those cases, you won’t do better than this folding, portable number featured in our Buy It For Life guide. French Alps-based Opinel has been making knives since 1890, and the No. 8 in particular is so well designed it’s been displayed in museums.

For Everyone

Save to wishlist Save to wishlist WIRED 1-Year Digital WIRED Subscription $24 WIRED (1 year)

WIRED is the gift that keeps on giving—stay in the know all year long with a digital subscription for only $24 for new subscribers. (It’s $48 a year after that.) It’ll get you access to WIRED’s brand-new app, as well as exclusive subscriber-only newsletters, livestream AMAs, and a limited-edition tote bag.

Tech.title: Meta Glasses Nova (Gen 3) Review: Not Much New
Tech.content:
The camera housing on my Meta Nova glasses is smaller than on the Gen 2 glasses. From a distance, they might even read as rivets at a glance. (I asked my colleague Reece Rogers how they looked on my face, and from a few feet away in the WIRED office, he didn’t even notice they were camera-enabled glasses at first.)

They feel and function the same as before. You can interact with an AI assistant or snap photos and video with the press of a button. Conversation Focus, a mode that helps hard-of-hearing people better pick up spoken words, is a feature that only works in early access on Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses. It seems very helpful, but my Meta-designed frames don’t have it yet.

They also don’t have integration with Meta’s Muse AI, which the company says is coming later this year. I’m intrigued by that, even if having access to a camera on your face will certainly help a service that seems better at surveilling than helping its users. That said, I’ve found Muse more useful than Meta’s current AI assistant, and I look forward to asking my entirely too cute AI buddy to assist me via my glasses.

Unfortunately, Meta’s current AI assistant on the glasses is still terrible. I tried to ask what features the glasses I was wearing had, and it failed miserably. The AI couldn’t get any of the details right, even when I told it specifically which frames I was wearing and let it snap a picture of the Meta product page for reference. I wouldn’t want to depend on the AI to help me sort out anything with some real complexity.

If you pretty much ignore the AI entirely, the Gen 3 glasses do just about everything Meta promises. They capture nice photos and video, all while maintaining an indicator light that has recently been made more tamper-proof. (That’s not necessarily enough to deter the creeps.) The frames are wearable, and the software is competent enough. They’re also pricey, so maybe you can save some cash sticking with the Gen 2. They’ll all do what you probably expect them to do. Just maybe don’t be weird about it, all right?

Tech.title: I Got a First Look at Vitamix’s First Juicer, and I’m in Love
Tech.content:
When a company enters a new product category, I’m always skeptical. As a Vitamix fan, a brand known for its blenders, I had reservations when I heard it was releasing its first cold-press juicer. Yet, I got a first look at the product and can safely say that this juicer lives up to the Vitamix name.

Announced on Monday and available for purchase on Oct. 15, the MaxExtract Cold Press Juicer uses slow-masticating technology to extract juice from fruits, veggies and leafy greens.

The MaxExtract is easy to operate

Assembling the juicer took less time and effort than I expected. Then, all you have to do is chop your produce into 2-inch pieces, throw them into the juicer’s 5.3-inch hopper (which can hold a surprising amount of ingredients) and let the MaxExtract handle the rest in minutes.

More from CNET

The light-up front dial makes it extra simple. Turn it to the on position to start the juicing process, to the off position when it’s done and reverse it when there’s a clog. However, I haven’t experienced a clog after making several batches of juice.

The dial has a light behind it. A nice touch. Anna Gragert/CNET

It comes with everything you need

The MaxExtract includes a pusher to push ingredients down, a cleaning brush, pulp and juice containers and two strainers: a fine-mesh for less pulp and smoother juice and an easy-clean for more pulp but an easier clean, as the name suggests.

I especially appreciate that the juice container includes measurements on the side.

The juice container also has a handle, making it easier to pour the liquid into a glass. Anna Gragert/CNET

All detachable parts are dishwasher-safe

I love that all the detachable components are dishwasher-safe on both the top and bottom racks. The pulp outlet can also be opened to make removing pulp and cleaning even simpler.

As someone who has never used a juicer, I have to say that the MaxExtract has converted me. It creates a smooth, fresh-tasting juice and takes any effort out of the process, including cleanup.

One of the most satisfying parts is watching the pulp emerge. Anna Gragert/CNET

Size is to be expected

The user manual lists the MaxExtract as 17.7 by 8.5 by 7.7 inches and 8.14 pounds. However, you can remove the hopper and chamber from the base if the full unit is too tall for your cabinets.

By comparison, the MaxExtract is narrower and shallower than the $599 Nama J2 Cold Press Juicer, which measures 17.7 by 9.8 by 9 inches and weighs 12.1 pounds. CNET’s best budget juicer, the 11.14-pound Hamilton Beach Easy Clean, is shorter but wider and deeper, measuring 15.31 by 13 by 9 inches.

Before purchasing any juicer, make sure it will fit in your space. Anna Gragert/CNET

Vitamix MaxExtract availability and price

Available in black or white with a glass front on Oct. 15, the MaxExtract will be $500. You can buy it on Vitamix.com or Amazon and it comes with a five-year limited warranty.

Tech.title: CNET Finds Nearly 1 in 3 US Adults Plan to Shop Early Holiday Sales. Will Deals Help Smaller Budgets?
Tech.content:
Early holiday sales are only a few days away. Next week, retailers including Amazon and Walmart will lower prices on many giftable items, like tech, toys and kitchen gadgets. But holiday shopping could look much different for US adults.



CNET’s annual holiday shopping survey shows that nearly one-third (32%) of US adults plan to start holiday shopping for deals before November and 27% plan to shop during sales. However, US adults will be juggling a smaller tech budget of $808. That’s $123 less than CNET’s survey findings last year.



Finding savings on must-have devices is paramount this year if you want to squeeze more out of your budget, but how can you spot a good deal during October’s holiday sales? CNET’s director of commerce content, Russell Holly, weighed in on the data and shared expert advice to help you make a shopping plan and stay within your price range.

Key findings

Nearly one-third (32%) of US adults plan to start holiday shopping before November, and 27% plan to shop during sales.

US adults plan to spend less on holiday shopping compared to last year. This year, holiday tech shoppers plan to spend an average of $808 on consumer tech products and services – that’s $123 less than last year’s holiday shopping average.

Most shoppers (84%) expect purchasing frustrations such as misleading discounts (43%), instant product sellouts (39%) and inflated baseline prices (35%).

US adults plan to buy toys and kitchen items more compared to tech items like headphones, phones, TVs and laptops.

US adults have already started holiday shopping

CNET found that close to one-third (32%) will start holiday shopping before November and aren’t waiting for the usual Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. Many have already started or plan to start this month. Twenty-seven percent of US adults plan to shop in November. And as the holidays inch closer, 11% say they will shop in December.

Cole Kan/CNET

Over a quarter of US adults (27%) plan to take advantage of savings events, like Amazon’s and Walmart’s early holiday sales, while 18% of those shopping between October and November don’t plan to. The big question is whether the sales are worthwhile. Holly says it comes down to when you find a deal that’s worthwhile.

More from CNET

“The best time to buy is the moment you see something you want on an actual discount, because increased prices can come at any time,” Holly said.

Holly says even steep discounts aren’t lowering prices as much as before, but the right deals may make you reconsider.

CNET’s deals team spends hours making sure sales are legitimate — not just a fake price drop. And in the coming weeks, they’ll track deals on devices like laptops, headphones, wearable devices and smart home gadgets, plus alternatives to more costly tech, to help you determine what’s worth buying now or later.



You can also check an item’s price history to see if you’re getting the best deal by using price trackers like CamelCamelCamel and comparing prices across retailers before buying. But as Holly noted, if you want to upgrade your personal devices, don’t wait. Look for the best price you can find and buy it right away. Otherwise, prices may go up while you wait.

US adults plan to spend $123 less than they did on holiday shopping last year

Last year, CNET found that US adults planned to spend an average of $931 on holiday shopping. This year, shoppers are planning to spend less.

On average, they expect to spend $808 on holiday shopping. That’s $123 less than last year. Some generations plan to spend more, such as millennials, who anticipate an average holiday shopping outlay of $1,074. Boomers will spend around half that amount — $582.

Cole Kan/CNET

Higher everyday living costs could explain why holiday budgets are lower.



“Everything else being more expensive means less left over for gifts,” said Holly. “There’s very little indication that component prices are going to come back down anytime soon, so if you’re hoping for the kinds of prices you saw even two years ago, I would say you’re going to be waiting quite a while.”

Balancing holiday gifts and everyday basics on your usual income can be a lot to handle. Now’s the time to set holiday expectations, including a budget and a list of must-haves, along with more affordable options that still meet your needs.

Then keep checking prices and deals from your trusted retailers and be prepared to buy when you spot good savings. Most importantly, try to avoid using credit cards and buy-now, pay-later plans that can lead to debt. The Federal Reserve’s recent rate hike will push borrowing costs higher, making debt more expensive through higher credit card and loan interest rates.

Nearly 3 in 4 plan to buy tech this holiday season

CNET found that 73% of shoppers plan to buy tech products or services this season, but what most US adults plan to buy and how much they plan to spend may surprise you.

Thirty percent of shoppers plan to purchase toys, and 25% plan to buy kitchen items, such as air fryers and cookware. But shoppers don’t plan to buy as many personal electronics and home entertainment products. Only 20% plan to buy headphones or earbuds, and even fewer plan to buy video games for consoles (18%) or laptops and TVs (11%). More shocking is that only 13% plan to buy phones. We’ve seen prices increase across popular tech devices and brands due to the RAM shortage, which has led to low supply and high demand for memory chips.

Cole Kan/CNET

Some of the latest releases cost way more than the average $808 most US adults plan to spend. For instance, the $2,000 iPhone Duo by itself costs even more than the average $1,704 that millennials plan to spend on tech this holiday season. And less costly phones are still beyond holiday budgets, like the $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro Max, and even the iPhone 18 Pro is $1,200. Trade-in offers and sales can help lower that cost if you’re planning to upgrade, but shop around and compare deals before buying.

Increased prices may make you reconsider whether to stick with your current model or upgrade, but remember, you have options.

“If the current laptop works well enough, upgrading can either be viewed as a luxury purchase for later or shifted to buying used or refurbished models to save extra,” Holly said.

You may also consider a slightly older model of the device you’re looking for. It could still have all of the features you need, but cost less. Another money-saving option is to consider refurbished tech that’s in excellent or good condition from a certified refurbished retailer. You may still notice some price increases due to demand, but it could still cost less than the newest models.

US adults are bracing for higher prices and fake deals

Most US shoppers (84%) expect the holiday shopping season to come with a few hurdles this year. Forty-three percent are concerned about deceptive pricing practices, such as retailers raising original prices before discounting them for a sale. Others are concerned about deals selling out immediately because of low stock or automated buying bots (39%).

Take Nintendo’s Zelda Switch 2 to commemorate the Legend of Zelda’s 40th anniversary. It costs $520, and preorders are sold out. But earlier this year, Nintendo announced a price increase for the regular Switch 2, which would start at $500, up $50 since its launch. So Zelda and Nintendo fans are juggling limited availability and higher prices for one item.

There’s not much you can do about preorders selling out or limited stock of an item, but it’s best to have a backup plan. Consider other retailers or device options that you’ll still be satisfied with — like a Nintendo Switch 2 and the digital download of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time when it’s released.

But if you’re more worried about fake deals or sales being a money grab by retailers, Holly said that historically, there have been some great sales ahead of the holidays. It’s still best to do your research before buying to make sure you’re getting a deal by comparing retailer prices before and after announced sales and using price tracking tools, like CamelCamelCamel. Heads up that many retailers, like Amazon, have flash sales with specific times of deeper discounts, and you’ll need to act fast, so it’s best to plan your holiday shopping now.

“The best thing anyone can do ahead of a shopping event is prepare,” said Holly. “Find your favorite price tracker tool before the event starts, have a general idea of what you’re looking to buy and be sure to keep an eye out for bigger discounts when you bundle things together.”

Methodology

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,615 adults, of whom 1,552 were interested in purchasing consumer tech products or services this winter holiday season. Fieldwork was undertaken Sept. 3-6, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).

Tech.title: Ready for Driverless Trucks? I Took a Ride in Kodiak’s Autonomous Semi
Tech.content:
Despite the growing number of players in the space, self-driving vehicles remain far from ubiquitous. In places like the San Francisco Bay Area, hailing a robotaxi is now nearly as easy as requesting an Uber. But in most cities, driverless cars have yet to surface at all.

Still, autonomous vehicles of all sizes and purposes continue to crop up in various regions. Kodiak AI is one company looking to shake up transportation and shipping in the near future. Founded in 2018, it set out to deploy semi trucks on highways without a human behind the wheel, and it’s getting close to realizing that vision.

The company’s autonomous driving system, called the Kodiak Driver, launched in December 2024, and has so far been deployed in 35 fully driverless trucks, which are owned and operated by Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin in New Mexico and Texas. The trucks haul frac sand, typically used during hydraulic fracking to help keep fractures in rock formations open, from depots to well sites.

Kodiak plans to deploy its self-driving trucks on highways in Texas by the end of the year. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Now, Kodiak wants to bring its fully driverless operations to the highway, starting in Texas with services for furniture giant Ikea later this year. That route will operate between Houston and Dallas, spanning 219 miles primarily along Interstate 45.

Massive trucks barreling down highways without a driver may be a daunting vision, but Michael Wiesinger, Kodiak’s chief operating officer, says they’ll make transportation more reliable and efficient.

“Lots of people, unfortunately, are getting killed in traffic, and many of those are related to truck accidents,” he said. “An autonomous truck [has a] 360-degree view of the world, [and] will actually never get drowsy, never get tired, never get distracted. They will make transportation safer.”

This is the sensor pod that houses the cameras, lidar and radar. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

In California, Kodiak’s driverless tech is already being used to ship produce from Fresno to Los Angeles, though a safety driver remains behind the wheel, ready to take over as needed.

I visited Kodiak’s headquarters in Mountain View, California, to ride in one of the company’s trucks and see its autonomous tech in action. As per current state regulations, there was still a safety operator onboard, ready to take control of the wheel if necessary. I wasn’t exactly nervous, but his presence nevertheless helped to assuage any trepidation, given how much bigger a semi truck is than a robotaxi from Waymo or Zoox.

During the demonstration, the Kodiak truck easily navigated surface streets, including making tight turns and dodging rows of parallel-parked cars and trailers. We made our way to the highway on-ramp rather slowly and carefully, picking up speed to 55 mph once we hit the roadway. When we really got going, it all felt remarkably ordinary, with the truck weaving through lanes and dodging construction cones without any trouble. After about 20 minutes, the truck navigated to an exit and we made our way back to Kodiak’s HQ.

Kodiak’s trucks run on diesel — the standard for heavy-duty commercial trucking — which allows them to travel over longer distances than if they were electric, the company notes.

The inside of the Kodiak semi feels standard — apart from the screen showing what the vehicle sees as it navigates autonomously. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

The growth of driverless operations brings with it mounting concern about lost jobs. Kodiak says deploying autonomous vehicles doesn’t mean humans won’t be involved at all.

“Before launching an autonomous truck, it gets inspected, it gets fueled, it gets prepared for the run,” Wiesinger said. “Those preparations are done by humans on the ground.”

He added that Kodiak is collaborating with truck-stop providers to help with refueling as it plans to eventually expand its driverless range across thousands of miles.

Kodiak isn’t the only company working on autonomous trucking. Other players include Aurora, Waabi and Gatik, while Tesla is making a push into this space as well with its all-electric Tesla Semi, which could one day adopt driverless capabilities, too.

Before climbing aboard Kodiak’s semi, it was hard to fathom how a Class 8 heavy-duty truck could navigate the complexities of residential streets and highways. As we passed other cars, I found myself wondering whether those drivers and passengers realized they were sharing the road with what could be the future of long-haul trucking. Then again, some of those folks were cruising in a Waymo robotaxi, so perhaps the existence of autonomous trucks won’t be such a tough pill to swallow for everyone.

Check out the video above for my ride-along in Kodiak’s self-driving truck.

Tech.title: Meta’s ‘AI Tamagotchi’ Looks to Me Like a Smartwatch Preview for 2027
Tech.content:
I was in the audience at Meta’s Connect conference in late September when Mark Zuckerberg held up a pendant in his hands and surprise announced the Muse Charm, a little novelty-like device with Meta’s disarmingly adorable Muse AI agent onboard. Muse Charm is coming as soon as December this year.

But the funny thing is, while most people called it an AI Tamagotchi, all I saw was a strapless Apple Watch. Is that what the Muse Charm could be, eventually? A watch as well as a pendant? Is this Meta’s entry to wrist wearables in disguise? I’m still thinking about it…because smartwatches are also on their way to being AI assistants soon, too.

Reports of Meta working on its own watch wearable have been cooking for several years now. At Connect, there were smart glasses galore and even a new glasses-like VR headset coming next year. But things were suspiciously quiet on the wrist wearables front.

More from CNET

Meta already has one wrist wearable, the neural band that comes with the Ray-Ban Display glasses. But it received no hardware updates this year, which surprised me. The sensor-studded band uses electromyography, or EMG, to measure skin-contact electrical signals for a set of gesture controls to navigate the heads-up glasses display. Meta’s already ambitiously promised that EMG could open up all sorts of neural input possibilities, even testing the tech in a smart car dashboard prototype.

As far back as last year, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth told me that some sort of display or watch-like evolution of the neural band could be in the works next. And Meta already introduced a partnership with Garmin to link fitness tracking to smart glasses last year.

AI agents as Meta’s new priority

The Muse Charm, however, brings a different piece of the puzzle to the table. Muse AI is Meta’s biggest priority now, clearly, based on its widespread availability on desktops and smartphones and on the company’s intentions to put the new agentic AI on all its smart glasses and, eventually, Meta’s VR Glasses. And where else could Muse work well? Enter the Charm.

The Charm has another watch-like tell. It’s powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset, which already runs on Samsung’s latest smartwatches. The Wear Elite, as I learned from Qualcomm earlier this year, is optimized for a range of AI-ready wearables, ranging from watches to pendants to even glasses. There’s no reason why Meta’s Charm couldn’t easily get a wrist strap…and a watch OS to go with it.

Meta’s neural band doesn’t have a screen yet. Would it ever fuse with Muse Charm? Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Many reasons for a Meta smartwatch

A smartwatch would benefit Meta on several fronts. Clearly, the company wants to keep breaking into lifestyle wearables, and watches could offer another way onto people besides faces. Fitness and health tracking would give Meta data that Muse and its smart glasses could use. And watches are a key part of the glasses interface’s future. Google’s glasses will work with Wear OS watches soon. Apple’s rumored glasses will likely work with Apple Watches.

And Meta has to find a better way to make its neural band more wearable. I find the first-gen neural band fascinating in theory, but an annoying extra thing to charge in practice. If it doesn’t become a watch, or at least a fitness tracker, why wear it at all? The neural band doesn’t even control anything other than Meta’s one line of display glasses right now, but chances are Meta’s going to try to figure out ways it could work with the rest of its smart glasses lineup, and VR too.

Last year I felt like Meta’s neural band felt naked without a watch display (Apple Watch on left, Meta Neural Band on right). Scott Stein/CNET

Google and Apple are already showing how quickly smartwatches are becoming more like AI companions. Gemini lives on Wear OS watches. Apple’s adding memory-assisting audio intelligence modes to its new watches later this fall. Both can tap into Gemini and the new Siri, respectively.

Meta has Muse now. And a charm by the end of the year. Is the watch after that? Meta didn’t have any comment on the topic when I reached out to ask, but I think we’re seeing the beta test in action right in front of our eyes. Or is this the pivot to a modular idea that could be a pendant and a wristworn device, without committing to either?

One thing’s clear, no matter what: Meta’s looking for ways for that disarmingly adorable Muse mascot to be with us all the time, even without glasses. And the Charm looks like the experiment.

Tech.title: Why the Moon Is a Legal Wild West
Tech.content:
For $3,495, you can send your pet’s ashes to the moon.

Celestis calls itself “the most compelling pet memorial service on or off the planet,” allowing customers to send a “symbolic portion” of their pet’s ashes to live forever on the lunar surface. (Prices are the same for human remains, Celestis says.) It’s part of a growing wave of companies looking to capitalize on the regulatory gray area that the moon inhabits.

A Japanese beverage company sent up a payload that looked like one of its Pocari Sweat energy drinks in 2014. Artist Jeff Koons sent up 125 mini-sculptures in 2024; each one corresponded to an NFT that collectors could purchase back on Earth. One man has even raised $227,000 to put a giant cross on the moon. All told, humans have left nearly 500,000 pounds of stuff on the moon’s surface to date, most of which consists of government-sent lunar landers, surveyors and other dead spacecraft.

More from CNET

This explosion of commercial lunar activity is technically legal, says Steve Mirmina, a professor of space law at Georgetown University and former NASA attorney.

“I searched and searched the law, and unfortunately, there’s no law against launching race cars,” he said, referring to Elon Musk’s launching of a Tesla Roadster in 2018. “We don’t have a government agency with the legal authority to regulate what happens on the moon.”

Existing US law doesn’t sufficiently regulate what we actually send to the lunar surface, Mirmina argues in Lawful but Awful: U.S. Regulation of Commercial Activities on the Lunar Surface, published Sept. 19 in Air and Space Law. Without a more sustainable legal framework, we risk turning the moon into “Earth’s junk drawer.”

Who regulates the moon?

To date, 118 countries are parties to the Outer Space Treaty, which was originally enacted in 1967 during the height of the Cold War. It stipulates that space is free for use by all countries, and that they have a duty to avoid harmful contamination in space.

The 2020 Artemis Accords further enshrined norms of space sustainability into international law. While not legally binding, it constitutes “soft law” norms that shape best practices in space.

Countries are left to enforce compliance on the private space companies within their borders. In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration governs rocket launches, and NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services program partners with American companies to deliver payloads to the moon. But Congress hasn’t given any one agency the authority to regulate what private companies are actually putting on those payloads.

“It’s not very useful that they can regulate launch if they can’t regulate what happens after the rocket’s in space,” said Mirmina. “Basically, NASA, the FAA, even the State Department – they’re all kind of pointing at each other, hoping somebody did something. And then nobody had the legal authority to do anything.”

Real-world costs of unchecked commercialization

No one wants to gaze up at the night sky and see an energy drink . None of this activity has affected our view of the moon so far, and most of it falls into the “annoying” category more than the “truly reprehensible.” But Mirmina worries that there’s no legal safeguard in place to halt some truly awful conduct.

What’s happening on the moon right now has already stirred outrage from a number of different groups. Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren wrote a letter to NASA in 2023 asking the agency to stop sending human remains to the moon.

“It is crucial to emphasize that the Moon holds a sacred position in many Indigenous cultures, including ours,” Nygren wrote. “The act of depositing human remains and other materials, which could be perceived as discards in any other location, on the moon is tantamount to desecration of this sacred space.”

There’s also the question of how to be good caretakers for future generations. Moon landings produce something called “plume–surface interactions,” in which exhaust from descending spacecraft kicks up rocks and dust at speeds faster than a bullet. When new payloads land with increasing frequency, yesterday’s pet ashes or energy drink s could become tomorrow’s projectiles. Unlike on Earth, the moon has a very thin atmosphere with little erosion, so every item placed on the surface stays “forever,” as Celestis promises customers.

“They become shrapnel for future lunar missions,” Mirmina says. “It’s just a lot easier to prevent it than it’s going to ever be to try to clean it up.”

Stewardship before it’s too late

Everything is hard in space, especially agreeing on the right way to behave in a domain that seems so distant and invulnerable. But it’s also one corner of the government with rare bipartisan approval: Roughly three-quarters of Americans have a favorable opinion of NASA, and seven in 10 say it is essential that the US continue to be a world leader in space, according to the Pew Research Center. Most also support NASA’s goal of sending astronauts back to the moon in 2028.

“Before we’ve really even explored the moon, we’re already tossing up junk to live on there forever,” Mirmina says. “If you care about space or stewardship or the environment, we should preserve it for future explorers and not ruin it before they get there.”

Tech.title: I’ve Tested Phones for 15 Years and These Are the Most Bizarre I’ve Seen
Tech.content:
I’ve been a CNET journalist for over 15 years and I’ve tested everything from the latest electric cars and bikes to cameras and TV-controlling magic wands. I’ve even compared drones to barn owls. My main focus has always been the hottest new phones, and I’ve seen a lot of them in my time.

Names like Apple and Samsung have remained stalwarts in the industry during my time, but I’ve also seen the rise of brands like Xiaomi, Oppo and Huawei. Meanwhile, once-dominant names like BlackBerry, HTC, LG and more recently OnePlus have vanished from the mobile space. Even Sony doesn’t make much of a fuss over its phones these days, though it does still launch new ones.

I’ve seen phones arrive with such wild fanfare that they changed the entire mobile industry, while others quietly trickled into existence only to vanish just as uneventfully. But it’s the weird ones that stick in my memory. Those devices that tried to be different, that dared to offer features we didn’t even know we wanted or simply the ones that aimed to be quirky for the sake of being quirky. Like someone who thinks an unusual hat is the same thing as having a personality.

Here then are some of the strangest phones I’ve come across in my mobile journey at CNET. Better yet, I still have these phones in a big cardboard box in my office, so I was able to dig them out and take new photos — though not all of them still work. Let’s start with a doozy.

BlackBerry briefly tried to convince us that it’s hip to be square. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

BlackBerry Passport

At the height of its power, RIM’s BlackBerry was one of the most dominant brands in mobile. It was unthinkable, then, that anything could unseat the goliath, let alone that it would fade into total nonexistence. But the once juicy, ripe BlackBerry withered and died on the branch, but not without a few interesting death rattles on its way.

My pick from the company’s end days is the Passport from 2014, notable not just for its physical keyboard but its almost completely square design. The rationale behind this, according to its maker, was that business types just really love squares. A Word document, an Excel spreadsheet, an email — all square (ish) and all able to be viewed natively on the Passport’s 4.5 inch display with its 1:1 aspect ratio. Let’s not forget that all Instagram posts at that time were also square so it had that going for it too. YouTube, not so much.

In theory, it’s a sound idea. In practice, the square design made it awkward to use, as the physical keyboard was too wide and narrow. Its BlackBerry 10 software, especially the app availability, lagged behind what you’d get from Android at the time. BlackBerry quickly ditched the new shape. After trying to claw back some credibility with its Android phones — including the stupidly named Priv, a phone I quite liked — and by bringing on singer Alicia Keys as global creative director (because BlackBerry phones had keys, get it?), the company stopped making its own phones in 2016.

The Russian YotaPhone 2. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

YotaPhone 2

You’d be forgiven for having never heard of this phone or its parent company, Yota. Based in Russia, Yota made two phones: the creatively named YotaPhone in 2012 and the similarly inspired YotaPhone 2 in 2014, pictured above. Both were unique in the mobile world for their use of a second display on the rear. From the front, these phones looked and operated like any other generic Android phone. Flip them over though and you’d get a 4.3-inch E Ink display.

The idea was that you’d use your Android phone as normal for things like web browsing, gaming or watching videos, but you’d switch to the rear display if you wanted to read ebooks or simply have it propped up to show incoming notifications. E Ink displays use almost no power, so it made a lot of sense to preserve battery life by viewing “slow” content on the back.

The reality though is that beyond ebooks — which aren’t great to read on such a tiny screen anyway — there’s very little anyone might want to use an E Ink display for when out and about. It was difficult to operate, too, thanks to a slow processor and clunky software. After just two generations of YotaPhones, the company went into liquidation.

The HTC ChaCha and its Facebook button. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

HTC ChaCha

Remember when Facebook was the cool spot to be instead of just the place your parents and their friends go to publicly air their most troubling opinions? When I was at university, instead of trading phone numbers when you met someone, the default thing was to add each other on Facebook before you began “poking” each other. Facebook was so ubiquitous at the time that it was simply the way every single person I knew communicated.

Keen to capitalize on Mark Zuckerberg’s social media success, HTC brought out the ChaCha in 2011. The phone came with an utterly ludicrous name and a dedicated Facebook button on the bottom edge. Tapping this would immediately bring up your Facebook page, allowing you to post the lyrics to Rebecca Black’s Friday, ask what Fifty Shades of Grey is about or do whatever else it was we were all up to in 2011.

Facebook might still be around in one form or another, but HTC abandoned its phone-making business back in 2018. Unsurprisingly, phones with dedicated hardware buttons tied to social media haven’t caught on. Though if I’m being generous, there is strictly speaking an X button on every keyboard.

The Finney’s pop-up screen is ideal for crypto bros. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Sirin Labs Finney U1

“Bro!” I hear you shout, all too loudly. “Bro! You’ve got to check out what my Bitcoin is doing!” You’d then show me your phone and I’d watch while your crypto account plummeted, rebounded and plummeted again over the course of 12 seconds. The phone you’d be showing me, of course, would be the Sirin Labs Finney, a 2019 phone specifically targeted at crypto bros who wanted a device that would perfectly match their high-living, high-fiving crypto-trading lifestyle.

At its core, the Finney is just another Android phone, but a hidden second screen pops up from the back of the phone, with the sole purpose of giving you secure access to your crypto wallet. The phone had a whole host of security features to ensure that only you could access your Bitcoin or Etherium, and it allowed you to send and receive cryptocurrency without having to use a third-party online platform. Apparently that was a good thing?

If you were entrenched in the crypto world, this phone might have been the dream. But the wallet wasn’t easy to use and the phone was expensive, thanks to the cost of that second screen. Sirin Labs stopped making phones soon after and the mobile industry learned an important lesson about not developing hyper-niche devices that aren’t even that well-suited for the handful of customers that might be interested.

The Gemini PDA was part phone, part laptop. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Planet Computers Gemini PDA

Half phone, half laptop, all productivity. The Gemini PDA by UK-based mobile startup Planet Computers was a clamshell device in 2018 with a large (at the time) 5.99-inch display and a full QWERTY keyboard. It was basically a slightly more modern interpretation of a PDA, like 1998’s Psion 3MX, in that it was effectively a tiny laptop that would fold up and fit in your pocket. The full keyboard allowed you to type away comfortably on long emails or documents, while the regular Android software on the top half meant it also functioned like any other phone — apps, games, phone calls, whatever.

It had 4G connectivity for fast data speeds and a later model even got an update to 5G. But, like the BlackBerry Passport, its focus on business-folk and productivity above all else meant it was a niche product that failed to garner enough appeal to succeed. It didn’t help that it was utterly enormous and fitting it in a jeans pocket was basically impossible, so it didn’t impress either as a laptop or as a phone.

LG’s G5 was a nice idea, but it didn’t last. Nor did LG’s phones. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

LG G5

LG remains a huge name in the tech industry today, thanks to its TVs and appliances, but it also tried to be a big player in the phone world, too. I liked LG’s phones — they were quirky and often tried weird things which kept my days as a reviewer interesting, perhaps none more so than the LG G5 in 2016.

LG called the G5 “modular,” meaning that the bottom chin of the phone snapped off allowing you to attach different modules such as a camera grip or an audio interface. Like many items on this list I can say that it’s a nice idea in theory, but in practice the phone fell short. Swapping out modules meant removing the battery, which of course meant restarting your phone every time you wanted to use the camera grip.

It was an inelegant solution to a problem that never needed to exist. But its bigger issue was that the camera grip and audio interface were the only two modules LG actually made for the phone. It’s as though the company had this fun notion in creating a phone that can transform according to your needs but then forgot to assign anyone to come up with any ideas on what to do with it. As a result, the end product was uninspiring, over-engineered and expensive.

What once was big now seems small. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Samsung Galaxy Note

Samsung’s Galaxy Note series helped transform the mobile industry. It literally stretched the boundaries of phones, encouraging larger and larger screens — even creating the unpleasant and mercifully short-lived term “phablet.” But the first-generation model in 2011 was controversial, mostly due to what was then considered its enormous size.

At 5.3 inches, it was significantly bigger than almost any other phone out there, including Samsung’s own Galaxy S2 — which, at a measly 4.3 inches, paled into insignificance against the mighty Note. It was mocked for being so huge, with memes appearing online poking fun at people holding it up when making calls. And while times have changed and we now have Samsung’s 6.9-inch Galaxy S26 Ultra, the original Note’s boxy aspect ratio meant it was actually wider than the S26 Ultra. So even by today’s standards it’s big.

It was also among the first phones to come with its own stylus shoved into its bottom. It’s a feature that few mobile companies have mimicked, but Samsung kept it as a differentiator on its later Note models before incorporating it into its flagship S line starting with the S22 Ultra.

Nokia may have been well ahead of its time. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Nokia Lumia 1020

Nokia’s Lumia 1020 was my absolute favorite phone for quite some time after its launch in 2013. And it’s because of its weirdness.

Nokia had an amazing history of bonkers mobiles — 2004’s 7280 “lipstick phone,” for example — and while the Lumia range was much more sedate, the 1020 had a few things that made it stand out. First, it ran Windows Phone, Microsoft’s brief and unsuccessful attempt to launch a rival to Android and iOS. A rival that I happened to quite like.

It was also made of polycarbonate, with a smoothly rounded unibody design that strongly contrasted the angular metal, plastic and glass designs of almost all other phones launching at that time. Its look was unlike anything else on sale, and I loved it.

But the main thing I loved was its camera. With a 41-megapixel sensor, Carl Zeiss lens, raw image capture and optical image stabilization, the Lumia 1020 packed the best camera specs of any phone I’d ever seen. It made the phone a true standout product, especially for photographers like me who wanted an amazing camera with them at all times, but didn’t want to have to carry both a phone and a compact digital camera.

While incredible image quality from a phone is a given in almost all camera phones in 2026, the Lumia 1020 was an early pioneer in what could be achieved from a phone camera.

The LG G5 was the love child of a phone and a handbag. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

LG G4

LG, twice in one list? Oh yes, my friend, because the G5 seen above was not the first time LG went weird. Launched in 2015, the LG G4 had two main features that raised a few eyebrows. Most notably was LG’s decision to wrap the phone in real leather. Yes, real actual leather. Like what you’d get when you peel a cow. It even had stitching down the back, making it look like a handbag or a boot.

While it’s not a phone for vegans, I actually liked the look, especially as real leather — even the really thin stuff LG used on the G4 — naturally wears over time, gaining scuffs and scratches that give each phone a unique patina. It’s why I love my old leather Danner boots, and it’s why a vintage, worn-in leather jacket will almost always look better than a brand-new one. Still, with leather being an expensive — and arguably controversial — material to use on a phone, it’s no surprise LG didn’t return to this idea.

But it’s not the only weird thing about the phone — the G4 was among a small number of phones released around that time that experimented with curved displays. It’s gently bent into a banana shape, the theory being that it makes watching videos more immersive, as is the case with curved screens in movie theaters. The problem is that movie screens are immense, so that curve makes sense. On a 5.5-inch phone like the G4, that curve is barely noticeable and only really served to push the price up.

I designed this custom phone. You can’t do that anymore. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Motorola Moto X and Moto Maker

I’ve just pointed out how weird the LG G4 was for using leather and now I’m pointing out another phone that, as you can see in the image above, is also wrapped in leather. But the weird thing here isn’t that the Motorola Moto X came in leather — it’s that I personally got to choose that it came in leather.

With the Moto X in 2013, Motorola launched a service called Moto Maker that allowed you to customize your phone in a wild variety of ways. From different-colored backs and multicolored accents around the camera and speakers through to using materials including leather and even various types of wood, there were loads of options to make your Moto X look unique. Each phone would then be made to order and you could even have it personalised with lazer etching and provide your Google account for it to be prelinked on arrival.

If custom-making phones with a vast number of potential options en masse sounds like an absolute logistical nightmare, you’re on the same page as Motorola eventually found itself. Moto Maker only existed for a few years before the company retired its customization service.

It was a weird time. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Samsung Galaxy Fold

I’m ending on a wildcard addition with the original Galaxy Fold. It’s a wildcard because Samsung’s Fold and Flip range are now up to No. 8 and we’ve got foldable devices from almost all major Android manufacturers. Even Apple got in on the game with its iPhone Duo.

While the original Fold might have kicked off the foldable revolution, there’s no question it was a weird phone. I was among the first in the world to test it when it launched in 2019, and while I was certainly impressed by the bendy display, its hinge felt weird and “snappy” to use. The outer display was, let’s face it, terrible.

On paper, its 4.6-inch size is reasonable, but it’s so tall and narrow that it was borderline unusable for anything more than checking incoming notifications. Trying to type on it meant whittling down your thumbs to pointy nubs, so I spent most of my time interacting with the phone’s much bigger internal screen. Cut to today, when the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer screen measures a healthier 6.7 inches and, as a result, can function like any regular smartphone, with the bigger inside screen only required when you want more immersive content.

Looking back at the original Fold and its bizarre proportions, it’s honestly a surprise that Samsung persisted with the format. But I’m glad it did.

Tech.title: What to Expect From This Week’s Microsoft Windows and Surface Event
Tech.content:
Microsoft is gearing up to drop even more news for Windows and Surface laptops. The tech titan is hosting a Windows and Surface event on Wednesday in San Francisco, its first laptop-centric event in two years. This is everything we’re expecting to see — and no, sorry, Windows 12 is not on the list.

The event will be a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” according to Microsoft. That makes sense as Microsoft has been all-in on AI by incorporating Copilot everywhere and partnering with chip makers like Qualcomm to bring enough firepower to its devices to handle the computational load of generative and agentic AI tasks. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and the head of Windows and Devices, Pavan Davuluri, are slated to speak.

This event could be when Microsoft actually drops the Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch high-end variant first announced this spring at Computex. The Ultra is powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, so Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s slated appearance at the event is another sign toward the Ultra.

More from CNET

We already got two new Surface laptops this month, previewed at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit. At the Hawaii event, Microsoft upgraded its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface 13-inch laptops, running on Snapdragon Elite X2 chips, and introduced a new Surface mouse to go along with them. The new laptops have better cameras and “embody the PC-phone marriage Qualcomm promised years ago,” CNET’s David Lumb reports.

A big question will be prices. Computer hardware companies have raised their prices across the board, from Apple to Asus and Acer, over the last year to keep up with rising manufacturing costs. AI is at least partially to blame, with advanced chips in hot demand for data centers as well as laptops and phones. Other costs, like price increases in Windows licenses during the manufacturing process, may also be contributing to higher price tags. The result, sometimes called RAMageddon, is that it’s more expensive to buy new devices.

How to watch Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event

Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event begins at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET on Wednesday. It is being held in San Francisco and will be livestreamed on YouTube. CNET will be on the ground to bring you all the latest Microsoft news.

Tech.title: How to Get a Piece of Apple’s $250M AI iPhone Settlement
Tech.content:
Apple’s legal settlement over its allegedly misleading AI claims during the initial Apple Intelligence launch has finally reached the point where you can sign up to be paid from the $250 million pool via a live website.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. Bridget Carey/CNET

How to claim your portion of the settlement

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

Who is eligible for the $250 million settlement?

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

iPhone 16

iPhone 16E

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

Why is there a lawsuit over Apple Intelligence?

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

When can you expect to receive a settlement payment?

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.
